Mr. BARBOUR: This item is of a

and partly on account of the receipts

The salaries of Clerks of the Crown and
Peace who held office on the passing of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, are
paid from Votes of the Imperial Parliament, and the amounts are deducted from
the Northern Ireland share of reserved
taxes. When, however, a new appointment is made the salary must be borne
on this Vote and not on the Imperial
Vote. Consequently, of course, no
deduction will fall to be made from the
Northern Ireland share of reserved taxes
in respect of the salary of any newlyappointed Clerk of the Crown and Peace.
The provision which it is now desired to
make is to cover the additional salary
paid to the senior clerk in the office of
the deceased Clerk of the Crown and
Peace, who acted during the vacancy,
and also the salary of the new Clerk of
the Crown and Peace for the small part
of the year during which he has been in
office. This additional provision will, as
I have explained, be offset by an increase
in the residuary share of reserved taxation payable to Northern Ireland.
The staff in the offices of the Clerks of
the Crown and Peace are engaged not
only in duties appertaining to the Crown
and Peace Office, but also in Land
Registry duties, the portions of the
salaries of these officers attributable to
the latter duties being recouped by the
Imperial Government. In the original
Estimate the proportion of the officers'
time which it was expected they would
devote to Land Registry work was overestimated and, consequently, the receipts
in respect of salary recouped are less than
was anticipated. There was also a slight
overestimate in the fees received by the
Clerks of the Crown and Peace in respect
of the revision of Jurors' Lists. I beg
to move.

The PRIME MINISTER: I hope that
the Committee will agree to pass the sum
of money put down in this Supplementary
Estimate for the expenses of those who
went out to Canada on behalf of Ulster.
I should explain that we, as a Government, were invited by the British Government to join with them in proceeding to
Ottawa in order to help in the delicate
negotiations that were then taking place
in order to come to some arrangement
whereby not alone our country, but the
Dominions themselves, should benefit by
whatever arrangements were made.
Although the results of the various agreements reached may not be apparent so
early, I can assure the Committee that
had Ulster refused the invitation of the
British Government to go to Ottawa, we
might be in a very much worse position
than we are in to-day. We stand to
benefit pari passu with Great Britain
both as regards industry and agriculture.
Our representatives were selected very
shrewdly and cautiously for the duties
As to flax and linen, Mr. Lewis Gray
very kindly undertook to represent that
important industry, and I think that his
firm showed great generosity in sparing
his services, not in the interests of his

under a deep debt of gratitude to him for
the way in which he was able to work in
the interests of the linen industry. By
the action taken, backed up, of course,
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance, the Canadian duties on linen
were entirely removed, and that, of
course, is a great benefit to the trade.
Modifications were also obtained in regard
to the embargoes on our exports to
Australia and other Dominions. I can
only say that if at any time a similar
opportunity occurs I shall not hesitate to
acquiesce in the invitation to send representatives, in view of what the British
Government think, that when Ulster
interests are so materially affected we

to help.

Conference has put them in a
position than they were in before.

in the direction of adding to the range
of goods already being manufactured in
the Province and of creating a market
in Ulster itself for the new goods thus

point out to the hon. Member for Pottinger and to the right hon. Gentleman,
as well as to the Committee, that we are
discussing a vote for £10.
We are,
it
seems to me, on the verge of discussing the
whole trade policy not only of this part
of the United Kingdom, but of the whole
of the United Kingdom. I cannot see how
we can do that within the narrow compass
of £10.
Mr. BEATTIE: Some of this money is
for the Ulster Industries Development
Association, and I think I am within my
rights in saying that the waste of money
in advertising should not be continued.
The CHAIRMAN: If the hon. Gentleman had stopped there, the debate would
have been over ten minutes ago.
Mr. BEATTIE: I tried to conclude,
but the right hon. Gentleman wants to
know about the attendance of the people
at picture-houses and football matches.
Mr. POLLOCK: And how does the
Co-operative Society pay so much money
in dividends?
Mr. BEATTIE: I hope you will not be
able to get your way and be empowered to
put a tax on that society. I am quite
willing to see money applied in a useful
way, but you are asking people to do something that it is impossible for them to do.
It is uneconomic and why do you insist on
spending money on an uneconomic proposition? In Great Britain they have their
own difficulties, and they do not come over
here to purchase Ulster articles, with the
exception of linen.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: It has been
stated that it is a waste of money to contribute to the funds of the Ulster Industries Development Association. If a man
and his wife and child have only 25/2 a
week, it is unfortunate, but it must be
admitted that that Association cannot
increase that sum, either directly or indirectly, but they can advertise in such a
way as to encourage the spending of that
25/2 so as to give employment to other
workmen throughout the Province of
Ulster, rather than spending it so that
the money goes to the Continent or some
other place and thereby increases the
amount of unemployment at home. Therefore, I feel that we are perfectly justified
in supporting this Vote.
I agree that very good work has been
done by this Association. The suggestion
has been made that practically all that we
are doing is to advertise on the other side
of the Channel. I had not been in contact with this organisation until a fortnight ago, but I have seen some of their
work at close quarters, and I can assure
you that every penny voted here has been,
is being, and will be well spent. I know
that within the past ten days they have
sent circulars to over 35,000 residents of
Belfast asking them to buy Ulster goods,
and encouraging them to spend their
money in such a way as will help to increase employment in this Province.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should just like to
say this that it is impossible for the goods
to be purchased on the basis of 25/2 a
week. That is my objection to the whole
scheme.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolutions to be reported to-morrow.
The remaining Orders were read and
postponed.

(Captain Dixon.)
Mr. BEATTIE: Perhaps the right hon.
Gentleman will state the order of business
for to-morrow.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is proposed tomorrow to take the Exchequer and Financial Provisions Resolutions and Loans
Guarantee (Money), Committee. I think
that will occupy the House for the great
part of the sitting.

Thursday, 2nd March, 1933.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.
Oral Answers to Questions.
LAND PURCHASE ANNUITIES.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been called to a resolution passed by the
Higher Officers of the Ulster Farmers'
Union declining to make any claim for
a reduction or remission of the land
annuities; and, whether, in view of this
generous gesture on behalf of the farmers' representatives, he can see his way
to grant their request in respect of this
matter.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, to reply.
I have followed with interest the Press
reports of the meetings of the Ulster
Farmers' Union, both at headquarters
and in the country, and I am pleased
to note that the more responsible members of the organisation realise that a
reduction or a remission of the land purchase annuities is not within the realm of
practical politics.
Mr. NIXON: Do I understand the
Minister to convey that he will be kind
enough to allow them to pay?
RETIRING AGE OF CIVIL
SERVANTS.
2. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether, in view of
the many protests against the fixing of
the retiring age of civil servants being
changed to 60 years as against 65 years,
he will give a considered statement on
the matter and indicate the possible savings to the Exchequer from this means.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have to give a
lengthy reply to the question asked by
the hon. and gallant Gentleman as some
detail is necessary in order to make the
position perfectly clear.
The hon. and gallant Member for St.
Anne's Division has apparently been misinformed, since no official steps have been
taken to fix a rigid retiring age limit
of sixty years for civil servants in the
Departments of Northern Ireland.
Under Article 15 of the Order in Council
of 10th January, 1910, it is laid down-
"It shall be competent for the head
of any Department to call upon any
officer of such Department to retire at
any time after reaching the age of sixty
on such pension as by the length of his
service he is qualified to receive.
"Retirement shall be compulsory for
every officer on attainment of sixtyfive years of age."
The provisions of the Article quoted are
still operative.
The only recent decision affecting the
matter is one under which immediately
before he reaches the age of fifty-nine the
case of each civil servant is specially examined by. the head of his Department
in order that he may decide whether
there are substantial grounds for retaining the officer's services for a further
period after the age of sixty. In
making that decision, due weight is given
to all the relevant circumstances, particularly the efficiency of the Service,
the general interest of the State, and the
desirability of maintaining a measure of
uniformity in our small Service. With
these considerations in view, it is determined whether the retirement will take
place as from the sixtieth anniversary of
the officer's birth, or whether he will be
retained for a year thereafter. A like
procedure is followed annually in all
cases of prolongation.
From the representations which have
reached me in recent months, I am satisfied that in some cases there is uneasiness
arising out of the annual review to which
I have referred. With the concurrence
of the Prime Minister, I have, therefore,
decided to waive that annual review and
to be content in normal circumstances
with the one examination which takes
place when the officer reaches fifty-nine
years of age. This change will be without prejudice.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
2 MARCH 1933
(1) to the statutory power of the head
of the Department-
(a) to require any offier to retire at
any time between the ages of sixty and
sixty-five;
(b) to retain any officer with his consent beyond the age of sixty; or
(2) to the existing right of an established officer to retire on reaching the age
of sixty or at any time thereafter.
Owing to the system under which
pensions are assessed on length of service,
and to the fact that salaries are fixed
with annual increments, some savings in
Estimates would possibly arise as a result
of general retirement at the age of sixty.
It would obviously be a matter of some
difficulty to calculate the amount of such
savings, which would vary from year to
year.
In this whole matter, the interests of
the public service must, of course, continue to be the paramount consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he is
prepared to consider sixty years as the
retiring age for all pensionable purposes
in the State.
That
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER :
rather goes outside the scope of the
original question. Perhaps an additional
question may be put down for that.
Major MCCORMICK: Would the
Minister say that the changing of the age
under the conditions which he has
mentioned and the subsequent increase of
pensions would not be retrograde to the
declared policy of economy?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, on the contrary,
it has been beyond all question proved
by the British Government that the retention of the 60 years contributes to
economy. It is impossible in reply to a
supplementary question to enter into
what is really an actuarial examination of
the position. Of course, exceptional
cases naturally arise where it is to the
advantage of the Service to retain
specially qualified officers beyond the age
of 60 years. Take, for example, the Post
Office Service in Northern Ireland. There
is only one case in which a supervising
officer has been allowed to remain after
sixty years. I have a note here before me
of a question asked in the Imperial
Parliament by one of the Members on the
retirement of officers in the Post Office.
Sir Kingsley Wood said:
"The hon. Member would appear
to be misinformed. There is at present
only one supervising officer in
Northern Ireland over sixty years of
age."
I only mention that to show the House
the practice in this matter, but I need
hardly say there is no intention of making
a hard and rigid rule in regard to a 60
years retiring age.
Mr. NIXON: Can the Minister give
us the name of the accountant who
worked out that extraordinary problem
which gives such extraordinary results?
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I do not
think that arises. There are nineteen questions on the Order Paper, and every hon.
Member who has put a question down
should have an opportunity of asking it.

FATAL MOTOR ACCIDENTS IN
BELFAST.
5. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been called to the Press
accounts of the strictures made by the
Belfast City Coroner (Mr. T. E. Alexander) on Friday, 24th inst., on the alarming number of fatal motor accidents
in the city; and whether, in view of his
suggestion that
of
a large number
drivers are not qualified to drive, the
Minister will take action to ensure the
safety of pedestrians by making more
drastic the regulations under which
driving licences are issued.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen
the remarks of the Belfast City Coroner
as reported in the Press.
The statistics of accidents collected by
the police over a number of years show
that a very minute fraction of the accidents only about one in every 200-is
due to inexperience on the part of the
driver. More than half the accidents
are due to the carelessness of pedestrians
and pedal cyclists, and of the remainder
the great majority are caused by the
negligence of drivers of experience who
have become over-confident and who take
risks that the inexperienced driver is
careful to avoid.
All experience goes to show that the
imposition of any practicable test would
be ineffective to prevent accidents. Tests
could only show ability to manipulate a
car under ordinary circumstances, but
would give no indication as to how a
driver would act in case of emergency
nor whether he would be careful or
negligent in his behaviour on the road.
I am not satisfied, therefore, that any
change in the regulations in the direction
indicated by the hon. Member, even if
it were within my power, would have the
desired effect.
Mr. NIXON: Is it true that a person
with defective vision and hearing and
even a disabled person can get a licence
to drive, provided he is respectable and
pays the fee?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, that is
not the case.
Mr. NIXON: I am glad to hear it.

2 MARCH 1933
BELFAST CORPORATION BUS
ROUTES.
6. Major McCORMICK: asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state if he considers the withdrawal of
certain bus routes by the Belfast Corporation, which are recognised as being
established routes, such as the Cregagh
route, is justified, in the interests of
residents of this district; and whether it
is an accepted principle of the Motor
Vehicles and Road Traffic Acts that the
convenience of the travelling public should
be the first consideration.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Before considering the application for the withdrawal of the bus service on the Cregagh
route I insisted on a long experimental
period, and it was only when I was satisfied, from careful examination of the
results, that the service could not be continued in fairness to the travelling public
in Belfast as a whole, that permission was
given to withdraw it.
For a period of 2 years the service was
run at a heavy loss, and during that
period the receipts steadily declined,
although every device was tried to
improve the position.
The mere fact that the receipts did not
cover the operating costs would not
necessarily involve the withdrawal of the
service, but in this case the receipts were
so far below the cost of operating the
service as to show that the service was
not availed of, nor appreciated, by the
residents of the district to an extent that
would justify its continuance.
The route is served by an excellent
tram service, and it was conclusively
shown that the bulk of the traffic carried
by the buses came from that part of the
district which is fully served by the trams
and not from the portion of the route
which diverged from the tram route.
I fully agree that the underlying
principle of the Motor Vehicles and Road
Traffic Acts is to secure the best possible
service for the public as a whole.
Major MCCORMICK: Is the Minister
aware that under private management
this route was a paying one and suited
the convenience of the people resident
there?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I am not
aware of that.
R.U.C.
CADETS-ELIGIBILITY OF
MARRIED MEN.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he can state whether
married men are eligible for appointment as cadets to the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and, if so, under what regulation; whether he can state the names
of any cadets appointed during 1932,
and the names of any gentlemen who
were nominated but found unable to
pass the medical tests; and whether they
were married or single.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer
to the first part of the question is in the
negative under Article 663 of the Code.
In the year 1932 two cadets were
appointed, viz., Mr. Peacock and Mr.
Crawford. Both of these gentlemen are
single.
It would not be in the public interest,
or fair to the persons concerned, to give
any information in regard to the medical fitness or unfitness, as the case may
be, of prospective but unsuccessful candidates for the R.U.C., as they may be
seeking other appointments and their
prospects might thereby be prejudiced.
APPOINTMENT OF R.U.C. CADETS.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he can state whether it
is considered necessary to appoint any
further cadets to the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and, if so, whether the appointments will be subject to Civil Service
examination as formerly.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not
anticipated that further vacancies for
cadet appointments, as distinct from promotion appointments, to the officer rank
of the R.U.C. will arise until 1935. If
and when such appointment is being
made, the appointment will be made by
a Selection Board.
Mr. NIXON: Whoever is in power.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Exchequer and Financial Provisions
(Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
The CHAIRMAN: I should like to
explain to the Committee that the first
of these Resolutions which now comes to
be considered by the Committee deals
with a matter about which there will on
a subsequent Order Paper be a certain
Motion set down. It is a rule of our
procedure that a Motion set down for
discussion shall not be anticipated. It is
a rule that the Orders of the Day shall
be debated. It is also a rule that any
speech made by an hon. Member may not
be repeated in the same Session, nor may
he repeat another hon. Member's speech.
The difficulty here is to find some middle
course to reconcile these apparently conflicting rules. A White Paper has been
issued for the information of Members,
and what I propose to do in the circumstances is to open the debate somewhat
wider than a strict interpretation of the
rules permits, so that hon. Members may
not find themselves in either of the difficulties I have pointed out. That means that
on this particular Resolution in relation
to the Road Fund I will allow a much
wider latitude, for the reasons indicated,
than would otherwise be possible, but
it must be clearly understood that to do
that anticipates the Motion set down in
respect of the same matter and will
largely limit the discussion upon it when
it comes up for debate later on.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: On the
point of order. From what you have
said then it is clear that my Motion on
the Road Fund would be better taken
to-day, but as that cannot be done I
understand the debate is to be widened.

Mr. BARBOUR: Thank you very
much. The most important item covered
by the first Resolution relates to the
transfer from the Reserve Fund to the
Exchequer, for which provision was made
in the Budget of my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, last May. It is
only due to the impossibility of passing
legislation to implement that Budget
before the House rose last summer, that
legislation is being introduced at the very
close of the year.
The reason why we consider it right
that the finances of the present year
should be assisted by this special withdrawal was explained in the Budget
Statement, namely, that it represents a
fortuitous accretion to the surplus of last
year; just at the close of last financial
year, that is, shortly before 31st March,
1932, in response to the Imperial Chancellor's appeal, there was a very heavy
payment of income tax and surtax in
Northern Ireland, much above the usual,
and accordingly, the revenues of the
current year were diminished to that
amount. It was felt to be right, however, that the surplus of revenue in
1931-32, together with a surplus arising
principally from tobacco duties in 1930-
31, should be utilised to help the revenues
of the current year, thereby, to an
extent, averaging the yield of the
reserved revenues over the three years
involved, or, in other words, eliminating
the abnormalities. The actual adjustment, although based on these facts, was
justified by other circumstances. Under
the formula governing the financial
relations of Northern Ireland with Great
Britain, any excess yield of reserved
revenues would normally augment the
Imperial contribution. It was pointed
out to the Imperial Treasury and the
Joint Exchequer Board, however, that
the Budget of the year 1931-32 contained
two items peculiar to Northern Ireland
which should not be used to augment the
contribution. These were the allocation

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : Dealing
with the Resolution on the Order Paper,
in conjunction with the White Paper, I
should first like to speak about the money
that is being transferred to the Exchequer
from the Reserve Fund. Hitherto I
understand it has been the practice, when
we had a surplus, that the amount finally
decided upon by the Joint Exchequer
Board was transferred to the Reserve
Fund (Capital Liabilities) under the
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act,
1927. Conversely, when the account had
gone against us, the deficit was met by
issues from the Consolidated Fund to the
Imperial Treasury. To get a picture of
the whole situation, I think you want to
cast your eye back over the last few years
and look at the heavy calls made on this
Reserve Fund for payments made in any
previous financial year. Looking back at
the finance accounts, you will find that
for the year 1924-25 a sum of £665,000
was returned to the Imperial Exchequer.
In 1927-28 £208,000 had to be returned.
Coming down to more recent times, I
find that in the year 1928-29 £159,000
had to be returned, and in the year
1930-31 £9,000 odd had to be returned.
Therefore it seems to me that only the
most stringent financial conditions of the
times justify our drawing from this
Capital Fund moneys which come as a
surplus. From what the Minister of
Commerce has said, I understand that the
£250,000 surplus of last year was due to
the pressure exercised on the income tax
payers who came forward and paid up.
I think it is wise to consider that for the
current financial
the income tax
year
payers will not be able to meet in full
their liabilities, and that our revenue will
be reduced. The result will be that in
future years, when the Joint Exchequer
Board comes to determine our final share,
we may have to meet a deficit. Are we
not laying ourselves open in the future
to have to meet such a deficit-if there
is one-from revenue and not from the
Reserve Fund?
When the Minister of Finance comes to
reply, I should like him to make it quite
clear that we are not jeopardising our
future by having to call up £350,000
from the Reserve Fund, and that if we
do have liabilities we will be able to meet
them. The point is this, the income tax
payers last year met their liabilities in
full,
but this year there may be a decrease
in revenue from this source. I wish to
make this point plain, that I consider the
withdrawal of these sums, which by
Statute were placed to the credit of the
Reserve Fund, requires serious consideration, and that it is only in an emergency
such as we are faced with at the present
time in order to meet our expenditure
that such a course is allowable. In other
words, necessity is driving us to this
course. I should like the Minister of
Finance to make it quite plain that we
are not depleting this Reserve Fund to
such an extent that in future, when we
have to pay money to the Exchequer, we
will not be able to meet our liabilities.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The Road
Fund. When the Budget was opened
last year very brief reference was made
to the state of the Road Fund. On the
11th May, 1932, the Minister of Finance,
in his Budget statement, dismissed it in
a few words. What he actually said was:
The Road Fund payment of £559,000
represents the corresponding receipts
from motor taxation. The Budget
estimate was £540,000, showing an

increase has been maintained during
the past few years.
That is all that was said about the state
of the Road Fund. In that statement
the Government did not take this House,
fully into their confidence by elaborating further the state of the Road Fund.
In this House in 1930 an Act of Parliament was passed whereby the Road Fund
was enabled to borrow against its current
revenue, and that Act stipulated that
such borrowing should and must be repaid at the end of the current year.
What in fact has happened? In the year
1931-32 the Road Fund borrowed from
the Exchequer £65,000, and when the
end of the year came it was not in a
position to pay that money back. This
difficulty was met by obtaining £49,000
from the Civil Contingencies Fund. May
I point out that no Road Fund account
has been issued for last year-it is now
three months late and ask why this
account has not been laid before the
House? Again, I ask why no Civil Contingencies Fund account has been issued
since 1930. I made inquiries in the
Library two days ago, and was told that
it was going into print to-day.
These
accounts would enable Members to follow
the finances of the Road Fund, and they
should be presented in due and normal
time, and not, as it were, kept back.
In this connection of borrowing from
the Road Fund, I would call the attention
of the House to the opinion of the Comptroller and Auditor-General on these transactions. There was no Statutory Authority
enabling the Road Fund to borrow,
and, the Road Fund having borrowed,
this Financial Resolution which we have
before us to-day, is going to legalise what
there was no legal authority for. The
Comptroller and the Auditor-General
states:-
Prior to the passing of the above Act
the N.I. Road Fund had no power to
borrow. Section 8 of that Act empowered the Ministry of Finance to
make temporary advances from the Exchequer to the Road Fund, such
advances to be repaid before the end of
the financial year. Sums amounting to
£65,000 were borrowed from the Exchequer in 1931-32, but it was subsequently found that the Fund was not
in a position to repay that amount
before the end of the year and at the
same time to pay the sums due to Local
Authorities. To relieve this situation
the Ministry of Finance made a temporary advance of £49,000 from the
Civil Contingencies Fund to the Road
Fund.
The result of the year's transactions
was that the Road Fund balance of
about £132,000 on 1/4/1931 had been
reduced to £888 on 31/3/32, and the
Fund owed £49,000 to the Civil Contigencies Fund.
Carry this further. The White Paper
shows, and the Minister of Commerce
said, that further attacks were to be made

I worked it out myself from information

had to serve seven years for Rachel, and

the
for which it was created.
purpose
As one who has had something to do
with the finances of County Antrim for
the past fourteen or fifteen years, I say
it is becoming increasingly difficult for
those who are trying to do their best to
finance their various schemes owing to the
way this Road Fund is being administered. I am very doubtful if it will be as
easy to fill seats on the various county
councils in the future as it has been in
the past, because it is so difficult to get
things done in a way they can be understood. So far as I am able to understand it, Memorandum B explains that
the £360,000 that is to be taken out of
the Road Fund-from which it ought not
to be taken-to finance schemes in relief
of unemployment, is to be principally
given to the City of Belfast.
In one
single journey from Ballymena to Belfast
I met seventeen large motor waggons
laden with goods from Belfast, and if
they pay the largest share of motor taxation they use the country roads. If you
are going to contend that because Belfast
pays the larger share of motor taxation
that city should have a similar proportion
of the Fund spent on its relief works, you
had better do like China and build a wall
round Belfast and then see if Belfast can
live without the country. The Minister
of Finance mentions Derry, but I do not
think that is a sound argument.
It is only right that the country should
share to the full in this motor taxation
fund. The reason I say that is that out
of a sum of £102,000 taken out of the
Road Fund up to October, 1932, no less
than £97,000 was given to the Belfast
Corporation, and the remaining few
thousands of pounds was distributed

expense
I note that the Consolidated Fund is
repaying the Road Fund the sum of
£360,000 which on the face of it looks
a satisfactory settlement, but when you
go into the Memorandum further you
find, as the hon. and gallant Member
for East Down said, that the sting is
in the tail. Although we are apparently
getting that £360,000 paid back again,
the Road Fund is to contribute £50,000
per annum for the next seven years to
the Exchequer. What will that mean?
The Road Fund has increased by about
£30,000 a year, taking an average of the
last six years. By having to pay this
£50,000 a year we will not only lose that
£30,000 annually, but the balance of
£20,000. If the Road Fund does not
continue to increase in the same ratio the
result will be that the grants to local
authorities to keep the roads in order will
be reduced. Indeed, the Minister of
Home Affairs has already notified local
authorities that they will have to curtail
their road programmes, and the result
will be that more money will be given
to the City of Belfast. The plain fact of
the case is that the Road Fund is bankrupt, and its bankruptcy is caused by the
Government. Now the Government are
compelled to recoup the Road Fund out
of the Consolidated Fund, but to my mind
this is only a book-keeping transaction,
as we will have to repay to the Exchequer
a sum of £50,000 a year for the next
seven years.

Antrim Road Fund. It was the Northern Ireland Road Fund. It was

money without

part of the credit account in order that
our Budget for the past year should be
balanced. We have balanced our Budgets

Ulster are the only countries in the world
that have balanced their Budgets.

The major part of the debate has
ranged around the question of the socalled raid on the Road Fund. Let me
say at once in regard to that that the
Road Fund is not sacroscant. It is part
of the revenue of Northern Ireland just
as the Road Fund of Great Britain is
part of the revenue of that country.
Year by year the British Government has
had no hesitation in taking a certain
proportion of the revenue of the Road
Fund under what they call a luxury
statute, and not only so, but they have
actually on special occasions taken very
considerable sums of money from that
Fund for the purpose of doing what all
Governments aim to do, and that is to
balance their accounts. It may, perhaps,
interest the House to know what happens
in Great Britain. From an amount of
£105,000,000 the British Government
have taken £46,000,000, approximately
half of the total contributions to the Road
Fund, for the purpose of balancing their
accounts. I do not think the parochialism
introduced by the Member for Antrim

this money is being used for the purpose
for which the Fund was created, it does
not very much matter whether it is spent

of Belfast or on the roads of Northern
Ireland. What is the exact position in
regard to the application of Road Fund

I would like to say generally in regard

has arisen. The Government loaned to
the Road Fund a certain sum of money to
meet the liabilities that had accrued, in

grants to local authorities should not be
reduced. The Government simply provided that a comparatively small amount

lent. Is there anything very mysterious

I want the House to remember that
there is one method of reducing taxation, and that is by reducing it at the

I ask if there is any Member in this

should be reduced. Is there anyone who

mittee. It is not the administration of

All that I ask the House to do is to

their such conditions, and bearing these.
conditions in mind I hope hon. Members

PROPOSED BELFAST COR-
PORATION ZOO.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture if he can state
whether he has power under the Diseases
of Animals Act to exclude wild animals
being brought into Northern Ireland for
the Belfast Corporation Zoo.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir E. M. Archdale): The reply
is in the affirmative, but I would only
be justified in exercising such powers of
exclusion if I were satisfied that there
was a risk of the introduction and spread
of disease.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is it not a
fact that there is a scheduled area roughly
south of a line drawn between the Humber and the Mersey from which animals
cannot be imported?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Only
animals that chew the cud are subject to
foot and mouth disease, and I do not
think that lions and animals of that sort
would be dangerous.
SLAUGHTER YARDS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
5. Major McCORMICK asked
asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state what abattoirs or slaughter yards
in Northern Ireland do not comply with
the conditions of the Slaughter of
Animals Act, 1932.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Slaughter of
Animals Act does not lay down conditions
with regard to abattoirs or slaughter
yards in Northern Ireland, but it requires.
that all animals slaughtered therein must
be killed with the humane killer, used
by a person duly licensed by the local
authority for that purpose.
The sanitary authorities are responsible
for the administration of the Act and
penalities are provided for contravention
of its provisions.
No offences against the provisions of
the Act have been brought to my notice.

OTTAWA CONFERENCE.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state what benefits have accrued
to
farmers of Northern Ireland from the
Ottawa Conference.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: One of
the objects of His Majesty's Government
at the Ottawa Conference was by agreement with the Dominions to secure a rise
in the wholesale price level of agricultural
products in the United Kingdom, particularly stock and stock products, which
constitute 75 per cent. of the agricultural
income of the United Kingdom. This
was secured by one or other of two
methods-the adjustment of existing
tariffs or by the limitations of imports.
Adjustments in the then existing tariffs
on eggs and butter have been successful
in maintaining the level of wholesale
prices for butter at about the 1932 level,
and in effecting an improvement in the
wholesale prices for eggs.
With regard to meat and meat products,
agreements were entered into with regard
to the limitation of imports. Pending the
necessary legislation and reorganisation,
voluntary agreements have been made
with foreign and Dominion countries
sending bacon, beef, mutton and lamb
to the United Kingdom, which have
resulted in the curtailment of imports by
15 to 20 per cent. of the quantities
imported in 1931-32. As a consequence
of these arrangements, the wholesale
prices of pork, beef and mutton have
shown a very substantial improvement in
recent months.
For example, the price of pork has
risen from 38s per dead cwt. at the beginning of November to over 52s per dead
cwt. at the end of February.
an
Store cattle prices have increased on the
average by about 2s per live cwt. between
November and February, while in the
case of fat cattle there has been
increase of about 8s per cwt., or 25 per
cent. in the average prices ruling in
Belfast in February as compared with
November.
Every sheep breeder in Northern
Ireland is aware of the very substantial
rise in sheep prices which has occurred as
the direct and indirect consequence of the
restriction on the importation of mutton
and lamb agreed to at the Ottawa Conference.
Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the
right hon. Gentleman's statement that the
farmers are benefiting to a certain extent
by the Ottawa Conference, will he
explain why it is that the farmers all over
the country are stating that they derive
no such benefit and that the conditions
are worse since that conference took
place?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: All the
farmers have not said that; only some
have.
Mr. HENDERSON: If the Minister
would go to any of the agricultural areas
he will find that he can get sheep for the
taking of them away.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: That is
not the case.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the
Loans Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922 to 1932, by extending to the
31st day of March, 1935, the period within
which the Ministry of Finance may give
guarantees under the Loans Guarantee
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922.—(Governor's Recommendation signified.-Mr.
Pollock.)
Mr. POLLOCK: The Government has
again decided to recommend Parliament
to adhere to its policy of keeping alive the
Loans Guarantee machinery, and the
Resolution which I am about to move has
accordingly been tabled. As shown by
the quarterly returns which are furnished
to hon. Members, no fresh guarantees
were issued last year-a result which reflects the melancholy condition of industry
and the shipbuilding industry in particular.
I do not propose to reiterate and investigate the considerations which have
led the Government to ask Parliament
to make available for a further period,
the credit facilities provided by the Loans
Guarantee Acts. Last year, when moving
a similar Resolution in relation to the 1932
Bill, I dealt with the various issues involved in detail, and in particular with
such important questions as the risk of
loss, and the difficulties which already face
the Exchequer in respect of past Loans
Guarantee commitments. I, therefore,
feel that it is unnecessary for me
to go over this ground a second time.
The one outstanding feature is that our
shipyards, in common with most of the
shipyards in Great Britain, are at the
moment practically empty and, in the
opinion of the Government, the present
time is inopportune to think of removing
from the Statute Book any means of helping to remedy the position.
Happily, there are signs that our shipyards may not, throughout 1933, present
the same derelict appearance, and without wishing to appear too optimistic, I
think I am justified in saying that the
prospects in 1933 are such as to lead us
to hope that, with the help of the credit
facilities which are the subject of this
Resolution, additional employment may
be secured.
The Resolution is limited in effect to an
extension in point of time; there is an
adequate margin in point of the financial
limit within which the Ministry can
engage in new transactions. It will have
been noted from the quarterly returns for
the period ended 31st December last, that
of the guarantees which have been
given, amounting in the aggregate to
£12,131,247, a sum of £3,330,100 has been
repaid, leaving guarantees outstanding of
£8,801,147. There remains, approximately, £4,000,000 available for any
guarantees that may be necessary for the
Government to extend during the year
that lies ahead of us. I beg to move.

Those two cases, I submit, are a very
fair illustration of the position and condition of single men and men without
dependents in Northern Ireland. It is
not for me to find a plan for this. It
is for the Government to find a plan. The
Government are in power for an unprecedented period, and they are going to be
in power unless numbers of these young
men coming on the labour market and
not getting labour get so overpowering that the Government will be
glad to run away, or will welcome defeat.
Emigration is stopped. I doubt if there
ever will be emigration again in our day.
There is no country that we know of that
has not surplus labour. No one can
find any trade for a young man now.
If he does serve an apprenticeship there
is, generally speaking, little work for him.
after he completes it. The only thing the
Government have done for youths, as

figures cannot be disputed, which show

be dealt with separately from the rest of
Northern Ireland. Besides, the hon.
Member's Motion sets out that work is to
be found for women also. Now no
Government that I know of has been

without interfering with private enterprise. Women, of course, are not suitable for the ordinary relief schemes such
as are being carried out by men. But
supposing we were to comply with the

£2.000,000, and therefore, the total cost

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 8th March, 1933.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.
Paper Presented to Parliament.
Ministry of Finance:
An Estimate showing the several Services for which a Vote on Account is
required for the year ending 31st March,
1934. (By Command.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
County Officers and Courts Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This Bill, which it is my duty
to present to the House for Second Reading, is of a miscellaneous character
treating of the functions of County Court
Officers and, to some extent, of the
functions of County Court Judges. The
Bill, which I presume hon. Members have
in their hands, deals mainly with
administrative and not judicial matters,
and falls naturally into four parts. The
first part, including Clauses 1 to 6, deals
with the appointment and payment of
certain officers and with superannuation
matters. I think it will be convenient if
I take the different Clauses of the Bill
categorically and explain them in some
detail in order that hon. Members may
be fortified when the Bill reaches the
Committee
discussing
Stage in
features of the Measure.
the
Clause 1 enables the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland to pay a consolidated
salary to a new Clerk of the Crown and
Peace who is not an "existing officer"
within the meaning of the Government of
Ireland Act, 1920, and this salary will
cover all the functions which he may by
law be required to carry out, including
those relating to reserved matters, that is
to say, his functions in regard to Registration of Title and the preparation of
the Voters' Lists. The Clause is complementary to Section 7 of the United
Kingdom Northern Ireland (Miscellaneous
Provisions) Act, 1932, which provides for
the cessation of payments to a new Clerk
of the Crown and Peace in respect of
these two functions.
Hitherto the payment of salaries to
Clerks of the Crown and Peace has been
made in three different parts, one covering the normal duties of Clerk of the
Crown and Peace and the other two
covering his additional duties in respect
of Registration of Title and Voters' List
work. This piecemeal payment is the
outcome of the imposition of certain
additional duties by Statute after the
original Act of 1877 dealing with county.
courts was passed, but there is now in
some cases no proper relation between the
payments which are made for the
original Crown and Peace duties and
those made for the additional duties.
The responsibility of the Clerk of the
Crown and Peace, for example, in relation to Land Registry work is probably
now as great as, if not greater than, his
responsibility in connection with the work
at Quarter Sessions and Assizes, and is of
a more continuous character.
This was felt so much that in the year
1919 a Viceregal Committee was set up
by the British Government to inquire
into and report on the duties, salaries
and allowances of the Clerks of the
Crown and Peace in their several
capacities, and this Committee reported
in June, 1920. One of the recommendations of that Committee was the placing
of the clerical staff in County Court
Offices on an established footing. This
was carried into effect by legislation
passed by this House in the year 1925.
The other suggestion, namely, that the
salaries of Clerks of the Crown and
Peace themselves should be consolidated,
remains to be given effect to, and it is
this which the present Bill proposes to
carry through in so far as concerns all
Clerks of the Crown and Peace who are
not protected by the Government of
Ireland Act of 1920. One such appointment has already been made, and in
anticipation that the present Bill will
County Courts Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
become law, the newly-appointed officer
has accepted office on the basis of the
payment of a consolidated salary.
I come now to Clause 2, which provides for the appointment and payment
of temporary Clerks of the Crown and
Peace to fill vacancies caused by death
or other reasons. There is provision in
Section 23 of the County Court Officers
Act, 1877, under which, in the case
where a Clerk of the Crown and Peace
dies or becomes incapacitated during the
holding of the Quarter Sessions, the
County Court Judge is empowered to
appoint a person to discharge the duties
of the office during the rest of the
Sessions; but the Act made no provision
for such temporary appointment in the
interval between Quarter Sessions, where
it is not possible to make a permanent
appointment immediately. There is in
existence an Act of 1906, the Recorders,
Stipendiary Magistrates and Clerks of
the Peace Act of that year, which has
once or twice been used as an authority
to make such appointments; but its provisions relate rather to English than Irish
jurisdiction, and it is considered preferable to legislate specially for Northern
Ireland, the English Act being, in the
main, followed.
of
Clause 3 relates to Registrars of
County Courts outside Belfast. The
present statutory provision is that the
County Court Judge appoints his own.
registrar subject to the approval of the
Minister of Home Affairs, and as existing County Court Judges cannot, by
reason of the protection given by the
Government of Ireland Act, have their
rights and privileges curtailed in any
way, the present Clause has to be limited
in its scope. It is proposed that, subject
to such limitation, future registrars will
be appointed by the Governor
Northern Ireland on the recommendation of the Ministry of Home Affairs;
thus, continuity of service will be
ensured irrespective of changes in the
County Court Judgeship, as automatically the appointment of a registrar
now terminates on the judge's retirement or death. As, however, a County
Court Judge may prefer to waive his
present rights of appointment in the
event of a future vacancy, or may be
willing that his present registrar should
be entitled to obtain the greater fixity
of tenure which the proposals in this
Clause would bring about, provision is
made, subject to
subject to the County Court
Judges' agreement, to existing registrars
coming within the provisions of the Bill,
or for future registrars to be appointed
by the Governor even though the County
Court Judge concerned may still hold
office with all his privileges under the
Government of Ireland Act.
It is proposed that, under this Clause,
registrars, while continuing to be parttime officers, should be paid an annual
salary instead of, as at the present time,
a daily fee in respect of their attendances in court.
Mr. BEATTIE: How much?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is not arranged
yet. The present men receive a daily
sum of £3 15s, which is inclusive of
maintenance charges where transport
fares have to be paid in moving from
place to place. Clause 4 removes the
necessity for the giving of security by
Clerks of the Crown and Peace and by
Registrars of County Courts for the due
their
performance of
duties. Such
security is considered to be unnecessary
in the case of Clerks of the Crown and
Peace who are entitled to superannuation rights, and besides this, the great
increase in the amount of money held in
the county court owing to the development of Workmen's Compensation, etc.,
renders the security afforded by the
present statutory requirements illusory.
In view of the different changes that
have taken place recently in regard to
the functions of these officers and the
fact that they become transferred to the
Civil Service with all the civil servants'
advantages of superannuation, it is considered that that in itself is a sufficient
security, and therefore, as I say, it is
proposed in this Measure to remove that
requirement of a bond and to promote
the officers to be appointed under the
ordinary rules governing the Civil
Service. As regards registrars, the
giving of security is also considered to be
unnecessary, as the amount of money
actually handled by them is negligible.
With the waiving of the requirement
of a bond, it follows as a matter of
course that Clerks of the Crown and
Peace should not be regarded as personally
responsible to the parties in any action,
suit or proceeding in respect of any act
or matter which they have carried
through in the course of their legal
duties.
County Courts Bill-
Second Reading
8 MARCH 1933
Clause 5 proposes to give effect to this
waiver. On the other hand it is proposed in a later Clause, namely, Clause
8 of the Bill, to substitute an audit of
their accounts and of all funds held in
court by the Comptroller and Auditor-
General. At the present time, although
there is an audit of such accounts in
Great Britain, there is no statutory audit
of accounts in Northern Ireland, and this
defect it is now proposed to remedy by
the Clause referred to. You see we are
behind the British arrangement in regard
to this matter.
Clause 6, which has been inserted at
the suggestion of, and after consultation
with, the County Court Officers' Association, is largely a re-enactment of
provisions in the County Officers and
Courts Act (Northern Ireland), 1925, and
is designed to bring the conditions of
service of County Court Officers,
especially as regards superannuation,
into closer conformity with those of
ordinary civil servants. The Clause does
not confer any superannuation rights
over and above those existing under the
1925 Act.
Clauses 1 to 6 form the first part of the
Bill. The second part of this Bill includes Clauses 7 to 10 and deals with
county court administration. Clause 7
provides for the use of a seal on judgments and orders of the county court
and is a result of one of the recommendations made by a committee
appointed some years ago by the Lord
Chief Justice to inquire into the amount
of work transacted by the Recorder of
Belfast. The object of this provision is
to relieve the judge of the necessity of
personally signing all decrees and orders
of the Court.
Clause 8 I have already dealt with.
Clause 9 clarifies the position regarding
the investment of moneys paid into the
county court.
Clause 10 relates to the disposition of
moneys which may have lain unclaimed
in the County Court for a period of
fifteen years after the action to which
they relate has been dealt with. Existing legislation makes provision for the
transfer of such dormant funds, if they
are in the Supreme Court, to the Exchequer after a period of years, and in
Great Britain such legislation operates
not only as regards dormant funds in the
High Court, but also as regards such
funds in the county courts. I wish hon.
Members to realise the distinction between the Supreme Court and the Court
of Quarter Sessions. For some reason no
statutory provision exists in Northern
Ireland in connection with the county
courts, and it is to remedy this defect
and to clear the books of the county
courts of a considerable number of small
accounts containing negligible balances
that this Clause is introduced. At the
same time, power is given for the court
to order the repayment of any part of
this money to which claim may ultimately
be laid and approved by the county court.
Mr. BEATTIE: Whom does the money
belong to?
Mr. POLLOCK: It will belong to the
Exchequer of Northern Ireland provided
no one claims it after fifteen years.
Mr. BEATTIE: Whom did the money
belong to originally?
Mr. POLLOCK: To litigants whose
cases came before the court and whose
money came into the hands of the Clerk
of the Crown and Peace and was held, as
I have said, until it was claimed. If
no claim appeared for fifteen years it
automatically merged into the Exchequer
of the country-of our Exchequer in
Northern Ireland, but, as I repeat, if
any person can establish a claim, subsequent to that fifteen years, against the
Government, arrangements are made by
which repayment will be made to the
person in question. This Measure will
cover that right.
The third part of the Bill deals with
the jurisdiction of County Court Judges
and the appointment of
of deputies.
Clause 11 is designed to render the
County Court Judiciary more elastic.
The judge's jurisdiction is no longer to
be restricted to the county to which he
is appointed in the first place but may
be extended to any other county by
direction of the Governor after consultation with the Lord Chief Justice. That
will be a matter of convenience, because
in the past it has been necessary to
appoint outside legal men to take the

The next thing I would like to ask is

abolished. I fully agree with the

the individual upon whom his livelihood

There is a certain amount of authority

you should give authority over these
appointments to outside individuals. I
know that appointments under the jurisdiction of the courts in the past, and up
to the present, have been made on a
sectarian basis. I know that when Protestants were required for an appointment there was a particular gentleman
asked to recommend Protestants, and that
when Catholics were supposed to be
appointed a particular gentleman was
approached to recommend Catholics. I
am absolutely against that system, and
you will not do away with it if you continue to give power of appointment into
the hands of those outside your own
Ministry. Therefore, I say that full responsibility for these appointments
should be placed in the hands of the
Minister of Finance, and then, perhaps,
we will have more satisfaction in regard
to appointments to the county court service in Northern Ireland.
The other point to which I wish to
refer is the provision that County Court
Judges should be transferable.
I agree
that they should be transferable, but not
at their own choice or right.
They should
be transferable to any area in which

something like what are paid in New
York. I do not agree with that, and I
do not agree that any authority should
be given to these people in connection
with appointments to any positions.
I see that the old surety bonds are

to clear out. We want persons in these

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: With
regard to the point made about the
County Court Officers, the House should
know that they are all appointed since
the Act of 1925 through the machinery
of the Civil Service. Prior to 1925 a
number of these officials in the County
Courts were the personal appointments of
and personally paid by the Clerk of the
Crown and Peace. It was found necessary to put them on a proper footing in
1925, and they are all now members of
the Civil Service. So far as I know,
since 1925 there has been no substantial
complaint either as to the rate of pay
or conditions of service.
One question of some importance was
raised, and that is as to the jurisdiction of

from time to time that county court jurisdiction should be increased. I would ask

in the

If hon. Members are anxious to see the
criticisms passed on the English county
court system, where the jurisdiction has
been increased with increased cost, they
should look at an article which appeared
last month in the "Nineteenth Century
Review." You will see there a very
trenchant criticism of the great cost of
litigation in the English county court. If
you make the jurisdiction of the county
court too high, you bring into the county
court all the evils which are inveighed
against with respect to litigation in the
high court, namely, that it is too protracted, too costly, and too complicated.
Our county court jurisdiction on the contrary is very simple. The proceedings
are never protracted, and the costs are
relatively infinitesimal. I think it would.
require a great deal of argument at any
rate before I would be convinced that
it is in the interests of the people as a
whole, that county court jurisdiction
should be increased at any rate to a very
great extent.
Another matter has been referred to
with respect to this Clause 13. The hon.
Member for Pottinger appears to have
taken exception to the fact that the
Attorney-General, under the law as it
exists at present, determines whether
cases go for trial or not. He also appears
to think that in some cases unspecified,
mistakes may be made. All I can say
is this: The Attorney-General of the day
only acts upon evidence, and upon
nothing else. He does not act upon
gossip, nor upon hearsay, nor upon
prejudice, but directly upon the evidence
that is laid before him, as to whether the
case is to go to trial or not. And I
have rigidly adhered to that principle
during the years I have been in office,
and will continue to adhere to it so long
as I am in office. But let me say this
further with reference to it. It is not a
fact that in law the determination of
the Attorney-General is final. In England a great number of prosecutions are
conducted by the citizens themselves,
private prosecutions. In this country, as
a matter of fact, the bulk of the prosecutions are conducted by the law department of the Crown, under the direction
of the Attorney General. But that jurisdiction is not exclusive, and it is open
to any citizen to present a bill in a criminal matter if he has evidence to
substantiate it, and to produce that
evidence himself for the purpose of prosecuting.
There have been cases during the time
I have been in office such as the one
referred to here, where the parties have
asked that the evidence should be put at
their disposal for the purpose of considering whether they would bring a
prosecution as a private prosecution if
dissatisfied with the decision of the
Attorney-General. I have always put
that evidence at their disposal, and they
can either proceed or not as they may be
advised. I do not pretend that the

I wish to draw attention to Clause 5 of
this Bill. All modern legislation is calculated to deprive the public of any
little rights or privileges they may have,
and this Clause goes in that direction.
The Clause reads:
"A clerk of the crown and peace
and any officereven a civil bill officer which the hon. and
gallant Member for St. Anne's (Major
McCormick) says is a very mean man-
"and any officer in the county court
service acting under the authority of a
clerk of the crown and peace, shall not
be liable to any action, suit or proceeding for or in respect of any act or matter
bona fide done or omitted to be done
in the discharge, or supposed discharge,
of any functions with the discharge of
which the county court service is concerned by virtue of sub-section (2) of
section one of the Act of 1925."
The latter part of this Clause has the
inconvenience of being legislation by
reference, and without seeing Section 2 of
the Act of 1925 neither I nor, perhaps,
the learned Attorney-General could explain what is contemplated in this. But
there is enough in it to show that those
officers are not liable for the mistakes they
commit, or are supposed to commit, in
discharging their duty, and that the
public have no jurisdiction over, and no
claim against them, good, bad, or indifferent, because all they have to do is to
plead this Section and say it was a bona
fide mistake; that they were not really
discharging their duty but were supposed
to be discharging their duty, because
supposed to be " is in the Clause. The
Bill gives no power to sue them or to
make them answer the charge.
Practically every Act passed in
Northern Ireland has had a Section or
Sub-section of that nature put into it. In
this case when the first person making a
claim against a county court officer in
regard to some mistake that officer has
made in the performance of his duty, or
the supposed performance of his duty,
goes to a solicitor; the solicitor will turn
up the Act and read that Section, and say
that the claimant has no case as this was
an officer of the county court who was
supposed to be discharging his duty at the
time. Consequently, there is no remedy.
If any other person makes a mistake he
has to pay for it. If any hon. Member
on his way home this afternoon makes a
mistake with his motor-car he will be liable
to have civil proceedings taken against him
and will be liable for damages.
This Clause will become law, I have no
doubt, in very short time, unless some of
our good friends in the Senate draw
attention to this matter. They will get
some hearing if they draw attention to it.
When this Bill becomes law any of these
officers, even the very mean summons
servers or civil bill officers, can make any
mistakes they like and claim the protection of that Section, while no other person
in the community is protected from civil
proceedings if they make a genuine mistake. Perhaps it would not be too much
to ask the Government to read that Clause
and, if necessary, re-draft it in Committee.

In such a County Court as
Recorder's Court in the City of Belfast
there are thousands of decrees and dismisses pronounced. All those have to be
presented to the judge for signature, and
the result is that the judge's time is taken

Mr. NIXON: He holds a lot of people

Mr. BLACK: What the Clause provides is that the persons who must be
responsible for seeing that the decree is
right, that is the officials in the Clerk of
Peace's Office should be entrusted with a

Member made is that it would be very

affix it to a decree. He appears to think
there is some sort of safeguard in having
a signature instead of a seal. To my
mind the man who would have the hardihood to go away and get a seal of the
Court forged and counterfeited would
very easily have the audacity to forge a
signature. To my mind it would be very
much easier for a malefactor to forge a
signature than to go to the trouble of
going to a person who makes seals and getting him to counterfeit a seal. The Clause,
as drawn, is a Clause which provides for a
commonsense procedure instead of a procedure which cannot be expected to
provide any safeguard, and which puts
the responsibility for the issue of the
paper from the office, be it a decree or a
dismiss, on the persons who must really
be responsible, the responsible registrar
and officials of the judge and not the
judge himself.

Clause 2 refers to the guaranteeing of 1

I should like here to express my appreciation of the work done by the Trust
for the ex-Servicemen of Northern Ireland, and in particular to the activity
displayed by the two Northern Ireland

and Colonel Pakenham. The work of the
Trust in so far as the building of houses

maintenance of the houses, the policy
adopted is entirely one for the Trust
itself, and not a matter which comes
within the purview of this House.
Perhaps I might mention that the

Ireland was 1,046. By means of the
provision we made and the interest
accumulating upon the money invested
during the progress of the development.
of the work of the Trust 1,192 houses

Clause 4 relates to the advance of a
sum of £360,000 to the Road Fund from
the Exchequer in respect of distress and
unemployment relief schemes, and the
charge on the Road Fund of £50,000 per
annum for the next seven years as an
effect. The House will recollect that on

a very exhaustive discussion took place in

hon. Members will not expect me to enter

Clause 5 is fully explained in the paragraph headed C. in the White Paper, and
relates to the issue of Ulster Savings
Certificates, while Clause 6 refers to the
Sinking Fund set aside in respect of the
interest liability on the certificates.
Clause 7 relates to the Government
Loans Fund. At the present time if
money has been raised by means of Ulster
Loans Stock, and has been temporarily
invested pending advances to Local
Authorities and other bodies who draw
from the Fund, it is not competent for
the Ministry of Finance to feed the Fund
out of temporary borrowings. It must
realise the Fund's temporary investments
even though a financial loss may occur.
It is to obviate this that the present
Clause is introduced. It will enable the
Ministry to avoid such a loss by means
of a temporary borrowing until the
temporary investments held by the Fund
appreciate.
Section 8 also relates to the Government
Loans Fund, and as it is legislation by
reference, which is frequently objected to
and sometimes rightly objected to, I shall
explain a little fully what is proposed.
The Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Act of 1926 made a provision that, except
in the case of Local Authorities, loans
were not to be issued out of the Government Loans Fund to meet existing indebtedness. The reason for this is clear.
The Fund should only be used for the
purpose of financing new capital works
and not for the purpose of transactions
on the money market. It has, however,
happened in a few cases in the past that
the condition has been found to be somewhat restrictive, where a body which has
the right to come to the Government
Loans Fund for a loan has made some
temporary bank accommodation until its
actual requirements were known. Usually
this temporary accommodation forms but
a small proportion of the whole loan
desired, and it has proved an incon-
Financial Provisions Bill-

venience for the borrower to look to the

to the original purpose and intention of
the original donor. I contemplate, of

£360,000, I have no doubt, will be used

and the effect of this Measure will be that
for the year ending on the 31st March,
1940, that is the last of the seven years,
the Road Fund will still have to supply
the sum of £50,000. Now, that is all
very well, but in taking the step which he
has taken, I think the Minister of Finance
has looked forward to the future, as he
has a perfect right to do, in a
optimistic frame of mind than I would
be inclined to take. Seven years is a long
time to look ahead. We do not know
whether those seven years will be like
the seven fat kine of Pharoah's dream, or
whether they will be like the seven lean
kine. I sincerely hope and trust that
those seven years will be a great deal
better than the years which have preceded
them (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and
I feel that the Road Fund, after all, is in
a position to spare a sum of £50,000 a
year.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McNeill]
May I just put forward another consideration which occurs to me? Failing
recourse to the Road Fund in what way
are we to balance our Budget and meet
the claims of our unemployed population?
It may be said that we could reduce the
cost of administration in Northern Ireland. I have not the slightest doubt that
certain reductions could be made, but,
looking at the thing from the broad point
of view and from the economic point of
view, I do not believe that even the most
stringent restrictions in the administration of our great civil service and in our
Northern Parliament would lead to any
appreciable benefits to the unemployed
population of Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. McNEILL: I am forced reluctantly
to that conclusion. On the other hand,
in order to obtain revenue I cannot
suggest at the present time that the
Government under their transferred
powers should impose new taxation upon
this community. In fact if new taxation
were imposed I believe that we would have
reached the straining point when the last
straw breaks the camel's back. Again, if
new taxation were imposed it would mean
that, as compared with Great Britain,
Northern Ireland would be the more
highly taxed community, and I am sure
that is not the desire either of any hon.
Member of this House or of any member
of the community. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
For these reasons I am compelled to
give acceptance to the explanation of the
Minister of Finance. As I said at the
outset of my speech, had I been in his
position I would have acted in the same
way. We are under the necessity of
balancing our Budget. We are under the
necessity of maintaining our unemployed
population, and in my opinion within a
very limited frame of reference, to use a
scientific term, the Government have really
and consistently attempted to do everything in their power both to alleviate the
distress of our unemployed population and
to maintain the financial credit of Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 9th March, 1933.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.
LOCAL BILL.
Ballymena Urban District Council Bill.
Read a Second time.
Ordered: That the Clerk do carry
the Bill to the Senate.
Oral Answers to Questions.
CENSUS OF POPULATION.
the
1. Major McCORMICK asked
Minister of Finance whether it is proposed to take a census of the population
of Northern Ireland during the present
year.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The reply is in the negative.
OPENING OF NEW LAW COURTS.
2. Major McCORMICK asked. the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
when it is proposed formally to open the
new Law Courts.
Mr. POLLOCK: The formal opening
of the new Law Courts is a matter for
determination by the Imperial Authorities as a Reserved Service in consultation with the Lord Chief Justice, who
is the head of the Judiciary in Northern
Ireland.
So far as the building itself is concerned, the Imperial Office of Works
hope to have it completed and available
for full occupation by the month of June
next.
LOANS GUARANTEE ACT.
The following question stood on the
Paper in the name of Major McCormick:
3. Major McCORMICK.-To ask the
Minister of Finance whether, in view of
the great assistance given to employment
by the Loans Guarantee Act, he proposes to extend its benefits to other industries.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER With regard to question No 3, this question may
not be asked in view of the fact that a
Bill is at present before the House dealing with Loans Guarantees. A Bill of
that kind may not be anticipated.
IRISH LANGUAGE IN PUBLIC
ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS.
4. Mr.
GRANT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether there is on sale at
H.M. Stationery Office, Belfast, a document entitled, "Statutory Rules and
Orders of Northern Ireland, 1932, No.
113," from which may be seen the attitude of the Northern Government,
through its Ministry of Education,
towards the teaching of Irish in public
elementary schools; whether, prior to the
issue of these latest regulations, dated
11th October, 1932, Latin, French and
Irish were the languages included among
the extra subjects for the satisfactory
teaching of which a special fee of 9s each
was paid to the teacher; and whether it
appears from these new regulations that
Latin and French are no longer thought
worthy of study, and that Irish alone.
is of sufficient importance to warrant
payment of the fee of 9s per pupil.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The regulations referred to by the hon. Member
are on sale at the Stationery Office.
No fees for teaching Latin or French
in public elementary schools have been
paid by the Ministry or the Commissioners of National Education for at
least 25 years.
Fees for Irish have been paid for the
last 50 or 60 years.

COTTIER HOUSES IN COUNTY
ANTRIM.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
numerous cottier houses in County
Antrim have been unroofed and are
crumbling into ruins, and what steps
have been taken by the Antrim County
Council and the various rural and
urban district councils in the county to
effect clearances under the Northern Ireland Town Planning and Housing Act,
1931; and further, whether he proposes
to issue circulars to the various councils
urging them to put the Act into
operation.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware that in
the County of Antrim a number of
cottier houses have fallen into disuse and
become dilapidated.
I assume that the hon. Member has
in mind the provisions of Section 13 of
the Planning and Housing Act, 1932,
which relates to the removal of unsightly
and dilapidated structures.
The operations of the local authorities under this
Section do not require the approval of
my Department, and I am unable to say
what steps have been taken by the local
authorities in individual cases.
I understand that negotiations are
taking place between the county council
and the district councils as to the delegation of the powers of the county
council under Part I of the Act to the
district councils.
My Department have already issued a
comprehensive circular to all local
authorities pointing out their powers and
duties under the Act, but, as the hon.
Member is no doubt aware, I have no
compulsory powers in the matter.
ALLEGED SALE OF UNSOUND
MEAT-HEARING OF CASES.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
at Ballymoney Petty Sessions Court, on
the 20th February last, two persons were
tried for exhibiting for sale unsound
butchers' meat; whether both cases were
dismissed; whether, in order to ensure
that no unsound meat is exhibited for
sale, he will consider the propriety of
amending the law so that such cases will
be tried by resident magistrates.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact
that proceedings were taken against two
persons at Ballymoney Petty Sessions on
the 20th February last in respect of
alleged offences in connection with the
sale of butchers' meat. The cases were
marked, "Dismissed on the merits."
The suggestion contained in the latter
part of the question involves issues of a
far-reaching nature, upon which I am
not prepared at the moment to express
any opinion.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the
neglect of these magistrates in the carrying out of their duty is the right hon.
Gentleman not prepared to have the cases
dealt with by resident magistrates?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not pre
pared to say at the moment that these
magistrates acted mala fide.
COLLECTOR OF RENTS,
BALLYMONEY.
7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
how many years Mr. John Hanna, of
Ballymoney, served as collector of
cottage rents; what was his remuneration for that service and what pension
was granted on that account.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Mr. John
Hanna retired from the service of the
Ballymoney Rural District Council in
1921, and I have no information as
regards the length of his service as rent
collector.
His remuneration was at the rate of
5 per cent. of the rents collected by
him, and I understand that no superannuation allowance was granted in
respect of his service in this capacity.

to

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Mr. POLLOCK: When this matter
was raised on the Money Resolution it
was discussed very fully and exhaustively,
that is to say, the question of the continuance of the Act which has now been
in existence for a considerable number of
years empowering the Government to
guarantee loans in connection with
capital expenditure in Northern Ireland.
I do not think it is necessary to enter
into any of the arguments to justify the
Government's action in asking Parliament to continue this power, because
hon. Members, without any exception,
know that the power given under this
Act has given an amount of employment
in Northern Ireland, the absence of which
would have resulted in a calamitous condition of things. I think that goes without saying.
I explained in moving the Money
Resolution that during the past year
there were no applications to take advantage of this Act, which, of course, was
a true reflection of the depressed conditions that have existed not only in the
United Kingdom, but also in the world.
These conditions have resulted in the great
restriction of trade, which, unfortunately,
has been known to us, and which, at the
moment, does not seem within a measurable distance of finality. I think it is

Mr. YOUNG: I would like to congratulate the Government, especially
after the most lucid explanation given by

would like the House to realise the
position the Russian Government stands.
in at the present time. The financial
capitals of Europe are flooded with
Russian Treasury bills. The principle
on which the Russian Government pays
for everything is by issuing a six months
bill. When the six months bill falls
due it is renewed, and then it is renewed
again. Things have reached such a
stage now that the owners of the Treasury
bills cannot turn them into cash. About
six months ago a businessman told me
he had got too many of these Russian
Treasury bills and wanted to try to get
relief, and told another business man that
a bank could give him some millions of
these Treasury bills at 80 per cent., or
20 per cent, discount. The reply of the
other business man was, "My dear fellow,
that is nothing. I could buy these bills
in Paris at 40 per cent. discount." It
has got to the stage that Russia is simply
paying for everything in these trade bills
which are by degrees becoming worthless.
If you want to buy anything from Russia
you have to pay 50 per cent. or 60 per
cent. cash on the spot three months before you get delivery, and you have to
pay the balance on the date of delivery.
I would like to congratulate the Government on that point, and I am glad
of this opportunity of showing the credit
of the Russian Government at the present
time.
