to be brought here to reply to me.
did tell the Minister to-day that I would
be compelled to make some criticism of
the administration of the Fund, and that
that criticism would be criticism of the

of two decisions of the umpire. By the

of the Ministry of Home Affairs (Mr.

The first case is the case of Mrs.
Martha Weir, of 65 Paris Street. She
is a married woman. She had nine
years' work practically without a break.
We were told yesterday, and properly
told, by the learned Attorney-General
(Mr. Babington) that he gives decisions
on evidence, and on evidence only. That
is a very proper attitude on the part of
the Attorney-General or any other legal
gentleman called upon to elucidate the
law. But from this document that I
hold in my hand I find that the umpire,
who gets £1,800 a year, makes his decision without taking evidence, and relies
on his own knowledge, although that
knowledge may possibly be at fault, as it
is in the present case. The decision says:
"On the evidence before me my
decision is that the claim for benefit
should be disallowed. The claimant is
a married woman, 28 years of age, who
is registered as a tobacco stripper, and
had a splendid record of employment
until she lost it on 8th May, 1932,
owing to approaching confinement.
Her employment was with a tobacco
firm in town, which, it is well known,
does not as a rule employ women who
get married and have a family. She
stated to the Court of Referees that
she was awaiting work, but my experience has been that this firm is most
unlikely to take the applicant on again,
and I think she was well aware of that
fact when she got married. She has
not had work since her child was born,
and she cannot be regarded as available for work at present."
In the latter part of that judgment the
Umpire relies on his experience, and says
it is most unlikely that the firm will
take this woman on again. But there
is not one word to show that he has any
evidence whatever, good, bad, or indifferent, of the statements that he puts
forward in support of his decision against
that claim.
Furthermore, I am informed by people.
who know just as well as the Umpire-if
these cases are to be decided on the
opinion or local knowledge of legal people
that his opinion in this respect is not
quite right, and I submit this is no way
whatever to treat a married woman with
the splendid record of this lady. I may
say, first and foremost, that her claim
was referred to the Court of Referees;
the Court of Referees granted her claim;
then the insurance officer referred it to
the Umpire, and the Umpire gave that decision, which is practically entirely based,
according to himself, on what purports
to be his own knowledge of conditions
in Gallaher's tobacco factory. No judge,
no person exercising jurisdiction with any
training in the law would rely on anything except evidence produced before
him, and I am surprised that a man
of the experience and high standing of
the Umpire should even commence to base
his decision on any such thing as that
on which he has based his decision. Of
course it might have been the Deputy
Umpire. I do not know which of them
it was, because there is no name to this.
The second case is the case of Catherine
Adair, and the Umpire says:
"On the facts before me my decision
is that the claim for benefit should be
disallowed. Claimant is aged 23, and
had a fair record of employment prior
to her marriage, which took place on
1st February, 1930. She was also
employed from November, 1931, to
April, 1932, when she had to give up
her employment owing to approaching
confinement, and she has not had any
work since then. The child was born
on 5th July, 1932. Having regard to
her record I see no reason why the
claimant should not have been employed except for her marriage and the
arrival of the child, and I do not think
she can be regarded as available for
employment until she obtains a substantial spell of employment.”"

In the latter part of that judgment there

Umpire says he cannot regard the claimant
as available for employment until she has

position now. Until she gets work and is

Another very remarkable case, though
somewhat different-the Minister has had
this case before him; it did not go to the
Umpire is the case of Margaret Lowry,

they allowed her claim. A couple of days

events, the strike was on-to go to Dunmurry for work. She did not go to Dunmurry. She could not go to Dunmurry,
and I say it was an audacious thing to
ask her to go to Dunmurry with the railway strike in progress. And, remember,
it was in the early stages of the railway
strike when the buses were overcrowded,
and when practically no one could get on
a bus in that direction unless he were a
subscriber. Most of the people up there
are subscribers, and a lot that were not
subscribers became subscribers when the
railway strike took effect. That was on
the 1st February, and she is ordered to
go to Dunmurry for work. It would not
be so bad if they had allowed the decision
of the Court of Referees to stand for any
considerable length of time. But they did
not do that. They struck by saying, "You
have won before the Court of Referees,
but we will trap you; we will fix you.
Go out now to Dunmurry and work."
That was two days after the Court of
Referees had admitted her claim, and because she could not do the impossible her
claim is disallowed.
Now this House has recently endorsed
the methods of the Minister in giving out
relief work. The Minister knows that I
referred to him a gentleman who was
making statements with which I did not
agree. I did not think his statements

would not get work because he was not an

but no matter what they did or how long

an excuse and there was no work for them
at the Labour Exchange.
These men are not all from my constituency. They are not all from the same
part of the City of Belfast. The first is
James McCartney, of 160 Canmore Street,
who has been unemployed for two years
and five months. The next is Robert
Sales, 61 Grosvenor Road, who has had

I know, and I have often reiterated it in

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to have
a fuller knowledge of the reasons why the
Minister of Home Affairs refuses to
sanction the resolution passed by the Coleraine Rural District Council to reduce the
rents of labourers' cottages. When I
asked the right hon. Gentleman to give
his reasons at question time his answer
was very brief. When the Coleraine
Rural District Council held two special
meetings in regard to the reduction of
rents of labourers' cottages, I think they
knew what they were doing, and as they
are the representatives of the ratepayers
of the district, I think the Ministry should
have taken notice of their resolution and
given immediate effect to it. Instead of
doing so the Ministry absolutely refuse.
to carry out the wishes of the ratepayers
of that area.
Coleraine Labourers' Cottages 826
Adjournment-
9 MARCH 1933
Sir DAWSON BATES: That statement is entirely incorrect.
Mr. BEATTIE: Then I should like to
know your reasons for not giving effect
to it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Council
passed a certain resolution which is now
the subject of an inquiry as to whether
or not their request should be acceded to.
The Ministry has not yet come to a
decision in the matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: I appreciate the
position the Minister is in. I do not say
you are not sympathetic to a reduction
of rents, but in this case you know you
are imposing a burden on a class of
labourer who is not able to fulfil his
obligations to pay the rent demanded.
I want to know why an inquiry was
necessary when a resolution had been
passed by two special meetings of the
representatives of the ratepayers who
seem to have agreed that the resolution
should be put into effect immediately.
They now state that owing to the Ministry's refusal to sanction the reduction the
whole thing is being held up, and the
people concerned are being very badly hit.
I ask the right hon. Gentleman to tell
the House when this local inquiry will
take place, and the earliest date when
those concerned will know the result of the
inquiry. I should also like to know what
the terms of reference will be, because,
in my opinion, the only terms of reference
that would be applicable would be the
economic position of the tenants of these
houses.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member has asked me why I delayed to
give my decision, and the reason is that
not alone have I a duty to the tenants
but I have also a duty to the ratepayers.
It occurs to me that it is a peculiar thing
that this rural district council in other
times never thought of passing a resolution of this character, which, if adopted,
would impose an additional burden of
9d. in the £. They would not have
passed that resolution prior to derating.
Many members of the rural district
council do not pay a shilling in rates. It
is immaterial to them what the rates go
up to, but it is a very material thing to
those who have to pay rates in the town.
If this were adopted it would mean an
addition of no less than 9d in the £ at
the present time. I suggest to my hon.
Friend that this is not a fair suggestion
from any point of view. It is not fair
to the ratepayers and it is not fair to
the tenants. The resolution asks that
the rents of labourers' cottages should be
reduced to a flat rate of 2s a week. May
I remind my hon. Friend that the whole
policy of the urban council, as certainly
it is mine, is to try to ease the burden
on the real poor? The hon. Member by
his proposals wishes to have a flat rate,
so that those who least can pay will have
to pay more, and those who can pay will
have to pay less. May I just quote a few
cases of these so-called down-trodden
tenants which the hon. Member-
Mr. BEATTIE: It is Coleraine Urban
Council you are speaking of.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I take
one case? One man pays 2s 6d, and the
hon. Member wishes to reduce his rent
to 2s. What is the income going into
that house? There is £2 5s from the
occupier of the house, who is a hearse
driver. In addition his son gets 8s,
another son gets 10s, and a daughter,
who is a maid, gets 2s a month. Another
case. I am taking these at random.
This is the case of a farm labourer
receiving 21s a week-one son gets 148
a week, and two sons get 10s a week.
My hon. Friend wishes the rent of that
house also to be reduced to 2s a week-

1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the names
of the stockbrokers who transact Government business in Northern Ireland; and
whether such business should not be
divided equally between all the members
of the Stock Exchange in Northern
Ireland.
The MININSTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Pollock): The following is the panel.
of stockbrokers who transact business for
Government Departments in Northern
Ireland:
Messrs. W. F. Coates & Company,
Messrs. Josias Cunningham & Company,
Messrs. Adam Duffin & Company,
Messrs. A. D. M'Ilwaine & Company,
and
Messrs. W. J. Richardson & Company.
The Ministry originally selected these
brokers because they were the panel
already employed by the Supreme High
Court in Northern Ireland for the investment of court funds.
In view of the small amount of Government business involved, I see no reason
for increasing the numbers on the panel.

DUNDONALD SEWERAGE SCHEME.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state on
what date work will be commenced upon
the Dundonald sewerage scheme.
Mr. HANNA: I am informed that the
negotiations between the Belfast Corporation and the Castlereagh Rural District
Council as to the terms on which the
sewers belonging to the Corporation may
be used by the District Council are nearing completion, and it is hoped that work
will be started at an early date.
TUBERCULOSIS IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of persons in Northern
Ireland diagnosed as suffering from
tuberculosis.
Mr. HANNA: It is not possible to
state the number of cases in which tuberculosis was diagnosed, because notification
is only required where the medical man
in charge is of opinion that the circumstances of the case are such that there is
danger that the disease may be communicated to others, and further notification
is not compulsory in all districts.
Perhaps, however, the hon. Member's
purpose will be served if I state that the
number undergoing treatment in the year
1931 was 10,890. This is the latest year
for which figures are yet available.
FATAL MOTOR ACCIDENTS.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
the number of deaths through motor
accidents in Northern Ireland since
January, 1932.
Mr. HANNA: As the answer is somewhat lengthy, involving a number of
figures, I shall, with the hon. Member's
permission, circulate it with the Official
Report.
The answer is as follows:
Deaths through motor accidents since
January, 1932.
During the year ended 31st December,
1932:-
(a) 47 deaths were caused by motor
vehicles.
(b) 8 deaths occurred as the result
of accidents in which motor vehicles
were involved, but in which the accidents could not be attributed entirely
to the motorists.
(c) 11 persons were killed as the
result of accidents in which motor
vehicles were involved, but where the
accidents were caused by pedal cyclists.
(d) 53 pedestrians were killed in
accidents in which motor cars were involved, but in each case the pedestrian
was solely responsible for the accident.
Total deaths, 119.
During January, 1933, there were 7
deaths, one of which comes under
category (a) above; one under category
(c), and 5 under category (d).
The totals for the 13 months ended
January, 1933, would, therefore, be:-

6. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in view
of the disaster that has taken place in
England owing to a landslide, he is prepared to recommend the Antrim County
Council to widen the Coast Road to eighty
or ninety feet, and thus make it safe for

Mr. HANNA: No representations
have been presented by the Antrim
County Council on the lines indicated in
the hon. Member's question, and it is not
likely that such representations will be

the proposition outside the region of
practical politics.

INDUSTRY
UNEMPLOYMENT
INSURANCE SCHEME.
8. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state what
rights applicants for benefit have under
the Industry Unemployment Insurance
Scheme (Northern Ireland),
1931;
whether they are entitled to appear
before a Court of Referees under the
scheme, and what right of appeal they
have to a higher tribunal.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Insurance Industry
Unemployment Insurance Scheme provides for the determination of unemployment benefit claims by a claims officer
appointed by the Insurance Unemployment Board. The applicant has a right
of appeal from the claims officer's
decision to an Appeals Committee
appointed by the Board, and with the
leave of the committee may appeal from
its decision to the umpire.

assure the hon. and gallant Member that

HOUSING AND SLUM CLEARANCE
BILL.
the
11. Mr. HENDERSON asked
Prime Minister if he can state whether
the Government of Northern Ireland propose to introduce legislation on parallel
lines with the Housing and Slum Clearance Bill of the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. HANNA: I have been asked to
reply.
The Minister of Home Affairs has been
following with interest the provisions of
the Housing (Financial Provisions) Bill
which is, at present, before the Imperial
Parliament, and I may add, that an
informal conference has already taken
place between representatives of my
Ministry and of the Belfast Corporation
on the subject of the introduction of
similar proposals into this Parliament.
As the hon. Member is no doubt aware,
the Bill in question involves—
(a) The abolition of the existing
subsidy arrangements in Great Britain;
and
(b) The substitution of the principle
under which the Government and local
authorities, conjointly, will guarantee
a percentage of advances made by
building societies to their members for
the purpose of building houses.
The representatives of the Corporation
who attended the recent conference at
the Ministry of Home Affairs, while
anxious that the principle of guarantee
should be introduced into Northern
Ireland, desired, at the same time, that
the principle of housing subsidy, provided
for under the Northern Ireland Subsidy
Acts, should be continued.
The whole matter is still under consideration, but the hon. Member will
appreciate that in the present financial
position it will be impossible for the
Government of Northern Ireland to go
further than the British Government and
introduce the new principle of guarantee
side by side with the principle of subsidy.

14. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether in view
of the distress which exists in the linen
industries of Northern Ireland, he will
make representation to the Imperial
Government to take steps to stop the
importation of foreign linen, flax, and
yarns into Northern Ireland.
Mr. BARBOUR: In reply to the hon.
Member's question I would remind him
that under the Import Duties Act, 1932,
a new tribunal, the Import Duties'
Advisory Committee, was established for
the purpose of examining tariff representations on the lines he presumably has
in mind, and further that the linen
industry has set up a Joint Tariff Committee to deal with questions relating to
tariffs. Any representations in regard
to tariffs should, therefore, emanate not
from the Government but from the
industry itself through this committee,
with whose deliberations my Ministry is
kept in close touch.
The existing rates of duty on imports
of manufactured linens and linen yarns
are those fixed by the Imperial Government after inquiry by the Import Duties'
Advisory Committee. Flax, I would
remind the hon. Member, was placed on
the Customs Free List in
to

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Ardglass Dock and Harbour Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Mr. BARBOUR: The Measure to
which I have to direct the attention of
the House this afternoon provides for the
merging of the dock at Ardglass with the
harbour at Ardglass for legal and
administrative purposes.
The harbour at Ardglass is, as the
House will be aware, a Royal Harbour,
that is to say, it is a harbour owned by
and administered by the Crown. Its
area is about 60 acres at high water, but
its value lies in the fact that it is adjacent
to the herring grounds, and during the
last ten years considerable attention has
been given by my Department towards
making it a more suitable port of call
for drifters and for the landing, pickling
and export of herring.
Whilst, apart
from the drifters, the harbour is mainly
used by coasting vessels up to 150 tons,
carrying coal and agricultural produce,
berthing accommodation is available for
vessels up to 500 tons, and as many as
90 drifters have been berthed in the harbour in a single day.
County Courts (Money) 838
Ardglass Harbour Bill
14 MARCH 1933
When the harbour at Ardglass was
taken over by the Commissioners of Public
Works under the provisions of the Ardglass Harbour Act, 1876, the dock at the
north end of the harbour remained in
private ownership. Following the bankruptcy of the owner, it fell into a bad
state of repair, became choked with silt
and obstructed by decaying and derelict
vessels. This state of affairs continued
for many years, until in the year 1925
the Ministry of Commerce acquired the
bed of the dock from the Official Receiver in Bankruptcy. The dock was then
dredged and made available for fishing
and small trading vessels. At a later
date, in 1927, certain lands around the
dock were purchased by the Ministry from
a private owner who had acquired them.
on the sale of the Beauclerk Estate at
Ardglass.
The dock is not a large one; in fact the
whole area acquired, including that of the
lands adjoining, does not far exceed 1
acres. It has proved a useful adjunct to
the harbour, its principal merit lying in
the fact that it provides a place of refuge
for fishing and other small vessels.
Twenty-nine such vessels made use of the
dock last year, while four cargoes of coal
were also landed from the dock. At the
present time, however, and this is the
anomaly which the Bill before you seeks
to remedy, whilst the Ministry of Commerce administers both the harbour and
the dock, the statutory powers exercised
in respect of them are different, for whilst
the Ardglass Harbour Act, and the bylaws and dues made and charged thereunder, apply to the harbour they do not
apply to the dock, which is regulated
by the Ardglass Dock Order, 1878.
There is no sound reason why this dual
code should continue to apply at Ardglass,
and in this Bill we make provision for
repealing the Ardglass Dock Order, 1878,
and for applying to the dock the provisions of the Ardglass Harbour Act,
1876, and of the by-laws and scale of
charges made thereunder, reserving
liberty, however, to frame special by-laws
and regulations hereafter as may be found
necessary. In Clause 3 of the Bill we are
seeking power for the Harbour Master
to regulate the laying up of vessels in the
dock. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Clause 10 of the Bill proposes that

balances as the judge directs shall be paid

that the claimant is entitled to the sum,
the necessary issue will be made from the
Consolidated Fund. The object of the
second part of the Resolution is to impose
this contingent charge upon the Consolidated Fund. I beg to move.

the Parliamentary Secretary, the

So far as an officer

determines.

Shipbuilding.
Mr. NIXON: I beg to move the following Motion standing in my name:
"That in the opinion of this House
owing to the failure of the Prime Minister
to redeem his various promises to relieve
unemployment, and to the fact that there
are now close on 40,000 men totally unemployed in Belfast, the Government
should encourage shipbuilding by offering
to shipping companies 45 per cent. of any
wages actually paid to men working on
any new ships which may be laid down
and constructed in Belfast for two years
as from the 1st April, 1933, and that a
relative portion of the money now paid as
unemployment benefit, distress relief,
etc., be set apart and used for this purpose."
I cannot conceive any Member of the
House or anyone outside saying to me,
"What do you know about shipbuilding,"
To any question of that sort there is
obviously only one answer. In fact, to
ask that question is to answer it. A
few years ago I would not have ventured
to express an opinion on any financial or
economic question. At that time I
thought that when any person with a
reputation for finances or economics made
a statement it was the last word, but,
without being construed as applying my

of the whole tonnage of the world. Today the picture is a very different one.
German, Italian, and French shipbuilders
are building ships of the very finest type
with tremendous speed, a speed that will
outpace any ships we have on the ocean,
and they are doing it for the purpose I
have stated.
Therefore, I think myself that the
British have been too complacent, but
how are they to combat that? Is it going
to be a race between Governments as to
which would offer the biggest subsidy?
What picture can you draw of the conditions of things that would arise under
those circumstances. The British Government have opposed it on the ground that
such competition would be disastrous
internationally, and they base their
policy on the inducements which they
think they can offer foreign Governments
to discontinue the principle of providing
subsidies and resort to equal competition.
Whether they will succeed in that or not
I do not know. The United States
Government particularly provides a subsidy of an extraordinarily large amount,
so much as £10,000 on a voyage of six
weeks duration. I repeat that if that is
to go on one does not know where it will
stop.
To crystallise the argument, it would be
impossible for us here in this little limited
area to start a competition which would
only have disastrous results to ourselves,
and in the end perhaps even increase the
unemployment already in existence. That
is the position our Government takes up,
and I think that is the only position it
would be possible for us to adopt. It is
a very great problem. It seems a very
attractive thing, when you have technical
young men unemployed, if you could
transfer them to work and pay for a proportion of that work in order to force the
provision of work, because it will force it.
Our Loans Guarantee Acts are intended
to force work, and these Acts have in
the past forced work, and the prospects
ahead of us go to indicate that they will
be similarly effective in the future,
perhaps in the near future.
The Prime Minister mentioned that
my presence in London happened to
synchronise with his own, and the object
of my visit was to endeavour to expedite
orders which we know are looming ahead,
and which we had hoped would have been
started before to-day. Therefore our
Loans Guarantee Act is operating, and it
is the only thing we can do with any

(Mr. Barbour): If hon. Members will look
at the Vote on Account Paper which was
circulated last week, they will see in
column 2 the total figure for Estimates
for the coming financial year, namely,
£8,820,595. The total figure for the
financial year now closing, including
Supplementary Estimates, is given in
column 3, and the difference between
these two columns is about £159,000,
which is the net decrease for the coming
year. Of this £159,000, however, a sum
of about £109,000 represents the saving
owing to the completion of the building
of Stormont and the approaching completion of the new Law Courts an expenditure which, as hon. Members are
aware, is offset by a direct payment from
the British Exchequer to the Northern
Irish Exchequer, which is not reflected
in the Votes. The net decrease, therefore, including the figure of £109,000 is
approximately £50,000. On a Vote on
Account, as hon. Members are aware, it
is not customary to enter into any detailed explanation, as such a discussion
is appropriate to the Estimates themselves, which will be published shortly.

Question proposed: "That the Clause

Mr. BLACK: There is, I think, a
slight difficulty arising in regard to this
Clause. The Clause, roughly, provides
that every process issuing out of the court
shall be sealed with the seal of the court.
Now, in the county court, proceedings
are ordinarily instituted by a civil bill,
which is popularly termed a process, and
it might be considered that this Clause,
as at present drawn, would apply to civil
bills and would require civil bills to be
issued under the seal of the court. As
a matter of fact, civil bills in one sense
are not issued from the court; they are
drawn up in a solicitor's office and sent
out to process servers for service after
they have been stamped.
There is a real doubt arising as the
Clause is at present drawn, and I think
some words ought to be inserted in it to
show that civil bills are not required to
be sealed with the seal of the county
court, and that it is sufficient that they
should be issued, as at present, over the
signature of the solicitor who issues
them. The object of this could be
carried out easily by inserting after the
word process, " in line 13, the words,
"other than civil bill." I suggest to
the Ministers in charge of the Bill that
some such words should be inserted in
the Clause, to make clear a matter which,
at anyrate, may give rise to serious
doubt. One does not wish to have any
doubt arising on the operation of this
Measure.

Mr. BLACK: The reason for making
out this list is not for the purpose of
informing the public at large what
moneys are lying dormant or unclaimed
in the county courts, but to ascertain
the sums which might reasonably be
transferred to the Exchequer under the

the Clause, as I understand it, is this:
These sums which are lying in the county
courts are mostly moneys which have
been lodged in court during something of
the nature of administration proceedings,
say.
During those administration proceedings you may find that some particular individual-perhaps one of the
next-of-kin of a person who has died intestate is entitled to a share of £30 or
£40, and that person cannot be traced.
It may be that he has gone to America
many years before, or that his parents
went to America and all that is known
is that he was born in America, and the
ordinary advertisements have not enabled you to get in touch with him.
That man may come in after many years
and find that he is entitled to that
amount, and may want to claim it. The
provision in this Clause is that if a man
does not claim the money after the substantial time provided here, I think it
is fifteen years, it shall be transferred
to the Exchequer. But even if it is
transferred and he comes in after that
period there is a provision made for the
retransfer, so that the man may get his
money.
The reason why this list is to be made
out in consultation with the County
Court Judge is that the County Court
Judge is the person who has charge of
those administration proceedings. Take
the case of any sum lodged to the credit
of any particular
particular individual. The
County Court Judge will know something of the proceedings that have taken
place, at what stage those proceedings
stand at the moment, what evidence has
been before him, what inquiries it is
necessary to make, and will be able to
form some idea of whether it is worth
while allowing that sum to be transferred to the Exchequer, or whether it
is probable that some claimant might
turn up in the near future. There is no
use in transferring the money if the
chances are that some person who is entitled to a share may come of age shortly,
or that some other claimant may come
in and prove his title to it. That is the
whole reason for the provision as set out
in the Clause.

Mr. POLLOCK: As the Committee

The old method was adopted because,

THE IRISH LANGUAGE.
1. Mr. GRANT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he can state the amount in
special fees for the teaching of Irish which
has been paid each year to elementary
schools by the Ministry of Education; the
names of the schools that have claimed
such fees and the amounts paid to each
of them during the period mentioned; why
there is a distinction drawn in favour of
Irish as against French, German and other
useful languages; and whether, in view
of the fact that the Irish language is of no
commercial or business value in any part
of the world, he will consider the advisability of discontinuing payment of such
fees.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The information asked for in the first part of the
question is given in the Annual Reports
of the Ministry; for the hon. Member's
convenience I am, however, circulating a
statement of the figures with my reply.
To give the details asked for in the
second part of the question which would
include the names of each school in which
Irish has been taught during the last 10
years with a statement of the amounts of
fees paid to each, would necessitate a prolonged investigation of the Ministry's
records and would involve a considerable
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
amount of clerical work, and the statement which I am circulating and which
shows the number of schools earning fees
in each year may, perhaps, be sufficient.
It would be difficult within the limits of
a reply to a Parliamentary question to
explain fully the considerations which influence the Ministry in drawing a distinction between Irish and useful modern
languages such as French and German, in
regard to the payment of fees for extra
instruction. Irish occupied a peculiar
and special position in the schools prior to
the establishment of the Ministry, and the
Ministry decided, after very careful consideration, that it was on the whole desirable to continue the system of making
grants for instruction in Irish as an extra
subject, though for a much more limited
number of pupils than was formerly the
case under the Commissioners of National
Education.
In reply to the last part of the question,
I would remind the hon. Member that the
commercial value of a subject is not the
only consideration in drawing up the most
appropriate syllabus for a public elementary school, and it seems proper and desirable, having regard to the general educational and cultural interests involved, that
considerations other than those of business
utility should be allowed due weight.

The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the

Oral Answers to Questions.
HIGH POWER BROADCASTING
STATION.
the
1. Major McCORMICK asked
Prime Minister whether he will make
representations to the British Broadcasting Corporation with a view to having
the proposed new high power broadcasting station for Northern Ireland placed
in a central position in the Province in
order that it may give equal service to
all.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
Tests are being made at the present
time with a view to finding the most
suitable site for a new high power transmitting station in Northern Ireland The
object of the British Broadcasting Corporation must be to secure the best service for the greatest possible number of
listeners throughout the Province, and
this consideration will guide them in
their ultimate choice of a site. The
hon. and gallant Member will readily
appreciate, however, that such a site may
not necessarily be situated in the
geographical centre of the Province.

was instituted against a railway company
during the period mentioned by the hon.
Member in which a conviction
obtained.

Mr. HENDERSON: I rise to offer
some criticism of this Measure. In doing
so it will be necessary for me to go into
many small matters, but it is not my
intention to speak at any great length
on this Bill to-day. It was my intention
a short time ago to speak at some length,
but I will not now take up so much of
the time of the House. I think this is
an opportune time to draw the attention
of the taxpayers of Northern Ireland to
the very costly form of Government there
is here. The Prime Minister and the
other Cabinet Ministers will not take any
exception to what I am going to say, and
I hope they will not regard it as in any
way personal. I wish, merely, to show
how costly the administration of the Six
Counties is in comparison with that of
other countries.
It has been admitted that this is the
most costly Government of its size in
the world to-day-(Hon. Members: No,
no) and I would like to draw attention
to one very important matter. As I
said before, there is nothing personal in
this. Take our Prime Minister. We
have got to realise that this Parliament
sits only six or seven weeks in the year,
a very short period for a Parliament to
sit in view of the fact that unemployment is more rife in Northern Ireland
than in any other part of the British
Empire. (Hon. Members: No, no.)

There is no denying the fact that in
Northern Ireland the unemployment
situation is more critical than in any
other part of the Empire.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

Mr. HENDERSON: There is no doubt

The PRIME MINISTER: I think it

Mr. HENDERSON: I withdraw that

I am not criticising him personally; I
am criticising the office. Even if the
office was held by one of my greatest
friends I would criticise it in the same
way. I hope, therefore, that anything
I say will not be looked upon as offensive.
This is a very costly office. The Prime
Minister has a permanent secretary, who
is allowed £1,725 a year. What are the
duties of this gentleman? I never saw
him doing anything useful for Ulster. I
am going to point out that other Prime
Ministers are not so well paid as our
Premier. There is no necessity for a
permanent secretary at all, because there
is no work for him to do. This Parliament, as I said, only sits about six or
seven or eight weeks in the year, and the
business done by the Government, so far
as anything useful is concerned, is
practically nil. This has been proved
during the last two or three weeks that
the House has been sitting.
The Prime Minister's residence is
situate in an estate of 250 acres.
A very
large section of the ground surrounding
that residence is cut off from the general
public. This ground, which is the most
beautiful part of the estate, should be
free to the people of Northern Ireland,
who own it. I contend that the Cabinet
itself should deal with this matter and

is no use in their talking about patriotism

are not prepared to make some slight

proportion of the people are in poor
circumstances through unemployment.
Up to the present time no action has

to a reduction in their salaries.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 22nd March, 1933.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.
THE RAILWAY DISPUTE.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Labour whether he
can state if there is any new development in the railway dispute with a view
to a settlement.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The reason that I asked the
hon. Member for Pottinger yesterday to
postpone his question to me until to-day
was to give me an opportunity of obtaining, in the meantime, an authoritative
statement from each of the parties as to
their respective positions.
The companies have furnished me with
a statement as follows:
"The financial position of the railway companies, with their expenditure
actually exceeding their receipts, is
such that it is imperative that at the
least they should receive the full benefits of the Irish Railways Wages Board
finding of 10 per cent., or its equivalent, which includes the previous cut
of 43 per cent. awarded in 1931. Their
original demand was for a cut of 15
per cent., which they consider they are
fully entitled to get on the merits of
the case, and even more SO now on
account of the strike with its resultant
loss in traffic.
"The companies' representatives are
also still willing-they have already
offered to consider making concessions
to the lower paid men, such as minima
and making these reductions to those
men in two cuts.
"The companies' representatives have
made their position abundantly clear
and are quite willing at any time to
meet the trade union representatives
and enter into negotiations with
them."
This is the companies' statement of
their position.
The trade unions on their part have
informed me that, as stated by Mr.
Cramp and Mr. Squance:
--
"They do not want any more abortive conferences, but if there are any
indications that the companies are
willing to approach the issue in
a new spirit and are earnestly
anxious for a settlement the unions will
be willing to meet the companies again
in conference."
Mr. BEATTIE: Supplementary to
that reply I would like to ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether he is prepared
to call a further conference of the parties
concerned at a very early date.
a
Mr. ANDREWS: I am glad that both
parties express in their statements
willingness to enter into further
negotiations and, if they will give some

prospect of a useful purpose being served
by a conference, I will be glad to facilitate bringing them together. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Moneylenders Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Bill which I have
Moneylenders Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
comthe privilege of submitting to the House
to-day is, I believe, one the principles
of which will receive general approval.
I do not propose, therefore, in
mending it to you to paint any lurid.
pictures of the miseries of those who have
fallen into the clutches of the less reputable moneylenders, but rather to
address myself to the task of explaining
as clearly and as temperately as I can the
main provisions of the Bill, and the
various evils which they are respectively
designed to remedy.
In passing, may I remind hon. Members that the British Act upon which
this Bill is to some extent based, was the
result of one of a series of Bills the
first of which was introduced into Parliament by Lord Carson of Duncairn. It
was largely due to his eloquence and
persistence that the English Bill ever
reached the Statute Book, and that
admirable contribution to modern social
legislation will ever be honourably
associated with his name. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Before, however, I proceed to the explanation of the individual Clauses of the
Bill, I think it well, by the way of
preface, to make a few preliminary
observations, first in regard to the
general principle of the governmental
control of moneylenders; and, secondly,
and very shortly, in regard to the degree
of control exercised under the law as it
is in operation in Northern Ireland at
this moment.
Historically, the business of moneylending is of great antiquity, and from
the very earliest days the evils likely to
arise in connection with it were clearly
recognised. In ancient times the taking
of interest was regarded as unnatural,
since it was considered wrong for money
to breed money; while right through the
Middle Ages usury-which in those days
meant any bargain in which one party
had an unfair advantage-was regarded
as an ecclesiastical crime. For this
reason few Christians engaged in it, and
it was not until the fifteenth century, and
the expansion of trade and commerce
which then took place, that native
Englishmen began to take part in those
financial operations which have their
counterpart to-day in the activities of the
banking companies and the great financial
houses, pawnbrokers, and the class of
persons with which this Bill deals, namely,
moneylenders.
Gradually contemporary thought swung
round to the view that economic
questions, such as the propriety, or otherwise, of lending at interest were secular
matters, which should be under the control of the State rather than of the
Church and, at the same time, had come
to realise that those who lend money play
a useful and legitimate part in the growth
of commercial enterprise. Accordingly,
during the latter half of the sixteenth
century, the first usury laws were passed
by Parliament, permitting the charging
of interest, provided that the rate was not
excessive.
It will be seen then that the principle
of the imposition of legal restriction upon
the profession of moneylenders, as distinct
from its total abolition on the one hand,
or an entire absence of State control on
the other, has a considerable history
behind it, and all subsequent legislation,
including the important Acts now in
operation, namely, the Moneylenders
Act, 1900, and the Moneylenders Act,
1911, are based upon it.
Any attempt to prohibit moneylending
would be doomed to failure since the practice would merely be driven underground,
and abuses, so far from being eradicated,
would merely be less liable to detection.
The Bill, therefore, is drafted on the
assumption that moneylending is a legitimate business with which, if it is properly
carried on in accordance with the law,
the State can have no quarrel.
What is the position of moneylenders
in Northern Ireland under the law
to-day? The principal statutory enactments relating to moneylenders are contained in the Moneylenders Act, 1900, to
which I have already referred. They are:
A moneylender is required to register
himself once every three years, and must
pay a fee of £1 in respect of each registration. He can only trade under his
registered name and at his registered
address, but no moneylender can be
refused registration, that is to say, on the
ground that he is not a suitable person
to carry on the trade of moneylending, or
that he has been convicted of an offence
in connection with moneylending.
A court may reopen any moneylending
transaction brought before it either by the
lender or the borrower, which it finds to
be harsh and unconscionable. This is, in
fact, the most important enactment on
the subject of moneylending but, un-
Moneylenders Bill-
22 MARCH 1933
Second Reading
fortunately, as I shall point out later,
there are methods by which it can be
evaded, and one of the objects of this
Bill is to render those methods of evasion
ineffective. After this very brief
reference to the existing state of the law,
I shall now pass on directly to the provisions of the Bill.
In the first place, I shall refer to
Clauses 1 to 3, which relate to moneylenders' licences and certificates. After
the commencement of the Act a moneylender, who desires to carry on business in
particular premises, must apply to the
court of petty sessions of the district in
which those premises are situated for a
certificate authorising him to carry on
business there. The application will be
heard by a court consisting of one or more
Resident Magistrates sitting alone, and
they may refuse the application on
certain grounds set forth in Clause 2 (6),
namely, unsatisfactory character, and on
those grounds only. It is to be observed,
however, that even where the grounds
indicated are present, a court, if it is
satisfied that the applicant is otherwise
suitable, may grant him a certificate. An
applicant may appeal to the county court
from a refusal of the court of petty
sessions to grant a certificate.
If an applicant fails to obtain a certificate it would be illegal for him to carry
on business at the address proposed. If
he is successful in obtaining a certificate,
the certificate will, subject to his taking
out an excise licence, authorise him to
carry on business in the name mentioned
in the certificate, that is, his authorised
name, at the address referred to in it,
that is, the authorised address. A moneylender can be authorised to carry on
business only under his true name; the
name of a firm, where such name consists of the true names of the partners;
or the name of a firm not consisting of
the true names of the partners, where he
has been registered under that name for
three years, prior to the commencement
of the Act. This provision is designed to
prevent those almost protean changes of
name which make the identity of those
who shelter behind them so very elusive.
Having obtained a certificate the
moneylender must then proceed to take.
out an excise licence for which he will
be required to pay the sum of £15. The
Government believe that this charge is
not unreasonable, in view of the
remunerative nature of moneylending
and the extensive use which moneylenders make of the legal institutions of
the State in enforcing their contracts.
The procedure of obtaining a certificate.
and taking out an excise licence is, it
will be observed, closely analogous to the
procedure for taking out a licence by
that equally useful and sometimes much
maligned member of the community, the
publican. The procedure must be carried
out annually, and therefore the suitability of every moneylender to carry on
business must be reviewed by the court
each year. It is in this connection that
the provisions of Clause 3 are important.
This Clause provides that where a moneylender is convicted of certain offences in
connection with his business, namely,
charging an excessive rate of interest,
his certificate or certificates, and in the
case of a firm those of his partners, may
be suspended or forfeited, and must be
endorsed with particulars of the conviction and the court Order. Where a
certificate is endorsed, the fact of the
conviction of the holder will come to the
notice of the court when next he makes
application for a certificate, and the
court will therefore be able to take this
into account in coming to a decision as
to whether a fresh certificate should be
granted. If a certificate is forfeited or
suspended it becomes illegal for the
moneylender to carry on business, since
his excise licence is also automatically
suspended.
The provisions which I have described
will, it is hoped, prevent the carrying
on of the business of moneylenders except by reputable persons, and will deter
those who are authorised to carry it on
from committing any offences, conviction.
for which might entail their compulsory
retirement from business.
en-
The moneylender, having duly obtained.
his certificate and licence, is now
titled to carry on business. Here we
may notice certain provisions of the Bill
which govern the way in which he carries
on his business, quite apart from any
actual transactions into which he may
enter. Thus the provisions of the Companies Acts in regard to disclosing in
circulars, show cards, etc., the fact that
directors are not of British nationality,
are imported into this Bill. Such
documents and also newspaper and other
advertisements must show the authorised

name of the moneylender, and must contain the words "licensed moneylender."
Except in the case of newspaper advertisements, any name under which the
moneylender was registered in Northern
Ireland before the passing of the Act
must also be given. Moreover, a moneylender must not in any advertisement
make use of any expression which might
imply that he carried on a banking business. The object of this provision, as
hon. Members will appreciate, is
enable borrowers to know more precisely

render futile the use of those imposing

Loan Company, and so forth, with which

quite unwarranted feeling of security and
confidence to prospective clients.
a
I now pass to one of the most interesting and most important Clauses in the
Bill, namely, Clause 5, which deals with
the sending of circulars and the publication of advertisements by moneylenders. I may point out in passing that
the principle underlying it is already
embodied in the Betting and Loans
(Infants) Act, 1892, which forbids the
sending of circulars by moneylenders to
persons under 21. Clause 5 extends this
provision by making it an offence for a
moneylender to send a circular to any
person except at his written request.
This discrimination against moneylenders'
circulars, as distinct from those sent by
persons engaged in other trades, is not,
I think, difficult to justify. It is unfortunately notorious that many of these
circulars give a quite misleading account
of
into which
transaction
person addressed is invited to enter, and
rarely, if ever, do they show the rate
of interest which will be charged, or
whether it will be charged upon the sum
actually lent or on some other sum.
Moreover, these circulars constitute a
nuisance to many persons who would
never resort to moneylenders, and the
manner in which they flaunt temptation
before the eyes of many of our impecunious brethren is one which no one,
except possibly the moneylender, could
the
approve.
the
Sub-clause (2) of Clause 5 deals with
moneylenders' advertisements, and lays
down the only particulars which
such advertisements may contain. In
addition to the name which must be
included in order to comply with Clause
4, the advertisement may contain the
moneylender's address, his telephone
number, the highest and lowest sums
that he is prepared to lend, and whether
he lends with or without security.
any
This provision should have the effect
of preventing the issue of those alluring
and exaggerated advertisements with
which hon. Members are, I am sure,
familiar, even though, as I am equally
certain, their familiarity with moneylending does not extend further.
Sub-Clause (3) prohibits what is perhaps
an even greater and more insidious evil
than moneylenders' circulars and advertisements, namely, the moneylender's
tout. It is, I believe, a practice in many
parts of the country for these touts to
call at houses where there has recently
been a death and endeavour to persuade
the deceased's relatives to take a loan
in order to be able to give the deceased
a more expensive funeral than would
otherwise have been possible. This
practice, I believe, is not unknown in
the factories and mills of the City of
Belfast. The abolition of the moneylender's tout will, I believe, be entirely
an unmixed blessing. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The most important feature of Subclause (4) will be the effect which it will
have indirectly upon the rate of interest
charged by moneylenders. At present,
as
a rule, moneylenders scrupulously
avoid giving the rate of interest charged
by them as a rate per cent. per annum,
since to do so might bring home, much
too clearly to would-be borrowers, the
nature of the transaction into which they
are invited to enter. Under this Subclause moneylenders, if they refer to
interest chargeable upon a loan in any
document, must show it either as a rate
per cent. per annum or as a rate per cent.
as calculated in accordance
per annum
with the First Schedule.
I now pass on to those provisions of
the Bill which affect the actual transactions into which a moneylender may
enter. The first of these, Clause 6, provides that, in respect of every moneylending transaction, a memorandum must
be drawn up, showing the authorised
name of the moneylender, full particulars of the loan, including the rate of
interest charged as a rate per cent. per
annum, or as calculated in accordance
with the First Schedule. This memor-
Moneylenders Bill-
Second Reading
22 MARCH 1933
andum must be signed by the borrower,
and if the borrower is a married woman
totally dependent on her husband, by the
borrower's husband, and a copy of the
memorandum must be sent to the
borrower within seven days of the making
of the contract. For fairly obvious
reasons the lender will procure the
signature to the memorandum before he
hands over the loan, since, if he were to
wait until afterwards, the borrower might
refuse to sign, and the moneylender
would have no remedy. Thus it is
brought about that every borrower,
before raising a loan will have an opportunity of inspecting a document which
will give him clear information regarding
the transaction into which he is about to
enter. Further protection than this it
would hardly be possible for the legislature to afford in this particular respect.
It is also proposed; by means of this
Clause, to make an effort to prevent wives
from entering into moneylending transations without the knowledge of their
husbands. There is evidence that some of
the more unscrupulous moneylenders do
encourage wives to enter into transactions
of this kind, and are not unwilling to
take advantage of the wives' fear of
publicity by charging a high rate of
interest. If this provision becomes law
husbands, who have not signed for their
wives' loans, need have no fear of court
publicity; the moneylender will know
that to take the wife into court will be
objectless, as no recovery would be
possible. In effect, therefore, a moneylender will be incurring very considerable
risk in lending money to wives who may
be totally dependent upon their husbands,
unless he has obtained the husband's
signature to the memorandum.
Clause 7, besides prohibiting compound
interest, provides that where default is
made in repayment the rate of interest
may not be increased although, as is
quite reasonable, the moneylender may
charge interest at a rate not exceeding
the rate on the loan itself on the sum
due from the date of default until it is
paid. This Clause needs little explanation, and I shall, therefore, proceed at
once to the following Clause, namely,
Clause 8, which enables a borrower at any
time, on payment of one shilling, to get
full particulars of any loan into which he
may have entered, namely, how much of
the principal is still due, and how much
interest. At present. where a loan has
been complicated by default, the borrower
very often is quite ignorant of precisely
how much is due from him, and advantage is taken of this fact by some moneylenders. This Clause will put into the
hands of borrowers a remedy, of which,
I trust, they will take full advantage.
to
Clause 10 is probably one of the two
most important Clauses in the Bill. I
have already referred to Section 1 of the
Moneylenders Act, 1900, which enables a
court, in certain circumstances, to reopen
a moneylending transaction if the terms
seem to it to be harsh and unconscionable.
The object of Sub-clause (1) of this Clause
is to provide courts with some kind of a
standard which will assist them in deciding whether a particular transaction is
such that they would have
power
reopen it. Lord Darling, the eminent
English judge, expressed the opinion.
when the Moneylenders Act, 1927, was
before the Imperial Parliament, that the
then ineffectiveness of Section 1 of the
Moneylenders Act, 1900, was largely due
to the fact that courts had no standard to
guide them. The Select Committee
which considered the English Bill gave
considerable attention to this particular
matter, and after very careful consideration, fixed 48 per cent. as the standard.
I would impress upon hon. Members
that this provision does not prescribe a
legal maximum rate of interest to which
it might be expected that the general rate
for moneylending transactions might rise,
but merely fixes a standard, since it is
specifically provided that the court may
reopen a transaction even where the interest charged is less than 48 per cent. per
annum, if, in the circumstances, the rate
charged appears to be excessive. In considering the reasonableness of the standard regard must be had to the fact that
it will be applicable to all kinds of moneylending transactions, namely, where no
security is offered and the lender's risk is
very high indeed. I have no doubt that
the various provisions of the Bill, namely,
Clauses 6, 15, 19 and 20, will, in conjunction, have the effect of compelling
moneylenders to reduce, very substantially, the rate of interest charged in
moneylending transactions, and hon.
Members may rest assured that the standard which we are proposing to fix is not
unreasonably high when the object of the
Clause is properly understood and all the
relevant circumstances are taken into
account.

[Mr. Barbour]
Clause 11 is designed to empower a
court to reopen a moneylending transaction in circumstances to which it is
not certain whether under the existing
law Section 1 of the Moneylenders Act,
1900, applies.
Clause 12 prohibits the charging of
expenses for moneylenders' loans. It is
not unknown, I believe, for moneylenders to demand preliminary charges
from would-be borrowers, and then, when
the charges have been paid, for the moneylenders either to disappear or to raise
insuperable objections to the granting of
the loan. In neither case is the money
returned.
I would now draw the attention of the
House to the provisions of Clause 15,
which provides that where, as is usually
the case, the interest charged on a loan
is not expressed in terms of a rate, any
amount paid or payable should be appropriated between principal and interest
in the proportion that the principal bears

and the rate shall be calculated as shown
in the First Schedule. In connection
with this Clause, I would ask hon. Members to look at the definition of "principal" in Clause 20, which states that
"principal" means the amount of money
actually lent. At present it is not uncommon, where a person borrows, say,
£8, for him to be asked to give a note
of hand for £10; the £10 is then regarded as the principal and must be
repaid in full with interest, just as if
the sum handed over to the borrower had
been £10 and not £8. This provision
should be effective in removing abuses of
this kind.
I have now touched upon practically
all the Clauses which are suitable for
treatment in a Second Reading speech.
The remainder-with two exceptions, to
which I shall refer in a moment-relate
to special circumstances such as bankruptcies, assignments of moneylenders'
loans, etc., or to special classes of moneylenders such as pawnbrokers. If there
are any points in connection with these
Clauses upon
which information is desired, either I or my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) will endeavour to afford it
in replying to the debate.
The two Clauses on which I now wish
to say a word are Clauses 18 and 19.
These Clauses have no counterpart in the
British Act, and I may point out that
this is one of the cases where in adopting
British legislation we have not slavishly
imitated our model. They are Clauses
which are strongly supported by those
who know local conditions in our area.
The object of Clause 18 is to prevent
the employment by moneylenders of
special bailiffs. These bailiffs, whose
services can be obtained on applcation to the Sheriff, are employed very
largely by moneylenders, the reason
being that they are prepared to take
much greater risks of making wrong
seizures than ordinary bailiffs, who in
cases of doubt would make a return of
"No goods."
Clause 19 aims at excluding moneylenders from resort to a certain High
Court procedure in which they are enabled to enforce their contracts in the
office without coming into open court
and, therefore, without running the risk
of having their transactions reopened.
This is one of the means of evasion to
which I referred in the opening part of
my speech.
In conclusion, I may say that I am not
so optimistic as to believe that this Bill
will at one blow abolish all the abuses
which are to-day associated with moneylending. The difficulty, as hon. Members
will appreciate, in bringing the law to bear
upon moneylending transactions is that
the essence of such transactions is very often
secrecy, that is to say, the borrower
would rather pay anything than risk exposure either in a court or otherwise,
and this gives the moneylender. a very
strong hold over him. The Bill will, I
hope, go a very long way in solving this
particular difficulty. At present a
moneylender can say to a defaulting
clinet, "If you do not pay I will bring
you into court"; the client will now in
many cases be able to reply, "You cannot enforce this contract against me without going before a court, and the court
will probably regard it as harsh and
unconscionable. Not only, therefore,
will you not succeed in your suit, but
your certificate will probably be
suspended, and you may be obliged to
give up business." Thus will the client
be able to call the bluff of the moneylender who endeavours to take an unfair
advantage.
The Bill will not, however, give a dishonest borrower any unfair advantage
over the moneylender. The latter need
Moneylenders Bill-

have no anxiety by reason of the passing
of this Bill, provided that he conducts his
business in accordance with the law and
takes no unfair advantage of his clients.
I commend this Bill to the sympathetic
consideration of the House. I beg to
move.

the Minister has pointed out, that Act

This Bill goes still further, and it gives
the court a sort of measuring rod, because
it indicates that a loan involving more
than 48 per cent. as the rate of interest
will prima facie be regarded as harsh and
unconscionable. Of course it would be
very difficult to fix a definite rate of
interest beyond which the moneylender
could not go. In fact, I believe it would be
quite impossible, and it is still open to the
court to regard a rate of interest, say of
100 per cent., as not in particular
circumstances harsh and unconscionable.
There are many excellent provisions in
this Bill. With regard to the application
for a certificate to the magistrates this
does not include lay magistrates, but
resident magistrates-I think that is a
very sound principle. We are already
familiar with such applications in the case
of licensing applications in connection
with the spirit trade. The law has
always recognised that such applications
are matters which concern not the
applicant alone, but which concern the
general community at the same time, and
in the case of licensing applications they
have also insisted upon proof of character
and other proofs sufficient to enable the
licensing authority to grant the necessary
certificate.
There are, as I
say, many excellent
provisions in the Bill. I say that, in my

ations to send out circulars or to

The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.

doing. It prohibits moneylending except

are clearly set out in this Bill. Instead
of the old and common practice of charging
interest on the capital by payments weekly
or monthly, as the case may be, a practice

Under this Measure a moneylender

criminals and do not desire to break the

to purify the system of moneylending.

Mr. BARBOUR: The brief Measure
to which I invite the consideration of the
House this afternoon has been found
necessary to ensure the smooth administration of the Companies Act (Northern
Ireland), 1932.
The most important of the provisions
included in the Bill now in the hands of
hon. Members centres round the powers
conferred upon liquidators in voluntary
winding-up cases. At the moment the
powers of such liquidators are inadequate
to enable them to dispose of a company's
property. Moreover, representations have
been made to my Ministry not only that
such powers should be conferred upon
liquidators but also that those gentlemen
should be placed in the position of being
able to dispose of property in parcels
by means of fee farm grants or subgrants and leases or sub-leases. In
practice it has been found difficult to
secure an outright sale in certain cases,
though the disposal of the lands in parcels
by means of fee farm grants or leases
and the consequent sale of the rental would
be feasible. In Clause 3 we are proposing
to give liquidators the power to make
such fee farm grants and leases, while
Clause 5 confers powers of disposal upon
liquidators in voluntary winding-up cases.
The remaining provisions of the Bill
are of minor importance and arise out of
discussions which have taken place with
the Incorporated Law Society and other
interests to whom I would like to pay a
tribute for their ready co-operation in
placing at the disposal of my Ministry
their experience in the working of
company legislation. It has been pointed
out to my Ministry that the proviso in
Section 158 of the Act of 1932, which
enables the Local Bankruptcy Court to
have powers to wind up a company in
certain circumstances, is unnecessary and
should be repealed. Such a provision has
been in existence for many years, but I
am given to understand that it has never
been resorted to. Provision is accordingly made in Clause 2 for its repeal.
Again in Section 156, which deals with
the case of a bankrupt contributory, it
has been represented to me that it would
more accurately express the intention of
paragraph (1) to use the phrase "his
assignees or trustee in bankruptcy in
substitution for the phrase "his trustee
""
in bankruptcy "which now appears in
the section. The latter words were
brought forward from the Companies.
(Consolidation) Act, 1908, and have therefore applied in Northern Ireland for

Probates and Letters of Administration
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): I beg to move, "That the
Bill be now read a Second time." This
is a short Bill, and it is designed for the
purpose of making it possible for banks
to act as executors of deceased persons.
The House will see that according to the
first Clause of the Bill where a trust corporation is named in the will as executor
it shall be competent for a court to issue
a grant of administration. Up to the
present time that has not been possible,
and it was always found a very great
inconvenience.
There are a number of ancillary
matters dealt with in the first Clause, one
of them being that at the present time
there are a number of cases in which
persons are nominated on behalf of corporations to act as personal representatives, and though they act in their own.
capacity, in fact the work is done by the
bank. Hon. Members are probably
aware that in some cases bank managers
agree to act as executors. They act in
their ordinary capacity, but the work is
carried out through the bank. This will
be a great convenience, because there are
numbers of people who find it difficult to
get an executor, especially persons who
have been abroad.
They are not in touch with people at
home, and they are sometimes involved
in litigation and trouble owing possibly
to the fact that there is nobody to look
after the management of the estate upon
whom they can rely, and also to the fact
that the executor may die or in some
other way cease to act as their personal
representative. As a consequence a great
deal of trouble is involved, and this,
while not compulsory, will give a person
the option of choosing a bank as sole
executor or as one of two executors.
That is all carried out in the first Clause
of the Bill.
The second Clause is to fill a gap. It
is to give the high court jurisdiction to
appoint a personal representative although
there are no assets. The foundation of
high court jurisdiction in probate depends
entirely upon assets, and there are cases
from time to time in which it is necessary
to have a personal representative where
there are no assets. To give one example.
The executor or personal representative of
a deceased person may have a claim upon
some other estate, and if there are no
assets it is impossible to make a grant to
a person to prosecute the suit. There are
also cases where for other purposes it is
necessary to have a grant of administration although there are no assets.
Clause 3 provides for the making of
rules of court to carry out the provisions
of these two Clauses, and Clause 4 is the
interpretation Clause. There is nothing
else in this Bill. It is a small matter,
but it is a very necessary amendment of
our law. I beg to move.

understand it has been the practice in law

That in itself would warrant me in feeling that the Bill is not just everything
that the Attorney-General has set forth,
as I would have many friends in this
House who would agree with me that the
banks have done nothing in their experience free of charge. I am certain that

In view of the position which has been

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: When
a person makes his will according to our
existing law the executor is not entitled
to charge for his services, but if the person
making the will wishes the executor to be
reimbursed for his services he can state
that in the will. That, as a matter of
fact, is constantly done in cases in which
the testators choose professional men such
as solicitors as executors. If they wish to
enable a solicitor to be recompensed they
have to state so in their will because the
law is that a person who accepts the office
of a trustee is not entitled to make a
charge in respect of his duties as such
trustee, but the person who makes the will
can provide that the trustee or executor is
entitled to charge.
Here the bank is left in the same position as anybody else. If the testator says
they may make a charge then they may
make it, but if the testator does not say
they may make a charge then they may
not make it. Of course, it is open to them
if they like not to accept the trust. So it
is really a matter for the testator and not
for the bank, as no power is given to the
bank by this Bill. It is merely to enable
private citizens to commit their affairs to
a bank if they think that is the most convenient way.
The hon. Member need not
fear that the banks will be in a position to
levy any charges which are not reasonable
under this Bill.

It is an insult to the intelligent people of

affairs should exist. It is regrettable

body protest against the neglect of the
Ministry of Education in not compelling
the local authorities to provide proper
school accommodation for these
children.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 23rd March, 1933.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
SPEAKER from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to
the Standing Order.

Oral Answers to Questions.
SALE OF PORK, ETC., IN
BALLYMONEY.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Commerce if he can state whether pork
and other commodities brought into
Ballymoney for sale have to be weighed
on the weighbridge of the Ballymoney
Market Company, Limited, or whether,
if weighed on a private weighbridge, the
vendor has to pay a fee to that company;
and whether the company has a legal
right to this monopoly, and how it has.
accrued; and whether any other towns
possess a weighbridge under the control
of their borough or urban district
councils or boards of town commissioners.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply.
While I have no jurisdiction in connection with the question of private
market rights, I understand that the
company referred to owns, in pursuance
of Charter, the market toll rights in
Ballymoney.
It is a fact that certain local
authorities in Northern Ireland own the
market rights themselves.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does the monopoly of
this weighbridge by a private individual
benefit the farmers of that area? Would
it not be better to establish a public
weighbridge for the benefit and protection of the farmers?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend forgets that this House some time
ago passed an Act under which it is open
to local authorities to acquire market
rights.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am asking the
Minister whether he is prepared to compel local authorities to have a weighbridge to protect the farmers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I am not
prepared to compel the local authorities.
They are as good judges as I am as to
the necessity.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does this weighbridge belong to a member of the local
authority? Is the right hon. Gentleman
aware of that?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I am not.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will you investigate
this question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: This does not
affect the question at all.
FIRST-CLASS TEACHERS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the total
number of male and female first of firstclass teachers at present employed in
Northern Ireland, and the number of
each employed in the different counties.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

abolished in 1900, and there are no

WORKING-CLASS HOUSES IN
BALLYMONEY RURAL
DISTRICT.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he san state if
there have been erected in Ballymoney
Rural District, with the assistance of
subsidies under the Housing Acts, houses
for the accommodation of working-class
families and occupied by such families,
other than two in the townland of Ballygan; whether the subsidy scheme has
failed to provide the occupants of unsanitary houses in Ballymoney Rural
District with sanitary residences; and
whether he proposes to provide the necessary finance to have the suspension of the
subsidy removed from the Ballymoney
Rural District Improvement Scheme.
Sir DAWSON BATES: 84 houses have
been built in the Ballymoney Rural
District under the Northern Ireland
Housing Acts, as distinct from and in
addition to the 465 cottages which have
been built under the Labourers Acts.
Both classes of houses have qualified for
Government grant.
The housing subsidy payable by the
Government under the 1932 Housing Act
is still available for any person who desires to build houses qualifying for subsidy under that Act. I am sorry however, that the Ballymoney Rural District
Council have not seen fit to undertake to
supplement the Government grant, as
they are empowered to do under the Act.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister prepared to take drastic action in regard to
that Council and have the houses erected
by direct labour?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No.
CANVASSING FOR
APPOINT-
MENTS UNDER LOCAL
AUTHORITIES.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
there is a great dissatisfaction with the
manner in which canvassing is pursued by
candidates for appointments under county
and district councils and regional and
borough education committees, and what
steps, if any, he proposes to take to bring
canvassing to an end.
Sir DAWSON BATES: While I am
aware that, undoubtedly, in the case of
certain appointments made by local
authorities in Northern Ireland, a certain
amount of canvassing takes place, no
serious cases of improper conduct have
been brought under my notice and,
further, I think it well to point out that,
in many instances, the local authorities
in their advertisements relating to new
appointments, expressly stipulate that
canvassing will disqualify or else prejudice the candidate's chances of appointment.
At the same time, I understand that
the Minister of Education is, at present,
investigating certain complaints which
have been made to him regarding an
appointment under the Education Act.
MAGISTRACY IN IRVINESTOWN,
COUNTY FERMANAGH.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he was consulted in the recent appointment to the
Bench of Mrs. and Mr. O. Hermon, of
Irvinestown; why it was thought
necessary to appoint both husband and
wife at the same time; how many Roman
Catholics have been appointed to the
Bench in Irvinestown area since the
Government took office in 1921; and how
many in County Fermanagh in the same
period.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The circumstances regarding the appointment to the
Bench of the persons referred to in the
question were carefully considered before
the recommendations were approved, and
the hon. Member may rest assured that
the appointments were made primarily on
the grounds of the fitness of the lady and
gentleman in question to occupy the
Bench.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I would again remind the hon.
Member that religion is not a qualification or otherwise for nomination to the
Bench of Magistrates and, accordingly, I
have no information as to the numbers
of persons of different denominations on

TIME LIMIT ON SPEECHES IN
PARLIAMENT.
6. Major McCORMICK asked the
Prime Minister whether, in view of
tedious and useless discussion in this
House, he will consider the advisability
of setting up a Committee of this House
to revise Standing Orders to enable a time
limit to be placed upon individual
speeches, which shall be in the power of
Mr. Speaker to so determine.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): This is a matter for the
House to decide. I hope, however, that
the hon. and gallant Member will not
press his proposal, but will realise the
importance, in a comparatively small
community like Northern Ireland, of permitting the freest possible expression of
opinion in this House; that he will
also recognise that our Standing
Orders are modelled on those of
the Mother of Parliaments, where
no time limit is placed on Members'
rhetorical efforts, and that he will not suggest adding to Mr. Speaker's duties the
responsibility of deciding how long should
be permitted hon. Members to present
their case.
