now controlling transport in this area. I
feel it my bounden duty to oppose,
strenuously, a Motion of this kind at this
period. I think the failure of the
Government in accepting representations
from this House will show that their
interest in the railways is too much of
their own concern to allow them to interfere on behalf of the working people who
are walking the streets.
I ask the Prime Minister to withdraw
the Motion and get in touch immediately
with the railway companies and tell them
that dictation from England or the Free
State will not be considered in Northern
Ireland. We have no right to allow this
area to be made the battleground of
foreign enemies. We have allowed it to
be the battleground of foreign enemies
too long. What right have our people
to suffer because of the failure of private
enterprise? It is most outrageous on the
part of the railway companies to ask the
railway workers to reduce themselves to
a state of starvation.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: There is a
Motion before the House for the adjournment over Easter, and it is not competent
to enter into the merits of the railway
dispute which is in being on this Motion.
Mr. BEATTIE: I feel the day is fast
approaching when you will have to take
the reins in your hand and drive the
machinery according to the desires of the
people of Ulster. You cannot be led by
London or elsewhere on the road of private enterprise. You cannot allow your
own personal interests to enter into this
question which you are now putting off
to the 25th April. The people look to
you to be the medium by which a settlement can be brought about. If you make
a failure on this occasion then you are not
competent to hold the office of Government in this area. I ask the House to
reject the Motion and to call upon
the Government to get into touch
immediately with the railway companies
and tell them that in their view the 10
per cent. cut cannot be made, and that
a settlement of the strike must take place
at the very earliest possible date.
Mr. HENDERSON: I wish to support
the hon. Member in protesting against
this Motion. Considering that we have
only met a few days it is surprising that
we are asked to adjourn to the 25th
April, notwithstanding the fact that
there is a railway strike in
which
progress
is disorganising the whole transport service of the country and will ruin industry

if something drastic is not done.
Minister of Labour realises that there

in the way of a settlement. Unfortunately the efforts of the Minister of
Labour to try to effect a settlement were

being put back until after 25th April.
(Hon. Members: No, no.)
Mr. ANDREWS: Not at all.
Mr. HENDERSON: We are adjourning until the 25th April, and then we will
sit for a number of days and adjourn for

back to the House. Extreme hardships are

bankruptcy. There is an ever increasing.
volume of people joining the ranks of
the unemployed.
Mr. ANDREWS: No.

increasing.

Mr. HENDERSON: They are increasing by leaps and bounds. People
who are not signing on are increasing to

The suggestion of the hon. Member (Mr. Gordon)

I protest against this adjournment.
Nothing can now be done until the 25th
April. A few formalities have been gone

What has been done since this Parliament opened? Practically nothing.
Nothing has been done in the way of

Grey Seals Protection Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The grey seal has enjoyed protection in British waters since
the year 1914. This immunity from wilful destruction was first secured to them
by an Act of only one year's duration but,
both in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland, their protection has been renewed annually up to the present time.
The Bill to which I now ask the House
to give a Second Reading is intended to
replace the 1914 Act by a Measure of
indefinite duration.
The seals frequenting the waters
round the British Isles include two
distinct species, the common seal and the
grey seal.
To the common seal, which
is found in considerable numbers around
the Northern Irish coast, it is not proposed to afford any protection, the scope
of the Bill being limited to the grey seal,
which is much less numerous, even in its
normal habitat, the Hebrides, and which
is very rarely met with in Northern Irish
waters.
Prior to 1914 the grey seal had suffered
so much destruction at the hands of commercial hunters that it appeared to be in
danger of total extinction. The Act
passed in that year was, accordingly,
designed to allow of protection being
afforded only for so long as was necessary
to restore the grey seal population to a
reasonable level, beyond which it would
not be desirable, in the interests of the
fishing industry, to allow it to rise.
Investigations carried out in 1927 and
1928 by the Scottish Fishery Board,
showed that the grey seal population had
appreciably recovered, and that there was
then no danger of the early extinction of
the species. It was evident, however,
that the withdrawal of all restriction
would speedily bring about those very conditions which the 1914 Act had been
designed to remedy. With a view,
accordingly, to guarding against an
undue increase in their numbers and, at
the same time protecting the grey seal
against excessive destruction, the Grey
Seals Protection Act was passed by the
Imperial Parliament in May last. This
Act repealed the 1914 Act, provided for
an annual close season for grey seals, subject to variation at the discretion of the
Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries for
1061 Grey Seals Protection Bill-

23 MARCH 1933
Second Reading.
England and Wales and the Secretary of
State for Scotland, and prohibited the
killing of grey seals except under permit
and by approved methods.
This Measure did not extend to
Northern Ireland and, whilst, as I have
said, grey seals are rarely met with in
Northern Irish waters, it is considered
desirable that a corresponding Measure
should be enacted here in order to secure
uniformity of practice throughout the
United Kingdom. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. BEATTIE: This Bill means one of
two things. It means the protection of
grey seals and the destruction of the
fishing industry round Northern Ireland,
or the protection of the fishing industry
and the destruction of the grey seals.
Which of the two are you prepared to
support? The Government have decided
to choose grey seals, and to protect them
as against the interests of the hundreds
of fishermen round the coast of Northern
Ireland. I want to ask the Minister if
he is quite serious in trying to push this
Bill through the House to the detriment
of the fishermen, who are looking to the
Government for assistance in their
industry, and who object to obstacles.
being placed in their way. I am only an
amateur fisherman, not a professional,
but I am quite satisfied that this Bill, if
it is put into operation, will destroy a
large part of the fishing industry, and
will make it impossible for many fishermen to get a livelihood. As was stated
by the Minister of Commerce, very few
grey seals come to the coast of Northern
Ireland. If that is so, what is the
necessity for a protection Bill?
It has also been stated that the
majority of the seals that do come in are
common seals, but so far as the fishermen are concerned it is all the same; seals
are a danger to the livelihood of those
men. That being so, I say that this Bill
is uncalled for in this part of the world
at anyrate. The authority on grey seals
has stated that their extinction is not
near at hand. I am inclined to think
that they will increase rather than
decrease, owing to this protective
Measure, and when they do increase in
Northern fishing-grounds the fishermen
must have recourse to outdoor relief. I
ask the Minister if he had an interview
with the fishermen of Northern Ireland
before he intimated to this House that he
intended to bring this Measure forward.
Strong protests have come forth from
every fishing centre in regard to this Bill,
and I understand from the fishermen that
it is going to be a menace and a handicap to them in connection with their
industry. I hope the Minister will not
ask the House to do anything detrimental
to this useful class of the community, and
I think I can speak for the majority of
fishermen. As I say, I am only an
amateur fisherman, but I know that they
do not want this Bill, as it is going to be
a serious menace to their livelihood.
or
Major MCCORMICK: I beg to support this Bill, because I feel that it is
desirable to have co-ordination among the
fishery boards of England, Scotland and
Ireland, in order that the grey seals may
be kept within bounds. I believe that
this Bill will be beneficial to the grey
seals, but there is just the fear that unless
this Measure is operated in an elastic
manner we may have similar trouble to
that experienced from the common
black seal, of which I have heard so much
on the County Down coast. I understand that the Scottish Fishery Board
went very exhaustively into the question
of the dying out of the grey seal, and the
conditions under which they cohabit, and
came to the conclusion that there is no
fear of grey seals becoming extinct. At
the same time the regulations should be
closely watched, in order that the fishing
industry may be protected. In connection with the hon. Member for
Pottinger's statement, I should like to ask
him does he wish to see the grey seal
entirely obliterated.
Mr. BEATTIE: I have not suggested
that, but I am anxious that the fishing
industry should not be destroyed.
Major MCCORMICK: If this Bill will
be operated in conjunction with the other.
fishery boards of the United Kingdom,
and the regulations are carefully watched,
the results should be satisfactory.

MARKETING OF AGRICULTURAL

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Mr. Gordon.)
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I want to
raise on the Motion for the Adjournment a question of which I have given
notice to the Minister of Agriculture in
regard to the position that may arise
under the Marketing of Agricultural
Produce Bill. I realise that I am precluded from discussing the provisions of
that Bill, but there is one point I should
like to mention in order that anxiety may
be allayed now that the season for planting potatoes is commencing. As everybody knows this year's crop is quite
unmarketable, and naturally the farmers
want to know what the position is going
to be in the coming season. I can best
illustrate my point by quoting a case.
•
Supposing a man has 10 acres of
potatoes, when he comes to dig them in
the autumn what is the position going
to be? Presumably under the Act he
may be penalised, and if he is permitted
to market only five tons, what is going
to become of the remaining part of the
crop? This point must arise in the minds
of those who are working in the country
when the crop is going in. The Marketing Act is late for this year's crop, and
that being so I consider that a statement
from the Government is desirable as to
whether there will be free sale for the
full measure of the coming crop. A
definite statement on this point will help
to clear the air.
Another point I want to raise relates
to the various duties on potatoes. We
do not impose those duties in this House
-this is a Reserved Service-but I should
like the Minister of Agriculture to tell
us exactly what are the tariffs on new
potatoes and for how long those tariffs
exist. I should like the Minister to tell
the House the amount of the duties imposed on main crop potatoes, and whether
the Tariff Advisory Commission is considering any revision of those duties.
There are changes made from time to
time, and I think this point should be
cleared up.
If the Minister makes a
statement on this subject, it will be read
in the country, and farmers will know

Oral Answers to Questions.
OFFICE ACCOMMODATION IN
PARLIAMENT BUILDING.
1. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Henderson)
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
can state the number of rooms and offices
in the new Parliament Buildings.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked to
reply. Omitting the two Chambers themselves, the total number of rooms and
offices in this building (including
messengers' and attendants' lobbies) is
277, of which 47, required mainly for
storage purposes, are in the basement.
Of the remainder, 181 are used by the
several Departments for official purposes,
and 49 are used for Parliamentary purposes and for the accommodation of the
staffs of the two Houses.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the number
of rooms attached to Parliament, is the
Minister in a position to say that the
Opposition will have sufficient accommodation at their disposal at the next
meeting of the House?
Mr. BARBOUR: The 49 rooms used
for parliamentary purposes and for the
accommodation of the staff include the
library, writing-room, smokeroom, and
committee rooms, Mr. Speaker's and
Ministers' rooms; and the allocation of
these rooms, as Mr. Deputy-Speaker has
already ruled, is a matter for the discretion of Mr. Speaker.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask whether
the number given there includes the two
locked rooms in. this house, and, if so,
whether the right hon. Gentleman will
state that the Government will have a
consultation with Mr. Speaker with a view
to giving accommodation for Members of
the Opposition?
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: As that is
solely a matter for Mr. Speaker, it would
be better for the hon. Gentleman to
await his return.
UNEMPLOYMENT-PROPOSED
CONFERENCE.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Henderson)
asked the Prime Minister whether, in
view of the large numbers of male and
female persons unemployed in Northern
Ireland who are receiving no unemployment benefit, he is prepared to call a
conference of the captains of industry in
Northern Ireland to consider what steps
can be taken to secure new industries.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
to reply. I am satisfied that those who
are responsible for the guidance of
industry in our Province are sparing no
effort and losing no opportunity of providing additional employment for our
workers. The hon. Member will be aware
that the world trade depression is due to
complex causes far beyond the control of
any local influences, and I am accordingly
doubtful whether the moment is opportune for calling a conference such as the
hon. Member suggests.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask whether
the right hon. Gentleman is prepared to
adopt the suggestion that single persons
should get married as a solution of the
unemployment situation amongst single
persons in Northern Ireland.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: As that is
a question of policy it would seem to me
to require some notice.

On a careful study of the interests
involved, the Ministry has come to the
conclusion that nothing should be done
which would discourage the teaching of
algebra and geometry in the public
elementary schools. These are most useful and, indeed (for boys), almost indispensable subjects of instruction, and until
some better arrangement for their encouragement can be devised it is essential
that the extra fee system should continue.
With Irish instruction the
case is
different. The Committee is aware that
since the establishment of the Ministry
grants in restricted form-that is,
restricted as compared with those formerly
given by the Commissioners of National
Education-have been available for the
teaching of Irish as an extra in the public
elementary schools. The continuation of
such grants showed, at any rate, that the
Government was not without regard for
what was believed to be the wish of a
section of the minority in our area.
an examination of the operation of the
grant over the past ten years discloses
that a comparatively insignificant number.
of those schools which might be expected
to avail themselves of the privilege of

probably than one in every seven schools
under Roman Catholic managers.
this surprising.
But
Nor is
There has been, as the Committee
knows, a considerable improvement in the
facilities for secondary education, and
scholarships to secondary schools are now
generally available. The result has been
to remove the teaching of languages,
apart from the mother tongue, to an
increasing extent from the present day
elementary school, which is not, as a rule,
the appropriate place for such instruction.
In view of these considerations and
in the interests of economy, it has been
decided to give notice that the payment
of extra fees for Irish will be discontinued
at the close of the present school year,
that is, after the 30th June next. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Managers and
teachers will be at liberty to continue the
teaching as heretofore, but no extra
remuneration will be available.
I would ask the Committee to note that
the Ministry of Education is well aware
of the necessity for the strictest economy
in expenditure, and I am sure that, if
the country were not now passing through
a dire period of financial stringency, it
would be necessary for the Ministry to
push on with several reforms in the system which would in ordinary times considerably increase the facilities for the
better education of the pupils. One of
the most important of such reforms would
be to secure a more liberal staffing of the
larger, and particularly the senior public
elementary schools, that is, those large
schools now being erected in Beifast and
other centres which provide a full course
of instruction, both practical as well as
intellectual, for pupils over ten years of
age.
Such schools would gain much in
efficiency if the classes were smaller, but
smaller classes mean more teachers, and
such an increase would seriously add to
educational expenditure.
The present arrangements for staffing,
devised on the general basis of one assistant teacher for every 45 pupils in average
attendance, with the principal teacher
thrown in almost as an extra, suit more
or less satisfactorily the circumstances of
schools of less than 250 or 300 pupils, but
are scarcely adequate to meet the needs
of the very much larger schools now being
built. It is true that the Ministry has
recently made a new regulation modifying
to a certain extent the adjustment of the
staffing arrangements in large senior
schools, but this alteration of rule merely
secures that the staffing will keep more
closely in step with the actual attendance
of pupils, and does not meet the fundamental requirement of smaller classes,
and until, as I have said, the financial
position is easier, I fear it will not be
possible to apply the proper remedy.
Another problem which is rapidly becoming urgent if our educational system
is to receive its fullest extension in bearing useful fruit after the pupil has left
school is the question of providing parttime education of a technical character for
boys and girls from 14 to 18 years of age.
The Ministry have never believed in the
policy of raising the compulsory school
age to fifteen; they look for more practical
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
and useful results in the institution of
compulsory part-time attendance at the
technical school for every boy and girl
over fourteen, not already attending
secondary or junior technical schools, so
that the young worker of either sex may
continue to receive appropriate instruction
suited to his or her occupation and attainments for a period equivalent to at least
one full day per week whilst learning at
the counter or in the workshop or on the
farm the practical realities of everyday
life. But here again a development of this
kind which is engaging the minds of
educational people almost everywhere
must, I fear, wait for better prospects in
the commercial and industrial world.
To return to the Estimates, the charge
for training colleges, £22,855, shows a
slight increase over last year, amounting
to £590. As the Committee is aware,
the Ministry has reduced the numbers of
the students in the training colleges successively in each of the last four years so
that the 398 students of 1928-29 fell to
324 in 1931-32, and the cost from
£27,360 to £22,265. Last September it
was found that the reduction was going
too far, and the number had to be increased so that at present there are 338
students in training.
In this connection I may mention that
the Ministry has noted in the last two or
three years a somewhat marked falling off
in the number of candidates for admission
to the colleges, and the decline is unfortunately not only in numbers, it also extends in some extent to the quality of
the answering at the entrance examination. It may be that the erroneous
impression that existed some time ago to
the effect that a large number of exstudents were unable to secure employment in the schools has affected the supply
of candidates, but whatever may be the
cause it points clearly to the necessity
of avoiding any steps that would tend to
diminish the attractions of the profession
as a career.
There is still an upward tendency in
the numbers of pupils in the public elementary schools and the increase of £5,700
in the estimated cost of salaries and
capitation grants is mainly due to an increase of about 2,000 in the attendance,
which now stands at about 175,000. An
increase of 2,000 pupils would normally.
mean an increase in cost of staffing of
some £15,500, but owing to the savings
effected by the process of amalgamation
of schools which still continues to a substantial extent according as new schools
are erected, the estimated additional expenditure due to this increase in
attendance is put at £10,200. As against
this increase, there is a saving of about
£1,600 in the charges in connection with
the pupil-teacher system, which is due to
the operation of the new rules in regard
to pupil-teachers' appointments and the
abolition of the monitorial system which
has been merged in the former. I may
say that the new arrangements appear to
be working satisfactorily.
Coming now to building grants under
Section 10 of the Act of 1930, the
Estimate for last year was £30,000, but
of this sum only £23,228 was actually
disbursed by the Ministry down to March
31st last. This sum was in respect of 14
cases of new voluntary schools, of a total
estimated cost of £91,148 11s 2d. The
Ministry's share, 50 per cent. of this
expenditure, is £45,574 5s 7d, and as the
works are not yet completed, there still
remains to be paid the sum of £22,346.
During the current year it is anticipated
that further grants amounting to £27,000
will be sanctioned, making a still outstanding liability on the Ministry of
nearly £50,000. Of this sum it is
believed that about £39,000 will accrue
for payment before the end of March,
1934, and as the Estimate for 1932-33 for
this service was £30,000, the amount now
asked for shows an increase of £9,000.
These works include large new schools,
three in Belfast and one each in Londonderry, Portadown, Newry, Clogher and
Newtown butler, as well as a substantial
scheme of reconstruction to the Irish
Society's Schools at Coleraine, and all
these are works of urgent necessity in
the interests of the pupils.

The moneys to be voted for secondary
education amount to £160,750,
increase of £5,600 on last year's Estimate.
There is an automatic growth in the total
cost of the incremental portion of the
teachers' salaries which falls to be paid
in full by the Ministry. This year the
increase amounts under this head to
£4,300, after allowance has been made
for savings due to retirements on pension.
In the commencing years of a new
system of teachers' salaries such as ours
this growth in expenditure is inevitable,
and merely represents the realisation of
an anticipated liability. There is also an
increase of £1,300 in the provision for
the capitation grant to the schools, due
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
25 APRIL 1933
partly to a small increase in the total
numbers of pupils, but mainly to the fact
that there is a substantial increase in the
proportion of pupils enrolled in the
highest or post-intermediate departments
of the schools, in which the grant is at
its maximum. From the educational
standpoint this is a matter for congratulation, as secondary education fails of a
great part of its advantages if cut short
before seventeen or eighteen years of age.
The direct grants in aid of technical
education show little change, but some
economies will be made in science and
technological and trade scholarships. Of
the former only three, instead of four,
will be in operation this year, and the
number of the latter is reduced from 80
to 60.
The liability for teachers' pensions,
accepted by Parliament in 1926, is
responsible this year for a sum of £80,000,
an increase over last year of £17,000.
This sum represents the amount required
to supplement the income of the Pension.
Fund, in order to meet the outgoings of
the year in superannuation allowances.
The number of pensioned teachers, which
is still growing, now approximates to
1,400, and as the older pensioners retired
on small pensions consequent on the low
salaries paid before the year 1920, the
fund experiences little relief according
as their places are taken by the much
more highly paid teachers now reaching
the age for retirement.
I do not propose to occupy the time of
the Committee any further at this stage.
The past year has seen no marked changes
in the schools; the system established in
the last few years has continued to
develop on lines now familiar to us all.
We are gratified that-when money is so
scarce it has been found possible for the
borough and regional education committees to continue their efforts, to which
I gladly pay a tribute, to improve the
school accommodation, and to extend
further the facilities for the comfort,
health, well-being, and, in short, the
better education of the pupils. I beg to
move.

something about our Irish language. I
do not, for one minute, agree that we
should regard Irish as a party or political
contrivance.
Apart from that observation I have
every reason to congratulate the Ministry
of Education on the report which has
just been presented with these Estimates.
It is unfortunate that we have not the
means at our disposal of increasing the
compulsory age limit by another year,
that is of extending it to fifteen years
instead of fourteen, as at present. It is
now some forty years since the Irish
Education Act of 1892 fixed fourteen
years as the compulsory school age, subject
to several exceptions. Those exceptions
were eliminated under the Act of 1923,
and it is now time that we endeavoured
to extend the age limit to fifteen years.
We have some 233,000 children attending our primary schools in Northern
Ireland. Thousands of those children
leave school at the age of fourteen, and
we know that, owing to the tremendous
economic impasse which exists at the
present time, the great majority of those
children have nothing to do, that they
have no employment which they can take
up, that they have leisure thrown upon
them which they cannot utilise to the best
advantage, and that they are not entitled to the benefits of our insurance
schemes until they attain the age of some
15 years and have made the necessary
contributions. At the present time, and
while waiting for the good times which
we all hope will yet come, we in Northern
Ireland should try to set an example to
the rest of the world by increasing this
age to fifteen years. I do not know
whether the Ministry have calculated the
cost. I presume they have.
If so, I
would like to hear from the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb) whether
it would not be possible at the present
time to do that in the best interests of
Northern Ireland.
There are not many other matters on
which I wish to touch. I had intended

for civil rights, but I hope I will not be

at a later stage if necessary.

Professor JOHNSTONE: I do not rise

The Ministry of Education carry on the

There are one or two other points on

are being made of our system of primary

I do

system of inspection. They may be
totally wrong, but that is a criticism
which is always heard.
Every Easter, in the reports of the proceedings of the various societies of school
teachers, you find the same criticism,
that the system of inspection is radically
bad. I do not know whether it is or not,
but I think we should have some defence
of it, and if there are faults they should
be remedied. One very grave fault
which is constantly alleged against the
system, and which, if true, is sufficient to
condemn it, is that the inspectors do not
take the opportunity of bringing to the
notice of the teachers in one school what
changes for the better have been adopted
in other schools. I think that, if that is
true, it is certainly a very damning
criticism of the method of inspection.
The inspector ought to ensure, as far as
possible, that any improvements that are
effected in one school should be introduced
into the next one that he visits, so far
as they are suited to that school. That
is one form of criticism which one hears
constantly repeated.
Another criticism which I hear from
my commercial friends, I am sorry to say,

average schoolboy who leaves school at the

the education of the average boy who left

My hon. Friend, the Member for

set in the same clerical class
as the
schoolboys formerly could be set. I do

well.

Professor JOHNSTONE: He should

wish that the average schoolboy would
learn the English language and

May I say that the cultural

this area. The reason why the change
has been made in this case is quite simple.
Upon investigation of what happened
during the last ten years when facilities
were given for the teaching of the Irish
language as an extra subject to children
in elementary schools outside school hours,
it was found that very little advantage
had been taken of that opportunity of
teaching and that on the whole the results were not worth the money expended

The hon. and learned Member mentioned two other matters-medical inspection and school feeding. With regard to
medical inspection I agree with him on
the importance of that subject. There is
hardly anything which was introduced in
1923 into our system which deserves
greater support and greater praise, and
from which we must expect better results,
than the medical inspection of school
children. I am glad to say that in all
the areas of regional committees certain
provision is being made, and we hope as
experience grows the provision will improve and the results be correspondingly
greater. As regards the feeding of school
children, I am sorry to say I have not
got the full figures, but I can say that in
Belfast and County Down and certain
other districts good work is being done in
this direction, and that as occasion requires and as necessity is impressed upon
the Ministry, they endeavour to bring
before the regional committees the
necessity of making provision where such
may be necessary in other districts.
My other colleague from the University
(Professor R. J. Johnstone) asked that

the necessity for saving every penny that

repeated that he had heard complaints.
with regard to our system of inspection.
Secondly, he said he also heard that our
pupils emerging from the primary schools
are not so well educated now as they were
thirty years ago. He said that he himself did not know whether that was so
or not. I say without any hesitation or
qualification whatever, that the children.
emerging from our elementary schools today are better educated than they were
thirty years ago. The hon. Member repeated a complaint that men in business
say that the pupils coming from the
elementary schools now are possibly not
as fit to be put in jobs as the pupils of
thirty years ago were. May I point out
that possibly thirty years ago the cream of
the elementary schools went into business,
but nowadays the cream of the elementary
school do not go into business, because
by reason of the system of scholarships
and other aid the better educated primary
students now proceed to secondary schools
and do not go direct from school into
business. As regards the general level of
the educational pupils in our primary
schools to-day, I repeat without any
qualification that they are better
educated to-day than thirty years ago.
The other matter the hon. Member
touched upon was the system of inspection
in our area. He said it was about time
someone defended it. No one could fully
explore the advantages and disadvantages
of the system of inspection in primary
schools enforced in this area in the time,
I would feel justified in occupying the
House; but, at the same time, I would
put forward certain considerations touching our system of inspection which will be
informative, I hope, to most Members and
enlighten my hon. Friend, who has said
he did not know whether the system was
good or bad. In our primary schools a
Ministry of Education
Estimates-

25 APRIL 1933
large amount of public money is spent.
No one for a moment suggests, at least no
sane person suggests, that that money is
to be spent without the Government taking steps to see that it is properly spent.
That can only be done by some system of
inspection. It being then admitted that
you must have some system of inspection,
what is the difference between the system
that is in force in Northern Ireland and
the other systems in force in the other
parts of the British Isle?
The main difference is this.
In our
area where inspectors go into a school and
examine the work being done they not
only certify and report to the Ministry
that the work being done in this school
is up to the minimum standard, but they
go on and say that the work of particular
teachers reaches or does not reach a particular state of efficiency. Accordingly,
in our area, our teacher has assigned to
him after the inspection what is called a
rating. There are four ratings.
At the
top there is the highly efficient teacher.
Next below that comes the efficient
teacher. Then there is the fairly efficient
teacher, and, last of all, there is the nonefficient teacher. What are the advantages that accrue from that? The system
was set up upon this theory. The
Ministry of Education-of course the
Ministry of Education only succeeded the
Commissioners of National Education,
and I speak generally of the Ministrydoes not appoint teachers to the schools,
but it pays the teachers' salaries. The
appointments to schools are made by the
managers or by regional committees or
otherwise. It is not within the power of
the Ministry to reward work well done
in the schools by appointing to a larger
school the teachers of outstanding merit.
That is not in their power.
At the same time the Ministry desire
to reward and to encourage by reward
good work done in the school, and accordingly a system was devised whereby a
teacher who earned a highly efficient
rating in successive years should receive
a double increment. As the Committee
know, teachers are paid upon a salary
beginning with a basic salary and rising
each year of service by an annual increase
until they reach the maximum. The first
use to which this system of inspection
is put is that a teacher who receives
successive ratings of highly efficient may
at intervals of not less than three years
gain a double increment. They may get
two steps on the salary scale. Further,
a teacher who has reached his or her
maximum, and has enjoyed that maximum of salary for one year and continues
to have highly efficient reports is rewarded
by being allowed to proceed beyond the
normal maximum of his or her salary
to what is called a super normal salary,
which means that he or she can proceed
until he or she has received five increments over and above the normal maximum of the salary scales. That, in the
Ministry's point of view, is a great advantage and well worth the money it costs.
We believe that these monetary inducements are a sufficient incentive to good
work in the schools to make it worth
our while to pay them. That is the first
advantage.
But there are other advantages. If the
teacher is applying for a position in
another school his record is before those
who make the appointment, and if that
record shows that he has enjoyed a highly
efficient rating for a number of years, or
even for one or more years, he naturally
will have a better chance of appointment
to a better school. Those are the great
advantages there are under this system.
Then there is one internal advantage, an
advantage within the office, that is not
so apparent. but is at the same time
valuable in itself. Under the system of
inspection, as it obtains in England,
there is no record further than that the
teacher comes up to the minimum standard. There is nowhere a record kept of
teachers who are exceptionally good, industrious, or brilliant, but we have in
our Ministry, by reason of this rating
which is put upon the teachers from time
to time, a record, and an inspection of
that record can furnish anyone who wishes
it very quickly with an accurate estimate
of the teacher's abilities and work.
Now, we may ask, if these advantages
accrue to the teachers why do they object?
In the first place may I say that their
first objection is a sentimental one? They
say it is derogatory to their dignity to
be classified like school children. I
remember very well the first time the
teachers put that up to me. I said, "Is
not any system of inspection derogatory
to your dignity? If you are put upon
your honour from the start to carry out
your duties faithfully you do not need
any system of inspection at all." To that
some of them said, "Well, we do not
need any." But I do not think that
the general public is going to commit the
Ministry of Education 1112

[Mr. Robb]
teaching of its children without inspection to the teachers.
I believe there must be some system of
inspection. Why then should they object?
Their objection, as I say, is based on
sentimental ground in the first instance,
and, of course, one can very well understand that a system in which merit, and
outstanding merit, is recognised must
necessarily weigh heavily upon
the
weaker brethren. The majority of the
teachers are not fit to be rated as highly
efficient, and the bulk of the teachers are
naturally a little bit jealous of any mark
of distinction given to those of whom
their estimate may not be exactly the
same as the official estimate.
Their second objection is that ratings
are capricious sometimes and depend upon
a particular inspector, even on the state
of a particular inspector's digestion. Of
course, no system that has to be worked
through human agents is perfect, and it
may be that on particular occasions.
justice is not done at an inspection to a
particular teacher. But if that should
happen the Ministry's regulations have
made ample provision for a remedy. The
teacher is entitled to appeal against his
rating. If he is dissatisfied with the
marking that is given him he can say so,
and the first thing that happens if he
says that is that one of the very senior
inspectors, experienced and expert, at the
top of our service is sent to review the
work. He may confirm or he may alter
in any way the rating. At any rate, on
that occasion it cannot be said that the
rating depends upon the state of a particular inspector's mind at a particular
time.
But even if he is dissatisfied then he
has a second right of appeal. He may
appeal first of all to the Appeals Committee. That is a committee constituted
by the Ministry for the express purpose
of reviewing the rating of dissatisfied
teachers. It consists of three members,
one of whom is himself a retired teacher.
The second member is a senior inspector
of the Ministry, and the third, so that
the Board may if anything be weighted
in favour of the teacher, is the president
for the year of one of the teachers'
organisations.
Mr. BEATTIE: Which one?
Mr. ROBB: There are four teachers'
organisations, and by a rota which they
have established themselves each year the
president of a different association is
president of the Appeal Board. Could
any tribunal be fairer toward the teacher ?
What justification then can there be for
the suggestion that in the ultimate result
the rating assigned to any teacher is or
can be capricious? Everything the Ministry could do has been done to avoid the
charges and complaints that have been
made against this system, and the Ministry
is perfectly satisfied that the system in
itself is good and well worth the extra
cost it entails, and, further, that the
Ministry has done all that it can to safeguard the teachers against caprice in the
working of it.

CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £50,099 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1934, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Agriculture." (Note-
£17,000 has been voted on account.)
-
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): Hon. Members
will see from the papers before them that
this Vote shows a net increase of £60
over the figures for last year. Examination of the various subheads of this
Vote show certain small decreases which
have been made possible by closer estimating and a number of relatively small
increases due entirely to normal increments in salary.
In presenting the Estimates to you last
year I drew attention to the great
economic difficulty our farmers were
facing owing to the almost catastrophic
fall in the price level of agricultural
produce, and expressed the hope that with
the change in the fiscal policy of the
United Kingdom there would come a
gradual increase in the price level of our
produce and a consequent increasing
measure of prosperity to our agricultural
community.
Since then the most important event
affecting our farmers has been the undertaking by the United Kingdom Government, as the result of the Ottawa Conference, to restrict the importation of
bacon and hams, beef, mutton and lamb,
with the avowed objects of raising the
price level to the farmers and of securing
to them the first claim on the home
market. Pending the necessary legislation at Westminster restrictions on the
importation of these products have been
operating on a voluntary basis since the
middle of November last, and I am very
happy, indeed, to report that without any
material advance in price to the con-
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
sumer there has occurred a very substantial increase in the price to the farmer
of pork, mutton and lamb.
Mr. NIXON: What about flax?
In
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE:
November last the price of pork had fallen
to the calamitous level of 38s per cwt.
Since the operation of the restrictions it
has risen steadily to the present level of
62s per cwt., and has affected a much
needed measure of relief to our agricultural community. Furthermore, there
has been an increase in the price of store
cattle of at least 10s per head.
The
increase in the price of mutton and lamb,
although not so spectacular as in the case
of pork, has been substantial.
Hon. Members will have noted that concession to the United Kingdom farmers
of a limitation of imports has so far been
confined to stock and stock products. I
rejoice that at long last the predominant
part played by livestock and livestock
products, not only in Ulster agriculture,
but in the agriculture of the whole United
Kingdom, has been recognised, and I am
happy indeed to think that, through the
persistent efforts of my Ministry, ably
backed by the county agricultural committees and the farmers themselves, to
improve our stock, we are in the most
favourable position of any part of the
United Kingdom to take advantage of
the better times which have come and the
still better times which I sincerely hope
the future has in store for our farmers.
to
The undertaking which the United
Kingdom Government has given
restrict the importation of meat and meat
products has been accompanied by a
requirement that the home farmer shall
undertake the re-organisation of his
marketing system and an improvement of
his methods of production. I shall have
more to say on a later occasion concerning
marketing, but as a substantial part
of the expenditure covered by this Vote.
is occasioned by the operation of our
existing marketing schemes, I should like
to take this opportunity of emphasising
the fact that the very heavy and anxious
task which lies before us has been
facilitated immensely by the marketing
and development schemes which we have
put into operation during the past nine
years.
CO-
The Livestock Breeding Act, the
Marketing of Eggs Acts, the Grading of
Potatoes, the Meat Inspection Act and
the Fruit Grading Act have convinced the
great majority of our farmers as to the
necessity for concentrated and
operative action in improving the quality
of their produce and the method of
marketing and presentation to the consuming public. Perhaps the greatest
tribute that can be paid to our pioneering
efforts in livestock improvement and
marketing methods is contained in the
fact that these schemes, or ones corresponding closely to them, are now being
put into operation in England and Scotland. We have, however, reached the
stage at which it is necessary to take
another step forward, a big step, one
which will call for wise and careful
guidance. I feel certain, however, that
the Ministry will continue to receive the
support from the farmers of Ulster which
has enabled us in the past to improve so
successfully the quality of our produce,
or methods of marketing and, above all,
has enabled us to secure for our surplus
produce the top prices in the British
market.
Before moving the Vote, I should like
to refer to one other item of agricultural
produce, namely, potatoes. The past
season has been a disastrous one for those
of our farmers who depended for a substantial part of their income on the sale
of potatoes. The low price, indeed one
might truthfully say the almost complete
absence of a price, is not due to foreign
importations. The root cause of the
collapse in main crop potato prices is the
fact that home production exceeds, by a
considerable margin, the normal home
consumption. The increased acreage of
potatoes and the improved yields are the
causes of surplus crops of potatoes occurring with much greater frequency than in
the past. The remedy can only be found
in a control of production and sale by producers themselves. Plans with this object
in view are under consideration, and I am
hopeful that joint action by our farmers
with producers in England and Scotland
will shortly provide the means of restoring a permanent economic sanity to the
potato market.
In view of the very distressing time
through which our industry has passed,
it has been a source of great satisfaction
to me to witness the substantial improvement in the price level which has taken
Estimates--
Ministry of Agriculture
26 APRIL 1933
place during the past four or five months.
in some of our most important agricultural products. Times are definitely
better and all the signs point to a still
better future. I beg to move.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In rising to
speak on this Estimate, may I say that
I intend to review the markets this year
and last year and the prospects for the
future. I will deal with policy in
general.
The CHAIRMAN: It may be advantageous to the Committee if I point out
again that all questions of policy arising
upon any of the three Votes of this Ministry should be debated now as well as the
details of the particular Estimate before
the Committee. At a later stage the
details, but not the policy, of the two
succeeding Estimates may be discussed.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I will now
deal with policy in general. To begin
with, I would remind the Committee that
last year in introducing the Estimate the
Minister said that he was convinced that
the agricultural situation was definitely
on the mend. That was the statement
made this time last year. The fact is
that since last April prices fell continuously until the autumn. By then
there was not a single agricultural
product that was not far below the spring
level. Since the autumn, prices have
risen as the Minister has told you to-day,
but not all of them have risen to last
year's price level. I think that those
who observe the markets will realise that
to-day's prices show signs of sagging.
Beef to-day is anything from 8s to 10s
per cwt. live weight, less than last year;
that would be £5 on a 10-cwt. beast.
Pork is about the same level. Oats are
down 5s per cwt., and potatoes are
practically unmarketable.
As regards the live stock trade, we are
to-day at the beginning of the grass
season. The store cattle trade to-day is extremely dull instead of booming, and this
statement of mine is borne out by the
fact that reference to the Ministry's
returns will show that in the last three
months shipments of store cattle to England and Scotland have fallen by 10,000.
Last year, in the first three months of
the year, 36,000 store cattle went out of
the ports of Northern Ireland, and this
year the number is 25,600. Now, I ask,
what may this fall be attributed to? It
may in part be attributed to the Canadian
cattle having free entry into English
ports since the Ottawa Conference; in
fact, this week alone 1,850 head of cattle
are leaving the St. Lawrence River for
Glasgow and Birkenhead, and during the
season we may expect another 40,000 of
those cattle coming in. Further, I understand that the Canadian Government
intends to subsidise these exported cattle
by fixing a special rate of exchange which
will work out at a bounty of about 12
per cent. per head. I do not know
whether this is a fact yet or not, but I
should like the Minister when he comes
to reply to tell us if he knows anything
about this proposed move on the part of
the Canadian Government, and whether
it conforms with the Ottawa Conference.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is fully in agreement with it.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: May I tell
a story to the Committee? A very short
time ago I was in one of the big sales
yards selling baby beef. As the hammer
was going down on the sale of my beasts
a voice from the crowd remarked,
Now,
Colonel, what do you think of the fruits
of Ottawa?" The beasts sold at 10s a
cwt. less than this time last year. This,
I think, illustrates a good deal of the feeling throughout the country regarding
the shipment of these Canadian cattle.
I will now turn to and review the pig
trade. This time last year on the Estimates I spoke of the development of the
shipment of live pork to the English
markets and advocated the breeding of a
hard-skinned pig which would meet the
requirements of the other side so that this
trade should develop, and I am glad to
say that during the first three months of
this year we sent across the water 27,000
pigs. The total for the whole of last year
was only 31,000, so hon. Members will
see that in three months this year we
very nearly equalled the whole trade in this
particular branch of the pig industry of
last year.
I ask the Committee, what is
the future of this trade?
In the Bill now before the Imperial
Parliament-which I cannot discuss here
-there is a Clause which puts the Secretary of State for Home Affairs in a
position, when the marketing scheme is
set up in regard to any one article of
farm produce, to enforce a quota on
Northern Ireland. Here I wish to
impress upon the Minister of Agriculture
that it is his duty, acting in conjunction
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
with the Secretary of State for Home
Affairs, to ensure that this new trade
which is developing in live pigs and it
is a most important trade-is fostered
and increased, and that no rules should
be introduced which would in any way
hamper or restrict it in favour of any
foreign country like Denmark or any
Dominion like Čanada. The home market
should be for the home producer. This
must be insisted upon.
Again, in connection with this pork
trade, the farmers, not only here, but
throughout the United Kingdom, are most
anxiously awaiting the White Paper,
which will not be presented to this House,
but is due to be presented to the Imperial
House of Commons, to show the trade
agreements entered into with Denmark
and how the agricultural interests are
affected thereby. This White Paper, as
I say, is awaited with very great interest
by the farmers throughout Great Britain
and Northern Ireland.
The Minister dealt with the potato
trade and, as he said, this has been a
most disastrous season. Potatoes in the
country districts are practically unsaleable. I am going to ask, What are the
prospects for the coming year? What are
the prospects for our first early potatoes
which come on to the market in July?
Last year I speak of my own knowledge
--in the week ending 16th July, the
average price for early potatoes mostly
British Queens-was 8s a cwt., and by
30th July it had fallen to 2s 9d a cwt.
What was the reason? The reason was
the importation from Holland of 40,000
tons of potatoes in two weeks in July.
Recently the Minister told us in this
House that there was a duty of 4s 8d a
cwt. on new potatoes up to 30th June,
but on 1st July the duty was reduced to
1s a cwt. Just as our first early potatoes
will come on the market we have to compete against a duty which drops from
4s 8d to 1s a cwt. We have to compete
with Dutch and Spanish producers, and
in Spain especially the rate of exchange
is in their favour. So I ask again that
the Ministry will back up the efforts being
made by the Farmers' Union, not only
here but in Scotland and in England, to
see that the Imports Duty Advisory Board
does something before it is too late.
Let me deal now with the main crop
of potatoes. The Minister told us that
the failure this year in potato prices is
due to the large crop, and with that I
agree in part, but I would point out that
there is a duty of £1 a ton on the main
crop of last year. In spite of that duty
some 778,000 tons of potatoes came in
from abroad. Is that reserving the home
market for the home producer? It is not.
I fail to see why, when we have a bumper
crop of our own, the market is open to
all this foreign competition. Again, that
is a matter for the Imports Duty Advisory
Board. If, as the Minister has foreshadowed, a potato scheme is set up in
Great Britain, we must be given a quota
on the basis of production in preference
to those foreign countries sending in what
they like with a duty that does not act
in keeping them out.
I have reviewed, roughly and shortly,
live stock, pigs, and potatoes, what
happened last year, and what are the
prospects for the coming year, and it will
be seen that, while we certainly have
recovered from the plight of last autumn,
we are no further forward than we were
this time last year; in fact, we are not
so far forward as regards the prices then
ruling. The promise made generally
throughout the United Kingdom of putting agriculture an a paying basis has still
to be redeemed. Great expectations are
held out in Great Britain and here under
the Marketing Bill now before the
Imperial Parliament. We here have also
a Marketing Bill, which has received a
First Reading, but it has yet to see the
Parliamentary light of day. This
Marketing Bill is going to affect agriculture for the next generation. I ask why
is this Bill not before the House. I ask
the Government have the Cabinet yet
considered it. I want an answer to those
two questions, and I hope I get one.
This enabling Bill, which is on the
Table of this House but which has not
yet been seen, is going to affect very
large interests throughout the whole of
the Six Counties, and it is only right
and just that it should be studied by all
whom it will affect throughout the whole
Province. It is the duty of Parliament
to have it laid before them so that they
can study it now, and I ask the Minister
to put that Bill on the Table of the
House. No doubt I will be told in reply
that we must wait for Great Britain. In
Great Britain they are already making
plans for a pig census to be taken practically at once, prior to the introduction
of a pig marketing scheme which is to
come into force in July. Here we are
to-day on the 26th of April. The 1st of
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
26 APRIL 1933
July is a very short time away, and this
Bill has to be passed and the schemes
set up. It means that the whole legislation will be rushed and hurried. This
job wants tackling now and at once.
Surely we in Northern Ireland should be
able, using this Act of 1931 and the Bill
now before the Imperial House as a basis
on which to work, to produce a Bill so
that when the 1st of July comes we will
not have to rush and scramble to pass
the necessary legislation. Surely we
should be able to produce a Bill now
and so let us get on with the work of preparing this marketing scheme.
If I have spoken strongly on this subject of agriculture it is because I feel
strongly. In conclusion, I would say
that whether or not these Marketing Acts
will restore prosperity is a question I am
not allowed to discuss now, but I can
and will say that if the agricultural community have to go through another year
such as 1932 the effect will be disastrous
to those who are dependent on agriculture for their livelihood, and the reaction will be far-reaching. I hope what
I have said will receive the very earnest
attention of the Cabinet and the Government.
Mr. NIXON: Anyone who had been
living out of this country for the last
eleven or twelve years on hearing the
Minister's speech would be bound to come
to the conclusion that there has been remarkable progress in the agricultural
industry. But those who live here know
that the reverse is the case. We know

go on at the same rate for the next eleven

Even the Minister himself will not contest that statement.
On the Prime Minister's return from
his visit to Australia and New Zealand
we were told, and led to believe that he
had been collecting and had brought back

Six Counties from creamery to creamery,
I presume to spread the knowledge he
himself had collected. I do not see any
improvement.
Neither do the farmers.
Then we were led to believe that the
Ottawa Conference was going to bring
what we had been promised over and over
again. The hon. and gallant Gentleman,
the Junior Whip (Sir Basil Brooke), was
sent to that Conference to represent the
farming industry. After everything in
connection with his visit to Ottawa had
been arranged-I knew he was going-he
himself stated in reply to me that he was
not aware that he was going. If he was
not aware of it I was, and my reason for
mentioning it in the House was in order
that hon. Members, who represent the
people, should have an opportunity of
conveying their views to him as to what
he should do there on behalf of the farming community.
Now what did he do? Since the hon.
and gallant Gentleman came back there
has been an agitation amongst the farmers it culminated in a deputation to
the Prime Minister-about the land
annuities. The farmers had a meeting
down town somewhere. I was not at it,
but there was a Socialist at it. He came
there without an invitation and went on
the platform, and the Junior Whip used
that as a reflection on the farmers, although when he himself went to Ottawa
he went under the guidance of a Socialist,
Mr. Jimmy Thomas, who went there
officially. It was no harm for the hon.
and gallant Gentleman to do that, but
it was a terrible crime for a Socialist inadvertently to get on the farmers' platform. That is a fair sample of the way
the people of Northern Ireland are being
bamboozled and hoodwinked and-shall I
say?-deceived.
Flax growing in Northern Ireland is a
dead industry. The Northern Government, through Ottawa and on another
occasion, did their dead level best to contribute to that. It is a very serious thing
at the moment, because it is just a
question, having regard to the international situation, if we can get any flax
from abroad after the Government have
killed the industry at home. Mr. Lewis
Gray, chairman of the Flax Dressers'
Association, also went to Canada, and the

How that was going to help the flax

and the hon. and gallant Gentleman, the

Mr. POLLOCK: No. The Ropeworks

or

The consumer's objective is to get in

is very hard to bring about because of

farming to materialise with these two
extremes. You must give the consuming
man purchasing power so that he will be

from the producer on the land, and give

That is not the objective or the policy

That is the direct opposite to what they
are doing. You tax the farmer heavily

I find a nice quotation. As we know,

The PRIME MINISTER: The question we are really discussing to-day is,
how best can the Government help the
Ulster farming community through difficult times? My hon. and gallant friend
(Sir Basil Brooke) has said a few words
about Ottawa. The question of flax has
been raised by one or two Members. We
all realise our responsibility. We all wish
we could do more. As a matter of fact,
I believe I am on sound lines when I say
that so far as the future is concerned
it is brighter for the Ulster farmer than
for the English farmer. Flax is a very
old crop, and one which we would like
to see grown to the greatest possible extent, and if the hon. Member had only
been at some of the conferences I have
attended in connection with flax growing
he would know I am the last man to make
a charge against by saying that everything possible was not being done to
encourage the growth of flax in our area.
It so happens that the question is full of
difficulty, and no matter how many acres
were put down in flax it would still be
impossible for us to meet the requirements
of the trade. That is obvious to anyone
who studies the situation. However, the
Committee may rest assured that my right
hon. Friend is a real, true, and sincere
friend of the farmers, and has at his back
not only myself but all his colleagues.
Mr. BEATTIE: Such a failure!
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
Mr. MINFORD: I rise to congratulate

any blame on the Minister of Agriculture,

I thoroughly agree with the Prime

of Northern Ireland.
With regard to the resolutions of the

although he and I to-day do not agree,
I say this about him, that he did all that
was humanly possible at Ottawa. I must

store cattle. Might I remind the Junior
Whip that Canada is prepared to put
46,000 store cattle into England inside

the Ulster farmer to-day is afraid to put
his hand out and purchase any cattle at
any price.

Regarding potatoes, I think the Minister
of Agriculture made a true statement
when he said there was almost an absence
of prices. The figures I have are last
year's figures. In 1932 we imported
£2,000,000 worth of Spanish potatoes
during the months of March, April, May,
and June. One of the reasons I give for
the low price of potatoes is that the
market for early potatoes was taken away
by the Spaniards, and I very much regret
to say that this year they are ready to
export to our islands from 500 tons to
600 tons a day.
The Junior Whip has said we must put
up proper supplies before we can control
imports. I would like to ask him is there
any sane man to-day who would suggest
that a farmer should grow potatoes at £1
per ton when you having coming in 500
to 600 tons of potatoes per day produced
principally by criminal and underpaid
labour. So long as these imports are
allowed to come in so long will the Ulster
farmers be deprived of their rightful

available before preventing imports.
believe it is not of course in the hands

We are told that the great underlying
principle of the Conference at Ottawa
was to give a market to the Britisher
first; to the Colonial, second, and to the
foreigner as we required him.
If you
look at these figures for Spanish potatoes
I think you will agree that the Spaniards
are getting first place in the market; they
are getting 4/8 per cwt., because, according to their money market, our pound
is worth 25/- to them. I say without fear
of contradiction that so long as you allow
the Spaniards to dump their stuff in our
markets so long will the Ulster farmers be
deprived. I agree that Canada has a
right to send their stuff here, but I do
not agree that two wrongs make a right.
I do not for a moment agree that because
the Irish Free State sends her cattle here
Canada should do the same. After all,
during the war the British farmers were
able to feed not only themselves and the
industrial population, but practically half
of the troops in the field. What we did
from 1914 to 1918 we surely can do in
1933.
•
I feel that we will never get away from
this terrible depression in our industrial
and agricultural life until the Imperial
Government take some steps to sweep from
our markets these products produced
under conditions which we ourselves
would not tolerate. To-day in Northern
Ireland we have unfortunately a big list
of unemployed. There are upwards of
3,000,000 people unemployed in England.
Surely it would be a sane policy for the
Minister of Agriculture in the Imperial
House to advise his Government that it
would be better to give these men work
to produce food on which to live than
perhaps to starve in the midst of plenty.
The late Mr. Chamberlain said in his time
that the time would come when we would
have starving people in the midst of
plenty. I almost believe that that day is
here. There are to-day in Northern Ireland, in the farmers' fields and houses,
hundreds of tons of potatoes practically
not worth marketing. In the very city in
which we are to-day we have hundreds of
people practically on the verge of starvation. Our Minister of Agriculture has
done all that is humanly possible to help
Ulster, but what we do need is the help of
the Imperial Government.
Although I am painting a dark picture
at the moment, I believe that better times
lie ahead. This Marketing Bill, which
will be introduced in the course of the
next few days, will be an enabling
Measure to give to the farmers of Ulster
an economic price for their produce. But
I am afraid that if we do not take into
our hands the controlling of imports this
Marketing Bill may not be such a great
boon as it should be. When you think
that to-day we import, roughly speaking,
£400,000,000 worth of foodstuffs, while
we produce somewhere in the neighbourhood of £300,000,000 worth, I believe
that the farmers should be producing at least half of those imports. We
must not forget that true wealth lies in
the land, and as long as the basic industry
of a country is in the position in which
agriculture is to-day so long I believe will
our unemployment continue. It is quite.
true, as the Junior Whip has said, that
we would require to have better purchasing power before agriculture can get on
its feet, but I believe it is possible, by
prohibiting these potatoes from coming
in and by giving us economic prices.
for our other products, to enable the
farmers to employ much more labour.
In the year 1914 we had 1,000,000

One thing that has been talked about

if the Ministry could have provided us

be in the position that we are in to-day;
but, unfortunately, owing to the bumper

flooded, and there was no outlet for us.
I hope the time will come when the importation of foreign potatoes will be stopped
altogether, so that we may have a chance
in the market which we think belongs to
us and which we ought to get.
As regards Canadian cattle, we have
heard a good deal on that subject. I think
the low prices that we are receiving today are not altogether due to the importation of Canadian cattle; that may be a
drop in the bucket. After all, our stores
suit the requirements of the English and
Scottish farmers far better than the
Canadian cattle. We would urge the
Government to put before us immediately
the Agricultural Marketing Bill.
We
are living in hope. Hope is the one thing

no matter what depression they may
come through. Sometimes we are up

more than cover the cost of production,
and give us a living for ourselves and our
families.

Mr. YOUNG: I should like to join in
the congratulations that have been extended to the Minister of Agriculture on
the presentation of these Estimates.
should like to congratulate the right hon.
Gentleman and his Department on the
efforts which they are making to improve
flax seed and to propagate new varieties.
Anybody who knows anything about the
flax trade in Northern Ireland can recall
that shortly after the war the flax crop
in Northern Ireland was almost destroyed
by the introduction of the so-called White
Blossom seed. No doubt it produced a
very big crop, and from the farmers' point
of view gave a very big yield. As new
seed it propagated to a large extent, but
when it came to be used in the flax spinning mills the quality was found to be so
poor that no flax buyer would buy White
Blossom seed if he knew it to be of that
variety. It was only when he did not
know it that he bought it, and he rued
his purchase bitterly when it got into
the hackling department of the flax
spinning mill. The J.W.S. seed was also
introduced, but it grew too long. By growing too long, it was more liable to be
beaten down by rain and wind, which,
unfortunately, are very prevalent in this
country. Flax that is lying down is
hardly worth picking up, and when the
fibre is too long there is a good deal of
waste.
I should like to congratulate the
Ministry on the three new kinds of seed
which they have recently propagated. One
is called "Stormont Cosmos" and another
is "Stormont Cirus." These both produce an extraordinarily good quality of
flax. The third quality, Pure Linen
J.W.S., is hardly so good. Last season
I knew cases in which those two qualities
of Stormont seed yielded nine stone per
peck, and produced 10/- in the open
market. On the average, there are 5
pecks of seed to the acre. Taking it at
nine stone to the peck, we get 50 stone per
acre, and at 10/- a stone, that is £25
sterling to the acre. In my opinion, that
compares very favourably with potatoes.
A yield of eight tons of potatoes to the
acre at £3 10s a ton-and farmers would
give their eyes to get that price at the
present time-would produce £28. A
yield of six tons to the acre, which is a
much more likely yield, at £3 10s a ton,
would produce £21 to the acre. Unfortunately, the price of potatoes is much
more like £1 a ton.
I admit that 10/- a stone for flax, and
nine stone to the peck are exceptional, but
even if you take the average price for the
whole of last season's flax crop, 7/- a
stone, and take the moderate yield of
seven stone to the peck, at 5 pecks to the
acre, you have 38 stone per acre, and at
the average price of 7/- a stone you get
£13 10s per acre, which is as good as 30/-
per ton for potatoes. This compares
reasonably with the price of potatoes. The
acreage of Irish flax last year was 6,093
acres, and agricultural experts estimate.
that this year the figure is nearer 20,000
acres, so it would look as if the farmers
were beginning to realise that the flax
crop is a much better paying crop than
some people imagine.
The hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) said that flax-growing in Northern
Ireland was a dead industry. I am only
sorry he is not in the House to hear this
statement. Questions have been raised
time and again about the importation of
foreign flax. Hon. Members opposite
would like to see a 10 per cent. import
duty on flax coming into Northern Ireland. Unfortunately, I have not the
exact figures-I am only quoting from
memory-but hon. Members seem to forget that the total tonnage of flax produced
throughout the world is 645,000. All that
Northern Ireland produced last year was
1,600 or 1,700 tons of flax. With 645,000

have far more faith in the Lane-Fox

periods of the year for licensing. It so
happens that a calf calved after the 1st
July, 1932, would not be up for licensing
until about the 1st September, 1933. By
that time that calf has reached the age of
fourteen months. Those who know anything about cattle breeding know a calf
can be used from nine months old. Very
often, I am afraid, a great many bulls
that happened to be calved in July or
August are used several months before
the date of licensing comes round, and
they are rightly rejected by the Ministry's
inspector. I think something should be
done to reject unsuitable animals before
they have done a great deal of harm. I
think the Minister of Agriculture should
take note of this so that something should
be done to see that the bulls are rejected
before they have an opportunity of doing
harm to the cattle breeding of our area.
I hope I have made myself quite clear.
The right hon. Gentleman understands

The hon. Member for Pottinger was
very eloquent on the farming industry.
He was saying something for the downtrodden farmers of Northern Ireland,
but he rather put his foot in it when
he suggested that our farmers are not
nearly so well off as the farmers of the
Irish Free State. Representing an agricultural community, I can say without
fear of contradiction that there is not
a farmer in my constituency that would
want to transfer into the Free State,
even with the reduction in annuities
which Mr. De Valera has promised.
Even with the higher annuities, I believe
the farmers are more satisfied to remain
in Northern Ireland than to transfer to
the Free State, in spite of the glittering
prospects held up to them by Mr. De
Valera, that is, the reduction of the
annuities by one-half. If the hon. Member for Pottinger has not something
better than that to allure my farmer constituents to go into the Free State, I
am glad to say that bait will not be taken
by the farmers in our area.
May I say this also, that I have just
as much sympathy with the farmers as
any Member of this House, on either side
of it, and I know just as well perhaps as
any Member the hardships of the farmers
at the present time. I know the farmers
are up against it, but I believe that the
majority of them are quite prepared to
do their utmost, with the assistance of
the Ministry of Agriculture and the Government, to pay their annuity in full and
remain loyal to the people who have been
such friends to them in the past.
I cannot allow the statement made by
the hon. Member for Pottinger against
the landlord class to go unchallenged, because I was particularly favoured by
living under a landlord whose name 18
revered in that area, and who, I am
glad to say, treated his tenants in a way
that could not be excelled by any man.
In a short time-we may live to see it
-the farmers in Northern Ireland will
be able to step out into farms not only
free from annuity but, as long as they
keep this Government in power, free from
all rates. I am glad to say there is only
a small minority of grousers. But I do
think they do not return the thanks or
feel the gratitude to the Government
they are entitled to for having done so
much for them. The Government of
Northern Ireland, with the co-operation
of the Ministry, have done a great deal
to make the lot of the farmers easy.
They have relieved them of the intolerable burden of rates. They have provided cheap loans at a moderate rate of
interest. I believe that the farmers will
yet weather the storm, and with the cooperation and sympathy of the Government they will not be in a worse position,
at any rate, than the farmers of any
other area.
I congratulate the right hon. Gentleman
on what the Ministry have been able to
do. I know this, because I am in touch
with the Ministry, that no agriculturist
and no representative of an agricultural
community, coming to the Ministry of
Agriculture with any fair proposition, is
ever sent away without getting, at any
rate, an acknowledgement and, if possible,
getting his wishes complied with. I know,
as a member of the County Council and
of the County Committee of Agriculture,
we appreciate very much, not only the
financial assistance, we also appreciate
very much the helpful suggestive assistance we receive, not only from the right
hon. Gentleman himself, but from the
officials who co-operate with the members
and the farmers themselves. I support
the Estimate put forward by the right
hon. Gentleman whole-heartedly, and I
think that the schemes submitted by the
Ministry will, eventually, bring the
farmers to brighter and better times. I
am convinced if we are ever going to get
better times in Northern Ireland the first
thing we must do is to revive agriculture,
and if agriculture is not revived I think
we cannot lay any charge on the Government.

CLASS VI. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That a sum, not exceeding £86,272, be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending 31st March, 1934, to defray
the expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture in respect of agricultural education and research, improvement of livestock, agricultural development and
credit, afforestation and diseases of
animals, including sundry grants in
aid."-(Note-£28,000 has been voted
on account.)
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: This
Vote shows a net increase of approximately £10,500, but it is more apparent
than real. A sum of £1,000 is accounted
for by increased expenditure under the
Marketing of Eggs Act. Hon. Members
will recall that under the recent Act and
by agreement with the trade, a sum of
approximately £3,300, shown under subhead O, is collected from the trade to be
utilised by the Ministry in improving
marketing conditions at the producers' end
of the trade. The scheme, which has been
in operation for 18 months, has been an
outstanding success and has the enthusiastic support of our licence-holders. Hon.
Members will appreciate the wisdom of
the policy in developing this scheme
gradually.
Sub-head F1, grants to county agricultural committees, shows an increase of
about £7,000. This is due entirely to the
fact that the Development Fund which,
for the past six years, provided £7,000
per annum for placing premium bulls,
boars and rams in our poorer districts, is
now exhausted. I should like to take
this opportunity of thanking my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) for agreeing to
the provision of this sum in the Estimates.
As I have explained on previous occasions,
the major part of the sum is expended on
the placing of premium sires in our poorer
and backward districts. The continuance of our efforts to improve the type
and quality of our live stock was never
more necessary than it is to-day, indeed it
is a vital factor in our agricultural prosperity. The stage has been reached when
even the critic will admit the great
improvement which has been brought
about and is in progress in our live stock
population.
""
an
There is, however, one criticism which
I would like to refer to. It is only too
often maintained and insinuated that, as
far as cattle are concerned, our live stock
improvement schemes, whilst improving
the type of cattle, are "driving the milk
out of the country.' This is not true.
Our recorded heifers in 1924
gave
average yield of 440 gallons, and in 1931,
with five times the number of recorded
heifers, the average yield was 540 gallons;
a remarkably good average for heifers and
one which shows, without any possibility
of contradiction, that the Ministry's
policy of combining type and quality with
milk production, in other words, the
evolution of the dual purpose cow, is
succeeding beyond our confident hopes.
The only other item to which I need
refer is Sub-head M, Agricultural Credits,
which shows an increase of about £1,000.
This is due entirely to the cost of the
new loan scheme, which enables farmers
to borrow money for the purchase of stock,
fertilizers and feeding stuffs at
at the
exceedingly low rate of interest of 3 per
cent., a much lower rate than they could
obtain in any other part of the British
Isles.

Ministry have shown substantial reductions in expenditure. I think it,
however, advisable, to repeat the warnings
I gave last year. The proportion of our
revenue spent in the development of our

Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. NIXON: Last year I made some

often wondered as I read these Estimates
what they survey, what all the surveying
