Department under the Government that is
not surveying. The country was surveyed
long ago. A country does not get any
bigger, and it does not get any smaller,
unless in some places where erosion is
caused by the sea. I do not think there

another, and I cannot see how it takes

is not all by any means. I do not know

Mr. SPEAKER: Before we come to
the questions, the House will observe that
there are a large number of questions to
be asked to-day. Strictly speaking,
according to a ruling made by the late
Speaker, six questions are the limit which
one Member can ask during one day's
sitting. I propose to extend that in
future to between eight and twelve,
according to the number of questions
asked by other hon Members. In the
meantime, to-day I propose to take as
many of the questions as we can get
through before half-past Three o'clock.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

PORK PRICES IN BELFAST AND
PROVINCIAL MARKETS.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if, in
provincial pork markets in Northern
Ireland, a cut is made on the price of
heavy carcases on the grounds that such
are too heavy to secure top price, while
in the Belfast markets the heavy carcases
draw the better price.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir E. Archdale): Curers of bacon and
hams require pigs that are not above
certain weights, and when such recognised weights are exceeded it is the
practice to cut the price. I am not aware
that so far as purchases for curers are
concerned any different policy is adopted
in the Belfast market.
INSPECTION OF PIG CARCASES.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if pig
carcases before being shipped are inspected for disease, etc., while carcases
for local retail and consumption in certain parts of Northern Ireland are subject to no inspection.
Sir E. ARCHDALE: All pork carcases for export must be inspected and
certified to be free from disease under the
Regulation of the Agricultural Produce
(Meat Regulation) Act (Northern Ireland), 1930; so too must all carcases
entering bacon factories for curing. The
question of the inspection of fresh pork
for local consumption is a matter for the
public health authorities concerned.

TUBERCULOSIS.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can give a full
report on the tests carried out by the
Ministry of the Spahlinger treatment for
tuberculosis.
Sir E. ARCHDALE: A report on the
tests carried out by the Ministry of the
Spahlinger treatment for tuberculosis in
cattle has been published, and I am
handing a copy to the hon. Member. A
full report cannot be given until these
experiments are completed.

9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been called to the fact that musk rats
have now appeared in the Irish Free
State; and whether he proposes to take
steps to meet this new Border menace.
Sir E. ARCHDALE: The reply to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative. My Ministry has already made an
Order prohibiting the importation into
or the keeping in Northern Ireland of
musk rats.

BOGS AND LUCERNE CLOVER.
14. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime Minister
whether he can state the policy of the
Government in respect to bogs and also
Lucerne clover, and whether he can state
the present position in regard to these
matters.
Sir E. ARCHDALE: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Work on the reclamation of overcut
peat land with a view to ascertaining the
best means of bringing such land into a
condition suitable for the growing of
crops, has been in progress for some time
and is still proceeding. The results so
far have shown that with suitable drainage and proper manuring peat land may
be made capable of producing very satisfactory crops of potatoes of a quality
suitable for the seed trade. The scheme
of land improvement, in which unemployed labour is utilised includes appropriate work in connection with the
reclamation and cultivation of suitable
areas of peat land. The Ministry provides advice in regard to drainage and
reclamation work, and also in regard to
and the
the manuring and
varieties of
potatoes to be planted.
A number of tests in each of the six
counties to determine the suitability of
Lucerne for average conditions in Northern Ireland were inaugurated two years
ago. While the majority of the plots
laid down could only be regarded as
failures, in a few cases where the soil
proved to be suitable the results were
satisfactory in the first year.
principal difficulty in obtaining a successful crop was that of keeping down weeds
in all stages of growth.
The
In view of the experience gained from
these trials the Ministry is not in a
position to advise the general cultivation
of Lucerne as a farm crop in Northern
Ireland; where, however, the condition
of the land is suitable and the crop can
be kept free from weeds and properly
cultivated, there seems to be a possibility of producing a reasonably good
yield of produce.
Mr. NIXON: What is the nature of
the manure the Minister recommends for
bogs?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
must give notice of a question of that
kind.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Does the hon. Member
for Woodvale consider that answer quite
satisfactory?
Mr. SPEAKER: That is a matter of
opinion.

BELFAST INFIRMARY DOCTORS-
QUALITY OF FOOD.
32. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the resident doctors in the Belfast Union
Infirmary complained of the quality or
quantity of the food supplied to them
in the institutions; and what steps, if
any, he has taken or proposes to take in
order to ensure that the future supply of
food to the doctors of this institution will
be sufficient and wholesome.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The resident
medical officers in Belfast Infirmary made
a complaint to the Board of Guardians
in September last, regarding some fish
that had been served; also regarding the
lack of variety of the food.
A Committee of the Board of Guardians
inquired into the complaint and came to
the conclusion that the food was of proper
quality, and that the complaint was not
justified. Their conclusion was endorsed
by the Board of Guardians.
No complaints have been made since.
The Ministry was not asked to intervene in the matter, and there is no reason
why it should do so.

PENSIONERS IN UNION
INFIRMARIES.
36. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if boards of
guardians in Northern Ireland have been
stopping all or portion of pensions payable to old age and insurance pensioners
while in union infirmaries for treatment;
whether the master of the workhouse has
been paid a commission on the amount
deducted from these old people in addition to his salary; whether the guardians
in some cases allege that these deductions
are made with the consent of the pensioners concerned; and what steps, if
the Minister has taken or proposes to
any,
take in order to ensure that the alleged
consent is not obtained or given under
duress or pressure.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply.
Mr. NIXON: The Minister of Labour
is present and this question is addressed
to him. He has a personal knowledge of
what I am referring to, and it is really
not fair that he should avoid answering.
Mr. SPEAKER: That may be so, but
right hon. Members can always delegate
their questions to other right hon. Members if they consider the matter dealt with
belongs to the Department of the other
Minister and not their own.
Sir DAWSON BATES: From the
answer the House will see quite clearly
that this is a matter that belongs to my
Department.
I have been asked to reply.
Boards of guardians are authorised by
statute to recover from inmates of their
infirmaries contributions towards the cost
of maintenance where the inmate is in a
position to make such a contribution.
In a number of cases pensioners have
agreed to make payments of this character,
and have given authority to the master or
other official to collect their pension and
to pay it over in whole or in part to the
guardians.
Formerly the official concerned was remunerated by a commission on the amount
collected, but my Department issued a
circular last year requiring boards of
guardians to put an end to this method
of payment.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I have no reason to think that
the officials concerned have been guilty
of any impropriety in carrying out their
duties.

Minister whether it is a fact that it has
been known in the city of Belfast that oldage pensioners have lost their pensions in
this way without their consent, and in
view of that is he prepared to issue a
definite order that pensions must not be
stopped other than a relative proportion
of the pensions for the support of the
inmates?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
that any pensioner has lost his pension in
the circumstances referred to by the hon.
Member.
Mr. NIXON: Might I ask is it not a
fact that an official of the Ministry of
Labour had to be sent to the Infirmary
to see that his consent was properly
received?
Sir DAWSON BATES: There was no
necessity to send anyone.
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask if the
Minister is aware-I will have to refer to
Hansard that I proved a case to his
satisfaction where the board of guardians
had taken
a pension illegally from a
pensioner without his consent? He will
find that in Hansard.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE—
COURTS OF REFEREES.
37. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that there
is grave discontent amongst the unemployed with the decisions of the courts
of referees and the umpire; and whether
he will take steps to ensure that before a
person's claim is heard by an incomplete
Written Answers
Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
court the person's right to demand a full
court is verbally explained to such person.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): As the courts and the umpire
give very careful and impartial consideration to all claims, I do not think it is reasonable to assume that there is grave discontent amongst the unemployed with the
decisions, as the question suggests.
Of
course it is natural that when a claim is
rejected the claimant would prefer it to
have been otherwise, but obviously that
is unavoidable. I understand that it is
made perfectly clear on all occasions to
the claimants that they need not have
their cases heard unless the court is fully
constituted, and that before a hearing
takes place without the court being fully
constituted the claimant is asked to sign
a consent.
RECRUITMENT OF LABOUR FOR
ROAD WORK.
38. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether his attention has been
called to a newspaper report of the 25th
April, 1933, in which the hon. Member
for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) was alleged
to have stated at a meeting of the County
Council when discussing the system of
recruiting labour for road work, that "at
each of these exchanges there was a
number of men receiving unemployment
benefit while others were signing on for
work but got no benefit. It was likely
that men getting benefit would be allocated work so as to save the unemployment fund. Men who were merely signing on and others who were out of work
got no employment whatever;" whether
this statement is, in fact, an accurate
description of the policy of the Ministry
in selecting men from the labour exchanges for work, and, if so, whether he
will take immediate action to have this
policy discontinued.
Mr. ANDREWS: The statement attributed to the hon. Member for South
Tyrone does not set out correctly the
system of the recruitment of labour for
road work. The practice followed is to
submit a list of men to the county surveyor, in the selection of whom preference
is given to the most suitable persons, to
married ex-Servicemen with dependents,
and to those who have been longest out of
work. No preference is given to men
drawing benefit over men who are not.

It has, for example, been necessary to
make some changes in the messenger
staff, since a slightly larger number of
messengers is required during the actual
sittings of the House than was the case
when the sittings were at College Green.
The need for this increased staff is due,
partly, to the larger extent of the
premises, and partly to the increased
number of visitors and the introduction of
the annunciator system. As against
this, it is now a simpler matter while the
House is sitting to withdraw messengers
temporarily from the Administrative
Departments in which they are employed,
and it has, therefore, been found possible
to reduce the permanent staff of messengers by one and to make increased use of
messengers temporarily withdrawn from
the Administrative part of the building.
Hon. Members may rest assured that the
messenger staff employed in the House is
kept at the lowest figure that is consistent with the proper conduct of our
proceedings.
There is a relatively small increase of
£476 on the entire Vote. There have
been savings owing to the fact that it
has been found possible to dispense with
the services of a typist, a caretaker, and
the charwomen who used to be employed
to clean out the former Parliament Buildings. There has also been a considerable
decrease in the Estimate for incidental
expenses. The figure £925, in respect of

cleaning this building, and it will not, I
am sure, be considered excessive when

for the Members here as compared with

had in the city. The residue of the £925
is made up of the share of the cost of
telephonists attributable to the Houses
of Parliament. I beg to move.

The Prime Minister is not any more

than a hungry workman whose home
is bare of the necessaries for his

get the orders can book them the shareholders protest against the orders being
brought forward.
I represent what I used to call the

individuals. They meet perhaps in some
pleasant place down town. They hold a
meeting. That is the decision of the
Cabinet, and all the other Members
agree. No such thing exists in Northern
Ireland as a Cabinet. Therefore,
Cabinet Offices should go although they
are under their respective headings.
When I come to that I will move their
deletion.
But for the Prime Minister to have
three shorthand typists, one principal
and one higher executive, one permanent
secretary and one Parliamentary secretary, two policemen for driving his car,
£1,750 for a Daimler car and £120 for
running expenses of the car, and after all
that has been met, he charges the people
of Northern Ireland with £200 travelling
expenses back and forward to his own
home in England that is something
the people of Belfast want to consider.
I remember the outcry in the "Evening
Telegraph" and the Tory morning newspapers, when Ramsey MacDonald, now
your Socialist Prime Minister, received a
motor car from an admirer and the great
howl that went up from the Tory Press
about the conduct of this gentleman, who
was unpatiotic, who wanted the Germans
to overrun England, and who was not
in favour of the war. He declared for
the nationalisation of all industry. That
motor car he got was dearly earned by
his services to the country. When he
became Prime Minister he did not ask
for an official motor car to be sent to him.
He did not ask for two drivers costing
the State £550. He did not ask for the
running expenses of his car, nor yet did
he ask for two charwomen to do his washing, nor did he ask for two gardeners to
do his gardening. He went into office
without fee or reward.
Mr. ELLIOTT: He got his salary.
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes; he
got the
£5,000, and paid for the upkeep, and
with all his liabilities he was able to
place himself in a better financial position
than he was previous to going in. He
did not spend all the money on the
official residence. There is no official
motor car in London, no official motor
car in Canada, no official motor car in
America for Mr. Roosevelt, and
official motor car in the Free State.
These gentlemen have got to pay for the
upkeep of all their staff, the same as any
other individual Member who carries on
Parliamentary work in a big way, and
why the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland should ask us to pay for his staff
I have yet to hear explained by himself.
I am going to move that this salary be
cut down to £170 a year.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Gentleman must do it in one of two ways;
either to reduce the sum mentioned in
the Vote or to reduce the individual
items.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am trying to keep
myself in order in the Committee and calculate at the same time. I do not believe the barmaids (laughter)-the
charwomen should be allowed to him at
all. My wife has got to do all the
charing and her household duties.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I am sorry for her.
I
Mr. BEATTIE: You are sorry.
had better tell her. She has got to do
all because I am not in a position to get
the State to pay for it. No one pays
for my papers.
I think the total amount
of the reduction will be £5,000.
The CHAIRMAN: That is on the
Vote?
Mr. BEATTIE: On the total. I will
tell you how I make it up. The Prime
Minister's salary to be £170, as he has
got a free house and everything appertaining to the upkeep of it, costing us a
very substantial amount in the year running into thousands. After that he has
secretaries with very large salaries, who
do all the work for him. Therefore, he
has no work to do. He has a head
messenger, who has more money than a
Member of Parliament, to do all the
necessary town visits required, and I am
sure he does not get off very easily.
Therefore the Prime Minister does not
require a motor-car. He may require
one of the policemen to guard him against,
perhaps, some-
Mr. ELLIOTT: Socialists.

Mr. BEATTIE: We do not believe in
taking away life, because we cannot give

necessary. Give him one typist with a

think you will give him all that is
necessary for the job he has to carry out.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Stamp his card.
not
Mr. BEATTIE: No, we will not stamp
his card, because with £170 and £250 he
has over the £5 a week and he is not entitled to receive stamps on his card. I
want to know from the right hon. Gentleman what is the £200 travelling expenses
spent upon when he has £1,488 for
contingencies of his office. Does he get
a return ticket first-class to and from his
home? We in Ulster know that he lives
in London. Surely we are not paying
first-class fare to and from London. If
we do, then you are entitled to pay my
2d fare from the Holywood Arches up
here. Then you will have a motor-car
on your hands. What can you do with
it? Do not put it to Government
auction, because if you do you will get a
very small bid for it. But use it at that
door there for Members who have not
motor-cars, and who, on wet nights, have
to walk three-quarters of a mile before
they get to a tram. I notice this motor-car
is used for taking the Prime Minister
from that door to the Castle. Two men,
costing £550 and motor-car expenses £120,
to take the Prime Minister from the
entrance of this House down to the Castle.
He is too lazy to walk, though a good
walk would do him good. I hope that
when we have this revised Estimate there
will be a further reduction shown in consequences of sacrifices made by Ministers
of £500 each, and if that is done it will
assist to alleviate the distress in Northern
Ireland, and will help to feed the hungry,
who are clamouring for bread at the
present time and cannot get it. I have
the greatest possible pleasure in moving
that this Estimate be reduced by the sum
of £5,000.
Mr. NIXON: I think this Estimate
should be reduced, because the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland is, without
exception, the best paid Prime Minister
in the world. His allowance is not subject to income tax, which is a very substantial benefit and, in addition, he has
an allowance for travelling. On top of
all that he is provided with a motor-car,
and that motor-car is used to convey the
Prime Minister to political meetings,
which is absolutely wrong. This motorcar was voted for the use of the Prime
Minister only in his capacity as Prime
Minister, and he has no more right to use
it for political purposes than I have. Yet
he is so using it. Then I come to the permanent secretary to the Cabinet. He has
a salary of £1,720. It is a most extraordinary thing that when everyone in this
House, every Member of Parliament, and
every civil servant, was subjected to a
15 per cent. reduction he was exempted.
In connection with the visit of the
Prince of Wales to Northern Ireland, the
secretary to the Cabinet was made the
chairman of the committee which had
charge of the arrangements. As I
pointed out before, that committee should
have consisted of Members of this House,
with some outstanding man in the chair,
and the secretary to the Cabinet should
have been the secretary to that committee.
I do not know how he discharged all his
duties as chairman of that committee, but
I will give the Committee one illustration. Since he was the chairman of the
committee he was responsible for this
incident. There is nothing too good for
the Prince of Wales. That is my attitude.
You will recollect that the night the
Prince of Wales went away he inspected a
guard of honour of the Royal Ulster Constabulary at the Northern Counties Railway Station. The evening before that
a gentleman came in to the Town Clerk
of Belfast, and told the Town Clerk that
this inspection was to take place, and
that the place was badly lighted. The
Town Clerk got in touch with the Electricity Department. That department
does not keep a stock of lamps or anything like that, but, at all events,
nothing is too good for the Prince of
Wales, and the department got busy.
The result was that when the Prince of
Wales went to inspect that guard of
honour on his way home I think I could
have read the smallest type in the "Belfast Telegraph" on the far side of the
street. Any person with any natural
courtesy would have said "Thank you"
to the Town Clerk and to the Electricity
Department, but I can assure you that
that was not done, and it has not been
done since. That is evidence of very

bad manners and very bad breeding, and

The whole position is preposterous,
because this Cabinet Secretariat is not

private secretary, a principal at £1,044 a

Since the motor car was voted I cannot

to
The Prime Minister, according
what he said yesterday, prays every
day. I wonder if he remembers when
he takes this money that there are forty
thousand people totally unemployed in
Belfast alone. Yet he can indulge in
prayer and thanksgiving every day
that he selected the Minister of Agriculture for his position. He has a
lot in this Estimate to be thankful for.
I do not know where he prays. There is
not a church convenient, but perhaps,
when the spirit of devotion takes possession of him, he marches up the hill, step
by step, to the precincts of this House,
and on bended knees and with bowed head
offers his fervent prayer in the shadow
of the picture of the Pope, though I
doubt very much if the Pope would
have congratulated him on selecting the
Minister of Agriculture, of all men, who
happens to be the head of the Orange
Order.
Last year I moved a reduction of the
Prime Minister's salary by £2,000, and
he said he was hurt. I was glad of it

under the circumstances. I thought

the same subject.
But there is a more important thing
still, that the Prime Minister encourages
and tolerates, and it is a matter that is
condemned, as the Prime Minister knows,
all over England and Scotland.
The
Prime Minister standing there justified,
or attempted to justify, a number of
Cabinet Ministers being directors of companies. He accepted responsibility for
that, standing there. That is a thing
that is not allowed in the Mother of

arising here in Belfast. Important companies are beginning to think they will

which have a Minister at their head.
Whether they do or not it would be only

man was a factory or workshop inspector

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £15,655 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1934, to defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Commerce (15 & 16 Geo. V.,
c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 Geo. V., c. 4 (N.I.)"
-(Note-£5,100 has been voted on
account).
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Estimate before the
Committee represents the anticipated cost
to the Exchequer of administering the
various services performed by the
Ministry of Commerce during the
financial year 1933/34. This part of the
Ministry's Estimates is made up mainly
of expenditure on staff and on miscellaneous items such as postage and
travelling. Allowing for receipts appropriated in aid the total amount to which
the Committee is now asked to give its
sanction is £20,755 as compared with
Ministry of Commerce 1256
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
£20,214 last year, that is to say, a net
increase of £541. Hon. Members will
appreciate that these figures relate only
to Vote No. I and that, as will be seen
when they come to deal with Vote No.
2, the total sum which they will be asked
to sanction in respect of the two Votes
together is very substantially less than
the corresponding sum for the previous
year.
On previous occasions I have furnished
the Committee with detailed particulars
of the various services which fall to my
Ministry to administer, and I do not,
therefore, propose to take up the time of
the Committee with repetition of those
particulars with which, I have no doubt,
hon. Members are already familiar.
As regards what I may briefly term
"commercial intelligence services," I
think that it will suffice for me to say
that throughout the past twelve months
our manufacturers and traders have made
an increasing use of these services in
building up their selling organisations
abroad, in exploring the possibilities of
overseas markets and, generally, in enlisting the assistance of the Ministry in
those difficulties which inevitably arise
in the conduct of an export trade. I
should like, once again, to record my
appreciation of the assistance which the
Ministry has received from the Department of Overseas Trade, whose close and
cordial co-operation has been invaluable
in our efforts to foster the interests of
Northern Ireland trade. In this connection I should like to mention specially
the arrangements made by the London
Department for the inclusion of Northern
Ireland in the itinerary of those officers
of His Majesty's Diplomatic and Consular
Services serving overseas, who visited
Great Britain during the year.
There can be no doubt that the opportunity which has thus been provided to
Northern Ireland firms of meeting the
various British trade repesentatives in
our overseas markets is one which is of
the very greatest advantage to our exporting firms. During the financial year,
1932/33, visits to Belfast were paid by
the trade officers stationed in British
West Indies, Vancouver, the Argentine,
New Zealand and South Africa, and
seventy-eight firms availed themselves of
the opportunity of discussing their
business matters with these officers.
Another event deserving mention was the
visit paid to Belfast by the Manager of
the Export Credits Department, during
the course of which twenty-four firms
took the opportunity of discussing with
him the possibilities of using the Export
Guarantee Scheme in the conduct of their
overseas trade.
The financial year which has just
closed will always be memorable as
Britain's
having witnessed
dramatic
abandonment of her traditional free trade
policy. Almost in a night Great Britain
took her place among the protectionist
countries of the world. The imposition
of a general customs tariff was a matter
of greatest moment to Northern Ireland,
especially when it was followed by a
general revision of all the existing trade
agreements with the Dominions and the
Colonies. Hon. Members will appreciate that the opportunity thus presented
of securing for Northern Irish industries
such treatment as would enable them not
only to compete successfully in the home.
market but also to extend their trade
overseas, was one which my Ministry felt
bound to assist in developing to the full.
As was foreseen, when the Customs
Import Duties Act was passed and the
Ottawa Agreements were signed, foreign
nations have shown a disposition not
hitherto apparent, to discuss with Great
Britain ways and means by which
British trade could be accommodated by
them in return for concessions by the
United Kingdom. The Ministry of
Commerce has taken an active part in
keeping Northern Ireland's interests to
the fore both during the Ottawa
discussions and in the negotiations
which are still proceeding between the
British and certain foreign Governments.
Throughout these negotiations the Ministry has kept in the closest possible touch
with the Northern Irish trade interests
concerned and has taken steps to ensure
that their views are adequately presented
to the Imperial Department responsible
for the conduct of the negotiations on the
British side.
Before passing to the other functions.
of the Ministry, there is one other matter to which I feel hon. Members may
expect me to refer, namely the census of
production, for the cost of which provision was made in last year's Estimates.
I am glad to be able to inform the Committee that the taking of the census has
now been brought to a successful conclusion and that the report was placed on
sale at the beginning of this year.
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
2 MAY 1933
Hon. Members will recollect that in
introducing these Estimates in previous
years, I have referred to the participation
by Northern Ireland in exhibitions and
Empire shops which are organised from
time to time in the larger centres of
Great Britain by the Empire Marketing
Board, and of the policy of the Ministry
in taking advantage of the opportunity
for trade propaganda which these displays offer.
The continued success which has
attended our exhibitions and shops in
Great Britain is eloquent proof of their
utility from this viewpoint. As well as
providing a valuable medium of general
trade publicity, the exhibitions have been.
the means of introducing to the English
market new food products of Ulster
origin on a scale which could otherwise
have been attained only by an extensive
advertising campaign on the part of the
home producer.
At the five exhibitions at which sampling was carried on during the past
financial year, 29,582 samples of Ulster
produce were sold, and it may interest.
hon. Members to know that with every
sample package there is now enclosed a
card setting forth clearly the position of
Northern Ireland within the United
Kingdom. These exhibitions accordingly
afford us not only an opportunity for
propaganda for our foodstuffs, but they
also provide us with a means of bringing
home to the British public the fact that
Northern Ireland is part of the United
Kingdom and that trade with the
Province is free from the encumbrance
of any tariff or customs frontier. During the course of the year cases of misapprehension brought to the attention of
the Ministry have emphasised the necessity for propaganda of this kind.
As the Committee will be aware, the
conclusion of the Ottawa agreements has
raised the question of the future status
and activities of the Empire Marketing
Board, and this matter is at present being
considered by a committee in London.
Pending its report no provision has been.
made in the British Estimates for a continuance of the activities of the Board
after the 30th September next, and the
Estimate of my own Department has been
reduced on the assumption that the
activities of the Board in this direction
will be somewhat curtailed in the current
financial year as compared with last year.
As I explained in presenting last year's
Estimates the provision which is annually
sought in respect of Fishery Services is
no real measure of the Ministry's work
in that particular sphere. In point of
fact, the reduction of the State contribution to the Fishery Conservancy
Boards, even to vanishing point, would
be symptomatic of increased activities in
our inland fisheries, since the provision
which this Committee is annually asked
to make under this heading represents
the contribution from the Exchequer
necessary to make up the difference between the assumed expenditure of the
Boards and the revenue accruing to them
from the licence duties paid for commercial fishing engines and on salmon rods.
When fishery stocks are depleted the
revenue from licences naturally falls
while, in order to assist stocks to recover,
expenditure on their protection necessarily increases.
In such circumstances the Exchequer
is obliged to come to the assistance of
the Boards. Conversely, a state of affairs
in which, with our waters well stocked
with fish, all the professional fishermen
found full employment, and large numbers of anglers were induced, by the prospects of good sport, to take out licences,
would render the Boards entirely independent of Government assistance.
I am
afraid that I cannot hold out to the Committee any real prospect of this happy
state of affairs materialising in the
immediate future, but the repeated small
reductions which it has been possible to
make from year to year in the provision
under this head, indicate a trend in the
right direction.
While on the subject of Conservancy
Boards, I think that hon. Members will
be interested to learn that during the past
year the whole system of local fishery
administration has formed the subject of
an inquiry by a special committee. In
the course of the seven years during which
my Ministry has been responsible for
fisheries many matters have come to light
suggesting the need for a thorough
examination of the machinery which the
legislature has provided, and from time.
to time adapted, for carrying out the
executive functions which the various
Fishery Acts have brought into being.
The committee to which I refer has not
yet completed its task, but I am given to
understand that its report will shortly be
presented to me.
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
I am glad to be able to inform the
Committee that, despite the difficulty
experienced by herring curers elsewhere
in disposing of their cure, Northern Irish
cured herring, largely owing to the high
standard which has been set under the
Crown branding scheme, continue to enjoy the highest possible reputation in the
Continental markets, a reputation which
has ensured to them each year a ready
market at top prices. Before leaving the
subject of fisheries, I should inform the
Committee that our fishermen still continue to avail themselves of the assistance afforded in the purchase of gear and
equipment by the fishery loans scheme.
Each year a considerable number of fishermen are thus enabled to equip themselves
with nets, without which they could not
participate in the summer fishing, whilst
around the coast a substantial number of
fishermen now own well equipped fishing
boats, by means of which they are able to
earn an independent livelihood.
I need refer only in general terms to
the statutory functions of the Ministry in
connection with such matters as electricity, railways, canals, mines and quarries,
weights and measures, and with the registration of companies, friendly and industrial and provident societies. While it is
imperative that these functions should be
carried out with due regard to all the
interests concerned, they do not call for
detailed explanation here.
Hon. Members will observe that provision is made in the Estimates for continuing to utilise the services of the
barrister who acts for the Industrial
Assurance Commissioner in hearing and
determining industrial assurance disputes.
I have referred in previous years to the
increasing volume of work laid on my
Ministry by the Industrial Assurance
Acts. The past year has shown still
further increases. To avoid burdening
the Committee with figures it will be
enough for me to say that a large proportion of our people-most of them of
humble station-are covered by this form
of insurance and pay little short of a
million pounds per year in premiums.
The main volume of work consists of
the settlement of disputes referred to the
Industrial Assurance Commissioner by
policy holders, or by the industrial
assurance offices under the Act of 1924,
which empowered the Commissioner to
arbitrate on such matters. The numbers
of cases so referred has risen from 155 in
1925 to 970 in 1932-figures which are
eloquent as to the necessity for such provision, and to the extent to which those
whom it was intended to benefit have
availed themselves of the facilities. Unremitting care has been taken in these
cases, which often involve points of
principle of vastly greater importance
than is indicated by the amount at stake,
and the Committee will agree, I hope,
that nothing should be done to impair the
capacity of the Ministry to deal with
matters affecting the savings of a wide
public who, despite depressed conditions,
are giving such a striking example of
thrift.
Turning now to the details of the Estimate, the increase of £541, to which I
have already referred, is due to the award
of annual increments, the necessity for
increased typing assistance, and a reduction of £100 in respect of receipts
appropriated in aid. The staff of the
Ministry shows an increase of one typist
as compared with last year. In this connection, I should explain that following
the removal of the Ministry in June,
1931, from Wellington Place where it
was accommodated in two buildings-to
15 Donegall Square West, one typing
post, in addition to assistance rendered
to the typing staff by a telephonist, was
surrendered, and it was hoped that, when
the Ministry was concentrated in one
building, a slightly smaller typing staff
would be sufficient to meet demands.
This hope was not realised, however, and
it has been necessary, since June, 1931,
to make numerous applications for temporary assistance, and one additional
typist has been continuously employed
since October of last year. None of the
other sub-heads of the Vote would appear
to call for special mention. I beg to
move.

Major MCCORMICK: I rise to support this Estimate, and to say that I
am not particular whether there is an
increase or decrease of an infinitesimal
amount, or a large amount for that matter, so long as the returns or profits to
the community and the employment of
our people are satisfactory and worth
while. That is the real point. I give
the Ministry of Commerce full credit as
a Department that is a source of good to
the Province. It is a Department that
has justified its expenditure in furthering industry and contributing to the good
of employer and employee. These Estimates of the Ministry of Commerce give
one an opportunity of speaking not too
critically of large expenditure and of
being helpful by showing where savings.
can be effected or expenditure put to
better use.
In my advocacy of economy I confess
to a feeling of disappointment inasmuch
as the results have not been as fruitful
as I expected. I admit that large sums
have been saved, but whilst certain items
have been cut out there are extra items,
which, I grant you, may be quite necessary. But the net amount involved,
after all, does not necessarily represent
economy. In short, my interpretation of
economy is doing away with useless expenditure that does not of itself bring
any return to our people. No doubt the
hon. Member for Pottinger will point out
to me many items that would not bear
out that contention, but that is where
our views diverge, because his eonomic
and social standard and usages are
opposed to mine.

like to say a few words in reply to the
suggestion that excessive charges are
being made by the Electricity Board.
As a very large consumer and one
intimately associated with the tariffs in

that, in my opinion, the tariffs of the
Board compare very favourably with those
in Belfast. There is a charge for the
floor area, plus ad per unit for the first
2,000 units and d a unit after that, and
you will find that that works out at not
one penny per unit. I think the Board
is perfectly reasonable in its demands,
and that for the services rendered the
charges compare very favourably with
those of any other source of supply, either
for light or heat. It has also been said
that the Board's charge for a cooker is
32s per annum. I have to accept the
word of the hon. Member for Pottinger
(Mr. Beattie) that that is correct. I do
not know whether it is or not. But I do
know that the charge in Belfast is £1 per
annum. Taking into consideration the
huge demand in Belfast and the facilities
that exist for repairs and transport, you
will realise that 32s a year would be a
perfectly reasonable charge to be made
by the Board. Because you must remember that that includes maintenance, and
in view of the fact that a first-class
cooker will cost from £12 to £14,I do not

installation.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): This is the
outstanding occasion when either the
Minister or I have an opportunity of
discussing the general work of the entire Department and the policy in dealing with the multitudinous activities in
which it is engaged. When we talk of
social insurance-
Mr. BEATTIE: Socialist.
Mr. GORDON- we are apt to forget that it includes every phase of insurance connected with the Ministry of
Labour, and not only unemployment insurance. Social insurance comprises
various schemes organised by the State
to compensate the working classes for
losses sustained chiefly in the course of
their industrial life. Collective responsibility is substituted for individual responsibility in the assumption of
financial burdens that would otherwise
fall upon certain individuals. The
accumulation of funds aids the unfortunate in times of distress, unemployment, sickness and old age. Speaking
in Manchester in 1930, Mr. J. H.
Thomas-
Mr. BEATTIE: Another Socialist.
Mr. GORDON: Mr. Thomas said:
No nation in the world stood higher
in its social obligation to the people.
than this country.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
There are evidences of an awakening
public opinion in other countries that are
anxious to follow the British system and
make provision for the wage earner in
times of sickness and unemployment.
Mr. NIXON: Germany?
Mr. GORDON: Germany, yes. In
connection with these services, our
Government has recognised as a moral
responsibility that the benefits paid in
Great Britain shall apply in Northern
Ireland and, I am glad to say that, notwithstanding the crippled condition of
industry with consequent unemployment
and sickness, we have met these obligations both in the spirit and in the letter.
Had we failed or retracted, a fresh
burden would have been imposed on the
local authorities to meet the exigencies,
and the entire community would have
been called upon to share in the wider
problem. When we assumed responsibility certain services were handed over
to us; others have been grafted on in the
intervening years with additional obligation and with a corresponding increase in
the work of the Department. I propose
to give a general survey of the work of
the various Departments of the Ministry.
Mr. NIXON: Do not, please.
Mr. GORDON: It is for the Committee to determine whether they are
operated with care and in the general
interest of the insured population, and it
is for the hon. Gentleman who interrupted to make good any points he wishes
to bring before the Committee. We have,
roughly, 265,000 persons in Northern
Ireland insured against unemployment,
of which 154,000 are men, 92,000 women
and 19,000 juveniles. Our main industries which give employment to these
insured workers are the linen industry,
shipbuilding and allied trades, the building trade, distributive trades, the
tailoring and dress industry. I think
that unemployment has touched bed-rock
in the linen industry. We have had
times of good and bad trade, but on the
whole we have cause to be thankful that
this industry is in the position to give
so much employment to our women
workers, and I am sure every Member of
the Committee is anxiously looking forward to the time when every spindle in
our mills and every loom in our factories
will be humming.
Our shipbuilding industry has been
extremely depressed during the past few
years. The last quarter of 1932 has been
the worst period both in Great Britain
and in Northern Ireland. Only 7,400
tons of shipping was laid down, and this
was the lowest on record.
Mr. BEATTIE: How much in Belfast?
Mr. GORDON: I am coming to that.
Early in March two keels were laid down
in a Belfast shipyard-
Mr. BEATTIE: Sure they are not
finished.
Mr. GORDON: But it requires time
before the stage of construction is reached,
when great numbers can be employed.
The future of the shipyards grows
brighter and the courage of shipyard
workers is strengthened by this hopeful
movement in this industry.
There are 73,346 unemployed persons
signing the live register at our Employment Exchanges. While the figure is
higher in relation to the population than
that in Great Britain as a whole, there
are many of the large industrial cities in
Great Britain where unemployment is
considerably higher than in the City of
Belfast, as, for instance, Glasgow,
Sheffield, Sunderland, and South Shields,
and if we compare unemployment by
districts of a similar character across the
water, it will show that, while the figures
for unemployment here are high, districts
across the water are in a worse position
so far as unemployment is concerned.
Hon. Members will remember that
the Unemployment Insurance Economy
Order No. 2 limited the period for which
a claimant was entitled to draw unemployment benefit to six months. After
the expiration of that period benefit
could only be paid to the applicant if he
or she satisfied the statutory qualifications
and, at the same time, proved that he or
she was in need of assistance. The
necessity for these conditions was
lucidly explained by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, in a
recent debate in this House, that it would
be fatuous of me to say more than this,
that the House laid down rules under the
Transitional Payments Act, 1932, for
dealing with claims of applicants, and the
full responsibility has been entrusted to
the public assistance committees-

Gentleman is to become a member of the

Mr. BEATTIE: You are not afraid of
me?
Mr. GORDON: No, but I want to say
something regarding the public assistance.
committees. These committees have performed a public and voluntary duty with
great care and discretion. Local employment committees, of which there are nineteen throughout our area, continue to
function, and are composed of workers'
representatives, employers' representatives and other public interests. There
are over 500 members attached to these
main committees, and their principal
function is to advise the Ministry to
increase the opportunity for employment,
to assist ex-Servicemen by getting
employers to become members of the
King's National Roll, and lastly, by cooperating with local education authorities.
Technical and other continuation
classes have been formed throughout the
exchange areas which give instruction to
the unemployed juveniles. One hundred
and fourteen classes were attended by
almost 2,000 boys and girls under 21
years of age, which means something in
the lives of these young people. There
is always damage wrought by unemployment during adolescence, and these
approved courses of instruction under the
Ministry of Labour develop to a high
degree future fitness for employment and
enable immediate action to prevent deterioration during the most formative
period of their lives. Section 15 of the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1930,
made provision for these courses of instruction in addition to the normal
Ministry of Education grant. The local
education authority in Belfast was unable to promote classes for unemployed
juveniles owing to lack of accommodation,
and to cope with the emergency the
Ministry decided to open a Juvenile Instruction Centre on the advice of the
Juvenile Advisory Committee, where
unemployed boys and girls between 16
and 18 years of age could attend classes.
This centre aims at maintaining and
increasing the general handiness and
adaptability of the boys and girls with
the idea of maintaining and increasing
their efficiency and mitigating the ill
effects of idleness. I am not satisfied
that we have reached the limit of useful
work, and I regret that we have neither
the means nor the accommodation while
we may have the desire to bridge the gap
between the school-leaving age and the
age we receive these juveniles into our
training centre. They not only receive
instruction, but every effort is made to
find them suitable employment. I
observe from the daily papers of this
week that classes are now being formed
for the unemployed in the College of
Technology.
We are still continuing our schemes of

months schemes costing three-quarters of

Mr. GORDON: During the past twelve
months thirty trade disputes were reported to the Department, and seventeen
of these were settled without having recourse to the strike weapon.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about the railway strike?
Mr. GORDON: It was not our fault.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was your fault.
Mr. GORDON: If there are strikes or
lock-outs it is not the fault of the Department. The doors of the Industrial
Relations Branch are always open to
receive complaints, either from employers
or workpeople, and they endeavour to
bring a satisfactory position out of any
chaos that may exist in any industry. As
I was saying, during the past twelve
months thirty trade disputes were
reported to the Department, and seventeen of these were settled without having
recourse to the strike weapon. 218,000
days were lost owing to stoppages of work,
largely due to the railway strike, which
was responsible for approximately 198,000
working days.
The only other strikes of any magnitude
which occurred during the year were at
Coleraine and Londonderry in connection with the building trade, and these
accounted for
for 16,000 working days.
Strikes and lock-outs are regrettable
incidents in industrial life, and it is difficult to measure the waste and loss
resulting therefrom. I am glad to say
that we are not often troubled with disputes of a serious and prolonged character, due to the common sense of our
working people and employers, who resort
to the machinery of the Department in an
effort to settle their differences.
Our Department continues to enforce
the determinations of the Trade Boards
Acts both by routine inspections and
investigation of complaints. During
1932, 1,277 inspections and visits were
made. These visits covered 11,492
workers. It was found during the
inspectors' visits that 116 firms were not
complying with the decisions of the Boards
in paying rates applicable to various
workers, and arrears of wages, amounting
to £463, were recovered in respect of 418
We
workers spread over these firms.
investigated 72 specific complaints and
found it necessary to take legal action in
10 cases, which we assumed to be sufficiently serious, and we pressed for
penalties for infractions of the Act.
When Trade Boards were first introduced those responsible were of the
opinion that, whether viewed from its
economic or its social effects, underpaid
labour was undesirable. Under-fed,
inadequately clothed, poorly housed
workers, are discontented workers and
often become a burden on the community.
These Boards were formed for the purpose of determining a minimum wage
under which the worker would not fall,
and that the wages paid in those trades
under the Trade Boards would be similar
to the wages paid in industries of a similar
character. Enlightened employers have
long recognised that cheap labour is
expensive labour and I am glad to say
that the decisions arrived at by these
Boards become effective.
There are 18 Trade Boards working
under an independent chairman, and their
work is delicate and intricate. They fix
time rates, piece-work basis time rates,
minimum time rates, overtime rates and,
on the whole, there is a general feeling of
good-will between all members of the
Boards, each endeavouring to see the
other's viewpoint and each working for
the prosperity of the industry they
represent.

that all accidents

Workers become so familiar with their

safeguards. Accidents occur owing to
shafting being unfenced. One of the fatal
accidents in 1932 was caused through
this, and we have taken steps to warn
employers of the legal requirement that
all shafting must be securely fenced or
safeguarded by some other method, such
as preventing the worker approaching it
while it is in motion.
During the year under review we instituted proceedings against 12 employers
for contraventions of the Factory Acts,
the majority being in respect of illegal
employment of women and young persons, and the remainder for failure to
protect shafting. There were 6,697
inspections made in factories, workshops,
and other places and, I must say,
employers are anxious and willing, even
at considerable expense, to carry out the
provisions of the Factory Acts.

past year on the position of a number of
representative societies. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, and I
were worried and anxious. We knew
how the funds of societies were being
depleted and, in many cases, deficiencies
had accumulated, and so we asked for a
report in order to get an idea of the result
of three years' experience. This report
disclosed that, almost without exception,
there had been a marked deterioration in
the three years from 1929 to 1931, and
that even societies which had hitherto
been regarded as gilt-edged had not only
ceased to accumulate surpluses but had
commenced to eat into their accumulated
reserves. In the case of other societies,
very heavy deficiencies had accumulated
during the three years.
It is very
necessary that societies should exercise the
greatest care so as to conserve their funds.
During the year our Department has
kept in close touch with societies with a
view to improving their organisation and
assisting in solving the difficult problem
We attribute
of heavy expenditure.
much of the loss disclosed by the actuary

-to unemployment, resulting in a

Mr. BEATTIE: Due to the policy of

unable to pay the total arrears at the

I am glad to be able to inform the
Committee that there is a high standard
of compliance with the Acts. It is still
unfortunately the case that legal proceedings have to be taken, from time to
time, against obdurate employers for
wilful evasion of the Acts, and it has also
been found necessary to prosecute workers
for failure to present cards to their
employers for stamping, in order to evade
their portion of the contribution. The
number of employers and workers who
failed to fulfil the statutory obligations
during 1932 was 223, and prosecutions
were instituted in these cases.
Last year
reference was made to the efforts of the
Department to put a stop to the traffic in
used stamps, and I am glad to say that
these efforts have been successful, as only
one person was convicted during the past
year. It, therefore, seems clear that this
traffic has been largely eliminated, but all
stamps of a suspicious appearance are
carefully examined by a special process,
and I would again reiterate what has
often been said in this House-that proceedings will be taken following the
detection of any case of this nature, and
the law will be strictly enforced.

Ministry of Labour
3 MAY 1933
Medical benefit is the latest important
addition to National Health Insurance.
There are 370,000 persons entitled to
medical treatment. This includes 2,000
disabled ex-Servicemen who are not
insured, but are included by an arrangement with the Ministry of Pensions. Out
of this total 354,000 persons have selected
doctors, but those insured persons who
have not yet selected a doctor are entitled to treatment if required. The
money accruing in respect of these persons
is distributed amongst the doctors in proportion to the number on their panel.
The payment to doctors falls under
three heads. For medical treatment the
payment is 9s per patient per annum.
The amount available for this payment
in the present year is £170,000, but
should the economy deduction continue
throughout the year, £17,000 would be
contributed to the Exchequer out of this
amount. Then there is a mileage payment to country doctors out of a fund
made up of 4d for each of the insured
population. This fund brings in,
roughly, £6,400, and the final payment
is for the provision of medicines by
doctors where no chemists are available.
The amount payable to doctors in outlying districts for this service amounted
to £5,500 for the past year.
The number of prescriptions issued in
1932 was 636,000, at a total cost of
£36,500. From this amount, however,
an agreed economy deduction was made
and paid to the Exchequer of £2,300.
There was a reduction in the number of
prescriptions issued this year as compared
with 1931, of 55,000, at a cost of £6,000.
The reduction was achieved by the steps
taken to bring to the notice of the doctors
generally methods of prescribing, by
which unnecessary cost or extravagance
could be avoided without, in any way,
sacrificing the interests of the patients.

We are asking the Committee to grant
us the sum of £3,926,223.
This is a
net decrease of £105,688 on last year's
estimates. The only increases are in respect of employment services and
widows', orphans' and old age contributory pensions. The Contributory
Pensions Act of 1929 made provision for
certain statutory increases to be paid into
the Pension Account out of moneys
provided by Parliament, and the
increased sum of £35,000 is in accordance
with the provisions laid down in the Act.
The increased provision for employment
services is due to the fact that the cost
of certain unemployment relief schemes,
which were works of road improvement,
was charged to the Road Fund, but this
year it has been decided that such works
shall be borne by this Vote. We are,
accordingly, providing a sum of £210,000
to provide employment, instead
£137,000 which was provided last year.
of
Under the other four Votes there are
decreases. The National Health Insurance Vote is reduced by £12,115. Part
of this is due to anticipated reductions in
the incidence of sickness and amended
rates of sickness and disablement benefit
for women. There will also be a reduction in the State grant for the cost
of prolongation. Unemployment is expected to cost the Exchequer £156,000
less this year. Interest charges are
expected to be £40,000 lower, due to a
reduction in the general rates of interest.
£7,000 less is expected to be required in
ordinary State grant, and it is estimated
that the provision necessary for transitional benefit will, in the aggregate, be
lower by £109,200.
Last year the percentage of unemployment for which we had to provide
averaged 28.3; this year we are estimating on the average percentage of 25.
The other decrease is under the Vote for
old age pensions. Last year we had to
make provision for 53 pay days or weekly
payments in the financial year, whereas
this year there will be the usual 52 payments, and this accounts largely for the
decrease of £35,000. I am not going into
details.

By putting into a factory a machine
capable of doing the work of from ten to
twenty men they are displacing that
number of workmen, and at the moment
the amount of machinery placed in mills,
and factories, and shipyards is responsible
for at least 50 per cent. of the discharges
from industry. To replace those 50 per
cent. discharges in industry there would
require to be new industries established,

Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
because the 50 per cent. cannot be got

The machines are in their place. The
Government are not competent to have

The solution that has to be carried out
is this. In Northern Ireland we have got
a limited amount of work available, and
we have at the moment 100,000 unemployed. The available work can only
absorb 50 per cent. of those 100,000. You
must immediately put your house in order
for reducing the working hours of the 50
per cent. who are employed and bringing
into industry the 50 per cent. idle, thus
giving an equal distribution of work as
well as an equal distribution of recreation.
That must be done without recourse to the
reduction of purchasing power, because
once you bring in a reduction of purchasing power you not only injure the industry
that you bring it into but you injure
other industry outside that, because
every
each industry is interdependent one upon

than those of anyone else, because if

will come
from where it is. We have more money
in the world to-day than ever we had in
our history. But we have fewer people in
receipt of that money than ever we had
in the world before. Is the hon. Gentleman aware that 80 per cent. of the population are compelled to live on 20 per
cent. of the wealth, while 20 per cent. of
the population have divided amongst them
80 per cent. of the wealth? Is he aware
of that? And is he aware that in the past
ten years the wealth of the country has
been brought into even fewer hands, and
that in 1930 the financial position was
that 90 per cent. of the people were living
on 10 per cent. of the wealth, while 10 per
cent. of the people had 90 per cent. of the
wealth? Hence, the reason for the great
blockade and for the things we require not
being at our hand to consume. The distribution is all wrong, and well the hon.
Gentleman knows it, and the wheels are
going to become so clogged that the workers themselves will have to take over the
distribution. It is not that we are prevented from having the things we need
because of the fact that the things are
not there. Everything we require is in
the stores, and if not in the stores then in
the land; but we cannot get at it because
the means of exchange are not at our command and the distribution is all wrong.
That fact in itself will right our social
system. It will not take any revolution
to right our social system. It will right
itself if it is allowed to continue in the
way it is at the moment.

employment and its effects, not only

end. Is a complacent attitude or resignation the proper way to take this

What does the Minister expect to happen?
What remedies or palliatives can he suggest to meet such a period as confronts
us?
Are we to wait until British brains
bring forward some new scheme that will
show us the industrial road to travel?
No doubt the Minister will say some
solution must be evolved. Whether we
stand on the threshold of a great economic
change that will alter our whole industrial outlook or whether this age of mass
production and whirling wheels will prove
our Waterloo is something to contemplate.
But we must go on. We must not wait.
It would appear to be something like
Hobson's choice, if I may put it that way.
Are we to get left in the race or take
a second or third position? I say no.
We may be assured at once, indeed we
know, that nothing will happen as by a
miracle. I say we must bring this about.
We cannot afford to let it go on.
It has been said that man is very
largely a creature of circumstances. Are
circumstances to rule the creature? I
do not believe in the view that we should
be the victims of circumstances. I ask
the Minister not to believe in that
attitude of negation, but to be positive
and bring it about. Are the brains of
Britain the only brains or mental consultants we have recourse to? I am
not speaking in any slighting manner
when I say this. I am sure that in
following British legislation we have

received through being connected with
Great Britain and that our people in
every way should have all the social benefits that were given to the sister country.
I need not enumerate these various Acts.
They are well known to the Committee.
The position is that Great Britain in
this vexed question cannot help us so far

concerned. According to the figures
Great Britain has far more unemployed

shall they look in vain ? I have faith in

spend here on domestic services approximately £7 8s per head of the population,
while in Great Britain the figure is

in an industrial area.
I ask the Committee to consider how
this gap has been closed in the past. To
put it in another way, I am going to try
to show how we have been living on the

per cent. basis. The answer is that we
have balanced our accounts by means of a
reduction of the Imperial contribution.

account of the residuary share of the

I do not think anyone in this Committee

The point I want to make is that we
are here voting money when, as I have
already said, there is a visible gap of half
a million pounds for which we do not
know we have money available. May I
say that there is no scope for increased
taxation? Readjustment may be possible.
It is not a solution to add any further

put on the rates in that way. I think I
have clearly shown that, unaided, we cannot support our domestic services on the
same level as Great Britain, and that
higher taxation is not practical politics.
Where does the solution lie? And this
is the point I wish to make. We here
are members of the United Kingdom-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)—and I ask,
as a Unionist, may not the solution lie
in a closer union and less autonomy in
this country, by the amalgamation of
those services which are on the same scale
of administration as in Great Britain; or
as part of the United Kingdom may
we not look for assistance from the
£25,000,000 we paid in contributions
when times were more prosperous?
The answer may lie between those two
suggestions. Yesterday a step was taken
to advance a republic in Ireland by
severing the tie of allegiance to the head
of the British Empire. Should we here,
as Unionists, not take a step closer, if
such a step is possible? (Hon Members:
Hear, hear.) I will conclude by saying
that the Minister of Finance is in no
enviable position, but he has the support
of a Unionist Committee.

things left for the present Government.
They are financially bankrupt. They have
no foresight in regard to the industries
of Northern Ireland. They can either
get back to the Imperial Parliament,

get better service, or they can have the

EXPENDITURE ON FIRST-CLASS
ROADS.
1. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether about two
years ago he asked the county councils
to curtail the expenditure on first-class
roads; whether in September last he
wrote to the Antrim County Council
saying that the grant for reconstruction
of first-class roads for 1933 would be 72
per cent.; and whether, when that
i
Council decided to reconstruct the five
mile length of road between Antrim and
Randalstown, he would only give 60 per
cent.; and in view of the urgency of this
work will he reconsider his decision and
give the full 72 per cent. and thus enable
the work to be carried out immediately.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer to the
first and third parts of the question is
in the affirmative.
As regards the second and fourth
parts, I would point out that it was laid
down in the circular issued in September
last that reconstruction grants at 72 per
cent could only be given where the Ministry was satisfied that the circumstances
were most pressing and exceptional, and
that no cheaper form of construction
would suffice.
These conditions are not satisfied in
the present instance, and, therefore, a
grant at a higher rate than 60 per cent.
cannot be given.
Mr. MINFORD: Is the Minister not
satisfied that the conditions are pressing
in this particular matter?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I would
point out to my hon. Friend that the
primary object of the Road Fund is to
supply good roads.
Mr. MINFORD: As I am not satisfied with the answer, I will raise the
question on the Adjournment.

IRISH FREE STATE AND ULSTER
ARTISTS.
4. Mr. McNEILL (for Mr. Henderson)
asked the Prime Minister whether, in
view of the recent Free State boycott of
Ulster artists' work, he can state what
steps the Government propose to take
to protect our artists' interests from
being penalised in this manner; and
whether he is prepared to advise the
Government to encourage Ulster artists
and support home industry by giving
instructions that all official paintings be
painted in future by Ulster artists.
The PRIME MINISTER: With
regard to the first part of the question,
the hon. Member will appreciate that the
selection of works of art for exhibition
must be a matter wholly within the discretion of the Free State authorities
themselves, and that it is not one in
which this Government could intervene in
any way. With regard to the second part
of the question, however, I would inform
the hon. Member that my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Commerce, is
giving active consideration, in collaboration with his colleague, the Minister of
Education, to the formation of a Committee, the function of which will be to
recommend such steps as may be
necessary to forge a closer link between
art and industry in Northern Ireland and
thereby to improve the position of the
artist by securing a truer recognition of
his importance to the modern industrial
fabric.

Affairs. In the first instance, however,

These expenses
are ultimately recovered from the Road

The Committee is aware that the
activities of the Ministry fall generally
under two main heads-i.e., Home Office
services and local government services.
In connection with the administration of
the Home Office Division of the Ministry,
one of the most important aspects is the
preservation of law and order, and this
brings me, naturally, to the question of
the police forces.
In this respect I am glad to be able to
say that during the past year the police
forces of Northern Ireland have carried
out their duties in a most satisfactory
and even exemplary manner. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I am glad to find
from the reports submitted to me by the
Inspector-General that the discipline of
the force has been kept up to a very
high standard, and I am sure that the
Committee will share with me the high
sense of satisfaction that the people of
Northern Ireland have such a welldisciplined and efficient force. A policeman's duty is sometimes not a pleasant
one-
Mr. BEATTIE: Not in Northern
Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend will have ample opportunity to
make his remarks afterwards. I am glad
to be able to think that the duties of
the police force in Northern Ireland
have been rendered easier by the feeling

engendered in the minds of the people
of Northern Ireland. In this respect
one cannot overlook the influence which
the existence of the "B" Special Constabulary has in creating amicable
relations and relations of mutual trust,
between the police forces and the people
as a whole. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It was not uncommon in the old
days to find a spirit of antagonism, or, at
least, distrust, between our people and
the police, but the fact that many of
more reputable citizens are themselves members of the Special Constabulary has undoubtedly conduced to the
excellent relations which prevail
prevail at
present.
our
During the past year the Judges of
Assize have been able to make satisfactory references to the peaceful state of
the country as a whole, but it cannot be
overlooked that during the year in question there were two extremely regrettable
outbreaks of disorder. Feelings have
died down now and I do not wish to
stress the various features of the two outbreaks, but, at any rate, I think I am
right in saying that the police handled
the situations with tact and firmness.
The same remarks apply to the conduct
of the force during the prolonged railway
strike. The duties imposed on the police
during the strike were arduous and
difficult, and I am sure the Committee
will agree with me that they discharged
those duties in a highly commendable
manner.
We have during the year continued—
though perhaps in a modified way for
economy reasons-with our policy of providing new barracks and otherwise improving the accommodation. for our
police, and I am glad to be able to state
now that a start will soon be made to
convert the old barracks at Enniskillen
into a depot for the training of our police
recruits and, in addition, into a county
headquarters. The work will begin as
soon as the contract is placed, which I
hope will not be very long now.

Turning to another side of the picture,
I feel it necessary to say a few words on
the question of prison administration.
In the first place, I am sorry to have to
say that our prison population figures for
last year show a slight upward tendency,
being a daily average of 354.8 as compared with 317.4 for the previous year.
This is due primarily to the exceptional
occurrences referred to earlier by me.
I cannot pass from the subject of
prisons without once again expressing
my appreciation of the continued interest
which has been displayed by the visiting
justices of the various prisons and the
Board of Visitors of Belfast Prison. The
ladies and gentlemen who constitute
these bodies have been at all times most
helpful in putting forward recommendations as to improvements, and, on
the other hand, I am glad to able to say
that according to their reports they are
satisfied, as I am, that the various members of the prison service have carried
out their duties in a conscientious and
tactful manner.
I must also tender my thanks, and the
thanks of the Government, to the members of the two societies which interest
themselves in discharged prisoners. They
have continued their splendid, though
perhaps thankless, work in perhaps the
worst possible circumstances in their
endeavour to obtain employment for
prisoners on release. I am only sorry
that the splendid work carried out by
these societies does not meet with
greater measure of support at the hands
of the general public. I must also again.
take this opportunity of expressing my
gratitude to the ladies and gentlemen
who, under the auspices of Toc H and
other organisations attend at Belfast
Prison and help towards the instruction
and entertainment of the prisoners by
way of lectures, concerts, etc.
a
Turning from prisons proper to our
Borstal and Reformatory Institution at
Malone, I am glad to be able to say that
in this respect most satisfactory work is
being done. That this fact is appreciated by the courts is proved by the fact
that the number of Borstal inmates in
our Malone Training School at the
present time-82-is higher than it has
ever been before. This increase is not
due to any startling increase in juvenile
crime, but is a proof that the courts
recognise the value of the institution and
of the great advantages accruing from the
disciplinary and technical training provided in it.
The school is now a live organisation
and has already in its short period of
existence built up for itself a tradition of
sound discipline, coupled with personal
and individual consideration for the
boys. In this connection also I cannot
speak in sufficiently high terms of the
enormous value to the boys, and to the
community as a whole, of the services of
the Visiting Committee of the school.
The gentlemen on this committee, like
those on other committees I have already
referred to, give their services freely and
willingly and display the utmost interest
in every individual activity of the school,
and, perhaps, indeed, in every individual
boy in it.
I, myself, have taken every possible
opportunity of seeing the activities of the
school, under all conceivable circumstances, and on every occasion I have
come away heartened with the evidence
of good work, the evidence of interest
taken in the boys and taken by the boys
themselves in their work and in the
school. It was a matter of the utmost
satisfaction to me, and, indeed, to the
staff of the school and to the boys, that
so many Members of this Committee were
able to be present at the annual sports
last August. The athletic attainments
of the boys are most satisfactory in the
various forms of sport in which they
engage.
Every boy at the school, before
leaving, qualifies for the Royal Life.
Saving Society's award, and for the past.
five years in succession the School Boy
Scout Troop has won the Alexander Cup
for swimming, which is open to all Scout
troops in Northern Ireland. The football team keeps a good position in the
Northern Amateur League, and in boxing the school has been represented in
several boxing tournaments run under
the auspices of the Ulster Amateur Boxing Association. May I here be allowed
to
thank the organisers for having
allowed the boys to join? During the
past two years there has been a most
interesting boxing fixture arranged between Campbell College and the school.
The annual camp was held again at
Islandmagee last year, and I am glad to
be able to say that the behaviour of the
boys during their period in camp was
more than satisfactory. Through the
kindness of Mr. and Miss Montgomery,

of Greyabbey, we have been permitted

Turning to local government administration, one of the first matters that call
for notice is the question of housing. It
will be remembered that some years ago
a Government subsidy of £100, with
supplementary local authority grant not
exceeding £40, was available to builders
of houses of prescribed pattern. During
those years the average number per year
of houses approved for erection was
2,626. Subsequently, for financial
reasons, the Government found it
necessary to reduce the subsidy to £50,
and it was found that, as a result, the
number of houses approved for erection.
fell to 920 per annum.
Last year, owing to the condition of
financial stringency which prevailed, the
subsidy was again still further reduced to
£25, and I regret to state that, whether
from this cause or whether on account of
the financial depression, the housing
operations in Northern Ireland in connection with the provision of houses for
the working classes has fallen to 44.
These results cannot be considered satisfactory in any degree. The housing
shortage has not been met, and, apart
from that, there is the question of unemployment. Various proposals have
been submitted to the Government
designed with the object of further encouraging the building of houses. All of
these, as may be imagined, involve
increased financial charges on the Government, and all I can say at present is that
these various proposals are being carefully considered, and I hope that something satisfactory will be arrived at.
Turning from housing to water supplies,
it perhaps is not out of place for me to
refer to the fact that the great scheme

supply in the Silent Valley has now
reached its completion and
completion and will be
formally inaugurated by his Grace the

I am sure they will join with me in expressing appreciation of the manner in
which the difficulties were faced and overcome, and of the fact that Belfast and
district will now have a water supply
second to none in the United Kingdom.
Arising out of the development of this
scheme, which is capable of providing

for many years to come and still have a
substantial surplus, I thought it well,
some time ago, to invite representatives
of the Commissioners and of the local

and discuss, provisionally and informally,

As a result a rough tentative scheme,

Saintfield, Ballygowan, Comber, Newtownards and Bangor, was sketched out
