I now turn to the question of road
traffic, and here I find it necessary to
express concern at the fact that the toll
of road accidents still shows a tendency
to increase. Some years ago we had
hoped, from the statistics furnished by the
police, that conditions were improving in
this respect, but these hopes have not been
fulfilled. For the year 1929 the total
Ministry of Home Affairs 1414
Estimates-
9 MAY 1933
number of accidents on our roads was
1,417, with 126 people killed; for the
following year the number was 1,457,
with 115 people killed; for the year 1931
the number was 1,582, the number of
deaths being 114; and for the year 1932
the number had increased to 1,765, with
118 deaths. This appalling loss of life
and damage to property and person has,
naturally, been the subject of comment
and criticism. Some critics have suggested and urged that the Government
might, by further administrative and even
legislative measures, do much to remedy
this state of affairs, but these critics
apparently ignore the fact that the
attention of the Government and the
police authorities is constantly directed
towards this terrible problem. We are
satisfied that it is not by the issue of
regulations alone that the problem can be
solved, and in this view we are supported
by the authorities, both official and semiofficial, in Great Britain and other parts
of the world. In fact, those who are best
qualified to judge have expressed the view
that there is, if anything, too much
regulation and too much legislation. I
am satisfied that the problem can only
be solved with the co-operation, not only
of the motoring community, but also, and
more important still, of the community at
large, i.e., all classes of road users.
In proof of this it is only necessary for
me to explain in detail for the Committee
the last return of road accidents which has
been prepared, i.e., the period 1st March,
1932, to 28th February, 1933. The total
number of accidents for that period was
1,719, and the number of people killed
123. Of the 1,719 accidents only 271
could be attributed to negligent driving,
176 to faulty judgment on the part of the
driver, while no fewer than 745 were
attributed to pedestrians being at fault,
and this latter factor was responsible for
not fewer than 57 out of the 123 persons
killed. In addition, 243 of the accidents
were attributed to cyclists being at fault,
this factor being responsible for 12 of the
deaths.
Of the total number of 1,719 accidents,
only half were caused by vehicles of all
classes on the roads, the remaining half
being catalogued as not caused by
vehicles but being cases in which the
vehicles are involved. It has often been
suggested that drivers of ordinary motor
vehicles should be required to undergo
a driving test before being allowed to take
out licences Expert opinion is definitely
against such a principle, and the
statistics of the last few years are undoubtedly proof of the wisdom of the
experts.
Taking the return in question, from
which I have been quoting, only 8
accidents out of a total of 1,719 are
attributed to inexperienced drivers, a
proof, if proof be needed, that a driving
test would involve expense, time, and
trouble out of all proportion to the value
of the results obtained. Out of 1,719
accidents, buses, though involved in 64
accidents, were responsible for 20. Private cars involved in 766 accidents were
responsible for 290. Lorries involved in
254 accidents were responsible for 111.
Motor-cycles involved in 234 accidents
were responsible for 145. It is interesting to note that out of a total of 1,719
accidents only 12 were due to drunkenness.
The above short summary will, I
think, satisfy the Committee that even
although there has been a steady
increase in the number of motor vehicles
on our roads, the responsibility for
accidents cannot be placed wholly on the
shoulders of the motorist. Out of the
total number of accidents of 1,719, only
271 were attributable to negligent
driving and 176 to faulty judgment,
while, as already intimated above,
nearly 1,000 were attributable to cyclists
or pedestrians at fault.
I feel it necessary on this occasion to
appeal to all users of the roads, whether
pedestrians, cyclists, or drivers of horse
vehicles, to realise that they have a responsibility which is of equal importance
to the responsibility imposed on the
motorists. I feel also that it is only by
the strong pressure of public opinion
that an improvement can be effected.
We are doing what we can by inculcating
into the minds of school children the
principles of "Safety First," but we
want the help of every member of the
community in order to solve this problem.
of danger on the roads, by realising the
principles of "Safety First."

We have passed through a trying winter,

while conditions in Northern Ireland
have, as in other parts of the world, been

Mr. YOUNG: I should like to congratulate the Minister of Home Affairs
and the Government in general on having changed their policy in connection
with recruitment for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. I think they have followed a very wrong policy for the last
five or six years in allowing the strength
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary to decrease gradually. In 1929 the strength
of the force was 2,903, and by degrees,
through natural causes, it was allowed
to fall to 2,757 last year. To such
an extent did they carry that policy
of what I call false economy that
they closed the Recruiting Depot
altogether, and there were no recruits
coming forward for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary.
Last year, owing to several causes, such
as the little rows that happened on the
Border in connection with the Eucharistic Congress in Dublin, and the unfortunate riots in Belfast, they have opened
up the depot again, and I am glad to
see from the returns that there are 137
young recruits coming forward. At the
same time, the total strength of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary at 2,802 is 200 below
strength. In my opinion the Government, instead of taking on recruits in
large batches at times of crisis, which
means they have too many recruits coming forward at one time, should adopt a
regular system of taking on as many
recruits every year as would keep the
Royal Ulster Constabulary up to the
standard strength of 3,000. That policy
would be better and cheaper in the end,
and there would be less criticism of the
Estimates, because the cost of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary would remain at
standard throughout, instead of providing the critics with the chance of saying
that the Estimates for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary have increased.

since

so many years without demanding something in return.
I remember when the question was

Mention has been made of the great
number of motor accidents which still,
unhappily, occur in our streets. On my
way to the House to-day I passed a corpse
on the highway. I am glad to say it was
only the corpse of a dog, but the number
of fatal accidents due to the motorist
is still lamentably great, and I see very
little possibility of reducing the number.
There is one culprit, I am sorry to say,
whom there is a very natural inclination
everywhere to screen-a natural inclination and yet an unworthy inclination. A
serious accident occurred a short time ago
in the neighbourhood of Carrickfergus.
On the first occasion on which the facts
were investigated no reference whatever
was made to the circumstance that the
driver of the motor at the time was,
to a considerable degree, under the
influence of alcohol. That fact was never
mentioned. Apparently it was never
mentioned at the inquiry; certainly it was
never mentioned in the newspapers. Now
if this is a real culprit, if this is a circumstance in the augmentation of this
tremendous number of accidents and this
sad number of fatalities, I do not think
the circumstance should be cloaked over.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I think
the fact should be known in order that
individuals, drivers and others, might be
warned. Those who go out on to the
highway with great, powerful machines
under their control, and who have, in
even the slightest degree, impaired their
nervous faculties by alcohol, are guilty of
a great criminal action and should not be
protected by any mock modesty on the
part of the public. It is a well-known
scientific fact that alcohol, even a glass or
two glasses, inevitably retards the speed
with which a man can react to stimuli.
Major MCCORMICK: How do you
know that?
Rev. Professor CORKEY: If a motorcar is going at forty miles an hour a man
driving it, at a given sign, will react to
that sign within a calculable space of
time. If, however, he has taken an
appreciable amount of alcohol the time of
that reaction is considerably extended, so
that his car is liable to run from 20 to 30
yards further, and that distance may
make all the difference between life and
death. I mention this because the public
outside, to some extent, may hear or read
my words. I appreciate the fact that in
this matter the Government can do very
little.

heed to their wails and cries for a decent
standard of housing. If he refuses to
hear those cries perhaps that area will be
very troublesome in the near future.
Therefore, I hope the Minister will take
a different view of the housing of the
people in Northern Ireland from that
which he has held in the past.
The Rent Act has been put forward
here in a light with which I cannot agree.
I understood that when this Department
took control of housing they would also
have control of the law governing rents.
The Department has thrown off its
responsibility for the law governing rents.
I do not think that should be. The
Minister of Home Affairs should be the
person responsible for seeing that every
part of the law appertaining to housing is
carried out. When he presented a Bill in
this House he was asked would the contents of that Measure be conformed to by
the landlords. When I hear his answer
I will give him some enlightenment as to
how the landlord class are undermining
his last amended Act. I know the
sections put in for the protection of the
tenants are not being recognised by the
landlord class. The right hon. Gentleman in his Department is not taking a
note of these violations, and I hope he
will wake up and see that justice is done
under that Act of Parliament.
I had a landlord who pursued
the policy of sending to me people to ask
if I would sign a document whereby he
could let his houses, which were controlled, at 3s a week more than the
controlled rent. That landlord appeared
before the Rent Committee. That was
trying to intimate to me that he would
put obstacles in my way because of the
action I took in regard to that Act.
course, I took no notice of it, but when
the people went back to him to tell him
that Mr. Beattie said he had no authority
for altering an Act of Parliament, or
signing a document that would undermine an Act of Parliament, he abused
me to those people who were my voters

In regard to the Borstal Institution,
that is a reform with which I fully agree.
I also agree with prison reform. I have
spoken many times in this House about
the prison on the Crumlin Road. It is
cruel and unkind for any man to be
housed for a period of over twelve months
in the Crumlin Road prison. It was
meant to be a short-term prison, and I
question very much whether the law
allows the Government to use a shortterm prison for life prisoners. It would
be far better to some, I am sure, to see
life ended than to go into a short-term
prison for life sentences. I think the law
relating to prisons and the prison regulations would condemn the Crumlin Road
prison for life prisoners. If we must
have a life-term prison we should build
one and have it built according to the
regulations which every other country
adheres to in cases of this kind. We
want to do away with crime. Everyone
in this Committee would agree, I expect,
with that statement. There is only one
way to do away with crime, that is by
dealing with the evil that commences
crime. If you get that canker or evil
abolished there will be no crime.
Mr. McBRIDE: The millennium.
Of
Mr. BEATTIE: It will possibly be the
millennium, but it is also possible that
Hades will be experienced before that
millennium is reached. I want to say to
the Parliamentary Secretary that there is
no use in bolstering this thing up. Crime
is due to society persecuting the individual. To my mind the man who steals
because he is compelled to do so on
account of having insufficient food for his
wife and children does not commit a
crime against society. In my eyes that
man has the right to steal, if you call it
stealing. I do not call it stealing.
course, I do not believe that murder
should be included in that category of
exemption-no man should resort to
that at any time. But the majority of
charges preferred against the citizens in
the law courts every day in the week
should be charges against society, rather
than individuals, because of the uneconomic conditions under which they are
compelled to live. That is the state of
society to-day; it is creating criminals by
the uneconomic conditions under which
many people have to exist. Until
society provides those conditions which a
civilised country ought to provide, crime
cannot be abolished.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Abolish drink and
you will abolish crime.

drunkenness or that he was in any way

ment by myself, as

was so much impressed by the facts, which

was adjourned so that evidence might be
produced, not merely on behalf of the

When the trial subsequently took place,
while a verdict was found for the plaintiff

the learned judge was so convinced that
there was, in fact, no evidence of drunkenness or of any circumstances amounting to
intoxication on the part of the defendant,

to the facts. I am afraid, from the

bring back into the regulations, so far

of manslaughter, so that the guilt of an
individual may be fixed in the right
degree. I maintain that wild or reckless
drivers-I am almost inclined to describe
them as potential murderers-should be
charged with manslaughter directly a fatal
accident occurs.
We may point to what the Coroner of
Belfast has said recently in the way of
stricture. He has said that many drivers
are not efficient drivers; in other words,
that they are not able to handle their
cars when the moment occurs when judgment is necessary. I would appeal to the
Minister to see if he could not bring in
a regulation to the effect that when a
licence is applied for something in the
nature of a test should be given to the
driver, that he should be able to show
that in a congested thoroughfare he is
able to take his part and to use coolness
and judgment in avoiding accidents. My
hon. Friend (Rev. Professor Corkey) in
front of me suggests that part of the
regulations should be the signing of the
pledge. I do not agree with that at all.
In fact I would answer him in another
way and say that if you make a man
sign the pledge you might even have to
make him sign away something else. I
have remarked on the fact that the
Coroner has made these strictures, and
the Minister might possibly in his reply
give us some satisfaction on this point.
Much discussion has raged in the House
-and it comes under the Estimates
""
to-day-in regard to what is called the
raiding of the Road Fund. I have
expressed myself very plainly on this
matter on more than one occasion. I do not
mind how this Fund is raided. (Hon.
Members: Oh.) Of course I know hon.
Members will say Oh, it is plain he is
not a motorist," but I am a very good
pedestrian and a user of the road, and
I say that, whether the money is used on
country roads or on roads in Belfast, it
is all going to a good purpose. Vehicles
are used on all roads, and the employment
that has been given through this money
that has been taken from the Road Fund
shows that it has been used to a good
purpose, and I am perfectly agreeable.
I maintain my position in that regard.
Reference has been made by the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. Minford) to
one particular road leading from Antrim
to Randalstown. While I do not know
the merits of this matter, I do think that
where such a small percentage of the cost
is involved the Department might have
met it. I understand that in the neighbourhood of Antrim and Randalstown,
which is a very congested countryside,
there are numbers of farm labourers who
are idle and who would be very glad of
this work. It would be an excellent
thing if these men could be employed on
this much-needed work. I believe that
the percentage involved in this matter is
very small, and that the whole amount of
money involved is something like £30,000.
As we all know, in road work the greater
proportion of the money would be spent
on wages and, therefore, I think that if
there were co-operation between the Departments this matter could be settled.
Only last week I spoke in this Committee on the Estimates for the Ministry
of Labour. I made what I might call a
very moving appeal to the Minister of
Labour with regard to the state of unemployment in our Province. I spoke, as I
felt, after meeting these men who are
looking for work and unable to get it.
I must say that the Minister of Labour
is always sympathetic to any appeal of
that kind for the elimination of all classes
of unemployment. I have great faith
that he will tackle this. The Committee
has faith in him, and I believe that we
will not look to him in vain. When I
read my speech afterwards in Hansard it
seemed to me to be a very depressing
and sad speech, but it was made because
I know, as everyone knows, the loss our
Province is incurring physically, morally,
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs

and financially through unemployment.
It is indeed a sad position to be in.
Therefore, when I think over what has
been said about unemployment, and find
that this little matter of the road between
Antrim and Randalstown is held up for
the sake of a small percentage of the
cost, I feel that we are, as one might say,
like Nero-fiddling whilst Rome is burning. That may be a very strong term,
but perhaps it will meet the point, and I
ask the Committee to consider it.
So far as the Estimates generally are
concerned, I wish to congratulate the
Minister on them. He has given us an
excellent record of work in so far as the
constabulary and the various other
branches of his Department are concerned.
The Department of Home Affairs deserves
well of the community. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is responsible for
law and order, and, as we all know, law
and order have been maintained, and I
believe the Department is firm in the

say. I have much pleasure in supporting the Estimate.

Mr. BEATTIE: When we employ law
advisers and pay them the high salaries
we are paying we expect to get good sound
advice. In the year 1931 in this House
I asked the Attorney-General a question
as to whether the Totalisator was legal in
Northern Ireland, and if it was not, what
action was he likely to take to stop it
operating. If you refer to Hansard you
will find the reply given by the Attorney-
General, who is our law adviser. Since
then the law advisers in England have
had a similar question put to them, and
they have definitely stated that the
Totalisator is illegal in Great Britain.
I
do not agree with the kind of advice we
received from the Attorney-General.
When you return bad food you are not
asked to pay for it, but we got bad legal
advice on that occasion, and for that
reason I do not think the Attorney-
General is entitled to the fees he receives
under this Estimate.
The next suggestion I want to make is
that the law department of the Ministry
should fulfil the policy of equality of treatment in the administration of the law. I
have already made a statement to the
effect that in no case where a man, woman
or child was killed by a lorry did the
driver escape without having to face the
law. But there were other cases in Northern Ireland, such as the Dunmurry and
the York Street cases, as well as another
one, but in the first two cases the
persons
responsible never faced a court of justice
to determine whether or not they were
responsible for the deaths of the persons
concerned. Why that was so I do not
know. I want the Attorney-General to
give me the names of the persons concerned
in the fatalities which have not been investigated by a court of justice-the
names of the workmen who earn their
living by driving lorries. I am quite
satisfied that no man goes out in a motorcar with the intention of killing any
person. I think that is the last thing any
man would do, whether drunk or sober,
but accidents will happen to the best of
drivers.
The CHAIRMAN: I hope the hon.
Member will keep two matters perfectly
clear. One is the action of the police who,
in the first instance, take cognisance of
accidents, and for that, of course, the
Attorney-General has no responsibility.
The second is the bringing of these matters before the magistrates where either
party is or is not returned for trial. That,
again, is not a matter for the Attorney-
General. I am sure that in a grave
matter of this kind this debate, so far as
it goes, will be conducted with great care
so that there shall not be any improper
reflection, and the only matters that may
be discussed are matters for which the
Attorney-General himself is responsible.
Mr. BEATTIE: In the two cases I
mentioned the police and all associated
with things of that sort up to a point fulfilled their duty, but the party responsible
in the Dunmurry case, where a man was
killed, has never yet been brought to
justice. The position of the car on that
night and the owner of that car are well
known throughout Belfast at anyrate.
Why is not the owner of the car held
responsible for the accident on that night?
The other case was the York Street accident. It is well known in Belfast that a
man lost his life through a motor-car.
That does not mean to say that the man
who was driving was not competent. He
may have been as competent as any other
man, but no charge was preferred against
him. Nor have we found the Dunmurry
man although I am prepared to say that
the car and owner involved in that accident are well known to members of the
Government.
All I want to see is the law equally
administered. If the law holds a working
man guilty until the courts prove him
innocent then it should also hold the
owners of the two cars I have mentioned
in a similar way. There is no equality of
administration at all in the conduct of
affairs in regard to motor-cars. It is all
bunkum to say that there is. The cases

for tampering, might I say, with words.

There has been unequal administration.
of the law. I fail to see why we should

being so, the job should be a full-time

The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Gentleman knows that discussion of the private
business of any Member is not a matter
open to the Committee. That is so well
established a practice that I do not need

Mr. BEATTIE: The private work of
the Attorney-General has nothing to do
with me, but he has failed to live up
to the expectations of Members of the
Committee, and should be asked to apply
himself to the full-time job for which he
is substantially paid. There is no earthly
reason why that cannot be carried out.
Many able lawyers are not getting much

in the State, and everyone should get an

I say that the Attorney-General should

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: It is
very easy for the hon. Member to make

a specific case is under discussion. In the

When a case comes before me it comes
before me upon facts which are committed to hand-writing. They are taken
down in the presence of a magistrate,
are read over to the persons who give
the evidence, and the depositions are
signed. Outside the four corners of
those depositions I am not entitled to,
and do not, inquire who the persons are
or who they may be, what their position.
in life is, or anything whatever connected with them. The Committee are
aware that there are cases where names
come before me in this way with which
I am familiar, but I assure the Committee that when that is so I rigorously
shut out from my mind all previous knowledge I may have, and if I was not able
to do that I would not hold the position
I have the privilege and honour to
occupy.
The profession of the law teaches one
to be able to take cases apart altogether
from any prejudice or gossip and to treat
them merely as problems presented upon
certain evidence which has been submitted after it has been carefully sifted.
I am not going to deal with cases that
may have occurred at Dunmurry or elsewhere. I know nothing about them.
Unless the depositions were produced
before me in this Committee, and I was
able to read them over again and re-form
the opinion I must have formed when
they were before me in the first instance,
it would be quite impossible for me to
make any statement in this Committee
with reference to them. If I did I
might possibly be doing an injustice to
persons whose cases have now been
terminated, either by the decision of the
courts or by my decision, that they should
or should not be prosecuted in the courts
of the land.
One or two other matters have been
referred to by the hon. Member. He
has referred to the totalisator.
He says
I gave the Government wrong advice and
that I gave him wrong advice when he
asked me a question in this House. There
are many things which, the Committee
will understand, in law are very debatable. There are some practices which
have continued in some cases for nearly
one hundred years and have been
garded as being absolutely legal, but which
when challenged in the courts have been
found to be illegal, although advised as
legal by the most eminent lawyers not
only here but on the other side of the
water.
re-
Anyone who knows anything about
this question of the totalisator knows
that the matter was up for decision in
the House of Lords. Decisions were
given there which looked as if the
totalisator was not a contravention of
the Betting Acts, and those decisions
were acted upon not only in this country
but in England and Scotland. They are
acted upon in Scotland at the present
time. What happened was this: Some
enterprising policeman in England, who
thought he saw a fallacy in the law as it
was then observed, brought a prosecution,
and the case was taken to the Court of
Criminal Appeal in England, where it
was decided that the totalisator upon
greyhound tracks was illegal according
to the law as it stands at the present
time. I make no apology for not having
investigated that. The same
thing
happened in Great Britain-
Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of correction. When I asked you that question a
decision had been given in Great Britain
that the totalisators were illegal.
decision was read to you on that occasion.
That
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Unless
the hon. Member refreshes my memory
of the period at which this question was
asked I am not going to deal with the
matter upon that footing. I think the
hon. Member must be wrong in saying
that I ever gave the opinion that the
totalisator was legal in this country after
the decision of the Court of Criminal
Appeal in England, because it was obvious
to everybody that that was a decision
upon a statute which is in exactly the
same terms as the statute which governs
the matter in Northern Ireland, and that,
therefore, it was bound to have an effect
upon it.
Everybody knows that since
that statute was brought into force the
totalisator has not operated in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: Pardon me for again
interrupting, but when the decision was
given in the High Court the question I
asked was did that decision apply to Northern Ireland, and you said it did not
apply to Northern Ireland.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I cannot at the moment tax my memory with
the time these various cases were presented
to the courts across the water, but I can
assure the Committee that from the
Estimates-
Law Charges
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Attorney-General]
moment it was decided in the Court of
Criminal Appeal in England that the
Betting Acts apply to totalisators on greyhound tracks the totalisator has not been
operated in Northern Ireland. So far as
the advice was concerned, the same rule
was adopted in England as here. The
law officers in Great Britain took no steps
to prevent the use of totalisators upon
greyhound racing tracks, and not
until this case was brought before the
Court of Criminal Appeal in England was
it known that this particular practice was
illegal according to the Betting Acts in
force in both countries.
Another matter that the hon. Member
has referred to is the question of holding
persons in prison. He seems to be under
the impression that some action of mine
upon some occasion or other was
vindictive. As you, Mr. Moles, pointed
out, and as everybody knows perfectly
well, the Attorney-General does not hold
anybody in prison. If persons are
arrested or put into prison under the
Civil Authorities Act it is done by the
police on the advice of the Minister of
Home Affairs. On the other hand, persons arrested by the police have to be
dealt with according to law in a certain
definite time. I know of no case where
a person has been held in prison for
longer than was absolutely necessary for
the purpose of bringing a charge.
Everybody knows that if he is kept all
his advisers have to do is to go to the
courts for a writ of habeas corpus,
whereupon, unless some valid reason can
be advanced by the Crown for holding
the prisoner, he is bound to be liberated.
I think one matter upon which the Committee can congratulate itself is, that so
far as the administration of the criminal
law in Northern Ireland is concerned it
is very speedy. When the hon. Member
made the charges, which he saw fit to
make to-day, he did so obviously from a
very imperfect knowledge of how the
criminal law works. I have heard no
complaints of how that law has been
administered since I have had the honour
of being Attorney-General for Northern
Ireland.
I do not think there is anything more
I need say except this: I want to assure
the hon. Member and persons who think
as he thinks, that so far as these prosecutions are concerned everyone is treated
absolutely upon the same footing. I
have not got the figures before me now,
but he will find if he asks the question
from my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Home Affairs, who has the records,
that during the last year or two the
same rule has been applied to all classes
of the community. He is quite wrong in
saying that every lorry driver who has
unfortunately been involved in an
accident where there has been loss of life
has ipso facto been placed upon his trial.
It is not true.
There have been numbers of cases
where persons who have to make their
living by driving heavy vehicles upon the
road, and who unfortunately have been
involved in accidents which have resulted
in loss of life have been, some of them,
returned for trial by the magistrates,
who were not in a position to say definitely
whether it was a case that should go
forward or not. When they come before
me, I decide if they are proper cases for
prosecution. The hon. Member opposite
has only got to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs for the records of these matters;
they are open to any hon. Member to
look into them. I can assure the Committee that there is not a word of truth
in the charges that have been made by
the hon. Member opposite. Everybody
is treated upon an equal footing. If
some people think that persons should be
prosecuted who have not been prosecuted,
you will find that in a number of other
cases in which people have been prosecuted representations have been made to
me that these are cases that should not
be prosecuted. But somebody has got to
make up his mind with reference to those
cases, and I deal with them all upon
exactly the same footing. Is there or
is there not evidence which would show
that the person who has unfortunately
been involved in an accident has been
guilty of what a jury would consider a
criminal act?
You
May I say this in conclusion?
have only got to look at the number of

-am I to send up everybody, knowing

Estimates-
9 MAY 1933
evidence is not sufficiently strong? If I
were to do that our courts would be choked
with prosecutions in these cases. We heard
the number of these unfortunate accidents
read out here to-day. Only a small
number of them are due to criminal negligence. The greater number of them are
pure accidents, and to bring every case in
which there is loss of life before the
criminal courts, before the twelve members
of a jury, is only defeating the ends of
justice, because as case after case came
up, and the accused is acquitted by the
jury, the juries more and more are inclined to say that in none of these cases
will they convict a man of manslaughter
for what is merely an accident, unless
under some very aggravated circumstances,
such as being under the influence of drink,
or some other matter of that sort.
Therefore, the Committee will understand that all these matters have to be
weighed up. The matter has to be left
to somebody. It is left to me, and I, in
the discharge of my duty, weigh them
all up upon the evidence and upon
nothing else. I resent the suggestion of
the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie)
that in so deciding I make any distinction
either between class and class or between
creed and creed, or between whether a
man is a man of means or whether he is
a poor man. I can assure you, and I can
assure the Committee, that in every case
I deal with it simply as a business matter,
and as a matter of fact upon the evidence,
and I leave prejudice entirely to one
side when I deal with matters of this
description.

THE GRANT FOR FIRST-CLASS
ROAD RECONSTRUCTION.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.'
(Captain Dixon.)
Mr. MINFORD: The question I asked
the Minister to-day was in regard to
Antrim County Council. That Council
had recommended the reconstruction of
the road between Antrim and Randalstown, and I may give the House a short
history of what occurred. In November
we had in Antrim a big lot of men,
anxious to work, who could not get work.
A meeting was called in Antrim to see
what could be done for those people. At
that meeting a committee was formed,
including the clergymen of the different
denominations, the chairman of the
Urban Council, and other people in the
neighbourhood. At that meeting an
Road Reconstruction

announcement was made that those who
were destitute should wait after the meeting. When the meeting was over to our
surprise we found we had quite a large
number.
The committee were most anxious to
relieve these people, and they approached
the Rural District Council of Antrim, and
there, I may say, they got some little
help. But we found, after all, that the
numbers were so great that it would take
something more than a small scheme to
absorb these men. A deputation was
appointed to wait on the Minister of
Home Affairs, and that deputation waited
on him some time early in December. A
month then elapsed and the deputation
began to get rather anxious regarding the
condition of the people in Antrim and
Randalstown. They then approached the
Minister of Home Affairs again, and then
in January, I think the 9th, the Ministry
promised to make investigation. Sometime about the middle of January
Admiral Archdale came down to Antrim
and made investigation regarding our unemployed, and there he found that the
state of affairs that existed was certainly
not too good. The County Council gave
grants or allowed the unexpended balance
to be used by this committee in Antrim
for the relief of unemployment.
At
As time went on we found that something would have to be done to help these
men out of this deplorable position. I
think I am right in saying that in the
latter end of March a deputation met in
this building, and at that deputation the
hon. Member for Antrim, who is chairman of the County Council of Antrim
Finance Committee, was present.
that conference it was arranged-in fact
the Minister himself suggested to the
chairman of the Antrim County Council
Finance Committee that his Council should
take steps to reconstruct this corridor road
between Antrim and Randalstown.
that meeting may I say that he did
certainly suggest that 60 per cent. could
only be given for the reconstruction of
that road. After we left the conference
the next thing we heard was that the
Finance Committee had met and had
recommended the County Council to reconstruct this road with a grant of 72 per
cent.
At
The committee became rather alarmed,
and we then went to the Ministry of
Finance, and there we were told that we
might expect no more than 60 per
Adjournment-
Road Reconstruction
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
cent. We then went to Antrim
County Council, which met on April
15, and we put our case before them
the best we could. They decided, by a
vote of 10 to 5, they would adhere to the
decision of the committee at Ballymena,
recommending the reconstruction of this
road, provided they got from the Ministry
of Home Affairs the 72 per cent. grant.
Just for the sake of giving the Members
of this House what really occurred, I may
say the road between Randalstown and
Antrim is certainly of vast importance.
It is the leading artery between County
Derry and County Antrim, and owing to
the traffic diverted from the railway, it
means that that road has got to bear
certainly a very large amount of heavy
traffic. The maintenance of that road
costs £2,000 per year, £400 per mile.
The Government contributed 60 per cent.,
leaving the rest to be paid by County
Antrim. The reconstruction of this road
with four-inch concrete was going to cost
£30,000, £6,000 per mile. That £6,000
per mile meant a repayment in ten years
of £3,630 on the average.
The 60 per
cent. grant from the Government meant
a total of £2,178, and left an annual repayment on the Council of, I think,
£1,452.
The County Council made up their
minds definitely that they were not going
to move from the 72 per cent. grant,
and I do hope that the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs, has
not made up his mind. I expect he
will do what I consider the big thing tonight and will give the Antrim County
Council the 72 per cent. grant. I will
tell you my reason. To put it in a nutshell, the difference between the 60 per
cent. and the 72 per cent. on which these
two bodies differ is £427. That is what
they are fighting about. I am not concerned as to whether the Antrim County
Council pay the £427 or whether the
Ministry pay it. What I am concerned
about is this. In my constituency we
have unfortunately, I have got to admit,
somewhere in the neighbourhood of 800
or 1,000 people signing the register.
These people signing the register are not
all drawing benefit from the Unemployment Fund or from transitional benefit.
They are really depending on work, and
I should perhaps state that some of these
men are depending on outdoor relief.
I put it to the House, is it fair that
in a place like Antrim or Randalstown,
where a most loyal body of workers were
willing to work, people who do not make
a parade of their poverty, just because
of a dispute beteen the Antrim County
Council and the Ministry of Home
Affairs, they should be deprived of a
livelihood. This work would employ,
roughly speaking, 130 men for six months
and these 130 men who would be employed are men who have no money
either from unemployment or from transitional benefit,
benefit, but men who are
depending upon a day's work for food
for their wives and families. What is
going to be the position there? If the
Minister of Home Affairs is going to
stand firm on his grant of 60 per cent.,
and if the County Council does not go
on with the scheme, it will mean that
these 140 or 150 men will have to seek
shelter in the workhouse or look for outdoor relief. It is a pity in this most
beautiful part of Ulster that we should
ask these men to stoop to do what I consider is not right. These men, remember, were employed in some of the largest
factories in Ulster. On top of that, I
understand to-day that one other very
large factory will, perhaps, be closing
down in a month or five weeks, which
may throw another thousand on the
register. I wonder, after all, is it
fair or reasonable that these 140 or 150
men-and remember that these men are
people who have dependents-should have
to seek relief in this way. I believe that
if the Chairman of our Committee would
show the lists he could show at least
160 more young, unmarried men who
have dependents, perhaps brothers or
sisters or invalid fathers or mothers. As
I have said, I am not concerned regarding who is going to pay this. The Antrim County Council have estimated for
the reconstruction of this road at
£30,000, provided the Ministry of Home
Affairs would give them a grant of 72
per cent. If the Minister is going to
stand firm on his dignity-perhaps I
should not say that.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a
question of dignity at all.
Mr. MINFORD: Perhaps it is a
question of principle.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is.
Mr. MINFORD: Well, I think we
are living in times when principles should
go by the board. The Antrim County

The County Council have undertaken to

and that is cheap for reconstruction. It

the original foundation, which they will
rebuild. On the road from Belfast to
Ballymena I understand there are seven
inches of concrete three inches, then the

County Council, after all, have met the

the road at a cost of £6,000 a mile. In
ordinary circumstances it would take
£12,000 a mile. Supposing the Ministry

County Council advise their people to go

mile it will cost £60,000 and, instead of
the Ministry having to pay a sum of about
£2,600, they will have to pay a sum of
£5,200. I consider that that is not
economy, especially when you take into
consideration that during the past six
years the Road Fund has increased by
something like £178,000, and that the
County Council of Antrim has decreased
its expenditure by ten per cent. And
may I say also that the charge on the
loan fund will be £12,000 less next year,
because the first loan will be completely
wiped out. Surely with that programme
in front of him the Minister should not
really stop at this little obstacle of £427.
If he is going to have £12,000 wiped off
the loan fund of the Antrim County
Council and is only going to be asked to
bear the amount I have already stated,
surely he should be able to meet this £427
and allow this work to proceed so as to
give these people employment.
I dread to forecast what will be the
consequence if these men cannot get work.
Owing to the unfortunate depression in
agriculture fewer men are employed on
the land. These men of whom I am
speaking are not corner boys at all. They
have been for years in honest employment, and I do plead with the Minister of
Home Affairs this time to give this
amount of 72 per cent. for the reconstruction of one of the most important
corridor roads in Ulster. If he is afraid
that this may implicate him into giving
72 per cent. to other county councils he,
himself, can easily say—

Now, as I said before, what is the interpretation of exceptional circumstances?
Surely a road which is in very bad condition, that is costing £2,000 to maintain,
which is bearing a larger amount of traffic
than, perhaps, any road in Ulster, a

highways, between two counties and
another county, with a big number of

Mr. CRAWFORD: I intend to occupy
only a few minutes, and I do so because
the Antrim County Council has been
brought so much into this picture.
want to make it perfectly clear that no
blame falls on the Antrim County
Council in reference to this matter.
have been connected with a great many
boards in my lifetime, and I never came
across a more humane board or a board
more desirous of helping the public than
the Antrim County Council. I came
into this matter simply because I have an
intense desire to get the people work in
place of giving them money for doing
nothing. That is not a new policy with
me in this House, because I have advocated it again and again. I believe it
is a much better policy than the one we
have been carrying out for a great many
years. May I give a little history of
this matter additional to that given by
the Member for Antrim?
In December, 1930, a considerable
time ago now, a letter came from the
Ministry of Home Affairs to the County
Council promising 72 per cent. of a grant
for the reconstruction of first-class roads.
The letter also said the grant would be
confined
to cases of clear necessity.
Before we received that letter our Council
had passed estimates for the reconstruction of part of the Lisburn-Moira
road, and part of the Coast road. On
14th February, 1931, the Ministry
wrote declining to give a grant of 72
per cent., but offering 60 per cent., and
under the circumstances the County
Council turned down the work and did
not carry it out. Having refused to
carry out work in one part of the county
with a grant of only 60 per cent., the
hands of the County Council were tied
against accepting the same grant for
work in another portion of the county.
Therefore if the Ministry is tied on the
one hand, the County Council is also
tied by the fact that they refused to do
work on the basis of a grant of 60 per
cent.
At a later date, on 25th January,
1932, the Ministry said again that a
grant of 72 per cent. would be given
under pressing and exceptional circumstances. I submit that the matter under
discussion at the present time is both
pressing and exceptional, and I can see
no
reason in the wide world why the
Minister should not keep his promise.
On 10th February, 1932, the Ministry
referred again to their January letter,
and again reiterated that a grant of
72 per cent. would be available under
pressing circumstances, but asked that
work of this nature should be deferred
to enable the Ministry to save £70,000.
On 16th September, 1932, the Ministry
said that the grant for the reconstruction
of first-class roads for the year 1933-34
would be 72 per cent. under special and
pressing circumstances. That letter was
sent to us at the time we were drafting
our estimates for the present year, and

asked the Minister what grant would be

When I discovered that I got the

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Agricultural Marketing Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): In submitting this Bill for the consideration
and approval of the House, there are
several very important facts which I
should like hon. Members to bear constantly in mind during the debate and
also when deliberating as to the effect of
the provisions of this Bill on the welfare
of our agricultural producers.
The first thing I should like to make
absolutely clear to the House is that the
Bill is an enabling Measure. It enables
schemes to be prepared by the Ministry
for enabling farmers to undertake the
better marketing of their agricultural
produce, and it provides that in preparing these marketing schemes the Ministry
shall take into consultation representatives of the producers of the agricultural
product which it is proposed to regulate
by the scheme, and of any other interests
concerned. Immediately a scheme is
approved it will be submitted to Parliament, which has the right to revoke the
scheme if it is not satisfied with it and,
in any case, must within a limited period
formally pass a resolution approving the
scheme.
I have on more than one occasion been
criticised for not bringing before the
House a Bill similar to the Agricultural
Marketing Act, 1931, passed by the Parliament at Westminster, and which, as
hon. Members know, applies to Great
Britain only. The main purpose of that
Act was to give a majority of producers
in any area in Great Britain power to
form a marketing board which would be
endowed with the power to control the
marketing of the whole of that particular
product in Great Britain or any part of
Great Britain. Such marketing boards.
would have, amongst other things, the
power to control the quantity of the
product which might be offered for sale,
the terms on which it could be sold and
the kind, variety or grade of the product
which could be sold.
After giving the matter very anxious
consideration, I came to the conclusion
that the time was not then ripe for
Northern Ireland to follow the British
lead, and I will give you my reasons because they will help you to a fuller
understanding of the provisions of the
Bill and the policy which underlies it.
Under the British Act of 1931, marketing boards could be established for such
products as pigs, bacon, potatoes, eggs,
beef, mutton and so on; the board or
boards dealing with each product,
although it would have absolute control
of, say, all the eggs produced in Great
1477 Agricultural Marketing Bill-

10 MAY 1933
Second Reading
Britain, and be in a position to regulate.
the sale of all eggs produced in England
and Scotland, had no control whatever of
the quantity of imported eggs or of their
sale.
It was clear beyond argument that,
without some form of control of imports,
such farmers' marketing boards would
never function, and that if an attempt was
made it would probably end in disaster
and give, for at least a generation, a death
blow to this form of agricultural cooperation. In fact no attempt was made
in Great Britain to constitute a marketing board to deal with the home production of any agricultural product which is
imported into the United Kingdom to a
substantial extent until the National
Government gave an undertaking to
regulate imports.
The British Act looked like being a
dead letter when the Ottawa Conference
brought a dramatic change in the situation. His Majesty's Government at
Westminster undertook to restrict, by
means of quotas, the entry of most forms
of meat and meat products into the
United Kingdom. Much can be said on
the subject of quotas, both for and
against, but that is a matter of United
Kingdom policy, and my only concern is
to deal with the situation which has arisen
in its relation to Ulster agriculture.
The Agricultural Marketing Bill, which
is, at present, before the Parliament at
Westminster, contains the machinery for
implementing the agreements arrived at in
Ottawa. What in effect this Amending
Bill does is to give the President of the
Board of Trade, after consulting the
Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries and
the Secretary of State for Scotland and
the Secretary of State for the Home Office,
power to regulate the importation of any
agricultural product into the United
Kingdom if it appears to the Board of
Trade that unless the Order is made the
re-organisation of some branch of the
agricultural industry cannot be achieved.
Now it must be obvious to all hon.
Members that no Minister of the Crown
could take the responsibility of limiting
the importation of an essential foodstuff
unless he had definite assurance as to the
home produced supply. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Therefore, in the Bill at
present before the Parliament at Westminster, there is a provision to the effect
that if the importation of any agricultural
product is restricted, the three Ministers
concerned with agriculture in the United
Kingdom may, by Order, regulate the
sales of that product by persons producing it in the United Kingdom.
Let me try to make this quite clear by
means of an illustration.
If, as will
shortly be the case, an Order is issued by
the Board of Trade limiting the importation of bacon and hams into the United
Kingdom, and the farmers in Great
Britain and in Northern Ireland do not
set up a marketing board, which will
regulate production and sales at home,
then the three Ministers responsible for
agriculture in the United Kingdom will
do it for them by means of Orders in
Council.
Now, I think I have made quite clear
to the House the reason for this Bill and
its urgency. I have also, I hope, made it
quite clear that now that the principle of
control of imports has been conceded,
there is no longer an economic obstacle
preventing the farmers of Great Britain
and of Northern Ireland organising, with
a view to regulating, the production and
marketing of their produce.
There is no need, I feel sure, for me to
deal at any length upon the need for
improvement in our methods of agricultural marketing or to outline my views as
to the sort of problems which confront
producers of milk, pork, beef, mutton,
etc. I can best illustrate the sort of
problem which this Bill now before you
provides the machinery for solving, by
instancing the case of potatoes. In rough
figures the United Kingdom consumes 4
million tons of potatoes per annum, and
that amount is not affected to any substantial extent by fluctuations in price to
the farmers. For all practical purposes
the United Kingdom produces enough
potatoes to meet its own requirements.
In certain years the crop exceeds the home
requirement and, although less than 10
per cent. of the crop may be surplus, the
price the farmer receives falls from £5 or
£6 or even £8 per ton to vanishing
point.
Mr. NIXON: Flax?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: This
season, for example, there is a nominal
price of 15s to £1 per ton, equal to onetenth of a penny per lb. That is a state of
affairs which is not reflected in the price
to the consumer. It is, moreover, a state
of affairs which is not in the consumer's
interest. This Bill now before the House
1479 Agricultural Marketing Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Sir Edward Archdale]
contains provisions which enable the
farmers of Ulster to constitute a marketing board which will control and regulate
the sale of the crop, and which enables
them to work in unison with a marketing
board in England or Scotland, or the
whole of Great Britain. It will thereby
be able to maintain a more level price for
potatoes and prevent the disturbing
fluctations which result from a crop which
may be worth £5 to £8 a ton one year and
nothing the next.
In the Bill are set out the matters for
which every marketing scheme submitted
to Parliament must provide. These include power to grant exemption from the
scheme; power for requiring that no sale
of the regulated product may be made by
producers who are not registered under
the scheme or exempted from registration; power to the board to impose on
and recover monetary penalties from
registered producers who contravene the
provisions of the scheme; power for
securing that any producer who is
aggrieved may submit his case to arbitration, and power to raise a levy on
registered producers to cover the costs of
the board's administration.
In general the powers which will be
possesssed by the boards operating any
marketing scheme are identical or similar
to those which will be possessed by marketing boards in Great Britain, and it is
only necessary at this stage to say that
in no instance will the powers conferred
on boards in Ulster exceed the powers
which have already been conferred on
marketing boards in
in Great Britain.
Whilst, therefore, the Bill in its most
important aspects follows closely and is
indeed a complement of the Bill at
present in the Statute Book in Great
Britain, it does in certain minor, but
nevertheless important, matters deflect in
form from the procedure followed in
Great Britain.
In the British Act the initiative in
formulating schemes appears to rest with
the producers, but there is a provision
which enables the Minister to appoint a
Re-organisation Commission to prepare
schemes and to charge any board that
may be formed to operate the schemes
with the whole cost of the Re-organisation Commission. In the Bill before
you the Ministry of Agriculture is
charged with the task of preparing
schemes, and the reasons are not far to
seek. In the case of a product the importation of which is controlled, Northern Ireland must prepare and operate a
scheme, otherwise the sale of that product
will be controlled by Orders issued by
the Secretary of State for the Home
Office.
In other cases if a marketing
scheme is in operation in Great
Britain it would be extremely dangerous
for us not to have a scheme and
thus to refuse to co-operate with the
Great
marketing boards in
Britain.
Moreover, in the case of practically all
schemes it will be necessary to secure coordination between the Northern Ireland
and the Great Britain scheme. Clearly
the Ministry is in the best position to take
into consideration all the circumstances
and to decide upon a policy which is in
the best interests of producers as a whole.
It is significant that even in England
the nominal power to initiate schemes
which rests with producers has been little
exercised. Already the Minister of
Agriculture and Fisheries has appointed
three Re-organisation Commissions to
prepare schemes, namely, Re-organisation
Commissions for pigs and pig products,
for milk, and for fat stock, and further
Re-organisation Commissions are foreshadowed. It will be seen, therefore,
that the policy outlined in this Bill does
not differ in practice from that in operation in Great Britain.
May I, however, repeat that any marketing scheme prepared by the Ministry
under the powers conferred by this Bill
must first be submitted to all the interests concerned and then placed before
both Houses of Parliament.
Finally, just one word as to the constitution of the boards. Power is given
to the Ministry to nominate three members of any marketing board, one of
whom shall be chairman. I should like
to make it clear that with the exception
of the three members nominated by the
Ministry, all the members will be elected
by a direct vote of the producers, and
that the nominated members can never
be more than a small fraction of the total
membership of the board.
I have endeavoured to set before the
House a brief and, as far as possible,
concise outline of the policy underlying
the Bill. I am conscious of the fact that
there are other particulars which call for
explanation but it would only confuse the
issue if I dealt with them at this stage.
1481 Agricultural Marketing Bill-

10 MAY 1933
Second Reading
I would, however, like to add this
point: This Bill, together with the Agricultural Marketing Bill at present before
the Parliament at Westminster, establishes a principle of supreme importance
to us, namely, that Ulster agricultural
produce is just as much a part of the
home supply as that produced in any
county or group of counties in England
or Scotland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Furthermore, I am confident
that as long as the policy of controlling
imports of agricultural produce is maintained by the United Kingdom Government, this Bill does provide our Ulster
farmers with the means of securing a just
return for their labours without in any
way prejudicing the position of the consumer.
In conclusion, may I add this point,
and an important point, in support of
the Measure? We have discussed it
fully with the Farmers' Union, the
Ulster Agricultural Organisation Society,
the Consultative Committee of Agriculture for the Six Counties and with the
following County Agricultural Committes: Down, Tyrone, Londonderry, and
Fermanagh. It has received the unanimous approval of each of these bodies,
and it has been approved by a majority
of the Armagh County Agricultural
Committee. I am, therefore, in the
happy position of commending to the
House a Measure which has behind it
the support of every organised body of
agriculture in the country, with the exception of the Antrim County Agricultural Committee which is to consider the
Bill on Friday. I beg to move.

which the farmer of Northern Ireland

sure it must be a source of great satisfaction to the Minister of Agriculture to
hear that when the Member for Shankill
was in Kilkeel he spoke very highly and
very favourably of the right hon. Gentleman. I think that on that occasion he
exhausted most of the good things he had
to say, judging from his speech here this
afternoon. I hope that in future he will
find more satisfactory things to say about
the Minister. When I read over the
various Clauses of this Bill it came upon
me with a sort of shock that the Minister
of Agriculture was wanting to assume
for himself as much power in Northern
Ireland as the Bible tells us Pharach
placed in the hands of Joseph, so that
he might control nearly everything in
the country. However, when I looked
more closely into the Bill I discovered
that it is only a Measure to enable the
Minister to frame certain schemes which
will be placed before this House for discussion, with the object of creating
better times for the farming population
of this Province.
As I represent an agricultural constituency and have always been interested
in agriculture I welcome this Bill, because I do not think things can be much
worse than they are so far as farming is
concerned, and I am very hopeful that if
wise schemes are brought forward under
this Bill the times will improve. I see it
is clearly laid down in the Bill that the
Minister will not have this power entirely
in his own hands, and that before any
scheme is brought into operation the
people concerned will be consulted, and I
am very hopeful that this is the beginning
of a better and brighter era for the farming community of this country. As such,
I welcome the Measure very heartily.
The Member for Shankill found fault
with the Minister because he, in the words
of the hon. Member, duplicated Bills
brought forward in the Imperial Parliament. I am going to find fault with him
for putting something into this Bill that
is not in the Imperial Measure, and I hope
the right hon. Gentleman will reconsider
this particular matter and will agree to
take it out of the Bill. I refer to page 14,
Clause 11, sub-clause (2), paragraphs (a)
and (b), in which it is laid down that
part of the arrangements for a scheme
must be that the various marketing boards
will have to submit their accounts for
audit to the Comptroller and Auditor-
General. I would be the last man to
say one word against the Comptroller and
Auditor-General, of all the officials of
this Government. I have met him repeatedly in the Public Accounts Committee, and accounts could not be submitted to a better or more able man.
But when you consider that the marketing boards in England are at liberty to
appoint their Own auditor, and are
entirely free from the Comptroller and
Auditor-General, I see no reason why the
marketing boards to be set up in Northern
Ireland should be treated differently. The
Comptroller and Auditor-General's department is not a department of commercial auditors. Its duties are to audit
the income and expenditure of this
Government, and I think it would be a
considerable disadvantage to the various
boards throughout the country if they
were compelled to furnish their accounts
to the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
The British Government is going further
than the Northern Government, because
they are making loans to the various
bodies, and this Government is not proposing to do that. They are only offering
to become guarantors, and considering
that they will have the full security of
all the producers I see no reason why they
should have to submit their accounts to
the Comptroller and Auditor-General. In
guaranteeing loans to the shipping companies the Government did not insist on
any such condition, and I hope the
Government will not insist upon it in the
case of farmers. There is no reason why
agriculture should be treated differently
to shipping companies and industrial
concerns.
The Bill commits us to nothing, but it
gives the Minister of Agriculture what he
ought to have, namely, the power to frame
some wise schemes whereby better prices

prices that have to be paid for lorries and
other vehicles to bring the produce to the
retailer or to the ship; and unless he can,
through his influence in the Cabinet, get
the Northern Government to remit or
bring down that tax, there is nothing
whatever he can do that will be successful
or that will get the farming community
on its feet again.
Now looking down the Clauses of this
Bill I can easily anticipate that it will
mean a lot more restrictions and a lot
more inspectors.
Whether this will or
will not be for the benefit of the farmers
it is not for me to say. I see that Clause
2 deals with the constitution of boards to
administer schemes. We are going to
have a number of boards set up.
Clause
3 provides for the register of producers
and lists. Now every farmer that sells
anything is a producer. I want to know
will every farmer have to be registered
before he is qualified to be considered a
producer or to sell the produce of his
estate.
The next Clause deals with the regulation of marketing and encouragement
of co-operation, education, and research,
the next with joint action for determining certain matters under the schemes,
the next with the general provisions of
schemes and contravention of schemes,
and the next with the financial powers
and duties of boards. Clause 10
provides for the employment of officers.
and payments to officers and members.
That Clause clearly contemplates an increased staff of officers, and, of course,
those officers must be paid. I notice
that some of the Governments out in the
tropics are taking steps to combat
locusts, because they swarm over the
country out there and when they are
done with it it is good for no one.
Someone said there were SO many
inspectors in Northern Ireland-I am
not saying it, but it was said that they
swarm over the country like locusts
seeking whom and what they may
devour. I want to know what is going
to be the increase in inspectors and the
increase in the payments. We are
coming to the time in Northern Ireland
-and we are getting to it very quickly
-when there will be an official or two
for every farmer. Whether that is
going to be for the benefit of the farmers or not I am not going to say, nor
am I going to criticise the inspectors.
I presume that the inspectors when they
are appointed do what they are told.
If they did not do what they are told
they would not be there, though you
will get people to say that public officials
can refuse to do what they are told.
The next Clause deals with provisions
as to the expenses of the Ministry and
audit in certain cases. More expenses.
And then Clause 13 gives power to the
marketing boards to negotiate with
other persons. What other persons will
they negotiate with, or is there any room
going to be left at all for individual
initiative either in the farming industry
or any other industry? I remember
reading letters in the Press from
practical farmers appealing to be left
alone, but apparently when this Bill
comes into force they will not be left
alone.
Now we come to Clause 14-power of
the Ministry to make regulations and
orders. There is not a Bill brought forward in this Parliament that does not
give the Ministry concerned power to
make regulations and orders. They
make regulations, and nobody ever sees
them till those regulations begin to take
effect. I understand that the practice
and rule in making regulations is to
draft the regulation and put it in the
Library, where it stays for a certain
time, and after that time the regulation
has the force of law.
The next Clause deals with the inspection of premises and the furnishing
of returns. I would like to know what
premises are to be inspected. If the
premises of every producer are liable to
inspection then the premises of every

the furnishing of returns, there is
nothing a farmer or any other business
man hates more, because he is always
liable to make a mistake or to be trapped
in the furnishing of these returns.
people probably are fairly busy at the
present time furnishing returns for the
Valuation Department, but now, according to this, they will have to start
furnishing returns regarding their agricultural produce. In fact they will have
to keep a clerk and an office for furnishing returns.

-protection in many ways-protection

1519 Agricultural Marketing Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mrs. Parker]
The hon. Member also referred to the
question of unemployment. He asked
what this Bill was going to do in the
way of giving employment. If this Bill
fulfils the purpose which I am certain
the Minister of Agriculture has in his
mind-that of raising the farming industry from the plight in which it now finds
itself it is going to maintain in employment numbers of agricultural labourers
throughout the country who would necessarily be out of employment if the farmer
continued to suffer as he is doing at the
present moment. I hope the hon. Member will realise, therefore, that this Bill
is concerned with the agricultural
labourer as well as with the industry,
and it seems to me, therefore, that he
ought to support this Measure.
I do not want to detain the House at
this very late hour, but I should like
to point out the necessity for boards of
the nature which are intended to be set
up for dealing with the marketing of
produce in every aspect. Human nature
being what it is, the industry which supplies the larder is the one which has
been the last to receive protection.
Naturally the consumer, assisted by
Socialist propaganda which sinks into
a receptive soil, will be inclined to
buy the cheapest without regard to
the question of origin. When cheap
Danish bacon is obtainable he will
not ask for Irish, and as a natural consequence the tradesmen find it almost
superfluous to keep the article. In fact
in the County of Somerset in England,
with which I am familiar, I went into
every grocer's shop to try to get English
or Irish bacon, and was offered Danish
bacon in every one except the last. That
is one aspect of the question.
Then there comes the question of
quality which, I gather, will be dealt with
by the marketing board to be set up
under this Bill. It is very interesting to
find that in England we are generally
told that the butter which comes from
New Zealand is cheaper and is very much
better in quality and purer than the
butter supplied by the majority of the
farmers. I should like hon. Members to
realise that I am not referring to Ulster
produce in this case. I merely mention
that to show-not, as I say, with reference to Ulster butter, but with reference
to butter in general-how necessary it is
to see that all the articles we produce are
the very best of their kind, in order that
we may procure the markets of Great
Britain for our own produce. It seems
to me that what we need, to a certain
extent, is protection against ourselves,
protection in order to make us realise
what is best for the whole community and
not best for the individual. In that connection I think a little co-operation is a
Danish lesson which farmers want to
learn, and I cannot help feeling that this
Bill will assist them to learn that lesson
and to profit by it.
In conclusion, I should like to say, in
support of this Measure, that we in Ulster
are very proud of our Ulster spirit. It
has already been stated in this House
to-day, and I should like to endorse it,
that our farmers are faced with the great
shadow of bankruptcy. That 18 a
terrible state of affairs, and anything that
we can do to help them should not be
grudged, even should it mean an extra
inspector or two, if the end justifies the
means in that respect. But, as I have
said, we in Ulster are very proud of the
spirit which made our forefathers come
over here, establish themselves, fight their
way, and hold their own and cultivate
the stony soil of the hillsides. Although
hon. Members opposite referred to it as
the most fertile soil in the world, there
is a large area of stony soil and of bog.
But in face of all the disadvantages our
forefathers made this country prosperous,
and handed down a great inheritance to
their descendants. To-day those descendants inherit the same spirit, but they also
have inherited something which goes with
it, fear of the unknown and the unusual.
Therefore, I am quite certain that
although this Measure has been approved
by so many representative bodies, there
will probably be a considerable amount
of criticism and grumbling. But I am
quite certain that with the powers provided by this Measure, and similar ones
which the Minister of Agriculture has
brought in, we shall find that the farmers
will be able to recover the prosperity
which they have lost through no fault of
their own, and are able once more to hold
their own, as their forbears did, against
all competitors.

Bill of 1931, and its sire is the Bill now
before the Imperial Parliament.
offspring with which we are dealing today has a somewhat mixed parentage,
and therefore for that reason I propose
to go into the two Bills as combined and
produced in the Measure now before this
House. I only hope the result of this
union between a Socialist Bill and a
National Government Bill will not be
love's labour lost. With all due
deference to the Member for South
Derry, who said this was not a Socialist
Bill, may I say this? The basis of this
Bill is the Act of 1931, and if you take
the trouble, as I did two years ago, to
buy this Act you will find that whole
Clauses have been lifted en bloc from
the Socialist Bill and included in this
Measure.
It is necessary here to touch upon the
reasons why this Socialist Act failed. It
failed for this reason. It enabled schemes
to be set up for the marketing of produce, but the fact is that no such schemes
were set up, because if you set up a
scheme for taking control of imports you
were torpedoed and it was a useless
proposition. Then you had the Ottawa
Agreements Act, and you have now in
the Imperial Parliament the Agricultural Marketing Bill making further provision for the imposition of quotas, and
1527 Agricultural Marketing Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
it is on this Socialist Act and the
National Government Bill now before the
Imperial House that our Marketing Bill
is based. The whole success of marketing schemes is dependent on the proper
working of a quota system, and it is
useless to set up any scheme where the
control of foreign imports is not taken
by quota. We have had the recent
agreements made by the Imperial Government with Denmark and the Argentine, which I cannot discuss here, but I
will say this, that these agreements somewhat restrict the quota which we can
impose on certain foreign imports, and
I am very much afraid that when it
comes to trying to set up a quota for
cattle or beef it will be found very
difficult to work in view of these agreements made by the Board of Trade.
The reason why we have this Bill before
us to-day is the effect of Clause
2 of the Bill now before the Imperial
Parliament. This Clause empowers the
Imperial authorities to act by Order in
Council or otherwise so that when a
marketing scheme is set up in Great
Britain, if we here do not follow suit
they will do it for us. So to-day we are
introducing this Bill to obviate that
necessity. While I do not stand here as
a Socialist, and I hope I never will, I
will of necessity support this Bill in the
hope that the Ministry will try to make
the most workable schemes they can out
of it. In dealing with any marketing
scheme we must remember that we are
different from Great Britain, inasmuch
as we are an exporting country. We export cattle, sheep and lambs, bacon and
pigs, eggs and potatoes, and of all the
things we grow at home we make our
money on the surplus we want to place
across the water. Therefore any scheme
which may be set up under this Bill
must ensure that these markets are retained and increased as expansion takes
place in the home market across the
water.
Whether or not this Bill is the best
way to deal with these exports I am not
at all sure. It seems to me it would be
a much more simple proposition if,
instead of having this very involved
procedure as laid down in the various
clauses of the Bill, we were to make
use of our existing Marketing Acts
which deal with such things as eggs,
potatoes, and pork. Every dealer who
sends across the water has been registered
under the Ministry, and I would think it
would be a far more simple thing if these
dealers were registred with the boards in
England, and such producers as are in
Northern Ireland were registered here, so
as to obtain the benefits of this Act in
England without resort to the very complicated schemes that will have to be set
up under this Bill. It would be a more
simple and more direct method, and
would probably result in the same thing
in the end.
If you look at Clause 14, it lays down
at great length exactly what these boards
can do, and I have no hesitation in saying
that this is the socialisation of agriculture, which is one of the most conservative businesses in the world. It is
a great experiment, and naturally you
will find the farmer critical. As these
schemes are introduced it will all depend
on the manner in which they are brought
forward to the public whether or not they
can be worked. In the first place, in any
schemes which may be set up under this
enabling Bill it should be remembered
that the producer's interests must be
paramount, and the control must be his.
The schemes must be worked in close cooperation with the Ministry of Agriculture, which will be the liaison between the
scheme set up in Northern Ireland and
the scheme set up in England, so that
there will be no difference in the form of
working, and in order to keep the whole
thing as simple as possible. To my mind
any scheme must not be imposed on an
unwilling community, but must be, as it
were, built up from the bottom.
The question of inspectors and officials
was mentioned by some Members on both
sides. In my opinion these officials are
not going to be officials of the Ministry
of Agriculture; they are going to be the
servants of the Board of Control in which,
as I have said, the producers must have a
paramount interest. These officials will
be paid by the Board, and their wages
will come under overhead charges taken
from the producers, so that it is up to the
farmers to see that when they have
control no elaborate number of officials is
appointed, that unduly inflated salaries
are not paid, and that the whole thing is
put on a business footing. It has been
said before that this Bill does not set up
any scheme, but that schemes as they
come through on the other side have to
be followed here.
1529 Agricultural Marketing Bill—

10 MAY 1933
Second Reading
I think these marketing schemes are
going to be the acid test as to whether
agriculture will regain its
former
prosperity under control on somewhat
Socialistic lines, and in exchange for this
control we are going to get a fixed minimum price. This control is combined with
a quota system, but I am only too much
afraid that the Dominions, and both Denmark and the Argentine, are being let
in on far too favourable terms with rather
inflated quotas, to the detriment of some
of the schemes that may be produced in
the future. Hitherto I have tried to
Ideal with the policy under which the Bill
was introduced, and I will now deal with
some points that are actually in the Bill.
I was very glad to see that in his statement to the House the Minister gave a
pledge that all interests will be consulted
when a scheme is framed. If you turn to
the Bill you will see that Schedule 1
implements this pledge. I do not think
this House has any right to pass a Bill to
enable schemes to be set up without allowing all interests to be consulted. I am
told that some effort may be made to
remove this Schedule 1 from the Bill, but
I hope the Cabinet, which no doubt has
considered this Bill closely and in detail,
