without alteration. Another point is
that when these schemes are set up they
have to come before this House for
approval. I understand this House can.
accept a scheme in toto or can reject it in
toto, but cannot alter one comma in it.
Whether or not this is a good thing I am
not prepared to say now, and no doubt
this point will be debated on the Committee Stage.
I
In conclusion, may I say that I am
going to support this Bill. It is a Bill
we have got to have, but it is a Bill that
is going to be extremely difficult to work.
It will only be made a success by getting
all those interested in agriculture to work
the schemes set up in close co-operation
with the Ministry of Agriculture.
would say this: Let the Minister of
Agriculture not try to run the show as
the boss, but try to run it as the helpful
friend and servant of the producer. This
Bill, if it proves a success, will alter

it is up to all concerned now that we
have got to have it, whether we like it

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I should like
to join with other hon. Members of the
House in congratulating the Minister.
I feel that this Bill has at last shown
the realisation that agriculture is the
most important industry in the British
Isles. Up to recently agriculture has
been, although the most important, the
most unorganised and disorganised, and
this Bill which is of the same type as

is a Bill which allows for an organisation
which, as Major Elliott said recently in

will be the best organised industry in
the whole British Isles. I think that
possibly outside this House some agriculturists may not realise the great
difficulties which will be met in
the working of this Bill. There is a
general tendency in Northern Ireland for
each farmer to be an individualist. He
detests by nature any form of control,
and the result is that until a benefit
is shown he may feel that the
scheme is not worth working. He will
have at times to pay a levy on his produce
for reasons which are explained in the
Bill, and he may resent those levies, but
he should look at it in this way.
Up to date agriculturists have been
hard put to it to keep their farms in a
prosperous condition. They have found
difficulty in getting an economic living
from their farms, and if, as we all hope,
this Marketing Bill brings back a modicum of prosperity and secures an economic
price for produce, they must realise they
can only get that through the establishment of a board, and must of necessity
pay certain levies for keeping that board
going. I would appeal to all those
boards, the farmers themselves, and to
the Ministry to realise that these
difficulties may exist, that hard things
may be said, but that each should treat
the scheme with the utmost sympathy.
We should realise that the Ministry, the
various boards and the individuals are
all out for one thing, that is, the prosperity of agriculture. Although these
small difficulties may crop up we should
keep in our minds that whatever occurs
the Bill has that one object-the good
of the industry. Many of the difficulties
bound to arise will gradually be swept
away. Once the boards have been established and are on their feet I feel that
those difficulties will fade away and there
will be smooth working in the end.

Second Reading
[Sir Basil Brooke]

the
have
was
past agriculturists
suffered from a policy by which food was
to be bought in the cheapest market in
the world, and this was intensified in
recent years by the fact that various
countries had closed the doors to other
food-producing countries. As each door
was closed more bankrupt stock
dumped on the British market. It has
been likened to a man watching a clock
which has not been wound up, or a man
watching a fire which has not been stoked.
Both will go down unless the clock is
wound up or the fire is stoked, and unless
a fair price is paid to the producer the
produce will disappear, and in the end
a higher price will have to be paid for
food. The argument may be put forward by some urban representatives that
this Bill will entail dearer food for the
future. As a matter of fact the regulation of these agricultural supplies will
ensure that in the future there is no
shortage of food, but that a level and
economic price will be paid.
The schemes which will eventually be
brought before this House are to be
worked by the farmers or producers.
They who have, to all intents and purposes, complete control will be responsible
for seeing that the best is done for the
particular industry of which they have
full knowledge and in which they are.
deeply interested themselves. I do not
quite agree with the hon. and gallant
Member (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) when he
says that it would be much better to carry
on under the present marketing schemes,
because if that were done it would mean
that the producers, who are the most
important people, can have no hand in
the production and marketing of their
own stuff. He suggested that this was
socialising agriculture. I would point
out that it does not in any way interfere
with the production, and therefore it is
not socialising the industry. The hon.
Lady (Mrs. Parker) pointed out that one
of the leaders of the Socialist Party
denied that this Bill was a Socialist
Measure. The reason it is not a Socialist
Measure, although it is framed on the old
Socialist scheme, is because the National
Government, owing to Conservative
influence, has realised quite rightly that
there must be some form of protection for
the industry. The accusation that this is
a Socialist Measure is entirely wrong and
will not hold water for one minute.
With regard to the question of unemployment, which was raised by the hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Nixon), actually agriculture employs more men than are
employed in all the textile industries in
the British Isles. So far as the dairying
industry is concerned, it employs more
men than are employed in the whole
motor industry. There is this great
danger and it refers particularly to
towns if we do not assist agriculture and
agriculture goes down the hill, what does
it mean? It means you will have an
influx into the towns of those people who
are unable to find a livelihood in the
country. It means you will have your
unemployment lists swollen. Bad as they
are now they will be very much increased,
so that, though, perhaps, the urban Members may not be so interested in the
agricultural question as we in the country
are, they should realise that if they do
not support this Bill, if they do not give
it every assistance they can, it will mean
that the towns will be overcrowded by the
population from the country.
Now, I would like to make again this
appeal, that agriculturists in this country
should consider this Bill as a charter,
because it implements, as the Minister
said in his speech, the Ottawa agreements; and I am very glad some of my
hon. Friends, who did not see eye to eye
with me as to the success of the Ottawa
agreements, agree that this Bill will be
an excellent thing for agriculture. If it
had not been for the Ottawa agreements
this Bill would not be before us to-day.
It is only because Ottawa established the
principle that it was possible to introduce
a Bill of this sort. If it is properly
worked, if there is proper sympathy, and
a proper understanding, I feel that this
Bill may mark a very important day for
agriculture in this country. I can only
hope that the defects which, perhaps,
some of us see, will gradually disappear,
but it will require sympathy and unselfishness on the part of everybody who has
anything to do with the working and
organisation of the various schemes.

Oral Answer to Question.
TELEPHONE SYSTEM IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD asked
the Minister of Commerce whether his
Ministry has made any representations
to the Postmaster-General with regard to
the installing of modern telephone instruments in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): Up-to-date apparatus is
already available at Bangor, Londonderry, and a very large number of the
smaller exchanges in Northern Ireland.
In the Belfast automatic area, which
covers some 17,000 telephones, and includes Knock, Fortwilliam, Dunmurry
and Whitehouse, the work of installing
the most up-to-date automatic plant is
now in progress, and, it is hoped, will
be completed before the end of 1935.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
the work, which involves the provision of
new telephone buildings, new apparatus.
and new cables, is of great magnitude,
and I can assure the hon. Member that
it is being pressed forward with the utmost dispatch.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: Is
the Minister aware that the district
manager has already sent notices out to
certain subscribers to say that he is
putting in another apparatus different
from what they have but which retains
a fixed mouthpiece and the old antedeluvian system of hand bell ringing?
Mr. BARBOUR: The hon. Member
will appreciate, as I have already said,
the magnitude and complication of the
matter. The change over from one system to another, to which the hon. Member refers, is one of an engineering
character and is of a transitional nature,
and we will have to ask the public to bear
it with such patience as they can until
the completion of the automatic system,
which I can assure the hon. Member is
being pushed forward, and which we hope
to have completed by the end of 1935.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to ask if
the right hon. Gentleman would be prepared to make representations to see that
the charge for telephones is reduced so
that ordinary people may have the advantage of their use in their own homes?
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman answer that question, because
it is important that the high rent at
present charged for telephones should
be reduced?
Mr. SPEAKER: I must point out that
it is not in the power of the right hon.
Gentleman to take action, but he can
make representations to the
proper
authorities.

Mr. NIXON: Fortunately or unfortunately, I have at the moment an opportunity of making my first speech on these
Estimates, and if I attack the Government and it is likely I will-I want to
say it is certainly not an attack on the
Minister of Labour. But circumstances
compel me to attack the Government.
As I have often said, there is not a man
on the Government side would do the job
as well as the Minister. He is very
courteous and so is his Parliamentary
Secretary, but things are so bad outside
and complaints are so numerous I must
take advantage of the occasion to draw
attention to them. Now, it does not
matter what legislation is brought forward here nor does it matter what anyone
on either side of the Committee says, the
all important and terrible question cf
the hour is the question of unemployment. I hold that at the moment there
are 40,000 totally unemployed in this
city, and I do not see I hope I am
wrong-where the half of them are ever
going to get work. I will be glad if the
Minister can tell me. In addition to
that, I do not see where half the number of boys coming from school are going
to get work. Emigration is finished, so
far as I can see, in our time.
-
These are the facts as I see them, and
I submit that-I will not say the Minister of Labour, I will say the Government
-are taking no steps to ease that situation. The only steps they are taking is
to increase the staff. I am not blaming
them for that, because the staff must be
kept up. I was not here the other day
when reference was made to the distinguished gentleman who built this
House. He had a scheme, but the Government, I understand, have turned
it down. There was a scheme put forward from this side which simply meant
subsidising industry, not out of revenue as
was erroneously stated in the Press, but
subsidising a certain industry for a beginning out of the £2,500,000 paid out
last year in unemployment benefit and a
few other things. The figures are there.
I still submit that the scheme laid before

Take any young person who is not

thinks if he does not sign the form he

a consent to accept a court which is not
complete. Most likely there is no
workers' representative. There is rarely
a workers' representative at these courts,
the reason being that the remuneration
they get would not pay them for being
there. If a man is unemployed he is
hardly qualified to sit on the court, and
if he is working his employer is not going
to allow him out to sit on a court of
referees adjudicating on these cases.

The Minister, in appointing these chairmen of courts of referees, should at least
appoint gentlemen who have some experience of the world, who have some years
behind them, who have some experience
of human nature, and who have some little
experience of industry and working conditions. I also object to the appointment
as chairman of a court of referees of a

resident magistrate with a big salary
should have that salary supplemented by

referees. I find that one resident magistrate here got £136 16s during the year;

another £90. There are plenty of gentlemen in Northern Ireland with a

Making sheep drains to give employment.

Before I sit down I will put one question to the Minister of Labour, a question
which he will admit, and has admitted, is
a vital question. I ask the Minister of
Labour to state to-day in this Committee,
since the Government have rejected the
suggestions from this side of the Committee for the relief of unemployment,
since they have rejected the suggestion put
forward by Mr. Stewart, M.P., since
the position is gradually getting worse,
although we are told every year that we
at the turning point-I ask the
Minister of Labour, the kind and sympathetic Minister of Labour-no matter
what I say I am always bound to say that
-what are the Government going to do.
Something must be done, and if something is not done the position will be
serious. I warned the Minister before; I
think it was about the 1st of November,
from my place in another house that there
was a storm gathering in Belfast owing to
the policy of the Government in regard to
unemployment.
The Minister did not
appreciate that statement at the time,
but the storm broke; there were a good
many windows broken, a good many heads
broken, and some lives lost, and then,
after the storm had broken, after the
people were batoned and abused, and
after angry and bitter feelings had been
aroused, the Government stepped in and
did what they should have done months
and months before.
I say to the Minister before I sit down
that the present position cannot continue.
There are 20,000 men in Belfast who
under present circumstances will never get
work. The young men who can get no
class of work are accumulating every year,
and unless you produce a remedy of your
own, seeing that you have rejected other
people's remedies, the position will be
desperate in four or five years. There
will be no question of defeating the
Government, because nobody will want to
defeat them. There are very few men in
Belfast who, if there were an election
to-morrow, would be looking for a seat.
You need not be a bit afraid of that, but
the position in the city is getting
desperate. I ask the Minister again-
I do not like repeating myself, but I want
to be as impressive as possible-to tell
us what the Government are going to do.

delivered in this House on the question
of the apathy of the Minister of Labour's
Department in regard to providing work
for single unemployed persons. I think
that is one of the greatest crimes that
have ever taken place in the history of
Northern Ireland. This is a huge
Department, one of the best-paid Labour
Departments in the world, and yet it is
doing absolutely nothing to provide work
for the single unemployed persons who
are not in receipt of unemployment
benefit. I wonder if the Minister and his
Parliamentary Secretary ever consider
the plight of the single unemployed men
and women.
Major MCCORMICK: And the married
men.
Mr. HENDERSON: I will deal with
that aspect of the question afterwards.
According to the official figures of the
Ministry of Labour there are 26,000
children leaving school every year. Those
are not my figures; they are the figures
of the Ministry of Labour which appear
on a very large poster, almost the length
of this Parliament House, on the Shore
Road. There are two paintings, not
painted by a Russian artist, but by a
Belfast artist, of a boy and a girl, and
alongside is the slogan "Buy Ulster
Goods." Then attention is drawn to the
fact that there are 25,000 or 26,000
Ulster children leaving school every year.
There is no work for them and there is no
hope for them. Their plight is getting
more horrible every day. I feel that the
Chairman would not allow me to draw
any other Minister into the discussion, but
the Minister of Labour and his Parliamentary Secretary are in a better position
to understand the plight of these people.
They are in utter destitution. Many of
them are to-day inmates of workhouses
throughout Northern Ireland.
The conditions under which some of
these people live are absolutely horrible.
The Government can realise the plight of
a worker in Belfast with three children.
He is entitled to draw benefit for himself,
his wife and three children. He gets 25/3
for them. There are thousands of homes
where some of these men have to keep
two single unemployed young men who
cannot get work. The Minister of Labour
has not paid the slightest attention to the
plight of these persons and the unfortunate parents of these boys. A man

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That on and after the first day of
January, nineteen hundred and thirtyfour, there shall be charged on a licence
to be taken out annually by a moneylender in Northern Ireland an excise
duty of fifteen pounds, or, if the licence
be taken out not more than six months
before the expiration thereof, of ten
pounds."
Mr. BARBOUR: This Resolution is
necessary before the Bill that was passed
in this House on the Second Reading
some weeks ago can be discussed further
in Committee. Clause 1 of the Bill requires every moneylender in Northern
Ireland, whether in business alone or as
a partner in a firm, to take out annually
in respect of every address at which he
carries on business an excise licence on
which there has to be paid an excise
duty of £15, but subject, of course, to
certain provisos in the Bill.
of
It seems to the Government desirable
that the provisions in operation here relating to the issue of excise licences to
moneylenders should follow as closely as
possible the corresponding provisions in
operation in other parts of the United
Kingdom. The reasons for this are,
course, very simple. If, for example, the
statutory conditions governing moneylending were somewhat less exacting here
than in England and Scotland, there
might be a tendency for Northern Ireland to become a favourable centre for
carrying on this particular kind of business, especially with English and Scottish
borrowers, since many such borrowers
prefer, for very obvious reasons, to borrow by post from moneylenders at a
distance from their own homes.
An excise duty requires the sanction of
a Ways and Means Resolution, and it is
that sanction that I ask the Committee
to give now. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I thought when the
Government introduced the Moneylenders Bill it was really a sort of protective Measure for the unfortunate
victims of the system.

the Committee.
I

discover now that it is really going to be

are made all over the country, and the

You

never would have introduced the Bill if

Oral Answers to Questions.
DUTIES ON GRASS-SEED ENTER-
ING GERMANY.
1. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of
the enormous import duty, viz., £25 per
ton imposed on grass-seed entering Germany, and, in view of the enormous importance of this branch of the agricultural industry to Ulster farmers, he will
make representations to the Imperial
Government with a view to having these
duties removed at the earliest possible
moment.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply. The
answer to the first part of the question
is in the affirmative. As regards the
second part, I would inform the hon.
Member that immediately following upon
the German Government's announcement
of its intention to increase the then existing rate of duty on imported grass-seeds
my Ministry took steps to bring the
matter, in its special bearings upon
Northern Ireland industry, to the notice
of the Board of Trade, and that the subject is still engaging the attention of the
two Departments.
TOWN PLANNING ACT.
the
2. Major McCORMICK asked
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
will consider introducing legislation to
amend the Town Planning Act so that
compulsory action may be taken to deal
with roads and amenities of the Province,
which though common to everyone, rural
or urban authorities concerned take no
action to preserve for the use and enjoyment of all.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am not aware of
any grounds for amending the Town.
Planning Act on the lines suggested by
the hon. and gallant Member.
Major MCCORMICK: Will the Minister allow that this Town Planning Act
is practically inoperative at the present
time, and will he take into consideration
the fact that our coast roads and other
amenities of the Province, common to
everyone, could not be despoiled as they
are at present if local authorities took
action?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The whole
principle of the Act is to enable the local
authorities to have this power to preserve the amenities of the countryside,
and while it is perfectly true that some
local authorities have not taken steps, I
am glad to think that others have. The
Act is a very difficult one, because you
have to consider the rights of property.
I know that the Belfast Corporation are
bringing in a scheme at the present time.

PROFESSION.

protection of properly conducted hairdressing and beauty parlour establishments, consider the introduction of legislation along the lines laid down by the
Pharmacy and Poisons Act, 1925.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not satisfied that the public interest involved
would either necessitate or justify the
introduction of legislation of the character
indicated.

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask a
question which perhaps concerns you,
Mr. Speaker. Can information be given
regarding the stealing of a locker out
of the room used at present by the

That locker was in the room and
we used it for locking up our Parliamentary papers and attache cases,
but when we entered that room to-day

I feel that that action, whoever may be

to

A question was raised the other day on
the Adjournment of the House in regard
to public statements made by a part-time
officer of the Ministry. I was prohibited
from referring to this matter when the
Estimate was in Committee. I want now
to recall to the Minister of Labour an
incident that happened some time ago.
I
refer to the case of James Wood, solicitor,
who was a part-time officer of the Government. James Wood went to Hillsborough
and delivered a speech against the Government.
The Government called a Cabinet
meeting the following day and had James
Wood removed from his part-time position
under the Ministry. This is going to lead
us to a position in which a part-time officer
can make a speech in favour of the
Government and there will be nothing
said to him, but if he makes a speech
against the Government he will be dismissed immediately.
I do not stand for that, nor do I stand
for the dismissal of any person who fulfils
the functions for which he was appointed,
but I am going to have it either one way
or the other. The policy of the Government in the past has been that if any
part-time officer
officer speaks against the
Government he is removed. I have
nothing to say against the young gentleman in the present case. He gave me one
of the highest credentials any man in this
Province could have. He said to the
people of the Ballycastle district that if
they want a Parliament to take an enlightened view of politics they should be
Socialists and the people will return them.
I do not think anyone could give me a
better certificate than that. In the past
the principle adopted was one of dismissal, but when the speech was in their
favour there was a change of attitude on
the part of the Government. I hope the
Government realise that that can be
played by two parties. If they mete out
justice equally no one can have any
complaint.
It has been the policy of the Government where all decisions in regard to unemployment benefit are concerned to have
the signature of the chairman of the court
of referees appearing on all papers,
whether the decision is in favour of or
against the applicant. There is a hidden
hand operating in regard to transitional
payments. The Minister is responsible
for this hidden hand in so far as he allows
the committees to meet in secret. Then
when they give their decisions they are
under the signature of G. R. McConnell,
the Labour Exchange manager. The
Minster of Labour has deliberately stated
in this House that he and his Department
have no connection with the amounts to
be granted to the applicants.
Why then does this full-time official
sign the decisions of that committee which
are sent to the applicants? I ask the
Minister to withdraw the signature of G.
R. McConnell, as he has admitted he has
no connection with it; and when he
appears before the Governor for the
renewal of his licence for another term
to have all decisions from the public
assistance committees signed by the chairmen. No man who signs a decision
should be ashamed of the decision. The
chairman of one of these public assistance
committees which gives a decision,
whether reducing a grant, disallowing a
grant, or making a grant in full, should
not be ashamed to sign his name to what
his convictions brought him to give as his
ruling.

want the Minister to understand that the

The Minister has said that I made an

could not be justified, and that I got my

I want to inform the Minister that I received six letters-four signed and two

who recently received an appointment at
the juvenile exchange. One of the individuals who sent me an anonymous letter
is in the Ministry; hence the right hon.
Gentleman's reason for knowing that the
letter was anonymous. I had four signed
letters and I used them instead of the
unsigned ones, because it is not my practice to use anonymous letters either in
this House or anywhere else.
I am quite aware that no one uses
anonymous letters more than the Minister
for the purpose of detecting fraud in
regard to unemployment insurance. I
know that an anonymous letter has held
up a man's benefit for weeks, and then at
the end of the seventh or eighth week it
was discovered there was no truth whatever in the letter. Whenever a letter is
sent into the Ministry, whether it is signed
or unsigned, it is acted upon immediately,
but I want to convey to the Minister that
I do not act upon information contained
in anonymous letters. I act on letters
signed by the people who wrote them.

The whole administration of this

They are only getting a percentage out of

and employees is more than I can understand, except it be that you are really

the public.
I hope we will have, in the near future,

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill
which now comes up for Second Reading
is identical with the Act which was
passed last year in connection with the
1932 race, and as its object was fully explained by me in this House on the 12th
May, 1932, it is perhaps unnecessary to
dilate at any length regarding it. However, I feel it necessary to express my
pleasure that we are once again to have
the Tourist Trophy Race run over the
famous Ards course in 1933.
area.
As I explained last year, we were compelled to impose a charge of 2s 6d on
every car entering the race
It
will be seen from the Bill that a similar
charge is proposed this year, but at the
same time it will be observed that, as on
the last occasion, persons who live in the
race area or who have to enter it
for purposes other than seeing the race,
are exempt from the payment of this
charge. The gross amount raised last
year by the imposition of this small
charge of 2s 6d was £616, and this went a
very considerable way towards relieving the
anxiety of the local race committee officials
and of the financial burden imposed on
them. I need hardly say that it would
be more difficult still were it not for the
fact that we have had the good fortune
to be assisted by generous donors who,
through their interest in motoring, have
come forward and presented the prize
money, amounting to £1,500.
For this year I am happy to say that
we have again been relieved of any
anxiety in connection with the prize
money through the generosity of Sir
William Morris, who is known throughout the world not only for the fact that
he is the founder of the famous Morris
Motor Car Company, but also, more important still, for his deep interest in and
generosity towards every movement
associated with the sport of motoring and
the development of motor engineering.
I am sure the House will join with me
in saying how much we appreciate his
generosity towards us in connection with
the race. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I have never opposed
this Bill before when it was presented
to the House. The reason I supported
it the first time it was introduced was
because I thought some advantage might
come to Northern Ireland in the way of
employment. I may say that in company with the Prime Minister I was
speaking to Sir Herbert Austin during
the race before last, and during that conversation the Prime Minister put before
Sir Herbert a practical proposition, that
was to make a centre in Northern Ireland for the construction of Austin cars.
I thought it was a very good idea. I
think the suggestion made by the Prime
Minister is one that should get the support of every Member of this House.
I have waited to see the results of our
expenditure on this motor-car race in
Northern Ireland, and I have discovered
at the end of every race when the balance
sheet was made up that our loss was
greater than our income. If we are
living in hope that part of the motor
industry will be established in Northern
Ireland, we are not going to have that
hope materialised through the motor
race.
In this Bill the motorist who crosses the
course is to be charged. That charge is
for the purpose of giving some financial
assistance to the R.A.C. to carry on the
race. I go to see the race myself and I
pay to see it. I have noticed, on a very
large stand erected by the R.A.C. certain
seats reserved for members of the Government, from whom no payment is taken.
If the R.A.C. think they are going to
use the race to create class distinction they
are making a great mistake. At one time
there were as many members of the
R.A.C. sitting on this side of the House
as on that side, but since the R.A.C. got
this race run in Northern Ireland they
never recognised one Member on this side
worthy of being invited as a guest on the
grand stand.
On all occasions the R.A.C. have
selected their guests from the Government side of the House, thus making the
general public believe that the only support they ever received was from that side,
whilst the Members of the Opposition were
100 per cent. with them in making the
race a success. If the R.A.C. want to
run the race in Belfast let them pay for
it. They should not get a local authority
to impose a charge on a private motor-car
going on that course. What authoritv
is there for prohibiting the ratepayers of
that area from using the course during a
working day? None whatever? A legal

right should not be granted the R.A.C.
by this Bill to prohibit cars going on the

to assist Ulster industry, and if we hang
on to this thing we are only losing-
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER : Is the
hon. Gentleman not forgetting the rather
important fact that for the closing of the

Mr. BEATTIE: I fully realise that,

Are you prepared on this occasion to keep

It is stated here that persons residing
within the area can use the area without

Persons who live within the area were
compelled to pay because they could not

understand this.
Within the Ards circuit a number of
people own motor cars. It is definitely
stated in the Bill that the people within
the area could use motor-cars without a

the area wished to go over the course

business reasons can have exemption by
receiving a badge from the district

clearly known by everyone outside, because

On the night before the race last year
six buses were held up in the Newtownards
centre because they could not get exemption badges to pass through on the following morning. I came through on the
following morning. I had an exemption
badge for half a crown.
But here were public vehicles that use

and they were asked to pay for badges,
the proceeds of which were to go to the

could not get exemption badges up to

four buses went on the road the following

Let the owners clearly understand their

I ask the Minister to-day to do away with

Mr. BARBOUR: This Resolution provides for a short-dated loan facility to be

Edward Archdale), the Bill contemplates

own operations in a sound businesslike

afforded by this Resolution, by the introduction of a State guarantee, is really

It is expected that a board will be able
to obtain credit on the commodities committed to its charge by the producers when
it has been firmly established, but in the
ordinary way there must be difficulty in
starting out, and it is on this account

this Resolution relates that any guaranteed loan must be repaid within two years,

on the ground that he has not been resident in Northern Ireland for a period of
at least twelve months, but there is
nothing in the provision which makes it
obligatory upon a Court to refuse a certificate where this ground for refusal exists.
It has been represented to the Ministry
that this provision may make it unnecessarily difficult for a Northern Ireland
moneylender to dispose of his business,
since potential purchasers from other parts.
of the United Kingdom might feel chary
about entering into negotiations if, however excellent their character, etc., could
be proved to be, a Court might refuse
them a certificate on the ground that they
had not resided for the statutory period
in Northern Ireland.
It is accordingly proposed by this
amendment to provide that a Court may
only refuse a certificate under paragraph
(e) where the applicant proposes to set up
The Committee may rest
a new business.
assured that this amendment will not in
any sense weaken the Clause, since a Court
may still, if it has grounds for doing so,
refuse a certificate under paragraph (a)
or (b) to, say, a cross-Channel moneylender
proposing to set up in Northern Ireland,
even where he is not taking over an existing moneylending business.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
note or memorandum delivered or sent

Sub-Clause (1) of Clause 6 provides.
that a moneylending contract shall not be
enforceable unless a note of the contract
is made and signed by the borrower and
a copy of the note delivered or sent to the
borrower within seven days from the making of the contract. It is to this copy
that I desire to draw the attention of the
Committee. It has been held that a copy
in such a provision as this means an exact
copy, and the object of this Amendment
is to enable a court, where it considers it
proper so to do, to regard a contract as
not being rendered void merely by reason
of some immaterial defect in the copy. It
is not difficult to imagine circumstances in
which a dishonest borrower might seek to
evade his obligations by pleading some
trivial typographical error in the copy as
an unquestionable ground for upsetting
his contract.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

Major MCCORMICK: I beg to move in
Clause 10, page 12, line 32, to leave out
"forty-eight" ("exceeds the rate of fortyeight per cent. per annum") and to insert "twenty-four.'
""
I feel that the Committee will be with
me in this Amendment as being in accordance with the principle that a low or
reasonable rate of interest should be
charged. It may be asked what is a low
or reasonable rate of interest. The
obvious answer is that it would be difficult
to fix such a rate because we have different
degrees or values so far as the rate of
money is concerned. All I can say is that
most people would say that a much less
rate of interest than that set down in the
Bill, or than what is set down in my
Amendment, should be quoted. Indeed
they might say that ten per cent. was a
reasonable rate of interest. But what
should be looked at in discussing this
question of interest is that people
who resort to moneylenders, or who are
habitual borrowers, are prepared to pay
what we might call an extortionate rate
of interest-it may be said that that is
their own look-out-and are certainly prepared to pay a higher rate than the
ordinary banking institutions would charge
them. We must take into account the
fact that the risks which the people who
lend out this money take would naturally
be larger than those taken by a bank,
and, therefore, the rate of interest would
have to be larger than what is usual or
even permissible by a bank.
To my mind Clause 10 is possibly the
most vital part of this whole Bill. It is
most important for the purpose of the Act,
which is ostensibly to protect the borrower.
It is not to protect the moneylender.
The very genesis of the Bill is to
protect the borrower. I say that
this is a most necessary amendment,
and I put it forward believing it
to make for the successful working of
the Bill. I feel that forty-eight or fifty
per cent. is an iniquitous rate. Half of
that would be a reasonable rate of interest.
I might repeat what I said on the Second
Reading of the Bill. I said then that
this rate of forty-eight per cent. becomes

There are certain other considerations
to which I would also draw the attention
of the Committee:-
1. The charging of expenses is prohibited under the Bill, and so moneylenders in future will have to defray these
out of the interest which they receive.
2. The bulk of the moneylending
business in Northern Ireland consists of
the making of small short-term loans, repayable by weekly or monthly instalments.
The expenses of collection in the case
of such loans are disproportionately high
as compared with those in connection with
loans of comparatively large amounts repayable in one sum or in a small number
of instalments.
Other provisions of the Bill, for example, Clauses 6, 15, 19 and 20 will, in
conjunction, have the effect of compelling
moneylenders to reduce very substantially
the rates of interest at present charged.
In view of these considerations, I cannot
accept the amendment proposed by the hon.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Agricultural Marketing Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Framing and approval of
marketing schemes).
(1) A scheme regulating the marketing of an agricultural product may be
framed by the Ministry of Agriculture
(in this Act referred to as "the Ministry") for application to Northern Ireland, or to some part thereof, in any
case where the Ministry is satisfied that
such a scheme is necessary for the more
efficient production and marketing of
the said agricultural product:
If either House of Parliament,
within the statutory period next after
any scheme approved as aforesaid has
been laid before such House, resolves
that the scheme shall be revoked, the
scheme shall thereupon be revoked by
the Ministry, but without prejudice to
the validity of anything previously
done thereunder or to the framing and
approving of a new scheme.

Lieut-Colonel GORDON : I beg to

In moving this Amendment to Clause
1, I wish to try to divest any schemes
which may be set up under this Bill
of the rigid control of the Ministry as
opposed to the Minister himself being responsible. I wish to introduce the personal element into any scheme which may
be set up under this Clause 1. While
"Ministry" may be said to be the same
thing as "Minister," in my opinion it
is not. The Ministry as authorised in
this Bill can act first and come to the
Minister afterwards and say, "We have
done such a thing, you must back us up."
If the Minister himself acts first the
Ministry then will hesitate before putting
into force any order or scheme under the
Bill without giving it close consideration
and without consulting the Minister. In
my opinion, any scheme which may be
evolved under this Bill must be vitalised
by the individual touch of the Minister
and free from the creeping paralysis of
bureaucracy. The tendency to-day is for
the body bureaucratic to take control,
using the Minister as their mouthpiece,
instead of the Minister using his Department to give executive effect to policy.
I am quite well aware that in the

that "Minister" and "Ministry" are the

Bill. In the Act of 1931 "Ministry"

It is the Minister
has the sole responsibility. In the Bill

and working out these schemes, using the

Again, if you turn over the page of this

I do not know whether this Amendment

I have put down this Amendment to try

This Clause deals with the framing and
approval of marketing schemes. The
circumstances in which a scheme may be
prepared by the Ministry of Agriculture
may be divided into two categories. First
of all, the Ministry must prepare
scheme, when such is necessary, for subserving an Order regulating sales of an
agricultural product within the United
Kingdom, made under Part 1 of the
Agricultural Marketing Bill at present
before the Parliament at Westminster.
It is important to bear in mind the
circumstances in which an Order regulating sales of an agricultural product in the
United Kingdom may be made. This
El
1667 Agricultural Marketing Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Sir Edward Archdale]
will only occur when a quota has been
established in regard to the importation
of an agricultural product into the United
Kingdom.
Such a quota may be either a compulsory one, covered by an Order made
by the Board of Trade under the Agricultural Marketing Bill at present before
Parliament at Westminster, or it may be
a voluntary arrangement, such as the
Gentleman's agreement, made last autumn
with Denmark and a number of other
countries, restricting the exports of bacon
and hams from those countries to the
United Kingdom. Broadly speaking,
therefore, an Order regulating sales in
the United Kingdom will only be made
in cases where the quantitative control of
imports into the United Kingdom has
been introduced. Power to make an
Order is conferred by the new United
Kingdom Agricultural Marketing Bill,
which also authorises the Minister of
Agriculture and Fisheries, and the Secretaries of State for Scotland and Northern
Ireland, acting jointly to make whatever
provisions they think necessary for carrying it out.
It will be seen, therefore, that the
Imperial Authorities could make regulations governing the conditions under
which agricultural products could be sold
in Northern Ireland. In practice, however, it is intended that so far as Northern
Ireland is concerned the regulation of
sales of products grown in Northern
Ireland shall be carried out under the
authority of our own Parliament. This
will be done by the Ministry of Agriculture framing a scheme whenever it is
necessary to do so in order to carry out
control of sales of any agricultural product within Northern Ireland. Consequently, by the proviso to Sub-Clause 1 of
Clause 1 of the Bill, it is made mandatory
on the Ministry to frame a scheme where
such is necessary for subserving any purposes of an Order regulating sales of an
agricultural product made under Part 1
of the United Kingdom Act.
The Ministry will have discretion to
prepare a scheme in the following circumstances: (i) Where a scheme is in force
in Great Britain without an Order having
been made under Part I of the United
Kingdom Act regulating sales of that product. In those circumstances, however,
it may be that the Ministry's discretion
is more apparent than real. Once a
scheme is introduced in Great Britain for
a commodity which we produce and export
to Great Britain it may be essential that
we should introduce a scheme for the
regulation of the marketing of that product in Northern Ireland, particularly in
regard to that portion of the product
which is exported.
Let us take the case of milk, which was
referred to by the hon. and gallant
Gentleman (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon).
milk marketing scheme may be introduced
in Great Britain without the regulation of
imports, since imports of milk from
abroad are negligible. Consequently,
there will be no Order under Part 1 of
the United Kingdom Act regulating sales
of milk within the United Kingdom, and
it will be optional for the Ministry to
frame a scheme. Nevertheless, in view of
our export of milk and cream from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain, it
might prove imperative that we should
take steps to control the conditions under
which milk was marketed here.
We could not stand aside and allow
opponents of the English scheme to use
supplies of milk from Northern Ireland
to endeavour to break the scheme in
England. If such a development took
place it would react upon our farmers in
many ways, since if Northern Ireland produce was used for the purpose of undercutting prices in Great Britain it would
not be long before discrimination against
our produce was introduced either by the
British Government or marketing boards.
(ii) There remain instances in which it
may be considered desirable to introduce
a marketing scheme for Northern Ireland
in respect of a product for which no
similar scheme is in operation in Great
Britain. Turkeys might prove an instance. It is only in respect of a few
commodities however, that the Ministry
will have any real discretion in regard
to the introduction of a scheme.
cases where this discretion exists it is
needless to say that the very closest consultation with the agricultural community
will take place before a scheme is introduced.

be made. If an objection to the scheme

SO as to meet the objection, then the

the fullest opportunity will be given for

removal of any anomalies which may be

of consultations with producers and the

made at a public inquiry certain modifications may be made. Not until all these
steps have been taken will the scheme be
brought into force. This will be done
by the Ministry making an order approving the scheme as framed, or as subsequently modified, specifying the day upon
which the scheme shall come into
operation.
Immediately a scheme has been
approved it has to be laid before both
Houses of Parliament. When this is done
Parliament has the power to pass a
resolution directing that the scheme shall
be revoked. Consequently, if producers
are dissatisfied with the scheme they may
get their Member of Parliament to raise
the matter in the House and to submit a
resolution proposing that the scheme
should be revoked. It may be hoped,
however, that the circumstances in which
this action will be taken by producers will
never arise.
Even if no exception is taken to the
scheme when it is presented to Parliament a further safeguard is provided.
The operation of a scheme framed by the
Ministry is limited to two years, and at
some date before the expiration of that
period Parliament must pass a resolution definitely approving the scheme.
This means that probably at some date
within the second year of its operation the
Minister of Agriculture will submit a
resolution to Parliament inviting each
House of Parliament to approve the
scheme. The equivalent of a second
reading debate will then take place on
this resolution, and in order to enable the

I move this Amendment standing in

charges taken from the products of the

against that is and there may be something in it that the farming community,

experience, and so on, to act as chairman

CLAUSE 3 (Register of Producers and
Lists.)
(1) Every scheme shall provide for
the registration of any producer of the
regulated product who makes application for that purpose, and for the
removal from the register of the names
of persons who have ceased to be such
producers.
(2) The Ministry, as soon as practicable after any scheme has been framed,
shall cause a list to be compiled containing-
(a) the names of all such persons as the
Ministry has reason to believe to
be producers of the regulated product, not being persons to be exempted from registration under the
scheme; and
(b) the respective addresses of such
persons so far as known to the
Ministry.
When such list has been compiled, the
Ministry shall send by post to every
person named in the list particulars of
the scheme framed by the Ministry,
together with a form of application for
registration as a producer under the
scheme.
The annual agricultural statistics collected by the Ministry may be used for
the purpose of compiling the list aforesaid.
(3) The register of producers for the
purposes of a scheme shall be kept by
the board constituted under the scheme.
The register shall be open for inspection, and the board shall furnish a copy
of the register, or of any part thereof,
to any person demanding it, upon payment of such fee as the Ministry may

the Standing Order.

clerical officer grade

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I presume that by "wastage"
vacancies the hon. Member means vacancies which have arisen in the grade
owing to superannuation, resignation,
dismissal, death, or the promotion of
clerical officers to higher rank. The
total number of such vacancies which
have arisen in the lower clerical grade
since October, 1930, is 40.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the number of new entrants, male and female,
who have been appointed to the Civil
Service since October, 1930, in the lower
clerical officer grade, also the number of
female temporary clerks who have been
promoted to writing assistant or lower
clerical officer grade since October, 1930,
and the number of writing assistants who
have been promoted to clerical grade
since 1930.
Mr. POLLOCK: Since October, 1930,
there have been 16 appointments to the
grade of established male clerks; this
number includes 8 posts filled by the
establishment of ex-Service temporary
clerks and 8 appointments made as the
result of open competition.
Vacancies in the lower clerical grade
(women) are filled by the promotion of
established writing assistants, typists
and telephonists. There have accordingly been no appointments since the
date mentioned to the grade of established women clerk as a result of open
competition.
Three temporary women clerks were
appointed to the grade of established
writing assistant during this period, but
for the reason which I have already
mentioned no temporary women clerks
were appointed to the established clerical
officer grade.
Nine established writing assistants
have been promoted to the clerical grade
since October, 1930.

to Ireland.

When any offence under this Act,
committed by a body corporate, is
proved to have been committed with the
consent or approval of, or to have been
facilitated by any neglect on the part
of, any director, manager, secretary or
other officer of the body corporate, he,

shall be liable to be proceeded against

NEW CLAUSE (Exemption from
market tolls).
or
Notwithstanding any Act of Parliament or grant or prescriptive right
all agricultural products sold
offered for sale under any schemes set

Brought up, and read a First time.
Mr. MARK: I beg to move, "That
the Clause be read a Second time."
I am inclined to think that this is a
very important matter to the people of
Northern Ireland. If hon. Members
refer to the Clause they will see that it
does not interfere with any existing
right, nor does it interfere with the right
of an urban council to charge any toll
they may care to charge, which it is in
their power to charge, in regard to any
product which is not subject to the scheme
under the Bill, nor does it interfere with
the right to charge tolls on any product
which goes through their market. Those
things are, I think, perfectly clear in the
wording of the new Clause.
In any
event, any move made by the board in
regard to tolls must be made with the
consent of the Ministry. I think that it
is sufficient protection of all the interests
concerned in these matters.
My object in moving this new Clause
is to try to get some sort of uniformity
throughout the markets of Northern Ireland. Take, for example, any scheme
that might be put into operation, say a
pork scheme. Supposing the Urban
Council in Newry or Ballynahinch
charge 2s per head toll on any pork
coming into their market when Coleraine
or some other neighbourhood only
charge 6d per head, it is quite clear
it would be impossible for the buyer to
pay a fixed price so that the farmers
would have the same amounts of money
in their pockets.
con-
These charges would have to go into
the general expenses account in
nection with the running of the Act as
such would have to be provided by the
board. Every producer throughout the
whole Six Counties would have to bear
his proportion of the extra charges made
in some districts. Thus the people of
County Derry or County Antrim might
have to pay something out of their own
pockets to compensate the people of
County Down or County Armagh for the
extra charges that might be levied by
reason of the powers of the existing
authorities.
This Clause does not affect any
product which may come into a market
except a product that may be subject to
a scheme and under the control of a
board, nor does it affect any product,
whether in a scheme or not in a scheme,
if it goes through a market-I think
that is the strict reading of the Clause
-nor can it be put into operation without the approval of the Ministry. That
is a sufficient safeguard, in my opinion,
for all interests. I look upon this as a
vital matter for I cannot see how a board
can deal with all the questions that will
arise without some powers being given
to them.
There is another very big question
If under a scheme a board is empowered
to take over all pork, there will be no
bargaining for pork as it will be the
property of the board before it leaves the
farm. If there is a sale, where does that
sale take place? Would it be within the
ambit of the district where the local
authority rules, or would it be outside
that in the rural district and on the
farm? If that question arose it might
give very eminent lawyers a very happy
hunting ground for some months deciding where the sale took place and whether
the local authorities would have power to
charge any tolls. For that reason and
to dispel all doubts and to let the boards
and the producers know exactly where
they stand, I beg to move this Amendment, in the hope that it may clear up
any misunderstanding that may arise in
future.
I hope it will be met by the Minister
of Agriculture in the spirit in which it is
proposed, and that he will accept it, or
at least that he will give the matter his
full consideration until the Report Stage,
to see if in his wisdom he can suggest
anything better or any further guarantee
that fair play will be done to all parties
concerned. I have inserted the Ministry
as the party who would hold the balance
of power in this matter. If the right

hon. Friend (Sir Edward Archdale),

I am afraid the Government could not

Clauses, either the one put down by my

We, as a Government, in studying this
Bill did not realise, until the Amendments were placed upon the Paper, that
the general question of tolls would be
raised at all, but since we have studied
the matter we have been very strongly
moved to see that no private tolls that are
in existence, some of them passed not so
very long ago, should be abrogated by a
Bill of this general nature dealing with
the marketing of Ulster produce. We
must bear in mind that it was only in
1931 that the question of tolls in the City
of Londonderry was raised before a Joint
Committee of both Houses, and they got
sanction at that time to make all within
the area of Derry a market within the
meaning of the Act. I think that is
within the memory of everybody in the
Committee.
This Amendment, proposed to a Bill
which is not, strictly speaking, a Bill
dealing with tolls, is an attempt to alter
the law with regard to tolls throughout
the Ulster area. I have no particular
brief for the ancient City of Londonderry,
but I do know some facts in connection
with its affairs and where we could
render help we were only too anxious, as
a Government, to do so. When I tell
the Committee that the rates in Derry
City at present stand as high as 19/6 in
the pound, that it bears the brunt more
than any other part of our Ulster area
of the attacks that have been made
through the tariffs on the other side of
the Border-when we bear in mind that
it has lately incurred heavy liabilities,
and that to-day comes the news that the
Lough Swilly Railway is in a very bad
way indeed, this accumulation
burdens to be borne there moves me, at
any rate, and my colleagues in the Government, to see that we do nothing that
would curtail the revenue that they
receive from their markets or, indeed,
from any other source from which they
can raise revenue to keep that historic
city on its feet.

The
Ulster. I do so for two reasons.
first is that this is an enabling Bill, in

Whose wife?) His own wife. (Laughter.)
They went into a restaurant for dinner,

had not
used all the dishes. The

The
It has been stated that Belfast has
spent £400,000 on its markets. I would

(Mr. Nixon) that the beautiful Law

site was used as a potato market, a grassseed market, a vegetable market, and a
variety market. Did the Corporation

can go down to the horse fair. I do not

I object to Belfast Corporation and Derry
Corporation, or any other local authority
charging tolls when their markets have
not been used.
Let me make it perfectly clear. The

of toll when their goods pass through the

on produce which has not been within
miles of the markets. May I also say

The Amendment put down

of Derry. Now, every farmer who brings

It will be within the recollection of
most Members of this House, and especially of my hon. Friend who has just down,
that that Clause in the 1931 Act was the
subject of considerable opposition. The
whole matter was discussed at considerable length before a Committee of this
House. I am not aware of the actual

course, was not a Member of the Committee. But certainly the hon. Member
for Antrim is fully aware of the nature
of the opposition. The opposition, to a
very large extent, ranged round the subject of tolls on milk sold within the city
boundary.
A matter that the Committee took into
consideration was that this was not a new
right sought by the City of Londonderry,
but that it was the continuance of a right
or privilege-I care not by which word it
is described-granted to the City of
Londonderry not by this Parliament, but
by the Parliament at Westminster more
than forty years ago. That right had
been conferred on the City of Londonderry. It does not differ from the rights
existing in other cities. While in all cities
with which I am acquainted the market
tolls are not confined to the actual market
itself, certain prescribed penalties attach
to sales of commodities outside that market once it has been established.
In the case of the City of Londonderry,
it was provided by an Act, passed as long
ago as 1896, that in lieu of the penalties
that could be applied to articles that
might be sold in the markets and were sold
outside the markets, the toll would be
charged in connection with those articles
if they were sold within the city boundary.
That matter arose for discussion, and was
fully discussed before the Committee. The
views of the vendors of milk in the neighbourhood of Londonderry were put before
the Committee. The Committee had both
sides of the case argued at length before
it, and having considered both sides of
the case the Committee and this House
in the Act of 1931 gave sanction to the
continuance of the right which had existed
in the city of Londonderry for at least
forty years.
May I remind the Committee-it is not
necessary to remind the hon. Member for
Antrim, because he has already referred
to it that in connection with the opposition to the Londonderry Act my hon.
Friend was quite correct in saying that
he went to the city of Londonderry and

not a modus vivendi or agreement could
be arrived at between the milk vendors
and the Corporation of Londonderry. I
am very glad to say that as a result of
the reasonable attitude then adopted by
my hon. Friend, and also of the extremely
reasonable attitude adopted by the Corporation of Londonderry, an arrangement
was come to which, so far as I know, and
subject to correction by my hon. Friend,
was at that time agreed to both by him
and by those he represented, and by the
Corporation of Londonderry, and was
looked upon as a perfectly satisfactory
arrangement.
May I indicate the nature of that
arrangement? So far from the Corporation of Londonderry endeavouring to extract or to charge the maximum tolls, the
amount they could legally charge, the
Corporation of Londonderry came to an
arrangement by which these maximum
tolls would be reduced, and, furthermore,
in the case of any milk vendor sending
in milk into the city of Londonderry,
that milk vendor is now entitled to pay
a lump sum to the Corporation on his own
returns. The Corporation does not investigate the quantity of milk that he sends,
but accepts the figures given by the
vendor, and allows him to pay a lump
sum, which represents a considerable reduction on the tolls that are chargeable
in other cases.

New CLAUSE (Modification of Act
so as to be consistent with the United
Kingdom Act)-
(1) In the event of any amendment
being made, after the passing of this
Act, in the Bill for the United Kingdom Act, with such effect as to render
any provisions of this Act inconsistent
with the United Kingdom Act as
passed, then in that event the Governor
of Northern Ireland may, by Order in
the Privy Council of Northern Ireland,
modify the provisions consistent with
the United Kingdom Act.
(2) Any Order in Council made
under this section shall come into force
upon the date specified therein in that
behalf, but shall be laid before each
House of Parliament as soon as may
be after it is made, and shall cease to
have effect upon the expiration of a
period of twelve months from the date
upon which it came into operation, unless at some time before the expiration
of that period it has been approved by
a resolution passed by each House of
Parliament.
Brought up and read a First Time.
""
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I beg to
move, That this Clause be now read
a Second Time." As hon. Members are
aware, an Agricultural Marketing Bill
is at present before the Parliament at
Westminster. Just as in the Northern
Ireland Bill there are several references
to the United Kingdom Act, so in the
Bill which is before Parliament at Westminster there are references to our Bill.
In these circumstances it is essential that
the two Measures should complement each
other. The United Kingdom Bill is at
present in the Committee stage in the
House of Commons, and is unlikely to
be passed into law until some time after
the passage of the Northern Ireland Bill.
In these circumstances, and in view of
the paramount importance of securing
that marketing schemes in Northern Ireland shall be complementary to schemes
introduced in Great Britain, I have decided to move this Clause. It will be
noted from Sub-section (2) that the
operations of any Order in Council made
under the Clause will be of limited duration unless subsequently approved by both
Houses of Parliament.
Question put and agreed to.
Clause read a Second time and added
to the Bill.

:

Mr. BEATTIE: I do not usually

but in view of the unprecedented attitude

in my position I cannot but make my

in the circumstances. The Government
have not indicated why they wish to
adjourn the House until Thursday. If
it is a fact, which I am led to believe,
that a few of the Members of the Front
Bench have been invited by the reactionary Belfast Water Board to an
entertainment at the Silent Valley, where
they will have their thirst quenched and
hunger appeased, that is no justification
for this unprecedented Motion. I feel
that the position is not taken seriously
by the Government. It means the
breaking up of this Assembly, which is
superior to the Belfast Water Board, in

reservoir on which they have spent
thousands of pounds of the ratepayers'
money. I have not had the honour of
an invitation. That is not my complaint.
If I had been invited as a guest I would
not have gone.

The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Financial Statement, 1933-34.
Mr. POLLOCK (who was received with
general cheers): When I presented my
Budget statement to the House a year ago
I commented on the fact that, from the
point of view of commerce and industry,
the year of 1931 must be reckoned as, in
some respects, among the blackest in our
history. It was in that year that the
British people awakened from their long
spell of apathy and indifference and threw
off the shackles which have bound them
to an obsolete and effete fiscal system
which threatened the whole commercial
and financial structure of the country.
I had hoped at that time that the
coming year, that is the year 1932, would
have seen a change for the better and that
the universal depression and difficulties,
from which our Province was not immune,
would in some measure be relieved.
am sorry to say that this anticipation was
not realised.
I
Looking back, however, on the year
recently finished, I must mention that
one bright spot appeared. That was the
Ottawa Conference. At this monumental
gathering, representatives from all the
various parts of our Empire assembled
to discuss our common problems of
Imperial trade. As a result of this Conference, we in Ulster have already derived
advantages in some sections of
our
industry, and I have no doubt whatever
that when the measures adopted at
Ottawa sufficiently mature they will result
in a great impetus to Empire trade.
Otherwise, the year has left us, as the
one before it, with little or no change in
the conditions of the world which would
encourage us to hope for a revival of prosperity, unless it be that out of the very
welter and chaos, in which the nations of
the whole world find themselves, there
has been developed an urge and incentive
to come together and endeavour to evolve
a better system.
are
The meeting of the World Economic
Conference next month in London, in
which more than sixty nations
expected to take part, is an indication of
the desperate plight of all, and from this
conference our hope springs afresh for
better times.
I refer to these world conditions in
order to emphasise that which is, perhaps, too often overlooked, namely, that
our prosperity in Ulster, or our lack of
it, is necessarily affected by and bound
up with world conditions. We cannot
shake ourselves free from that fact. We
succeeded, in the face of many difficulties, in balancing our Budget last year,
and, though the margin is small, if we
allow for rightful contribution to
Imperial services, I think we should
derive more satisfaction from such a
battle hardly won in face of such strong
opposing forces than the more ample
victories in the past when circumstances
were more favourable and financial surpluses more easily produced.
It has been urged by some people,
even those in responsible positions, that
it would be better policy to disregard the
balancing of Budgets in order to provide
for a remission of taxation, which would
develop confidence and give an impetus
to the recovery of trade and business
generally. I cannot see, however, that
an unbalanced Budget has yet helped any
nation to progress.
In Great Britain
and in Northern Ireland, where Budgets have been balanced even in the
stress and strain of the last few years,
the conditions under which our people
have been living are better or, perhaps
I should say, less severe than in any
country with an unbalanced Budget.
There is also this important factor,
that the financial stability of the country
remains unassailable and that, I make
bold to say, could never have been the
case if the policy of deliberately budgeting for a deficit had been adopted.
(Hon. Member: Hear, hear.)
And now,
after these introductory
remarks, I should like to proceed with
the more concrete matter of the accounts
which I propose to discuss. Firstly, as
is customary, I will deal with the
accounts of the past year and endeavour
to show as between expenditure and
revenue how we balanced those accounts
and how they turned out. I hope hon.
Members will bear in mind that in the
figures I am about to give I am dealing
with the year that is past, which has
little bearing, of course, on the year
which lies ahead of us.
Minister's Statement 1834
The Budget-
23 MAY 1933
Expenditure, 1932-33.
If hon. Members will turn to Table I.
of the White Paper which has been
circulated, they will find statements comparing the estimated with the actual outturn of last year's finance.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure, we find that Consolidated Fund
Services, apart from the Road Fund,
accounted for £440,000, or £48,000
below the Estimate. The details will
be found in Table II. of the White
Paper and are as follows:-Interest on
Borrowings, £99,000; Sinking Funds,
£194,000; other miscellaneous items,
£147,000.
The reduction of £48,000 below the
Budget Estimate arose chiefly owing to
the low rate of interest paid in respect
of temporary borrowings, due to the
ample supplies of cheap money.
ROAD FUND.
The Road Fund payment of £559,000
represents the corresponding receipt from
motor taxation. The Budget Estimate
was £570,000, so that the revenue did
not quite realise the Estimate.
SUPPLY SERVICES.
save
The Budget Estimate for Supply Services (omitting the cost of Public Works
chargeable to the Imperial Government)
was £8,788,000, to which should be
added £42,000 for Supplementary Estimates, making a total of £8,830,000.
The actual expenditure for the year was
£8,637,000, so that not only was I able
to provide for the cost of the Supplementaries, but I was able to
£151,000 on the original Estimate. This
is £100,000 more than the figure
mentioned in my Budget speech last year
as the special savings which it was hoped
to make in the Supply Services. The
saving is mainly due to unemployment
insurance expenditure proving less than
had been anticipated, but I would like
to acknowledge that all Departments
have contributed by keeping expenditure
down to the lowest possible level.
PUBLIC WORKS.
Public buildings chargeable to the
Imperial Government under Section 34
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
account for £109,000; this expenditure
being balanced by a similar revenue item
on the other side of the account.
DEDUCTIONS FROM RESIDUARY SHARE.
We repaid to the Imperial Government sums collected by us from the local
authorities in repayment of loans made
before we took over control (£73,000),
and also collections of "New" Land Purchase Annuities (£284,000). The slight
drop from the Estimate is due to advances
being made by the Land Purchase Commission at a slightly slower rate than
anticipated.
The expenditure on the Services controlled and paid for by the Imperial
Government, such as Income Tax, Post
Office, Customs, etc., was £1,739,000,
which was £27,000 less than the Budget
Estimate.
Details of the more important items of
expenditure with which I have dealt will
be found in Table II of the White Paper.
In all, then, we find that the total
expenditure of the Province last year
amounted to £11,841,000, and I shall now
examine the sources from which we
derived the revenue to meet this expenditure.
Revenue, 1932-33.
TAX REVENUE.
Transferred taxes imposed by our
Government produced £902,000, that is
£40,000 less than the Budget Estimate.
