The drop in estate duties, as compared
with the averages of ten years past, is
something over £100,000 a year and,
although the amount of this tax is, for
obvious reasons, not readily calculable,
there is no doubt that the world-wide
depreciation in industrial securities
accounts for an considerable part of the
reduction in the amount.
The yield of stamp duties, although less
than my Estimate by £2,000, has, I am
glad to say, shown an improvement
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
(£8,000) on the figure for 1931-32, but
here again the return is a long way below
what it was when conditions were what
we now like to consider as normal.
Mr. NIXON: Why the fall?
Mr. POLLOCK: I dare say the fall
has been due to the conditions that I have
indicated the general depression in
trade.
Mr. NIXON: Excessive taxation.
Mr. POLLOCK: Motor taxation, as
I have stated above, produced £559,000,
and was transferred to the Road Fund.
RESERVED TAXES.
The Budget Estimate for Reserved
Taxes, collected by the Imperial Government, was £7,853,000. This figure has
been exceeded by no less than £124,000;
£55,000 of which is due to Customs and
Excise and £69,000 to Inland Revenue.
The new tariff policy adopted by the
British Government has resulted in considerable extra revenue accruing to our
Exchequer, and this fortunate result of
a tariff not primarily intended as revenueproducing was of considerable importance
to us at this time of decline in revenue
generally. As compared with the
revenue for 1931-32, there was, in
1932-33, from Customs and Excise an
increased sum of £1,078,000, of which
approximately 40 per cent. is due to the
above-mentioned cause, and the
mainder, for the most part, to the
collection of tobacco duties having once
again become normal. Hon. Members
will recollect that in March, 1931, considerable withdrawals of tobacco from
bond took place in the expectation of
increased duties, and this led to the duty
collected in 1931-32 being sub-normal.
re-
Liquor duties again declined, as
I
anticipated, and brought in £48,000 less
than in 1931-32.
It has been my custom from year to
year to comment on the consistent yearly
fall in the consumption of spirituous
liquors, and it may interest the House
to know that since the year 1924, the
revenue from strong spirit has fallen
from £1,610,500 to £816,000 in the year
I am reviewing.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: The use of beer, however, has only fallen in that period about
£50,000. However important and
gratifying this evidence of the temperate
habits of our people may be, the loss
of revenue accruing therefrom is a constant source of embarrassment to myself
in the effort to discover additional
revenue to take its place.
The collection of Inland Revenue produced £3,319,000, against the original
Budget Estimate of £3,250,000-thus
exceeding the Estimate by £69,000.
Here again this increase over the Estimate is very welcome in a difficult time,
and shows, I think, that the more
punctual collection of tax in the previous
year has been maintained.
The Transferred and Reserved Taxes
together, therefore, provided us with
£9,439,000.
NON-TAX REVENUE.
Amongst the items of Non-Tax
Revenue, there are two items to which
I may direct the attention of the House.
One is the item of £341,000, adjustment of residuary share transferred from
the Reserve Fund to the Exchequer. As
hon. Members will recollect, we took
power under the Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Act, passed before 31st March
last, to make a transfer of a sum not
exceeding £350,000 to the Exchequer,
and I explained at the time that this
the
represented adjustments in
residuary share made by the Joint Exchequer Board to the extent of
-
(a) £91,000 for the year 1930-31;
and
(b) £250,000 for the following year.
These adjustments we were entitled to,
partly by reason of economies which we
had ourselves effected, and partly because
we had increased our revenue by certain
emergency fund transfers.
The other item of Non-Tax Revenue is
the sum of £32,000 paid over from the
Ulster Savings Sinking Fund. This
transfer is made under the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Act to which I
have already referred. This fund has
now been built up to the point where it
can provide portion of the amount necessary to meet the growing interest
liability for Savings Certificates each
year.
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
23 MAY 1933
As a matter of fact this fund has
grown to a sum of £823, 585. It may be
of interest to the House to know that
our Ulster Savings Certificates are as
popular as they have ever been. Even
with a smaller return of interest than
was provided for the earlier issues, I find
that the average of £11,000 in weekly
savings is well up to the average of the
sales of the previous issues, notwithstanding the lower rate of interest
provided for the third issue of these
certificates. This, I need hardly point
out, is evidence of the thrifty habits of
our people. The certificates, of course,
were provided to encourage the people in
that direction.
I am sorry to have to record that the
profit of £14,000 on the working of the
Post Office for 1931-32 has been turned
into a loss of £1,000 for 1932-33. On
the figures supplied to me by the Post
Office, I had assumed a profit of £19,000,
and am naturally disappointed that,
whether owing to the continued depression in trade and business activities or
partly for this and partly for some other
reason, the forecast had not been realised.
I had also estimated for a
sum of
£97,000 as a contribution to our
Exchequer from Great Britain under the
Unemployment Insurance Agreement, but
no such receipt has accrued. While, on
the one hand, we have not had to call
on the British Exchequer for a payment,
on the other I am sorry for the underlying reason, which is that employment
in Great Britain, in comparison with our
own Province, has worsened. The effect
is that I found myself short of revenue
which I had expected by £97,000.
The other items of Non-Tax Revenue
were as follow:-"Existing" Land Purchase Annuities, £656,000; Church
Temporalities, £20,000; miscellaneous,
interest, etc., £263,000. We have very
large investments, as the House will
understand. We received from the
Imperial Government, being the cost of
public buildings under Section 34 of the
Government of Ireland Act, £109,000;
Imperial local loans repayments £74,000;
"New" Land Purchase Annuities amounting to £279,000.
In all, then, the non-tax revenue
(including the self-balancing items in
respect of public buildings, local loans repayments, "New" Land Purchase Annuities and residuary share adjustment)
amounted to £2,676,000, bringing the
total revenue of the Province available
from all sources last year to £12,114,000.
If we deduct from this the total expenditure for the year, £11,841,000, we are
left with a balance of £273,000 as the
amount available for surplus and
Imperial contribution. Our accounts at
the close of the year showed only a cash
surplus of £7,000, the difference between
this and the £273,000 being held by the
Treasury pending the final determination
by the Joint Exchequer Board of the
amount of Imperial contribution.
THE COMING YEAR.
I have dealt with the year that is just
past, showing a balance of £273,000,
secured in the face of difficulties of more
than ordinary proportion, and I think
we have reason to congratulate ourselves
that, notwithstanding all these tribulations, we are able to come through so
satisfactorily and without using adventitious aids to the ordinary sources of
national revenue.
I now come to what hon. Members will,
I am sure, be more interested in, the
conditions which lie before us in this
present year rather than that which has
disappeared into the past. Let me say
at once that the continued fall in revenue,
coupled with the heavy expenditure
resulting from the distressing lack of
employment, has given me more anxiety
and care in preparing my proposals for
this year than for any of the eleven years
during which I have had the privilege of
presenting Budgets to this House. However, the steps which I propose to take
will, I hope, show the financial strength.
of Northern Ireland with our Budget
balanced for the twelfth
in sucyear
cession.

the present basis of taxation Estate Duties
are estimated to produce £565,000, Stamp
Duties are estimated at £206,000, Excise
Duties, that is to say, principally Entertainments Tax and Liquor Licences are
expected to reach £128,000,
£128,000, Motor
Vehicle Duties we take at £570,000,

RESERVED REVENUE.
The Reserved Revenues imposed by the
Imperial Government present rather
more startling features. The Customs
The Budget-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

receipts show a considerable drop,

that the imports from abroad, and consequently the duties thereon, have fallen
away from their pre-tariff level.
Further, the relief given to the beer-drinker
is to cost our Exchequer this year no
less than £145,000, and in a full year
considerably more, and I am only compensated to a very minor degree by the
duty on oil, which is expected to produce
£35,000 this year, and £50,000 in a full
year. All these factors, together with
the growing temperance habits of our
people in the consumption of alcoholic
liquor, reduce the Customs and Excise
receipts by £269,000 as compared with.
last
year; the total amount being
£4,390,000.
INLAND REVENUE.
was
Now, as to our next great head of
revenue, the Income Tax, it
inevitable that we should expect a
smaller yield on account of the difficult
conditions prevailing last year. The
actual collection of tax within the Province is being maintained wonderfully,
but we lose nearly £250,000 as a result
of the lower dividends which our citizens
receive on their investments in British
stocks and the reduced profits of business enterprises. Then, on top of this,
comes the concession in the British Budget as to the proportions of Income Tax
to be paid in the two halves of the
financial year, costing us £170,000.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Socialist Government was not so bad.
Mr. NIXON: Income Tax is up.
Mr. POLLOCK: Happily this is not
a recurring loss. These negative quantities, together with a fall in the yield of
surtax of £82,000, and in excess profits
of £5,000, give a total yield of Inland
Revenue of £2,800,000, as against
£3,319,000 last year. This shows
startling loss exceeding £500,000 in the
year.

NON-TAX Revenue.
Coming now to revenue derived from
other sources than taxation, we have
Land Annuities transferred to our Exchequer, which are expected to produce
£656,000. I am bound to say that there
is rarely any great variation in the

not only of the honesty of the farmers,
but of their desire to live up to their

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The new Land Annuities, the

Church Temporalities revenue is responsible for £19,000. Interest on our very

Local loans repayments which are the

1931-32 in respect of the Unemployment

Expenditure, 1933-34.
And now I turn to the expenditure side

have been formulated by our Ministries

impressed by three facts. First, that we
had a non-recurring loss of income tax by
the alteration of the January liability
from 75 per cent. to 50 per cent.;
secondly, that we had a non-recurring
expenditure of £32,000 for issue expenses
of our 3 per cent. Stock; and thirdly,
that our possible losses on guarantees
were fit charges against any
reserves
accumulated in former years of comparative prosperity. I, accordingly, caused
investigations to be made and ascertained
that there is a considerable surplus in the
Capital Fund, which is accumulating to
provide for liquidating the deficit on the
Unemployment Fund, accrued prior to
the Re-Insurance Agreement in 1926.
This surplus of about £400,000 I shall
transfer to reserve and make available
for any possible Loans Guarantee losses,
thereby eliminating an item of expenditure amounting to £150,000.
Further, in view of the non-recurring loss
of income tax and cost of floating our
loan, I propose to take £100,000 out of

it has been brought to my notice that not

Mr. NIXON: There is more in the

Mr. POLLOCK: Hon. Members may
be surprised at the smallness of our contribution to Imperial Services, but I have
represented to the Treasury that we are
bearing exceptionally heavy burdens at
present, and they have shown great
sympathy with our difficulties. Assuming that the Joint Exchequer Board can
be satisfied as to the equity of our claim
in respect of our contribution, we shall
not be opposed in our contention that
for this year our Imperial contribution
should be provisionally assessed at a
nominal figure.
May I say that I sincerely trust that
this Budget marks the low water-mark of
our financial career. We have been very
hard hit, both by falling revenues and
rising social expenditure, but let us hope
the depression, which has been the cause
of both these symptoms, will at last be
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
23 MAY 1933
dispelled. There are glimmerings of
hope in the future, and we are doing all
in our power to help on the good work.
In closing, let me remind the House
that two years ago I ventured to predict
that we were approaching danger point
in respect to our expenditure, which was
then closely approaching our revenue.
Since then our Exchequer has undertaken
the cost of transitional benefit to unemployed workers, whilst at the same time
the British Insurance Scheme has failed
to provide us with any contribution.
These two factors, combined with a severe
fall in Income Tax and Customs and
Excise revenue, will, in my judgment,
render it necessary to take account of our
goings during the currency of the present
year.
Whilst we have very substantial
sinking funds, sufficient to assure the
financial stability of the Province, it is
absolutely essential that revenue and
expenditure in each year must be made
to balance. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Any other course can only lead
to ultimate disaster.
I would, therefore, issue a warning to
public spending authorities, that until
normal conditions in world trade give
assurance of resumed prosperity, all
unnecessary expenditure of every kind
should be suspended. There are some
indications of improved trade even now
visible on the horizon, but they are not
sufficiently developed to warrant any
departure from the most rigid economy.
It is either economy on the one hand, or
additional taxation on the other. It is
for the people of Ulster to choose between
these two alternatives. I beg to move.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Question proposed, "That this House
approves the proposals of the Government for meeting the financial requirements of the year."

different nature from our social services.
That is a very remarkable achievement.
It may be a source of anxiety and concern to this House to maintain those social
services at a high or reasonable level, but
it will be admitted that a Government
like our own, a twentieth century Government, is bound to maintain their social
services, if possible, at an even higher
level.

to make certain reductions in respect of
what we pay towards our unemployed
population. If we compare the Estimate
that was introduced to-day with that of
the past year we find that there is a reduction of approximately £150,000.

16 years of age, I say, from the higher
point of view of the age in which we live
and its scientific achievements, that that
sum is paltry and absurd. This is not a
laughing matter; it is a very serious
matter. I have investigated the figures.
I have studied the figures. I have read
the figures of Rowntree, whose name
hon. Members will remember as one who
wrote on economics before the war.
Rowntree proved, conclusively, that you
cannot give a child sufficient nourishment
on any sum less than 2s 3d a week. That
was Rowntree's figure. I compared his
figure with that in a recent medical work
on hygiene, and I found that the figure
given in that book was 2s 4d for feeding
alone.
I have read in the "Manchester
Guardian "' recent statistics to the effect
that out of his total amount of insurance

penny per day out of 2s per week. Of
course, I am not blaming the Government for that, but I think we have come
to the pass that we should not rest satis.
fied with our achievements in the past.
Every thinking man knows that we cannot maintain a reasonable standard of life
and provide all the essential requirements
of life on a pittance of 15s 3d a week,

is the dilemma in which this and other
Governments find themselves at the
present time. That is the dilemma in
which we are placed.
It has been said that our plight is
terrible in the extreme. I, myself, never
expected that we could suddenly turn
round a corner and see extended before us

look back to the past for guidance,
because the figures that I have heard to-

day, these figures for social services,

evinced the worst features of capitalism.
On the scientific side it looked to Huxley
for guidance, and it incorporated his biological doctrine into the field of economics.
On the economic side it looked to Manchester, to the doctrine of laisser faire,
and to the doctrine of devil take
the hindmost. That is a capitalistic
State which cannot any longer be maintained. I believe that here in Northern

Written Answer to Question.
BALLYMONEY RURAL DISTRICT
ELECTION.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the action of the Deputy Returning
Officer for the Ballymoney Rural District
Elections in receiving nominations after
the appointed time, 5 p.m., on 3rd May,
1933; whether this is legal; whether this
officer canvassed for nominations during
office hours on nomination day; what
action the Minister has taken against
said officer; and whether the Minister will
hold a public inquiry into these charges.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware it has
been alleged that this officer received
nominations after the prescribed time
had elapsed and had canvassed for nominations during office hours.
A nomination received after 5 o'clock
on the appointed day would not be valid,
and it would be most improper for a
Deputy Returning Officer to canvass for
nominations either during or outside
office hours.
I should, however, say that the
officer in question denies that there is any
truth in either of the allegations referred
to.
The conduct of a Deputy Returning
Officer is not subject to review by the
Ministry, and I have no power to order
a public inquiry of the nature suggested,
but as the hon. Member is no doubt
aware, Section II of the Ballot Act of
1872, as adapted, provides a legal remedy
to any person aggrieved by misconduct on
the part of a Deputy Returning Officer.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I misunderstood the hon. and gallant Gentleman.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I quite agree
with the hon. Member for Tyrone, who
has just spoken, and that is the reason
why we cannot accept this Amendment.
The object of this Amendment appears
to be to remove the power of my Ministry to exercise a general supervision
over the employment of officers of a
board and over the salary or remuneration of persons employed by the board.
In place of the approval which has, at
present, to be given by my Department
to all appointments, the hon. and
gallant Member proposes that these
matters should merely be submitted to
me for my consideration. I feel that I
would be quite unjustified in agreeing
to a limitation of the powers
of my
Department in this respect. It has been
argued that the money which will be
expended in the salary of officers of a
board and remuneration to the members
will be money which will be raised
directly from the producers themselves,
and that my Department should have no
supervision in the matter. I cannot
agree with this interpretation of the
position.
I would remind the House that in the
event of a loss being incurred by the
board in trading the Ministry may have
to authorise this loss to be made good
by means of a levy upon producers. I
feel that in these circumstances it is the
duty of my Department, to make certain
that the administrative expenses of the
board are kept as low as possible and,
therefore, the officers employed by the
board should be subject to the approval
of the Ministry.

Loans Guarantee (No. 2) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In moving the Second Reading of this short Measure, I need add
very little to the explanation given by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce, when moving the Money Resolution on the Bill. The purport of the
Measure is to enable our Government to
acquiesce in any proposal submitted for
the continuance of the guarantee of the
Government in a case where the borrower
is in a position to arrange with the
lenders for a lower rate of interest than
that for which the original loan provided.
The advantage to the Ministry of such an
operation is obviously a reduction of the
contingent liability assumed by our Exchequer under our original guarantee.
The plethora of money in most of the
financial centres of the world, and notably
in London, at present offers great opportunities for borrowing at exceptionally
low rates of interest, and it is not unnatural if advantage is taken of these
conditions by some of those whose
obligations were guaranteed by our Government at much higher rates than those
obtaining at present. It is a moot question whether our present Loans Guarantee
Act covers the powers of the Ministry
to continue the existing guarantee under
such circumstances, but it was considered
wiser to provide specific authority by
this short Bill.
I should like to point out that the Bill
may have a very direct bearing on employment in Northern Ireland. If you
take the example of a shipping company
being able to reduce the interest upon its
loans it means that a certain amount of
liquid resources will be available for the
purpose of providing for the construction
of new ships Therefore it is, in my
judgment, of direct benefit not only in

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: In
introducing this Measure to the House
this afternoon I am happy to say that
the Bill has the entire support of the
creamery industry in Northern Ireland
and of the Ministry's Advisory Committee on dairying. It has, indeed,
been introduced at the express request
of the Ulster Agricultural Organisation
Society, and has been supported by
representatives of other creameries in
Northern Ireland outside that organisation. As hon. Members are aware, the
Dairy Produce Bill-
Second Reading
29 MAY 1933
Marketing of Dairy Produce Act
(Northern Ireland), which was passed in
1929, came into operation on the 1st
January, 1931. Under that Measure
all premises used as auxiliary creameries,
as central creameries, as butter factories
or as wholesale depots for the despatch
of butter to Great Britain required to be
registered with the Ministry of Agriculture.
The Act and the regulations made
thereunder laid down the processes of
manufacture, treatment and trade in
butter, which could be carried on at the
various premises registered under the
Act. In regard to auxiliary and central
creameries the methods for the treatment of cream and the manufacture of
butter were specified, and a high standard of equipment and of qualifications
on the part of the staff employed has
been demanded. As a result of the Act
considerable expenditure was incurred
in improving the equipment of the
creameries in Northern Ireland and
modernising their plant. Unfortunately, however, the supply of milk in
Northern Ireland is not sufficient to
enable the creameries to run at full
capacity throughout the whole year, and
during the winter months our creameries
are working at only a fraction of their
capacity owing to the small supplies of
milk available.
Consequently, in order to reduce their
overhead costs and to keep their staffs
employed, it is necessary for many
creameries to deal in imported butters.
Hitherto the practice had been for
creameries to purchase imported bulk
butter and to cut this butter into rolls.
The butter is then sold locally, and this
enables the creameries to maintain their
connection with wholesalers and retailers
during the winter months, when they
have no butter of their own to sell.
butter is, of course, sold subject to the
requirements of the Merchandise Marks
Act, 1926, and Order, 1932, under
which imported butter must be sold
bearing a mark indicating the source of
origin.
The
In the proviso to sub-section 1 of Clause
1 of the Act of 1929, the creameries were
specially authorised to carry on this
business without liability to be registered as a butter factory. It is now
desired to extend the proviso so as to
authorise the creameries,
creameries, subject
to
conditions, to
undertake the
certain
process of blending butter. In this connection it is important to remember that
during the past two or three years the
local demand for Northern Ireland butter
has grown to such an extent that our
Northern Ireland creameries have not
been able, even in the summer season,
to produce enough butter to satisfy the
Northern Ireland demand, and within
the last few years there has been
marked increase in the consumption of
butter in our area.
a
The creameries believe that by their
and
large purchasing power
their
technical skill they can perform the
function of converting imported butter
from bulk (56lbs. boxes) to the usual
small 1lb. packages in which the butter
is bought by the consumer, and that the
service
performing of this
by the
creameries would be an advantage to the
public as well as helping the creameries
to maintain their staff fully employed
during the winter, and thus preventing
unemployment. It must be emphasised
that all the activities of the creameries in
this, as in all other directions, will be
under the closest scrutiny of the Ministry, and I am confident that as a result
of their technical skill the creameries will
be able to prepare a blend of high-class
butters which is more palatable and more
suitable for the winter trade than
straight cut imported butter.
The second Clause of the Bill relates
to the registration of premises, and will
operate only in the case of premises for
which registration is applied, subsequent
to the passage of the amending Measure.
At present, in considering the question
of registration, the Ministry has no right
to take into consideration the supply of
milk or cream in the area in which it is
proposed to erect a creamery.
As a
result it may be that a creamery will be
erected in an area where there is already
an adquate supply of registered premises
for dealing with the supply of milk and
cream available. The proposed Amendment will enable the Ministry to take
into consideration the needs of the
district before granting registration to
new premises. In the event of the
Ministry refusing to register premises
under this Clause of the Bill it will be
open to the persons interested to appeal
to the county court by virtue of the provisions of Section 15 of the Act of 1929.
I beg to move.

Mr. ANDREWS: This is a temporary
Measure, as the Title of the Bill very
clearly states. It is introduced to extend for a further period of not more
than one year certain statutory provisions
of several of our Unemployment Insurance Acts which would otherwise come to
an end on 30th June next. Hon. Members are probably aware of the fact that
the entire problem of unemployment
insurance was examined by a Royal Commission between December, 1930, and
November, 1932. The report and recommendations of the Commission have since
been occupying the attention of His
Majesty's Imperial Government,
legislation to reform the scheme has been
promised, but it has not been found possible to deal with it at the moment, and
therefore this Bill is being introduced, as
I have already said, to extend the time
in which several of the provisions in our
existing acts shall be effective.
and
I would like to point out to hon. Members that this Bill will have to pass without amendment because of the policy of
our Government to have similar legislation here in connection with unemployment insurance as in Great Britain-
Mr. NIXON: Step by step.
Mr. ANDREWS-and, secondly,
owing to the re-insurance agreement
which necessitates parity in connection
with unemployment insurance legislation.
Hon. Members cannot have it both ways.
We must either follow Great Britain,
which I feel is wise and proper, or else
we must claim our freedom and go on our
own. If we did so I am positive that
both our employers and our insured
workers would suffer, because the contributions would have to be raised and the
benefits lowered if we were to attempt
to carry on on our own. Therefore, it is
really foolish to suggest that we can have
it both ways.
I am perfectly certain that
the best we can do for our people is to
maintain the British standards, and this
is the only way, in my opinion, and in the
opinion of my colleagues, that parity with
Great Britain can be maintained in respect
of unemployment insurance.
The Bill is a very simple and clear one,
and if read with the explanatory memorandum no one can doubt what is intended. Clause 1 provides that the

G.S.W." condition for benefit and the
"reasonable period of employment in the

condition for transitional
payments shall continue not to be applied
so long as this Act remains in force.
Further than this, the list of dependents

of claimants for transitional payments,

means that they must disregard half of

Clause 2 gives power to the Governor in

Insurance Acts in Northern Ireland any
other provisions which may be included
in the British Measure. I want to explain why that provision is inserted here.
and why it is absolutely necessary that it
should be inserted. This temporary Measure has not yet been introduced at Westminster. We have an idea of what it
will contain, but we do not know exactly
what it may contain. It may contain
provisions which are not included in this
Measure, and, therefore, in order to
ensure that in effect it will be permissible
for us to do the same for our people here
as is done for their fellow-countrymen
across the Channel, we are giving his
Grace the Governor in Council power to
authorise payments on the same basis as
in Great Britain. That, obviously, is a
precaution to ensure that our people here
are not placed at a disadvantage as compared with the insured population in
Great Britain.
Clause 3 provides that this Act, when
passed, shall continue in force until Parliament makes further provision with
respect to unemployment insurance in
Northern Ireland, but in no case will its
provisions extend beyond the 30th June,
1934. It is
It is reasonably certain that
the Imperial Government will introduce
a very important and widespread measure
of unemployment insurance
in the
autumn. We here will follow suit. In
the meantime, this Bill is introduced to
ensure that the position here is maintained as it will be maintained in the
interval in Great Britain.
Hon. Members may feel that this is in
accordance with our rubber stamp policy,
as the hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) has said. I am not ashamed of
our rubber stamp policy, because I feel
that it is really, in effect, doing the best
possible for those in our community who
are deprived of the opportunity under
existing conditions of earning their daily
bread by their own efforts, as the vast
majority of them earnestly desire to do
It is not expected that the financial effect
of this Measure will exceed £3,000 per
year. I beg to move.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In resuming
the debate on the financial statement
made recently by the Minister of Finance,
may I join in the congratulations extended to him on the most able manner
in which he presented what must be to
him the most serious Budget with which
he has had to deal during the past ten
years as regards the gap between revenue
and expenditure. In the Minister's review
of the past year what stood out most was
the extraordinary rise in revenue from
reserved taxation. Inland revenue, the
Minister said, rose by £69,000 and customs
and excise by £55,000, a total of £124,000.
This is very remarkable, indeed, when
we consider that the corresponding taxes
in Great Britain show a fall of 22 millions.
To this rise in the estimated revenue of
last year, and the fact that the Road
Fund provided £133,000 on account of
relief works in distressed areas, may be
ascribed the fact that an Imperial contribution of £173,000 was handed over to
Great Britain. I do not propose to
discuss the past year any further, but I
want to try to analyse the position as disclosed by the Budget statement.
Mr. POLLOCK: May I interrupt the
hon. and gallant Gentleman to remind
him that the Imperial contribution was
£273,000. He said £173,000.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I thought I
said £273,000. I said that the two
figures I quoted, the rise in revenue of
£124,000 and the charge on the Road
Fund of £133,000, added together gave
£257,000, and the contribution to the
Imperial Government was £273,000.
When discussing financial policy on the
Finance Estimates on 4th May, I pointed
out that as far as I could see there was
then a possibility of a gap of half a million
pounds in our revenue this year as compared with last year; but
you, Mr.
Deputy-Speaker, told me that I could not
discuss then what would in effect be in
the Budget statement. The fall, I pointed
out, from the figures given in the White
Paper issued in the Imperial House of
Commons, would come to £650,000.
exact figures were revealed by the Minister
of Finance in his Budget statement-inland revenue, half a million; customs and
excise, £269,000, making a total of
£769,000 of a fall in our revenue this
year.
The
What we have to ask ourselves is how
do these figures react on our normal revenue, which is imposed and collected in
the current year, and on our normal expenditure, which we vote in this House;
and what is the clearest way to try to
bring this out. The Minister of Finance,
in presenting his Budget statement, took
the unusual course of dealing first with
revenue, instead of with expenditure.
Taking expenditure first, I find that the
Consolidated Fund Services, the Supply

Services voted by this House, and the

Since the Budget was opened, the

there has been a remission of this tax

that that remission will upset his figure;
it will have to be reduced. Dealing with

brought up to fill the gap, I will take

by £168,000. This appears to me to be
the weakest of the Minister's proposals.
Reference to our Estimates will show that
unemployment insurance I am sorry to
say is based on a 25 per cent. estimate.
If the Minister of Labour has to come
to this House with a Supplementary
Estimate I hope he will not have to do

Again, if you study the Appropriation
Accounts issued in the Blue Book, you
will see that last year the average percentage surrendered by all the Departments was 2.5. If you take 2 per cent.
off your Supply Votes you will find that
it gives you the figure which the Minister
hopes to save. Therefore the Departments are going to work on a .5—a half
-per cent. margin. This, I think, is a
very narrow margin. Some years ago,

By close estimating that was brought

Let me deal with the £420,000 adjustments of residuary share. I will recall
that the Minister in his speech last year
said we had a similar item. It was then
£340,000. It must be obvious to everybody that this cannot go on, and that we
cannot hope every year to have in our

share. In some years we have had

share as normal revenue. The next item
was the balance from the appropriation

It will be noticed that in the accounts

Fund were then by Act of Parliament

I suppose he will require to introduce an

£150,000 has been earmarked.
I hope
we will not have to spend the balance
later on. The next item is the taking
of £100,000 out of the surplus in the
Land Annuities Sinking Fund.
We are
extremely lucky to have this fund, but
I do not think we can continue, as it
were, to rely on being able to get
£100,000 out of it every year. I am not
going to discuss the £12,000 appropriation from the Constabulary Reward
Fund; it is a small item. The last item
I wish to discuss is the £100,000 taken
from the Capital Fund relating to
buildings. This is the fund mentioned
in these accounts as handed over
by the British Government. Now,
the last account issued-I have it
in my
hand-shows a credit balance
roughly of £400,000 on 31st March last
year. The amount spent was roughly
£300,000 leaving a balance of £100,000.
Owing to some profits the balance had
risen to £160,000, SO after taking
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
29 MAY 1933
£1,000,000 they had still £60,000 left,
which the Minister no doubt is going to
use for the building of the depot at Enniskillen which I suppose is the last building
which can be erected from this fund. It
will then be practically exhausted. This
is the last time you can come to this fund
for money as there will be no balance left.
There are various funds to which you can

May I ask where is all this leading us to?
About three weeks ago on the Finance
Estimates I dealt with the financial policy
as far as I was then able to go. I then
pointed out that our expenditure was out
of proportion to our income. This analysis
of the Budget clearly shows and I think
the Minister's speech clearly shows that
we are undoubtedly living beyond our
income, and I also think it is clear that
we will be unable to support the strain
imposed by maintaining our social services
on the same scale as Great Britain on our
limited revenue. That seems to me a vital
problem for us to consider as a whole. I
think we are extremely lucky this year, as
I said before, to get £400,000 on account
of former years. We are also lucky that
the Minister of Finance by his wisdom has
been able to pile up this reserve fund from
which we were this year able to draw
£362,000 to carry on with. But I do not
think we can go back to this fund too
often, and I wonder whether or not the
time is coming when we will have to try
to curtail our expenditure and, if necessary, recast some of our administration on
more economical lines.
Now the question of social services
throughout the United Kingdom is one
for the Imperial Government.
But on
this matter I think we will be on the right
lines if before the next Budget we were
to appoint a commission to revise and go
into all expenditure with a view to being
able to say to those across the water-
"We here have done everything possible
to cut down expenditure. We now wish
to maintain the social services on the same
level as you, and we now put forward the
fact that we here in Northern Ireland are
still part of the United Kingdom, and
are entitled to have the same basis of
social services as obtain in England."
And having first put our expenditure on
the lowest level we can for administration, and having cut down as much as we
can if necessary we can go across the
water and say with a clear conscience,
"We require your assistance to maintain our social services."
We all hope this will not be necessary;
that trade will improve; that the shipyards will get work, and that the burden
of unemployment will be eased. I think
it would be a great mistake to count too
much on this arriving quickly, and, therefore, I do think we here must seriously
consider between now and the next
Budget exactly how we are going to make
ends meet. As I pointed out, we have
had this year various sums of money
which I do not think we can possibly
expect again. In this matter the only
course would appear to be to use all the
time between now and the next Budget
to see how exactly we are going to work
things out. Before I sit down I would
like to congratulate the Minister on the
manner in which he has conserved these
reserve funds. I think the House will
realise how useful they have been. They
have saved taxation, and the thanks of
the House are due to the Minister for
maintaining these reserves.
I think we
will realise that we cannot always continue
to draw on them. With these words I
will now close.

and optimism in the financial resources of

""
The state of thankfulness for mercies
granted may be put in different ways. I
will illustrate it by the poor man who
asked for a meal from a restaurant
keeper. He was given a plate of cold
porridge, and in return said: Well, this
is better than heaven." On being asked
why he said that, his reply was: It is
said that nothing is better than heaven,
and this cold porridge is better than
nothing." The taxpayer may say this
Budget gives him nothing but cold comfort. That is a matter of opinion. Therefore I feel there is credit coming to our
people who put before themselves the
fact that they have to pay, and pay
cheerfully. If I might liken the Minister
for the moment to the Biblical Chancellor of Egypt, I could say that he saved
his country against seven years of famine,
but our Chancellor has even exceeded this
period of years by a goodly number.
Could I say more? In historical comparison that speaks for itself, and though
Joseph of old might not agree with the
system of our finances-visionary or
otherwise-still we all believe with the
Minister that there is corn in Egypt, or
rather in Ulster yet. This corn must be
saved. It is imperative, indeed, as he

cannot be placed on this.
Whilst I listened with pleasure to the
Minister of Finance expounding his
proposals and expectations of increased.
revenues, I took courage in the thought
that with increased trade we would get
additional revenue. But it does not
follow always. It is rather the other
way, and that is the fallacy from which
we are suffering to-day, not so much in
the high taxation we pay, because that
is inevitable owing to the times, but in
the inequality of this burden of taxation,
borne by, shall I say, a fast dwindling

Many people have been squeezed out by
taxation. My personal opinion of the
genius displayed by the Minister in

if he will keep to earth rather than soar

One would be a bold Daniel, a very
Horatius holding the bridge, who to-day,

to test the results of our teetotal education of the past ten years, and to watch
our friends who claim to have made a

I come now to the motor vehicle duties,

to the disparity in tax as between pneu-
This question is not a new one by any
means, and I understand that correspondence pointing out the grievance complained of between Mr. Robert M'Cann,
J.P., the secretary of the North of Ireland Motor Hirers' Association, and the
Home Ministry had no effect. The reply
of the Ministry is as follows:-
"With reference to your letter of
the 20th ultimo regarding an allowance
made in Great Britain in respect of
the taxation of goods vehicles of 4 tons
and upwards, when fitted with pneumatic tyres, I am directed by the
Minister of Home Affairs to state that
this matter was carefully considered
when the concession was first made in
Great Britain, but the heavy expenditure needed for the maintenance and
improvement of roads is such that the
Road Fund could not afford the loss
which would be entailed were a similar
concession granted in Northern Ireland.
That answer to me is beside the point.
It entirely avoids the merits of the case,
and it puts Northern Ireland motor
users in a different category, and for no
sufficient reason whatever, from English
motorists. Why should this be so? A
deputation which waited on the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Finance,
was informed of the concurrence of the
Minister with the principle and the reason
for this concession in England. I would
like to know from the right hon. Gentleman if I am informed correctly, and if
so, why this concession has not been
granted.
It is not a very vital point,
and the amount in tax might not be of
great moment. But it is surprising how
small things like these upset people, and
whilst motorists of all kinds are heavily
taxed to-day, a trifling increase of this
sort is much resented, and rightly so in
my opinion. The Minister would be
well advised to look into this matter and
allay much discontent. I make this
appeal to him in the interests of a
heavily taxed class.

The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major McCormick]
In regard to the Sinking Fund, I was
particularly struck by the clear manner
in which the Minister dealt with this
fund. It was to me a simple revelation
of great foresight, because in such
diminishing revenues as, for instance,
the Land Annuities, which amount to
£650,000, they may possibly expire
or run out in 60 years. To-day a fund is
in being to offset in a large part the
annual payments accruing from this
source, and thus to avoid a financial
vacuum, as it were.
This Sinking Fund, made up from
different sources, I understand will
amount to £362,000, and this with the
deficit of £347,000, plus the balance of
£15,000, which goes for the Imperial contribution, makes up the sum total. It
might be said that the fluidity of these
funds tends to the completion of this
happy result. Of course, the Joint Exchequer Board may have other ideas as to
our contribution, but as they have heretofore been very agreeable in meeting our
difficulties I think the Minister may safely
assume that they will be satisfied as to the
equity of our claims in respect of this
year's contribution.
Where our interests and the Imperial
Treasury conflict the diplomatic machinery of the Joint Exchequer Board, used
in a sympathetic manner, makes matters
easy of adjustment. This has been shown
time after time, and it bears out the contention that the true Imperial link that
binds us to the motherland of Empire is
recognised in a real feeling of loyalty and
love being engendered for the good of all.
Our interests, in short, are identical with
those of Britain.

I may revert in a brief manner to
the comments made by the hon. and
gallant Member (Lieut.-Col. Gordon) who
called attention to the very serious reduction in our revenue and the difficulty of
bridging the gulf. I would remind the
House that the real cause of our difficulty
to-day in balancing our Budget arose
from the fact that a most unexpected fall
took place in our revenue from customs
and excise, and also income tax, amounting to £770,000. That was really the basis
of all our troubles and difficulties, and
naturally it devolved upon me to endeavour
to discover some source of revenue that
would bridge that gap. Even that did
not stand alone, because the Chancellor
in his statement reduced, as the House
remembers very well, the tax upon beer,
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
29 MAY 1933
which had the effect of disturbing our
revenue by £270,000. Therefore, in
fact, we had to bridge a gulf of practically one million pounds, and I think
that when the House recalls the different
methods, without straining any one in
particular, adopted to reach that end,
it will be agreed that we have under the
circumstances fairly emerged from a year
of more than ordinary difficulty. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I would recall to the House that in
these difficulties we do not by any means
stand alone. We are apt to forget that.
There is not a country on earth outside
Britain, as I stated in my Budget statement, that was able to balance its budget
for this year. France yesterday was
reported to be some two hundred million
francs short in her estimate, and how that
will be bridged is something I cannot tell.
France and the United States are two
types of the difficulties that have arisen,
so that it need not be considered very extraordinary, with all the depression in
industry and in the trade of the world
and the tremendous reduction in the value
of all primary commodities having a
distinct bearing on our position, that we
should be under the necessity of adopting
rather exceptional measures which would
provide for the balancing of our Budget.
The balancing of our Budget means
that this year we are unable to give any
substantial contribution to Great Britain
as we have done in the past. However,
there is no use in being pessimistic over
this condition of things. We have companions in misfortune everywhere, and it
is not to be expected that the conditions
obtaining to-day will be permanent.
There is no reason in the world why our
revenue from customs and excise, for example, should not resume its normal
figure. Therefore, I hope for the time
when we will be able to resume our former
position and pay, as we are entitled to
pay, something substantial Great
Britain by way of contribution.

were adopted in order to balance our
Budget, with a care which does him

that the £35,000 estimate will
will be

saved. I would like to pay a tribute
to my colleagues in this matter, and
particularly to my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Andrews), who wholeheartedly
assisted me in finding an issue out of
some of the difficulties that faced me in

There were other features in the
Budget referred to by my hon. and

that the House will expect me to deal with

measures that were adopted in order to
reach the end I had in view. The use of
£400,000, which I proposed to transfer
to a reserve fund, and out of which I
drew £150,000 for the purpose of my
Budget, was commented on by the hon.
and gallant member. As I only wanted
£150,000, the question was asked why did
I transfer £400,000 to a reserve fund.
The reply to that is that it is the best
position in which any money could be
placed. Just as in business, a reserve
fund is regarded as one of a company's
greatest assets. The amount was not
used in its entirety.

Referring to the speech of my hon.
and gallant Friend, the Member for St.
Anne's (Major McCormick), may I say
that the rates of motor taxation were
not touched upon in my Budget for the
very good reason that no change could
be made. The hon. and gallant Member suggested that in this case we should
follow literally the rate of taxation imposed in Britain in respect of certain
motor lorries. Let me remind him that
the mileage we have to provide for here
is exactly three times the relative
mileage in Great Britain, and therefore
it is not reasonable to suppose that we
can necessarily base our revenue from
motor taxation on the same ground as
that of Great Britain. It is well known
that Great Britain has a very large
surplus. We cannot pretend that we
have. We are put to severe limits in
order to provide the local authorities
with the money necessary to maintain
the roads in good condition.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Business of the House.

(Sittings of the House) business be not
interrupted at half-past Six o'clock this

Adjournment of the House (Summer).
Resolved: "That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until 12 noon
on Tuesday, 13th June, and that after
the report of Royal Assent to Bills agreed
to by both Houses, Mr. Speaker do
adjourn the House without Question put,
until Tuesday, 3rd of October, provided
always that in the event of any Bill or
Bills being returned from the Senate with
Amendments, the House shall meet on
Thursday, the 8th of June, and shall
transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date, and at its rising
shall adjourn until 12 noon on Tuesday,
the 13th of June; and further, provided
that if it appears to the satisfaction of
Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the
Government, that the public interest requires that the House shall meet at any
earlier time during the Summer adjournment, Mr. Speaker may give notice that
he is so satisfied, and thereupon the House
shall meet at the time stated in such
notice and shall transact its business as if
it had been duly adjourned to that date."
-(The Prime Minister.)

Mr. Barbour.)
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The final paragraph of
the White Paper which was presented
in connection with this Bill sets forth
clearly the financial effect of its provisions, and it is, I think, hardly
necessary for me to add anything to the
explanation contained in the White
Paper.
The object of the Bill is to keep alive
certain important provisions relating to
unemployment insurance, and this Resolution is submitted to the Committee for
the purpose of providing the money
necessary in order to enable this to be
done. As hon. Members are aware, the
cost of transitional payments is, under
the Unemployment Insurance (Economy)
(No. 2) Act, 1931, borne out of voted
moneys, and it is for this reason that a
Financial Resolution of this House is
required in order to give effect to this
Bill.
The enactments, which it is proposed
to keep alive have, I think, been sufficiently explained at the Second Reading
stage of the Bill. They provide, inter
alia, for the continuation of the payment
of benefit to certain classes of dependents,
for example, the claimant's father or
step-father (if unable, by reason of
infirmity, to support himself), his
younger brothers and sisters, etc. They
also provide for an increase in the rate
of dependents' benefit for adults.
against this increased expenditure there

an
assurance from the Ministry, and I

Our Minister of
before Empire trade.
Agriculture is not Minister for the

Northern Ireland he should confine his

The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Minford) complained that it was difficult
to compete with the Free State in the
matter of butter, because the Free State
butter was subsidised to the extent of
60/- per cwt. I am sure he knows, and

it is correct. If that be so, I doubt
very much if they will be able to keep
up that subsidy very long, for I do not
see where they will find the money to do
it. But if they do it would certainly be
very injurious to the butter trade of
Northern Ireland. Under present circumstances I can hardly contemplate how
the Free State would be able to subsidise their butter so as to compete with
and to beat the producers of Northern
Ireland, though the hon. Member stated
that that is being done.
However, my two main reasons for
moving the rejection of the Bill are,
firstly, this ever-growing practice on the
part of the Government of Northern
Ireland of increasing monopolies and
wiping out the small man altogether,
and, secondly, because I entirely object
to the principle of the Government
legalising the doubtful practice of any
creamery purchasing foreign butter, remaking it, cutting it into rolls, blending
it, and selling it. A practice like that
is bound to be injurious to the butter
trade of Northern Ireland. It is bound
to be deceptive to the people who buy
butter in retail shops.
The Minister of Agriculture would be
well advised if he would confine his attention solely to Bills that would help the
farmers and producers of Northern Ireland. I am sure he is anxious to help.
I do not for a moment charge him with
not being anxious, but he would be well
advised to confine his attention to that
without bringing in a Bill here, because,
as he has told us, he was asked to do so
by the owners of the creameries. They
were unanimous in asking him to do so.
Why would they not ask him to do so
when it is for their benefit and for their
advantage? But that does not say that
it is for the advantage of the ordinary
producer, nor yet for the advantage of
the consumer.
I would advise the
Minister, next time he gets advice to
bring forward legislation in this House,
to investigate thoroughly the motives
underlying that advice, and the reason the
people concerned have for tendering that
advice.
It is marvellous how the creamery
owners of Northern Ireland can influence
the Minister to come forward with this
Bill, and it is marvellous how he and
those who support the Bill can get up
and make speeches and endeavour to convince the House and the country that
you will help the butter industry and
the butter producers of Northern Ireland
by purchasing foreign butter, bringing it
in here, remaking it, and selling to wholesalers and retailers. It is a new way of
helping a local industry. I, as a strong
Protectionist, can think of only one way
to help the farmers or any other industry,
and that is to put a tariff on foreign
stuff sufficient to keep it out. But the
Minister of Agriculture can go one
further than that. He not only can
admit the policy of allowing articles to
come in free, but he can bring forward
special legislation in this House to enable
people to purchase foreign agricultural
produce, bring it into Northern Ireland,
trim it up like our own stuff, throw it
on the market, and glut the market to
the detriment and injury of our own
butter trade. I beg to move.

accord generally with

Mr. Minford asked the Minister of

Mr. Barbour: My right hon. Friend

EX-SERVICE TEMPORARY CLERKS
IN CIVIL SERVICE.
10. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the salary
scale of ex-Servicemen appointed to the
clerical class of the Civil Service, and
whether it is the intention of the Government to put the ex-Servicemen clerks on
the permanent Civil Service staff, under
the same terms and conditions as obtains
in the Imperial Civil Service.
Mr. POLLOCK: Ex-Service temporary clerks selected for promotion to
the clerical class are placed on a salary
scale with a maximum of £200 per annum
plus cost-of-living bonus. The full scale
is set out in page 1 of the current
Estimates.
In the Imperial Service ex-Service
temporary clerks, after establishment in
an intermediate grade, are eligible for
promotion to the clerical class, in which
either of two scales (one rising to £180
per annum and the other to £250 per
annum) may be applied to them.
I am satisfied that, looking at the
matter broadly, ex-Service temporary
clerks selected for pensionable posts in
the Northern Ireland Service are treated
at least as generously as their colleagues
in the Imperial Service.

GOVERNMENT'S HOUSING POLICY.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD (by
Private Notice) asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is now in a
position to make any statement regarding
the Government's housing policy.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government have had under consideration for
some time past various suggestions which
have been submitted from the Belfast
Corporation and other sources on the
subject of the encouragement of the building of houses for the working classes.
Amongst other proposals it was suggested
that the Government should apply the
principle of the Loans Guarantee Acts
for the purpose of enabling public utility
companies to embark on comprehensive
housing schemes, but in this connection
it is to be remembered that the housing
of the working classes is primarily the
duty of local authorities, and it would be
out of the question for the Government
to interfere with or infringe on any of
the powers or duties already vested in
these authorities in this respect. Further,
the Government could not itself deal
directly with such utility companies in
the way suggested without establishing
special and costly machinery for the
purpose.
Keeping these principles in mind, and
in the light of its resources, the Government have decided to bring before Parliament proposals of an alternative character,
which it is hoped will tend towards the
further encouragement of the building of
workmen's dwellings. These proposals
may be shortly enumerated as follows:-
In the first place, the present subsidy
of £25 will remain available until the
end of the financial year, as well as the
powers vested in local authorities of
making supplemental grants. After
the 1st April next, the Government
propose that the subsidy of £25 will
be continued for a further period of
two years, subject to the condition that
the local authority makes a correspond
ing grant.
As an alternative to this direct subsidy principle, the Government propose
to institute a scheme under which funds
will be available at cheap rates to those
persons or bodies of persons intending
to build houses, whether local authorities, public utility companies, or private
individuals. The basis of the scheme
is that towards the interest charges incurred by local authorities in borrowing for housing purposes, whether from
the Government Loans Fund or outside
sources, the Government will make a
contribution of one-half per cent. for a
period of 20 years. The sums SO
borrowed under this advantageous
arrangement can be utilised by the local
authorities themselves for the purposes
of their own building schemes, or,
alternatively, may be passed on by
such authorities at the same rate to
persons or bodies of persons desirous of
building houses of the prescribed type.
A further alternative proposal to the
other two already mentioned will be on
the lines of the scheme already introduced into Great Britain by the Act
Message from the Senate 1964
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
recently passed by the Imperial Parliament, the basis of which scheme is that
under normal circumstances building
societies lend money to builders of houses
up to 70 per cent. of the cost of the
houses. In order to induce the
societies to lend up to 90 per cent. of
the cost of the houses, the Government
and the local authorities concerned will
co-operate by guaranteeing two-thirds
of the additional 20 per cent.
Accordingly, a person or body of persons in Northern Ireland who, under the
new arrangement, propose to build houses
of the prescribed type will have a choice
of three methods of obtaining financial
assistance from the Government and the
local authorities of the district in which
the houses are proposed to be erected,
while local authorities will have either of
the first two schemes open to them.

UNEMPLOYMENT IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Sir Basil Brooke.)
Mr. HENDERSON: I must apologise
to the Prime Minister and to the other
Members of the House for not having
given due notice of a little matter I would
like to take the opportunity of raising in
this House. I understood that there was
going to be no adjournment moved. Had
I known the adjournment was going to be
moved I would have given notice. I would
like to ask the Prime Minister a very pertinent question at the present time.
view of the fact that this Government is
going to have a very long holiday until
In
3rd October I would like to ask the Prime
Minister to state whether it is the intention of the Cabinet in the meantime to
take some action whereby work will be
provided not only for the married men,
but also for the single persons, many of
whom are in utter destitution.
poor
their
This matter is so serious that I demand
a reply from the Prime Minister, who is
responsible for the lives of these people.
To-day you have large numbers of married men running about unemployed and
nothing is being done for them. You
have a large number of girls throughout
Northern Ireland in utter destitution
and with no hope of securing employment. You have a large number of single men living on
parents who are unable to provide the
necessaries of life for themselves. You
can realise the terrible plight of these
young people thousands and
thousands of them signing the unemployment register day after day with no
hope of securing employment. And here
we are adjourning this House until the
3rd of October, notwithstanding the fact
that we have only sat two or three weeks.
One thing I would like to say and that
is this, the Cabinet Ministers of this
Government have no reason to be proud
of what they have done for these people.
You are leaving them now and no Member of the Opposition, or on the Government back benches, will have an opportunity of protesting. Of course the
back benchers opposite very seldom protest against the neglect of the right hon.
Gentleman, the Prime Minister, or the
Minister of Labour, in regard to providing work for the single unemployed
persons.
I hope the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Labour, will not draw some
red herring along the trail and reply on
behalf of the Prime Minister.
I am
asking the Prime Minister of this House
to reply, and I will protest in the
strongest possible way if the Minister of
Labour replies on behalf of the Prime
Minister. The Prime Minister is always
looked upon as the captain of the ship.
I do not want to create any trouble
for the captain. I want this ship to sail
along in untroubled waters. I cannot
allow the captain to sail the ship in
troubled waters all the time. At the
present time the waters are troubled. I
would like to suggest to the prime Minister that he should do the same as I do.

Unemployment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
You have to go into the homes of these
people and see where these boys and
girls live to realise the destitution and
hardship of the fathers and mothers of
these children,
children, who can hardly get
existence for themselves. I would like
the prime Minister to do this the first
time he is in the centre of the city after
10 or 11 o'clock. Let him take the
earliest opportunity of seeing the state
of affairs that exists in the city after 11
o'clock at night. I would not like to describe
publicly some of the things I have seen,
but if the Prime Minister does not want
to go along these streets himself, let him
send some of his secret service agents to
go and tell him what is taking place.
It is the duty of every Government to
provide work for the people under its
jurisdiction, but, so far as the single persons of Northern Ireland are concerned,
their plight was never so bad as it is at
the present time. I suggest that the
Minister of Finance, who has just come
into the House, can be of great assistance
to the Prime Minister in providing the
money necessary to create schemes of
employment..
Mr. POLLOCK: Where would I get
the money?
Mr. HENDERSON: You can forge it
so far as I am concerned. I realise the
difficulties of the Prime Minister and the

have done to provide work for the people.
We are going to adjourn this House until
3rd October, although the position of
married men who are out of employment
is as serious as it could be at the present
time. I know the Minister of Labour
does not like to hear matters like this
brought before the House, but I feel

Shankill district, an industrial constituency in which thousands of men are running about unemployed, some of them
with large families. In view of this
position of affairs I feel justified in protesting in the strongest possible manner
against this outrage of the House being

stated that I was talking nonsense.

Mr. HENDERSON: Is it not a good

will have ample time to consider schemes

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Bill which I have the
pleasure of submitting to the House this
afternoon is one which relates to a
number of miscellaneous and largely unrelated matters. Some of the Clauses
may appear to hon. Members to deal with
comparatively trivial details of administration, and if this be so, such a Bill
may, perhaps, be useful in bringing home
to the minds of hon. Members the close
control exercised by Parliament over
many aspects of the everyday administration of our Government Departments.
Secondly, I think the Bill may be taken
as an indication of the desire of the
Government, even in matters of minor
importance, to take every step which
would be conducive to efficiency and
economy in administration. I now pass
to the individual Clauses of the Bill.
more
As regards Clause 1, when this Government was set up the functions relating to
Ordnance Survey were, by Order in
Council, assigned to the Ministry of Agriculture, the corresponding Department in
Great Britain being attached to the British
Ministry of Agriculture. The Government is now satisfied that a
economical, and possibly more efficient,
arrangement would be the amalgamation
of the Ordnance Survey Department with
the Valuation Branch of the Ministry of
Finance, and it is in order to enable this
amalgamation to be effected that this provision is introduced. Hon. Members will
appreciate that certain types of work,
etc., performed in the Ordnance Survey
Department, are similar to some of those
carried out in our Valuation Branch,
which is now, by reason of the Revaluation Scheme, much larger than was the
case when the Ordnance Survey work was
originally assigned to the Ministry of
Agriculture. There can be little doubt,
therefore, in the new circumstances, that
the most appropriate allocation of this
work is to assign it to the Ministry of
Finance, as is now proposed. I may
say that I have the full support of my
right hon.
hon. Friend the Minister of
Agriculture in proposing this change,
which will take effect from a date to be
2005 Administrative Provisions Bill-
3 OCTOBER 1933

Second Reading
fixed by Order in Council. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I
With reference to Clause 2, hon. Members may be aware that many of our
Government Departments are required
by Statute, to publish annually certain
reports and returns dealing with their
activities during the preceding year.
wonder how many Members scrutinise
these reports. I hope that they do so,
because I am satisfied that they will find
in them much informative and interesting reading. I only wish that the public
as a whole showed a greater interest in
the administration of our Province by an
occasional purchase and perusal of these
documents.
It has been found possible without legislation to amalgamate many of these reports, etc., which were formerly published
separately, and considerable economies
have thereby been effected. It is considered, however, that by publishing reports
at longer intervals than a year and by
excluding certain unnecessary material,
further economies might be effected along
these lines without any inconvenience to
the public or any loss of administrative
efficiency. To enable this to be done,
however, Parliamentary sanction is
necessary, and the object of this Clause
is to obtain such sanction. It will be
observed that the Clause is not applicable
to any published documents relating to
Government accounts, the necessity for
which will be obvious to this House,
which preserves jealously its control over
all aspects of Government finance.
As to Clause 3, in certain Statutes,
more particularly dealing with Revenue
matters, and the Adaptation Orders made
thereunder by virtue of the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920, Departments are
referred to as having their head office in
Belfast. Owing to the fact that the headquarters of most Departments are now
situated at Stormont in County Down
a technical irregularity exists, and the
first sub-section of Clause 3 is designed
to meet this difficulty. The second subsection, which refers to the "Belfast
Gazette,' " is designed to cover an omission
in one of the Adaptation Orders under
the Government of Ireland Act.
I now come to Clause 4, which deals
with a highly technical matter, and I
shall, therefore, content myself with
giving a very brief account of its purpose. Under the Irish Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922, it is in
effect provided that a reference in any
enactment to the Lord Lieutenant shall,
in its application to Northern Ireland,
be construed as a reference to the
Governor of Northern Ireland. It is
doubtful, however, whether this enactment can be held to apply to those Acts
which were passed by the Northern
Ireland Parliament itself between June,
1921, and December, 1922, and it has,
therefore, been thought well to make it
quite certain that the expression "Lord
Lieutenant" in this small group of Acts
can be construed as referring to the
Governor.
A further difficulty which has arisen is
that there is some doubt whether the
expression, "Governor of Northern
Ireland," as it appears in Statutes of
this Parliament, can be regarded as
including the Lords Justices, who, in the
absence of the Governor, are sworn in to
exercise his functions. The Clause will
also meet this difficulty, since it will, in
effect, apply to the expression, "Governor
of Northern Ireland, the definition in
the Interpretation Act which contains a
reference to the Lords Justices. I beg to
move.
Mr. BEATTIE: The introduction of a
Measure of this kind reminds me of a
cheap bazaar which I once attended.
What does this Bill contain? Twopencehalfpenny matters, while the important
matters which count in this Province are
left untouched. The Bill is brought in to
cover several small reports issued by the
different Departments for the information
of the class interested in the matters
concerned. These reports are not to be
issued in their usual form but are going
to be amalgamated into one booklet, so
that instead of paying for one small report the purchaser will have to pay for
the whole lot.. The Government call that
economy. I used to be able to buy the
report of a Department for 3d, but now
if I want to get that particular report I
shall have to buy a booklet containing the
reports of several other matters, and I
presume the price will be increased although to the Government the cost will
be reduced. I do not think that will
enlighten the people of Northern Ireland,
nor will it give them any greater interest
in the matters contained in the reports as
they are now issued.
.
Administrative Provisions Bill
Drainage Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
I would like to correct a statement made
by the Minister of Finance. He said that
many of the reports issued are not read.
I, at any rate, read all reports that come
to me. Whether they interest me or not
is another matter. I do not think I ever
threw anything into the wastepaper basket without reading it, but that is the
suggestion of the Minister. Because some
people do not take a deep interest in
these reports he feels that he must amalgamate them with other reports of a
similar nature. I think that is foolish
economy, and I do not believe the Exchequer will benefit very much.
If the Government brought in an
Administrative Provisions Bill covering
say the cost of the Government and
of all the Departments which the
Government control we would have
something to work upon, and would
feel that revenue could be obtained
without injuring those concerned. That
is my reason for saying that this is only
a twopence-halfpenny matter to cover up
the larger expenditure of the Government.
I do not stand for this class of economy
which prevents those desiring information
from getting it because of the cost.
Then we come to another Clause in this
Measure. I think it deals with a paltry
thing, which statesmen or politicians
worthy of the name would have taken
no notice of. I presume that the right
hon. Gentleman and I have been moving
about this district since early childhood,
and we always understood that the City
of Belfast extended to the boundary. We
are now located at Stormont, in the Ballymiscaw area, and that gives to the County
Down authorities the right to get a contribution on behalf of rates which are
payable by the Government. But who
have spent the money on the roads leading to Stormont, and who have made the
site what it is to-day? Has it been the
Down County Council?
The Down County Council, I understand, forgot to control this part of the
county. The Minister of Labour knows
quite well that they did not trouble their
heads about it because they were afraid
that at a future time there would be an
extension of the boundary of the borough
of Belfast and that this place would be
taken into the borough of Belfast. If
the Bill for the extension of the borough
of Belfast had been introduced at its
proper time, that is when the increase in
values took place on this estate, we would
have had no reason to change the title
from "Belfast" to "Stormont,'
as Stormont would have been in Belfast. I
object strongly to the exclusion of Stormont from the borough of Belfast after
the enormous sums of money the ratepayers of Belfast have spent in improving
this part of County Down. From that
point of view I believe I would be justified in moving that this Clause be left
out of the Bill until such time as the
City Fathers and the Government get
together and the boundary is extended.
The other point in the Measure, I am
told, is one of no importance; it is only
a change in title in reference to the Lord
Lieutenant of Ireland. It will now be
the Governor of Northern Ireland. I do
not think we need those words in the Bill
as the time is fast approaching when our
financial responsibilities will have to be
faced up to, and the first sinecure which
will have to be abolished is this position
which is now included. Therefore, I
think this Measure, taking it from start
to finish, is not likely to be for the good
of the residents of Northern Ireland. I
think it is more inclined to do them an
injury so far as the dissemination of information is concerned. In my opinion
it should be a larger Measure to cover the
administration of the Government as a
whole. The other items are such that I
do not think this House need pay any
great attention to them. The Bill is one
which should be rejected on its Second
Reading.
