Mr. POLLOCK: In moving the Second
Reading of this Drainage Bill it crosses
my mind that hon. Members may think
that a Drainage Bill has become a perennial institution in our legislation. I
venture to offer, as an explanation of the
somewhat frequent recurrence of Drainage Bills, that it is not a simple matter
to frame general provisions in regard to
Drainage Bill-
Second Reading
3 OCTOBER 1933
drainage which are sufficiently adaptable
to provide for all the wide variety of
circumstances which arise in respect of
the different problems which have to be
faced. Indeed, considering the technical
difficulties that have to be overcome,
the conflicting interests that have to
be dealt with, and the shortage of available
hon. Members will realise
money,
that the code of legislation on the subject
is one that must be built up on the basis
of actual experience.
There are four matters being dealt with
in this Bill. Two relate to developments
of existing schemes-the Quoile and the
Erne-which possess certain features that
render it impossible to deal with them
under the ordinary machinery of the
Drainage Acts, and the other two amend
existing enactments so as to facilitate procedure in certain directions.
is
The first matter concerns the drainage
of the lower portion of the Quoile River
with a view to the relief of the extensive
flooding which takes place so frequently
in Downpatrick and the immediate neighbourhood. The problem, which
probably centuries old, is a peculiar one,
because it is necessary to cope with high
tides tending to rush upstream as well
as with floods coming downstream. During
the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries
works were carried out in order to ameliorate these conditions, and the existing
works now consist firstly, of tidal flaps at
three points below the Quoile Bridge,
which deal with minor streams, and
secondly-the main work-of a stone and
earthen barrier below the bridge, at one
end of which are inserted gates of the
ordinary type with which we are familiar
on canals.
These gates are closed by hand each
tide to hold the sea water back, and
opened as the tide falls to release the
river water. This was the position when,
a few years ago, a considerable portion
of the agricultural land in this area came
under the operation of the Land Purchase Acts and, by order of the Judicial
Commissioner, a sum of about £6,000 was
made available out of the purchase
moneys and handed over to the Land
Purchase trustee for the specific purpose
of maintaining the existing drainage
works, including the wages of the lockkeeper. The scheme under which the
money was made available provided for
the Ministry of Finance acting as agent
for the trustee in the maintenance of the
works. The Ministry, however, ascertained, on taking over control, that the
gates were in a state of disrepair and even
danger, and that inroads would have to
be made into the capital fund in order
to make the works more effective.
Simultaneously with this discovery on
the part of our Office of Works, the
Urban District Council of Downpatrick
approached the Ministry with a view to
seeing whether something could not be
done in the way of an improved scheme
in order to ameliorate flooding conditions
in the town. This necessitated consultation with the Down County Council, who
had an interest in this matter, although
perhaps, it was only secondary, as the
catchment area as a whole was involved,
and by arrangement the Ministry surveyed the entire area and prepared the
outlines of a comprehensive drainage
scheme. As, however, it became evident
that the benefits to be derived from it by
the rural dwellers were likely to be incommensurate with the charges on the
land, this scheme was not proceeded with.
Therefore, it was necessary to reconsider
the whole matter, and it was arranged
that our surveyors should devise some
means by which this trouble could be
remedied at lesser cost. Ultimately a
smaller scheme, designed primarily in the
interests of Downpatrick town, was drawn
up, the cost being estimated at £11,000.
For a considerable time the question of
the division of this cost seemed to be an
insuperable barrier in the negotiations between the Government, the Down County
Council, and Downpatrick Urban Council,
but ultimately, owing very largely to the
untiring efforts of the hon. and gallant
Member for East Down (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) a settlement was reached, and is
embodied in the schedule to the Bill as
an agreement. After taking about
£5,000 from the Land Purchase scheme,
the balance will be found in varying proportions by the Government and the two
Councils. I should like to add that I
consider that the Down County Council
has acted with commendable public spirit
in agreeing to make a substantial contribution to a scheme which is of only
secondary importance to them.
As regards the drainage works which
are being carried out, it may interest the
House if I give a short sketch of what
they comprise. Shorn of intricate
technical details, the basic idea is
Drainage Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
to insert in the present tidal barrier
self-acting sluices which will hold
back the tides on the one hand and
release flood waters without any manual
intervention. The existing locks will be
filled up when the new sluices are available. In addition, in order to facilitate
the flow of the river itself in the lower
reaches with consequential benefit higher
up, the channel will be deepened by
dredging between the railway bridge and
the barrier, a distance of nearly two miles.
This will involve the underpinning of the
present Quoile Bridge itself. This, then,
is the scheme in outline, and I hope hon.
Members will have a clear idea of what
is being done.
I should add that in order to take
advantage of the summer months considerable progress has already been made with
the works, as the Government's intentions
had already been brought to the notice.
of the House by means of a token provision in the Estimate for Public Works
and Buildings.
The second problem concerns the Erne,
which is a larger and much more difficult
problem, one, indeed, which has been regarded from time to time as almost insoluble. What we are proposing to do in
this case is, by arrangement with the
Lough Erne Drainage Board, to experiment with the operation of the sluice
gates at Belleek, at the entrance of the
Lough to the river which conducts the
waters to the sea, but these experiments
would have been useless unless some preliminary expenditure was first incurred.
Hon. Members may have read the Report
of the Drainage Advisory Committee on
the problem which was presented to this
House some years ago.
Hitherto it has
been impossible to exercise any adequate
measure of control over the level of Lower
Lough Erne by the operation of the
Belleek gates, because the Belleek Pottery
Company were entitled to a certain head
of water for motive power. As the Report pointed out the interests of the company were in direct opposition to those
of persons occupying land on the shores
of the Lough, who wanted the water to
flow away as quickly as possible. If the
gates were opened to their full extent
in flood time the accelerated current drew
away the head of water from the millrace and deprived the company of its
right to water which it had established by
legal process.
The solution recommended by the Committee, and now adopted, has been to
buy out the water rights of the Pottery
Company, and towards the cost of this,
amounting to £8,250, the Government
are providing £6,000 and the Fermanagh
County Council the balance. It is not
pretended that the operation of the sluice
gates will absolutely cure flooding. A
comprehensive scheme would be wholly
uneconomic, but the unhampered operation of the gates will certainly mitigate
the severity of spring and summer flooding, which is so harmful to farming
operations.
The general method of operation will
be to anticipate floods, this being possible
because of the great distance of current
flow through the two lakes. If the sluice
gates are opened immediately a flood is
indicated, the water of the Lower Lough
should be appreciably lowered before the
floods of the Upper Lough reach the
Lower, and thus a larger reservoir will
be created.
Owing to the vast area covered by the
loughs, experiments alone can show, with
some degree of accuracy, what the effect
will be of maintaining the lake at some
point which, while below the existing
statutory level, will not damnify persons
seeking reasonable use of the waters of
the lough. These experiments will be
carried out by the Ministry's engineers
during the next two years, and as the
result of these experiences decisions will
be taken as to whether any amendment in
the existing Drainage Scheme is either
possible or desirable.
The matters to which I have referred
are covered by the first four Clauses of
the Bill. I now come to Clause 5. This
Clause replaces the sections of the Drainage Acts of 1925, 1929 and 1931, which
relate to the cleaning of farm drains by
occupiers of land. These sections represent successive attempts to empower
county councils to compel landowners to
clean their drains, or, failing this, to carry
out the work themselves and recover the
cost from the landowners. In working
these sections the county councils found
that the difficulties were insuperable,
because in nearly every case they were
unable to prove the landowner's
occupier's liability. It is, therefore,
necessary that the county council's powers
in this respect should be strengthened,
and the most important section of this
Clause is that which is designed to effect
or
Drainage Bill-
Second Reading
3 OCTOBER 1933
this by definitely imposing on the
occupier of agricultural lands the responsibility for cleaning the drains which run
through them.
I may say that the Clause has been
brought before the Drainage Advisory
Committee, which contains representation from every county council, and has
their full support. The Clause may look
formidable, but a considerable portion of
it does not contain fresh matter. In order
to have a complete picture Clauses relating to the cleaning of drains have been
extracted from our earlier Drainage Acts
and are now consolidated here in a single
Clause. I have no doubt that the Clause
will be carefully scrutinised in Committee,
and my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Home Affairs, or myself, will be prepared to answer any points that then
may
arise. I have, however, put before the
House the cardinal point in the Clause
itself.
The object of Clause 7 is to place the
Ministry of Finance in the same position
as a county council or an urban district
council as regards eligibility for grants
from the Road Fund for the purpose of
repairing and improving the swivel
portion of the bridges over the Lower
Bann. Under the Drainage Act, 1929,
the Ministry of Finance, in connection
with the drainage works on the Bann,
took over the responsibilities of the Lower
Bann Navigation Trustees, including the
care and upkeep of the swivel portion of
these bridges. That responsibility involves
merely the maintenance of this part of
the bridges in a condition suited to the
traffic at the date that they were built.
From recent investigations the Ministry's
engineers are satisfied that these parts of
the bridges will not sustain present day
traffic without considerable and increasing risk, and instead of tinkering with
them it is proposed to bring the swivel
portion to a strength capable of carrying
modern traffic. It is, however, not right
that the Exchequer should be called on
to bear this extra charge, and accordingly
this Clause provides for the same contribution being made towards this work as
would be made to a local authority in
connection with works on the roads on
which these bridges are situated. I beg
to move.

District Council, and the Government to

This Quoile River has been an outstanding question for a very large number of
years. In fact the first time it is met
with was in 1638, when one, Thomas
Cromwell, was instrumental in getting a
grant for the building of a bank and
sluices. The next time mention is made
of this business was in 1748, when a
gentleman called Edward Southwell built
a dam with sluices to shut out the tide.
It may be interesting here to read a
letter written on the 8th July, 1749, by
his wife to her son, Captain Southwell.
In the evening they went down to
see the bank and flood gates to drain
the lake. They keep the sea out very
well, but the fresh water is not so easily
managed yet. I make no doubt it will
be in time.
That letter, written 185 years ago, said
they made no doubt the fresh water would
be managed in time. Now the time has
come 185 years afterwards. The problem
that is before the drainage experts and
the Government is a complicated one,
firstly, because the level of the land is
about nine or ten feet above ordnance
level, while the tide rises 17 feet. Therefore
when the tide has risen the gates have to
be shut. Now the area under drainage
is a water area of 3,000,000 square feet,
and the flow from this area when the gates
are open is about 60,000 cubic feet of
water per minute. Therefore the House
will realise that when the gates are shut
the water banks up, and the problem is
to devise gates that will deal with this.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In moving the
Second Reading of this Measure, may I
say that I do not anticipate that hon.
Members will find any difficulty in appreciating fully and supporting the objects
of the three short Clauses. Briefly, their
effect is to extend to Northern Ireland
certain statutory provisions which have
for some time been in force in Great
Britain.
The first Clause deals with the sending
of youthful delinquents to Borstal Institutions. Under the Criminal Justice
Administration Act, 1914, petty sessional
courts can, in lieu of sentencing such
youths, commit them to prison until the
next quarter sessions, when the presiding
Criminal Justice Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
judge may impose a sentence of Borstal
detention. Hon. Members will be aware
that it often happens that assizes are held
before quarter sessions, and it is naturally
very desirable that it should be possible
for these youths to be sentenced by the
judge of assize rather than that they
should have to be kept in prison until
the next quarter sessions. Provision to
enable these youthful offenders to be committed either to quarter sessions or to
assizes, whichever is the more convenient,
was made in England under the provisions
of the Criminal Justice Act, 1925, but
this Act does not extend to Northern Ireland. This Clause will enable petty
sessional courts in future to send these
lads forward for sentence at quarter sessions or assizes, whichever is the more convenient.
Consequential on the amendment I have.
just referred to, the Clause also amends
our Northern Ireland Criminal Appeal
Act of 1930, for the purpose of permitting
appeals, in the case of youths sentenced to
detention in a Borstal Institution, from
a court of assize as well as from a court
of quarter sessions, as is the case at
present.
In connection with Clause 2, I would
inform the House that, under the
Children Act, 1908, any person charged
with certain specified offiences and "any
offence involving bodily injury to a child
or young person" is declared to be competent but not compellable to give evidence, and the wife or husband of such
person is similarly competent but not compellable. A doubt arose in the working
of the Act as to whether, if a child were
actually killed, this would come within
the meaning of the expression "involving
bodily injury," and I may state that it
was found necessary in England to clear
the matter up by a provision included in
the Criminal Justice Act of 1925, which
declared that the expression "any other
offence involving bodily injury to a child
or young person" includes the murder or
manslaughter of a child or young person,
and also infanticide.
The Criminal Justice Act of 1925, as I
have previously stated, does not apply to
Northern Ireland, but I am satisfied that
the time has now arrived when we should
clear up this matter, in so far as Northern
Ireland is concerned, by adopting a provision similar to the English provision,
and this will be the effect of Clause 2.

think that the House will agree with me

I may state that the provisions of this

Wednesday, 4th October, 1933.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
MARKETING OF PIGS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
Mr. DAVISON (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
he can give any information with regard
to the working of the Pig Marketing
Scheme in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I am very glad
to have this opportunity of explaining
the position which has arisen in regard
to the marketing of pigs in Northern.
Ireland.
As hon. Members are aware a Pigs
Marketing Scheme was framed by my
Ministry, after consultation with the interests concerned, in order to enable Northern Ireland to keep in step with
developments which were taking place in
Great Britain where a Scheme for the
marketing of pigs, on lines somewhat
similar to those which had been adopted
in Northern Ireland, came into force on
the 15th September.
The object of the Pigs Marketing
Schemes in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland is to enable a better regulation of
the marketing of pigs at home to be
undertaken by the producers themselves
as a corollary to the limitation of imports of bacon and hams from abroad
which has been put into operation by the
Imperial Government. The Marketing
Schemes both in Great Britain and in
Northern Ireland are administered by
the producers themselves, and I wish
to
emphasise that my Department
has absolutely no responsibility for
the administration of the Scheme. Since
the 1st October when the Pigs Marketing
Scheme came into operation its administration has been entirely a matter for the
Board which administers it. Owing to
certain difficulties it was not possible to
bring the Scheme into operation in Northern Ireland on September 15th simultaneously with the Scheme in Great
Britain, but in order to enable the producers to have an assurance with regard
to the prices for their pigs the provisional
Pigs Marketing Board and the provisional
Bacon Marketing Board agreed to certain
standard prices coming into operation as
from September 16th.
As hon. Members are aware a surplus
of pigs on the Northern Ireland pork
markets occurred almost immediately
after the agreed prices came into operation. Since the Pigs Marketing Board
was not legally constituted until the 1st
October and had no power to intervene,
my Ministry made representations to the
bacon curers to clear the markets at the
agreed prices during the latter half of
September and I am very glad to know
that it was possible to do this. I should
like, in particular, to express my appreciation of the action of those bacon curers
who agreed to clear the markets in response to my representations on the
matter. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Unfortunately I am informed by the
curers that larger quantities of pigs than
they can absorb have continued to be
offered at the markets and, consequently,
the Pigs Marketing Board has had to
commence operations under conditions of
great difficulty. I am further informed
by the curers that owing to the existing
limitation of imports of bacon from
abroad being inadequate they are unable
to clear their stocks of bacon at a remunerative figure and, consequently, have
had to restrict their purchases of pigs.
This morning a joint deputation from
the Northern Ireland Pigs and Bacon
Marketing Boards was received at Stormont Castle and arrangements have been
made to impress upon the Imperial Government the difficulties of the situation
and the need for a tightening-up of the
control of imports.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply of the right hon. Gentleman,
may I ask can the question of the
paralysis of the pig trade since the introduction of the Marketing Scheme be discussed by a private Member on moving
the adjournment of the House or alternatively, as an administrative matter
when the business of the House is
finished?
Mr. SPEAKER: The position is that
once a Board of this kind has been constituted and set up by Parliament under

The Capital Fund, which consisted of

Mr. POLLOCK: I really feel a sense
of humiliation in that I am compelled to
reply to the exaggerated and nonsensical
statements made from the other side in
regard to the matters before the Committee to-day. All the objects specified
in connection with the Colwyn Fund, as
it is called-that is, the £400,000 Fundhave been provided for, and the £400,000
has been, or will be expended.
£100,000 is a surplus which has accrued
from favourable investment and interest
derivable on the money lying in that
fund. As there were no other objects
allocated for the expenditure of that
money, obviously it had to be applied to
something, and surely it could not have
been applied to a more praiseworthy
object than to balance the accounts of
Northern Ireland, a thing which is essential and which, I hope, will always be
regarded as essential in the history of this
Financial Provisions-

4 OCTOBER 1933
Committee
Province. Therefore, as I say, I really
feel a sense almost amounting to shame,
that I find it necessary over and over
again to assure the Committee as to the
utilisation of the £100,000 from that
fund.
Criticism has also been made in regard
to one or two other matters to which
out of courtesy I suppose I must repeat
the reply. The £30,000 is simply part
of our ordinary revenue that accrued to
us when the accounts between the British
Treasury and ourselves came to be adjusted. It did not matter whether that
£30,000 had come from Income Tax,
from Customs and Excise, or from any
other source of revenue; it was part of
the revenue of Northern Ireland, and,
therefore, was appropriate to be introduced, and, indeed, necessary to be
introduced into our returns.
As far as the Constabulary Fund is
concerned there seems to be a great deal
of misconception. Ample funds were
provided for rewarding the members of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary for any
praiseworthy acts they performed. There
never was any question about that. This
amount of £12,000, which has lain there
for some years unused, is simply the surplus after all the members of the Constabulary who had earned them were in
receipt of their rewards. Therefore, to
talk about robbing the fund-and especially to suggest that it has been done
to the prejudice of those members of
the Constabulary who deserved rewards
and who were rewarded-is nothing but
sheer nonsense. The fund has to be disposed of in some way, and there is no
other method of disposing of it than by
bringing it into the ordinary Exchequer
funds, and that is where it is. If it
were disposed of in the way in which
the hon. Member (Mr. Henderson) on
the other side suggests I suppose it would
be devoted to some of the beautiful
schemes, such as art and literature, which
were mentioned by him, and for which
the Belfast Corporation presumably are
responsible. But we have nothing whatever to do with these matters. Those are
local matters, entirely belonging to the
Corporation, with which we have no concern at all at the moment.
There is just one other thing I would
like to emphasise again, and it seems to
me that the necessity for referring to it
again only brings into relief the unbusinesslike ideas some hon. Members
on the other side of the Committee have
in regard to the treatment of money in
connection with our financial arrangements. This Sinking Fund is provided
out of the revenues of Northern Ireland,
and is designed to continue in perpetuity
the revenues now derivable from our land
annuities. If this were not provided for
they would become a terminable source of
revenue, and we would receive no benefit
from them when the date arrived for the
expiration of the payment of those
annuities. I wonder could I make it any
clearer than that. It has no connection
with the payment of the annuities by
the farmers. It is not the farmers'
money. This Sinking Fund is paid out
of the revenues of the Province to ensure
that there will be continuity of an
amount comparable to the annuities as
we have them to-day.
I hope I have made these matters clear,
and that all the visionary talk we hear
from the other side about the maladministration of Ulster funds will cease.
It is really humiliating that the Members
of this Committee should indulge in recrimination of that kind, particularly
when they wind up, as they generally
do, with suggestions as to the bankruptcy
of the Province. The Province has
balanced its accounts out of its own revenues from the day we started until
the present day. I doubt if, outside
Great Britain, another country in the
world could make that claim. Out of
our own revenues, remember, without
any assistance whatever from Great
Britain, notwithstanding all the talk
about our standing on the doorstep of the
British Treasury as mendicants out of
our revenues we have provided for our
expenditure. It is true that the great
depression in business renders it difficult
for us to balance our accounts, owing to
the fact that the revenues derivable from
Income Tax and from Customs and Excise
have fallen away, and that the people
who used to pay those taxes are not now
providing the revenue which would make
it easy for us to balance our accounts
and to pay an Imperial contribution. At
anyrate we have come through, and I
hope we shall come through to the end.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. POLLOCK: The three small and
unimportant matters dealt with on this
Resolution will not, I reckon, develop
much controversy. The first part charges
the expenses of issue of stocks or bonds
issued by the Government on the Consolidated Fund instead of charging the expenses on the Votes for the year, and will
have retrospective effect so as to cover the
expenses of issue of our 3 per cent.
Ulster Stock last March.
The second part of the Resolution
transfers from the Consolidated Fund to
annual Votes the cost of the provision of
furniture for new or reconstructed barracks, and is designed rather to simplify
administration than from any financial
motive.
The third part of the Resolution refers
to the spreading over a number of years
of the Exchequer grants made towards
the cost of building new voluntary
schools. The Committee will recall that
some years ago Parliament agreed that
fifty per cent. of the cost of certain voluntary schools should be provided from the
Exchequer. The amount of such grants
in the current year is approximately
£39,000. That is all that is involved in
the three parts of this Resolution, and,
therefore, I beg to move.

Mr. BARBOUR: The object of the
Resolution on the Order Paper is to provide for the contingency of the estimated
cost of the drainage works described in
the Schedule to the Bill being exceeded.
It will be seen from the scheduled agreement that the works have been estimated
to cost £11,000, and that apart from the
Ministry of Labour grant, Parliament is
not to be called upon to contribute to this
cost except in so far as it exceeds the
estimated total of £11,000. It is not at
the present juncture possible to say what
will be the excess over this sum. All
that I can say is that indications so far
point to the fact that the works will cost
more than the stated amount.
In moving this Resolution it is perhaps
only right that at this point in the
various stages of the Drainage Bill I
should make some comment on the suggestion put forward by the hon. Member
for South Derry (Mrs. Parker), namely,
that the Government should make more
substantial contributions to drainage
schemes generally. I am aware that recently Resolutions have been passed by
the County Council of Down and the
County Council of Armagh recommending that the cost of major drainage
schemes should be divided as to one-third
by the Government, one-third by the
County Council, and one-third by the persons in the area affected. The object of
this proposal is to attempt to convert
drainage schemes which, from the point
of view of the ratepayers in the area benefited, are uneconomic, into schemes, which
from their point of view would be economic,
that is to say, schemes in which the increased value of the land will not be
swallowed up in the rate struck to meet
the capital cost of the scheme and its
future maintenance.
I fully agree that it is extremely doubtful whether any drainage scheme carried
out at the present day can be profitable
without assistance from some outside
source. Existing drainage legislation
does provide one such source, namely, the
county at large, but as the hon. Member
pointed out in her speech yesterday, such
county contributions are the exception
rather than the rule. I hold the view,
however, that in a local problem of this
sort the county is the proper source of
assistance, and indeed the Resolutions to
which I have referred to some extent confirm this view. Exchequer assistance
should, in my opinion, and in that of my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, be confined to those larger
schemes which are, if I may use the expression, of a national rather than of a
local character. The standard examples
of such schemes are the River Bann and
the Lough and River Erne.
As regards the River Erne, I do not
think that any justification is necessary
of the action of the Government in contributing out of voted moneys a sum
equivalent to about two-thirds of the cost
of the purchase of the water rights at
Belleek. That preserves the same proportion as the Government's contribution towards the Bann Drainage Scheme
bears to the prospective contributions by
the various county councils in the catchment area.
To some extent the Government has
given assistance to local authorities in
their local drainage schemes, inasmuch as
it has made available the services of its
engineers, and no payment for these services is called upon where the engineers
are satisfied that the scheme in respect of
which they have carried out preliminary
surveys is likely to be wholly uneconomic.
By wholly uneconomic I mean schemes
which could only be carried out by the
assistance of a county at large contribution of such an amount as
no sensible
person could recommend.
The hon. Member for South Derry also
referred to the fact that in the case of

being made in the case of the Claudy

is evident as most of them are in areas
far removed from localities where un-

Thursday, 5th October, 1933.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
OUTBREAKS OF SHEEP SCAB.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
supply any information as regards the
number of outbreaks of sheep scab since
1928; also whether he can state the number of sheep or lambs which have been
held up at the ports of embarkation
owing to having been in contact with scab
cases.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): During
the period 1st January, 1929, to 30th
September, 1933, there were 600 confirmed outbreaks of sheep scab in Northern Ireland. In the same period 2,128
sheep or lambs were held up at the ports
of embarkation because of having been in
contact with animals found on inspection
at the ports to have been affected with
sheep scab.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In view of
the danger of losing our export trade
will the Minister see that there is a
tightening up of the regulations, and is
he aware that at present in Belfast there
is only one inspector for every 6,000
sheep on a Monday?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: We are
taking very considerable trouble about
that matter and have appointed extra
veterinary inspectors. That action was
taken for the reason that disease in the
in-contact sheep may be only in the
incubative stage and consequently not
observable at the time of veterinary inspection.
THE PIGS MARKETING SCHEME.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, in view of the
present unsatisfactory condition of the
pork markets and the inconvenience and
loss arising therefrom to the pork producers, he can state when the Pork Marketing Board will be able to relieve the
present congestion.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I would
refer the hon. Member to the reply I
gave yesterday to the question put to
me by the hon. Member for Armagh
(Mr. Davison) regarding the operation of
the Pigs Marketing Scheme. I would
add that the Pigs Marketing Board are
doing all in their power to relieve the
congestion in the markets and that they
have made an announcement regarding
the prices at which they are prepared to
purchase live pigs.
Farmers have further been warned by
the Board not to market dead pigs unless
they have made arrangements with curers
to accept the carcases after the pigs have
been killed.
Mr. NIXON : Is the Minister
ashamed?
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the Minister aware
of the fact that the prices adopted by the
Pigs Marketing Board are much lower
than those promised by the Pigs Marketing Board some time ago?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I do not
think the Pigs Marketing Board could
make promises before it was established.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is it not a fact that
the Pigs Marketing Board arranged that
the price should be 58s 6d during the
month of October?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: That is
the price the Pigs Marketing Board are
paying at present.
Mr. ELLIOTT: The Pigs Marketing
Board to-day are offering 43s——
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
making a statement. He should put it
in the form of a supplementary question
-a short, direct question.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the Minister aware
that the Pigs Marketing Board to-day are
offering 43s per cwt. live weight for pork,
which price is not at all equal to the
58s 6d promised by the Board?

Oral Answers

PURCHASE OF PIGS IN IRISH
FREE STATE.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of the
fact that several bacon curers in Northern Ireland are purchasing their pork in
the Irish Free State to the embarrassment
and loss of the pig producers in this area;
and whether he will have representation
made to the Imperial Authorities, with
a view to getting the duty on pork imported from the Irish Free State very
considerably increased.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I am
aware that a number of bacon curers in
Northern Ireland have for a great many
years obtained part of their supplies of
pigs for curing from the Irish Free State,
and that some of these curers are continuing to obtain supplies of pigs from
that area. The quantity of pork, live
pigs and bacon and hams imported from
the Irish Free State into the United
Kingdom is now restricted by quota
arrangements, however, and consequently
only a limited supply of pork from the
Irish Free State will in future be available for curing in Northern Ireland. I
am satisfied that the best interests of pig
producers in Northern Ireland lie in the
results which will eventually accrue from
the operation of the quota arrangements
which are being enforced by the Imperial
Government.
Mr. ELLIOTT: As I do not consider
the reply satisfactory, I propose to raise
the matter on the Motion for Adjournment to-day.
Mr. HENDERSON: Now for the fire
works.
IMPORT DUTY ON LINEN GOODS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can state the
amount of import duty at present on linen
goods coming into Great Britain; what is
the amount of import duty at present
on linen goods coming into Northern Ireland; what effect this duty has upon the
trade in Northern Ireland; when this
duty was imposed; what was the amount
and value of linen goods imported into
Great Britain during the years 1930-31
and 1932-33; what was the amount and
value of linen goods imported into Northern Ireland during the years 1930-31
and 1931-32.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In reference to the first
part of the question, I would remind the
hon. Member that, as Great Britain and
Northern Ireland form one fiscal unit,
the rates of duty applicable to goods.
entering either country from places outside the United Kingdom are the same
in all cases. The present rate of duty
on goods falling within the general classification of linen manufacturers is 20
per cent. ad valorem, while the rate
chargeable on embroidered goods is 30
per cent. ad valorem. Both classes of
goods first became subject to duty in
November, 1931, under the Abnormal
Importations (Customs Duties) Act, 1931.
Since April, 1932, they have been dutiable under the Import Duties Act, 1932,
originally at the rate of 10 per cent.,
increased as from September, 1932, to 20
per cent., and, in the case of embroidered
goods, to 30 per cent. as from June,
1933.
The effect of these duties on our local
linen trade cannot be measured with any
degree of exactitude, except in so far as
the reduction of unemployment in the
linen industry and diminished importation of foreign goods into the United
Kingdom may be regarded as indicating
increased consumption of Northern Irish
goods within the United Kingdom
market.
In regard to the statistics desired by
the hon. Member, I would point out that
in the trade returns published by the
Board of Trade, imports into Northern
Ireland are not segregated from imports
into Great Britain. Further, the annual
summaries published by that Department
relate to the calendar, and not to the
financial year. With the hon. Member's
permission, therefore, I shall quote the
published figures of imports into the
United Kingdom for the calendar years
1930, 1931 and 1932, as well as those for
the period January to August of the
present year. In 1930 the value of linen
manufacturers of all kinds imported was
£908,000, of which £590,000 represented
piece-goods measuring 11,769,000 square
yards. In 1931, the imports amounted to
£711,000, including £430,000 piece-goods
of 9,533,000 square yards. In 1932, the
imports amounted in all to £448,000, including £164,000 piece-goods of 4,451,000
square yards. For the period January to
August, 1933, the corresponding figures
Oral Answers
Oral Answer
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
were:-Total imports, £180,000; piecegoods, £62,000, measuring 2,218,000
square yards.
Mr. JOHN JOHNSTON: Is it not a
fact that the imports of goods since the
tariff was put on are about one-fifth what
they were previously? (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
ANCIENT MONUMENTS ACT-

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

BANN DRAINAGE SCHEME.
6. Mr. John JOHNSTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
what progress has been made in the Bann
Drainage Scheme and when it will be
completed.
Mr. POLLOCK : By the end of
October it is anticipated that about all
the soft dredging from the Cutts to the
Agivey Bridge-a distance of 6 mileswill be completed, and the same results
have been achieved on the stretch between
Toome Weir and Lough Beg.
As regards rock excavation, it is hoped
that before the winter rains set in the
whole of the rock excavation at the Cutts
and all the rock on the very long stretch
at Portna will have been removed, with
one small exception at the latter place.
Except for a few isolated reefs in the
river this completes the entire rock
removal work.
As regards sluices and fish passes, the
entire work has been completed at the
Cutts and Portna, while at Toome out of
five sluice gates, one is completed, one
nearing completion, and the foundations
of the third well forward. The anticipated date of completion of all works is
mid-summer 1936.
Mr. JOHNSTON: Can the right hon.
Gentleman state whether there will be
any appreciable diminution in the flooding during the coming winter as a result
of the work that has already been done?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a very large
question, and to answer it would require
much more engineering experience than
I could pretend to possess, but I have it
from the experts that the indications
show that the work done up to the present
on the Bann will permit of the amelioration of a great many of the troubles that
have arisen in connection with flooding in
the catchment area. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
TOOME EEL FISHERY CO.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether the property of the
Toome Eel Fishery Company is included.
in the list to be dealt with under the Revaluation Scheme and if not, whether he
will explain the reason why this company
is allowed to control the fishing rights of
Lough Neagh and contribute nothing by
way of taxation either to the Exchequer
or to local authorities.
Mr. POLLOCK: The property of the
Toome Eel Fishery has always been
treated as a rateable hereditament, and
will require to be dealt with under the
Revaluation Scheme.
As regards the implication in the
question that the company control the
fishing rights of Lough Neagh, I may say
that a discussion on the rights of the
company to control the catching of eels in
Lough Neagh could not be adequately
dealt with by way of question and answer,
but I understand that this right has been
the subject of a House of Lords decision.

My own position in this matter has

POLICE PROTECTION FOR
CHILDREN AT DANGER
POINTS.
11. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been drawn to the recent
resolution of the Irish National Teachers'
Organisation calling attention to the
necessity for rigorous police supervision.
at all danger points at lunch hour and
breaking up time of schools, in order to
safeguard the children attending daily;
and whether he will, in view of the
increasing number of accidents, stress
such important precautions upon the
Royal Ulster Constabulary.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have seen the
resolution referred to in the Press.
There is no evidence to show that the
number of accidents to school children is
increasing.
This matter was taken up by my
Department some years ago, and the
Inspector-General made arrangements
that police on beat duty should, so far
as possible, be at the more dangerous
crossings at the times when children were
likely to be going to or coming from
school. A9 the hon. Member will
appreciate, it is impossible to provide
police at all crossings, but as many as
possible have been covered.
So far as the immediate vicinity of the
school is concerned, I understand that in
many cases the teachers arrange to supervise the children crossing the streets, and
I think that in all cases the staff should
take this course, and I am making this
suggestion to my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Education.
As the hon. Member is no doubt aware,
arrangements have been made by my
Department for lectures and demonstrations in a number of schools for the
purpose of inculcating traffic discipline on
the children, and I am satisfied that this
instruction has been the means of preventing a very considerable number of
accidents.

POWERS OF PETTY SESSIONS
COURTS-DECREES FOR

Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is the intention
of the Government to introduce and pass
legislation extending the powers of Petty
Sessions Courts in connection with the

will see that these unemployed men are

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The employment of George
Osborne by his brother and subsequently
by his father between 20th October, 1932,
and 22nd June, 1933-in respect of which
28 contributions were paid-was ruled by
the Court of Referees as not bona fide
employment under the provisions of
Section 7 of the 1920 Act, as amended by
Section 5 of the 1928 Act. The 28 stamps
in question could not therefore be counted
towards satisfying the required contributions for the receipt of unemployment
insurance benefit.
Section 28 of the 1920 Act provides for
the refund of contributions only where the
said contributions have been paid "under
the erroneous belief that the contributions
were payable." Having regard to the

The third point relates to a proposal
which I am sure the Committee will consider reasonable. By reason of the existing
law, documents executed by local authorities or in connection with local government administration, for instance, rate
receipts and contracts, are treated
being exempt from ordinary Stamp Duty.
Originally documents relating to the
County Cess and Poor Law
alone exempted, but in process
time, by reason of administrative
action, and on account of the
ployment of the Poor Rate machinery for
the collection of all rates leviable in rural
areas, the exemption has been extended
far beyond the limits originally intended. There is no good reason why
documents of local authorities, or those of
one local authority rather than those of
another, should receive this special
exemption, which is not accorded to
other persons or bodies of persons in the
State, and it is therefore proposed that
in future Stamp Duty should be payable
by local authorities in the same way as
by other persons and bodies of persons.
The law in Great Britain only grants
exemption in limited cases, and therefore, as the law stands at present, local
authorities in Northern Ireland are in a
more privileged position than similar
bodies on the other side rather by the
accidental development of the law relating
to the Poor Rate than by the intention
of the legislature. This Clause now seeks
to remedy this unwarranted encroachment
into the Revenue laws of Northern Ireland.
The fourth point deals with an exemption from Entertainments Duty of certain
agricultural shows where the promoters,
in order to attract people to the show,
have introduced some popular items, the
effect of which would be to make the
entire show liable to Entertainments
Duty. Agricultural shows generally were
exempted from Entertainments Duty by
our Finance Act, 1927, and I now propose to go a step further and exempt such
shows even when a taxable item is included. I may add that there will be a
proviso to the effect that, in order to
qualify for such exemption, my Ministry
must approve of the inclusion in a show
of any particular item which, as the law
is at present, would have rendered the
show liable to duty. The effect of this
Clause, if accepted by the Committeeand I have no doubt that it will-will be
to encourage the holding of agricultural
shows in the interests of the farming community.
The last point which is covered by the
Resolution relates to the exemption from
Northern Ireland Estate Duty in certain
circumstances of the capital and interest
on securities issued by the Treasury, that
is to say, the issue of 3 per cent. Bonds
in 1932. Legislation was passed in the
British Parliament in 1931, exempting
from British taxation all such securities
which are in the beneficial ownership of
persons who are not domiciled nor
ordinarily resident in the United
Kingdom.
In this matter we have been consulted
by the Imperial Treasury and have
decided that our own legislature should
be asked to make corresponding provision
as regards transferred taxation. Accordingly, it is proposed by this part of the
Resolution to exempt from Northern Ircland Death Duties all such securities in
the beneficial ownership of persons who
are not domiciled nor ordinarily resident
in Northern Ireland, and the exemption
will be retrospective so as to cover issues
by the Treasury since the passing of the
British Act in 1931. I may say that this
matter does not materially affect us as
I do not think it has occurred in any
single instance, that has been brought to
my notice at any rate, that foreigners are
concerned with Estate Duty in Northern
Ireland. I beg to move.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman a question, as I
failed to catch exactly what he
said? Am I to understand that
people who reside outside Northern
Ireland are to be exempted from Death
Duties on 3 per cent. Conversion
Loan, while those who live in Northern
Ireland will be subject to those duties?
Mr. POLLOCK: The idea is that, in
order to avoid double taxation, foreigners
-not necessarily those outside Northern
Ireland, for it does not apply to Great
Britain-or those people who are not
domiciled in Northern Ireland, should
not be subject to the duties I have
mentioned. I do not think this need
give my hon. Friend, who has asked the
question, any great concern, because the
conditions at present will not be altered,
very materially at any rate, because of
the non-existence of cases of this kind.

NEW CLAUSE (Penalty for obtaining poor relief by fraud).
(1) If for the purpose of obtaining
any benefit or payment under the Poor
Relief Acts (Northern Ireland), 1838
to 1928, either for himself or for any
other person, any person knowingly
makes any false statement or false
representation, he shall be liable on
summary conviction to imprisonment for
a term not exceeding three months.

prescribing the time within which proceedings may be brought before a court
of summary jurisdiction, proceedings
for an offence under this section may be
brought within twelve months from the
date on which evidence, sufficient in
their opinion to justify a prosecution
for the offence, comes to the knowledge
of the Guardians of the union in which
the alleged offence was committed and,
for the purposes of this provision, a
certificate purporting to be signed by
the clerk of the union as to the date on
with such evidence, as aforesaid, came
to the knowledge of the Guardians shall
be conclusive evidence thereof."

Constabulary Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This short
Measure involves no new principles, and
simply provides for the continuation, for
a further period, of the existing arrangements in regard to the contribution of
£25,000 by the Belfast Corporation
towards the cost of the police in the City,
and in regard to the powers of acquisition of land which may be required in
connection with the erection of police
barracks. It will be remembered that
under the Constabulary Act of 1928 the
old "free quota" system, under which
the Corporation of Belfast would have
been liable for a contribution of approximately £40,000 per annum towards the
cost of police, was abolished, and provision was made limiting the contribution
M1
Constabulary Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
of the Corporation to the reduced sum of
£25,000 per annum for the period of
seven years ended 31st March, 1933,
and thereafter at such amount as might
be determined by Parliament.
I may point out that, although the
number of men stationed in Belfast, excluding headquarters' staff and men
engaged on points duty is approximately 1,140, costing approximately
£282,000, the
the Corporation are only
charged for 75 men or 9 per cent. of the
total cost.
The time has now arrived, therefore,
when the question of the future contributions to be made by the Corporation
must be determined.
This question as to the appropriate contribution by local authorities towards the
cost of police formed one of the many
matters taken into consideration by the
committee set up by the Minister of
Finance to inquire into the financial relations between the State and the local
authorities, and it may be mentioned in
this connection that in the case of Belfast
the committee recommended that the contribution in respect of the City should be
increased to the amount which would be
produced by a 6d rate, approximately
£42,000.
This matter, however, formed one item
only of many other far reaching recommendations of the Committee with which
it is closely bound up. These recommendations are still under the consideration of Government, and it is not,
therefore, desirable at the moment to
make any change in the existing arrangement in regard to the contributions to be
made by local authorities towards the cost
of police.
The first Clause of this Bill, therefore,
simply makes provision for the continuance for the current financial year of the
payment by the Corporation of the sum
of £25,000 towards the cost of police.
The second Clause of the Bill concerns
the powers given to the Ministry by the
Constabulary (Acquisition of Land) Act,
1924, to acquire land compulsorily for
the use or accommodation of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. The powers conferred by this Act, which would have terminated in the ordinary course in 1929,
were extended by the Constabulary Act,
1928, until the 28th May, 1934, when it
was anticipated that the programme of
barrack building would have been practically completed and the necessity for such
powers would no longer exist.
As hon. Members are, no doubt, aware,
it was necessary in 1931, for purposes of

THE PIGS MARKETING SCHEME.
BREAKDOWN OF THE PORK
MARKET.
Lieut.-Col. GORDON: I beg to move,
"That this House do now adjourn." I
do so in order to discuss
The necessity of the Government
taking action in respect of the grave
crisis that has arisen owing to the present breakdown of the pork marketing
scheme, and to suggest remedies.
In moving this Motion, I wish to say
at the outset that I am not going to make
any criticism or remarks on the administration of the Pigs Marketing Board. This
Board has a most herculean task to perform in trying to evolve order out of the
present chaos. My remarks will deal with
the matter from the Government point of
view. In dealing with this matter it will
be necessary that one should shortly refer
to the legislation which has been enacted
and which has caused this disorganisation.
First, a Marketing Act of the Imperial
Government passed in 1931, set up
schemes to deal with the control of market
products. This year a further Act was
passed linking up this control of
products with the control of imports
by the Government and the quota system.
In the Act passed by the Imperial Government there was a Clause which required
us in Northern Ireland to conform by
passing legislation on the same lines or else
to have products controlled by an Order
in Council from Whitehall. Naturally
the Government here introduced the Marketing Bill, which was passed, and received
the Royal Assent in June. It is under
this Act that the scheme now in force for
the marketing of pigs came to be set up.
Under this scheme the responsibility for
the organisation and setting up of the control of the products passed from the
Government here to the Pigs Marketing
Board and Bacon Board. In a statement
made yesterday by the Minister the point
was emphasised that the Government had
no responsibility for the administration
of the Marketing Act, which implied that
there was no responsibility on the Government or this House to take steps to deal
with the impasse which has arisen. I agree
with that, but the fact remains that
everyone of us in this House who supported the passing of this Act has a moral
Pig Marketing Schems 2124
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
responsibility to see that the scheme works
and does not result in a wholesale loss to
the agricultural community.
I may say that I do not raise this question in any political sense at all. I raise
it as an act of common justice. It will be
necessary then to touch on the factors
leading to this breakdown. That the markets are glutted is due to two or rather
three main reasons. First, I would recall
that on the Third Reading debate of the
Bill in this House I emphasised the point
that the keynote of success for the scheme
would be confidence that the Imperial
Government would regulate the quotas.
What has happened? During the week
ending September 9th the Imperial Government allowed 10,000 extra cwts. of
Danish bacon to enter this country, and
yet during the time that the debates on
this legislation were going on the farmers
were urged from every platform all over
the country to increase their stock of pigs
for the home markets. Therefore, the
position was that at the time this scheme
was coming in there was an extra flood of
Danish bacon synchronising with an increased home production of pigs coming on
the markets. That gave the scheme a very
bad start.
There is a further factor, and it is that
in the Free State to-day you can buy
pork at 40/- per cwt. To this must be
added 12/- duty payable to the English
Government, making a total of 52/-. If
you deduct the bounty given by Mr. de
Valera for taking the pigs off his hands
you find the net price to those buying
pork from the Free State is 40/- against
the controlled price here of 58/6. The
curers buying in the Free State are, therefore, getting their pigs at 18/6 per cwt.
cheaper. The farmers have been told not
to put their pigs on the market but to
keep them. That is a suggestion that
comes from people who know little about
the keeping of pigs. If you have pigs
ready for the market and you keep them
one day longer than that market you are
losing money. Members on both sides of
the House will, I am sure, support me in
that statement. You must put the products on the market as they are ready.
If you keep them one day longer you will
lose money by the extra feeding charges
and overhead charges. Pork when ready
must go on the market or else there is a
loss to the farmer.
It may be argued that pork can be had
in the live market. What are the prices
that have been set up? The average price
in the live market is 7/- or 8/- per cwt.
under the Board's own price for dead
pigs, and 7/- or so under the price in the
free and open market. Whatever course
is taken the farmer is at a loss. It will
result in a glutting of the market so long
as this continues, and the farmer will be
unable to market his pigs profitably, either
dead or alive.
In my Motion I put down a suggestion
as to what remedy and what steps can be
taken by the Government now and at
once to relieve the markets, so that no
further loss will fall on the farming community. We must assume the moral
responsibility which we all have here for
having passed an Act which is not having
the results we desire and make a better
and freer market for the products of the
farmers. It may be argued by many
that this impasse or disorganisation will
not continue for long-that it may end
in a week or two. I hope that will be
the case, but as far as I can
see this
impasse will not be righted for five or
six weeks, and there is always the fear
that a similar situation may arise in
England.
It is necessary for the Government to
come forward at once with some remedy.
I am going to suggest one; I am not going
to wait on the Government's suggestion.
The remedy is that the Government should
undertake through the Pigs Marketing
Board to relieve the markets of such pigs
as are not bought by the curers in the
dead markets, and these pigs should be
placed by the Government in cold storage
until such time as the Pigs Marketing
Board can absorb them. The cost of the
cold storage should not fall on the farmer
who has already had enough losses to
bear. What it will cost I am not prepared to say. That can be easily investigated through the organisation set up
under the Act. The Pigs Marketing
Board is composed of some eminent men
and they could consider this proposal.
To-day I went to the weekly market at
Ballynahinch. There were 150 live pigs
in the market. When I got there I found
there were 45 pigs unsold. I am glad to
say that after consultation with the
curers I was able to get the pigs purchased and taken off the farmers' hands.
I can quote you the case of a man I have
known all my life, and who is known to
my people for the last number of
generations.

of industry and of the Belfast Corporation
can rise to the occasion and come to the
relief of the agricultural community of
this area who, at the present time, are
pretty well down and out owing to the
inaction of the Ministry of Agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture stated in
reply to a question I put to him this.
afternoon that the Board could not make
the prices before it came into operation. I
think I am in order in saying that some
time ago a statement was issued under the
seal of the Pigs Marketing Board or the
Ministry of Agriculture-I do not know
which to the effect that an arrangement
had been come to with the curers that 57/-
per cwt. dead weight would be paid for
pork from 15th September to the end of
the month, and that from 1st October to
the 31st October the price would be fixed
at 58/6.
That statement was made, and I hold
that the Government are morally responsible to come to the relief of the agriculturists of this area who took the Ministry
and the Pigs Marketing Board at their
word and expected to get 58/6 for their
pork and are now faced with ruin. I hold
the Government are fully entitled to come
to the relief of the pig producers and see
that they receive the full 58/6 per cwt. to
which they are entitled. Realising the
position in which I stand, and feeling my
responsibility in the matter, I feel that
something must be done speedily.
whole-heartedly support the Motion put

that the farmers are relieved of their pork
and get the prices they were led to believe
they would get, and which I believe they
will not get unless something is done to
supplement the offer made by the Pigs
Marketing Board.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I was in

towns telling the farmers that their pigs

The hon. Member for South Tyrone
(Mr. Elliott) said that I had stated I had

Oral Answers to Questions.
POLITICAL SPEECHES-MR.
GEORGE B. HANNA, B.L.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he received a complaint.
in this House on 10th May, 1933, regarding George B. Hanna, B.L., a parttime official of the Ministry, making a
political speech at a Unionist Association; and whether the Minister has
taken, or will take, similar action in this
case to the action taken by the Minister
in respect of James Wood, solicitor,
when he made a speech at a meeting
which was not in sympathy with the
Government while he was a part-time
officer of the Ministry.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): As I explained to the House
when this matter was raised on the 10th
May, 1933, Mr. George B. Hanna, B.L.,
is not a part-time official of the Ministry;
he merely receives remuneration on a fee
basis for such duties as he performs as
one of the panel of Chairmen of Courts
of Referees, and I have nothing to add
to what I stated in the House as recorded in Volume 15, No. 31, of the
Official Report.
I also dealt in the House on the 16th
May, 1933, with a similar question that
was raised with regard to Mr. James
Wood, who also was at no time a parttime official of the Ministry, and the
hon. Member will find my statement on
that occasion recorded in No. 33 of the
same Volume of the Official Report.
Mr. James Wood was one of the several
solicitors to whom the Chief Crown
Solicitor allotted the conduct of prosecutions initiated by Departments of the
Government, but it is now the practice
for this work to be done, as far as possible, by a whole-time official in the Chief
Crown Solicitor's Department.

GREEN CARD SYSTEM.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether, in view of the many
complaints regarding the unfair method.
of issuing green cards for relief work by
the Labour Exchange Authorities, he will
reconsider the matter and abolish the
green card, thus allowing men to obtain
work on their merits.
Mr. ANDREWS: As I pointed out
in reply to a similar question by the hon.
Member on 12th November, 1929, as
recorded in the Official Report, Volume
XI, column 1123, I am not prepared to
abolish the "green card" system until
an alternative is suggested which would,
in my opinion, be at least equally fair
in general to the unemployed workers.
The system has been approved by the
Unemployment Relief Grants Advisory
Committee; by the Belfast Local Employment Committee; by the different
public bodies which have undertaken
relief schemes, and by numerous deputations which have waited on me in connection with the relief of unemployment.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister consider seriously the advisability of abolishing himself politically and handing over
that green paper he holds in his hand?
TOTAL NUMBER OF UNEM-
PLOYED.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the total
number of persons at present unemployed
in Northern Ireland as compared with
November, 1932; and whether he will
make a statement as to Government plans,
if any, for relieving the position of these
persons during the coming winter.
Mr. ANDREWS: The hon. Member
will be glad to learn that the number of
persons registered for employment at the
Employment Exchanges in Northern
Ireland on the 25th September, the latest
date for which figures are available, was
about 10,000 less than on the 28th
November, 1932, and over 14,000 less
than on the 23rd January, 1933, the
totals being 71,986 in November; 76,367
in January, and 61,991 in September.
As I observe by the Order Paper that
the hon. Member for Pottinger has put
down a Notice of Motion with regard to
the general problem of unemployment, I
propose, in replying to the Motion, to
deal with the matter more fully than is
possible in reply to a question.
Mr. NIXON: All I can say is that this
is not like the question I put down. Perhaps I made a mistake. I will look into
it. It appears to have been altered.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that 7,000 of the 10,000 that he claims
as a reduction in unemployment numbers
are now borne on the local rates of the
City of Belfast?
Mr. SPEAKER: That is a matter for
the debate that comes on at half-past
four o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Barnett's Road is
privately owned and the Corporation has
no responsibility or liability with regard
to it.
The road is in bad condition, but the
owners have a contractor working on it
at present.
The work is being carried out in

completed, the question of taking over
and maintaining the road will receive
consideration by the Corporation.
Major MCCORMICK: Do I understand the Minister to say that the road
belongs to the Corporation?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I did not say
anything of the kind.
the

BORSTAL INSTITUTION AND
MALONE TRAINING
SCHOOL.
5. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
if it is a fact that the same regulations
regarding the insurance of staff and pupils
apply to the Borstal Institution and
Malone Training School as to other
educational centres in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that some time ago the Ministry of
Education circularised education authorities and managers of schools generally,
suggesting that they should protect themselves by insurance against any legal
liability in respect of accidents sustained
by teachers or pupils under their charge,
and I presume that it is to this advice
that the hon. Member refers.
The position in regard to the Malone
Training School is, of course entirely
different. The established staff of the
school is, in the first place, covered by the
provisions of the Superannuation Acts
and the sick leave regulations of the Civil
Service. If injury in the discharge of
duty, resulting in retirement, occurs,
special superannuation terms are granted.
In the case of unestablished staff, the
Ministry of Finance insures against its
liability under the Workmen's Compensation Act.
In the case of the inmates of the school,
no legal liability is involved, and the
question of insurance does not, therefore,
arise.
PIGS AND BACON MARKETING
SCHEMES.
Mr. MINFORD (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Agriculture if, as
a result of the deputation which was received last week by Mr. Walter Elliot,
he is in a position to state what, if any,
steps have been taken to secure a more
satisfactory control of the imports of
foreign bacon, and generally if, in view
of the lack of confidence suggested by
certain sections of the Press, the Minister could give the House some assurance
as to the future of the Pigs and Bacon
Marketing Schemes.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE: (Sir Edward Archdale): In
reply to the hon. Member, I should
like to make it quite clear that
beginning in November last, the British
Government have been steadily curtailing the import of foreign bacon and
hams with a view to reaching the level
recommended by the Lane Fox Commission by the time the Pigs and Bacon
Constabulary Bill
Oral Answers
10 OCTOBER 1933
Marketing Schemes came into operation
on September 15th. Between November
and September last, the imports of
foreign bacon have been reduced by one
million cwts.
The time table of reduction has worked
with considerable accuracy. Unfortunately the last reduction which was to
have come into operation on September
15th did not actually come into operation until October 4th. This delay
caused a weakening of the bacon market.
But I should like the House to realise
that from October 4th the full reductions
have been put into operation and that
total supplies are now down to the rate
recommended by the Lane Fox Commission. As a consequence, the market has
already resumed a healthier and firmer
tone.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, I can only
assure him that there is now
no risk
of the scheme breaking down. Owing
to the increase of 30 per cent. which has
taken place in our pig population, we
are in a position to secure a much larger
share of the British market than has
ever been possible before, and I should
therefore like to thank all those who
through their work helped to put Ulster
in this fortunate position.
Mr. NIXON: Cold storage.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: During
the month of September, the marketings
of Northern Ireland pigs in our pork
markets were 10 per cent. above the
quantities for the corresponding period
of last year and were therefore not such
as to cause a glut. The greater part of
the initial difficulties has been due to
the lack of confidence in the import control and as a consequence a reluctance
to buy. These difficulties have now
been removed and I am happy to tell
the House that both the Bacon and the
Pig Producers' Board are satisfied with
Mr. Elliot's assurances on this point.
Initial difficulties are inevitable in
bringing into operation a scheme of this
magnitude. Hon. Members will, I feel
sure, realise that but for the scheme the
price to producers would have been 35s
or less, instead of 58s 6d as at present.
I would ask all concerned to go forward
with steady confidence, realising that the
position is clearing rapidly and that

within a very short time the troubles
which are inevitable in bringing into
operation such a big scheme will have
disappeared.

In the month of July, 1932, there

Another thing for which I object to

I notice that their address is 35 High

object to the
the Government using the

Another thing to which I object is the
Government using the police to find out

they want to know anything about the
Ulster K.K.K. they can find it all from a

Another thing to which I object is the

to the G.P.O. to take possession of letters
and to make photographs of letters going

belong to the Government party. I
object to that absolutely. Why in the

Government. I say it is disgraceful, and
this Government are abusing the power

Now here is a report, dated 12/3/32,
by an officer concerning the Shankill
Road district. You would imagine by
this report that everyone in that district
was a law-breaker, but what are the facts?
If you analyse the whole report you will
find that it only deals with petty little
offences which children might commit,
kicking football, flying kites, and various
things like that, things that any good
sensible policeman would deal with without a summons at all. But it would not
Constabulary Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
do, according to this officer, if they would.
not prosecute, take the whole of the
people before the courts, and make the

is this:
"While supervising beat duty in your
districtthat is the Shankill Road-
"during the early afternoon, about 1
p.m. on this date, I noticed, when
going round in my car, a great many
cases of kite flying, roller-skating,
playing football, etcetera, going on
without any effort on the part of the

These pasttimes were not confined to the back
streets-
I deny that. It is not true.
"but were being carried on in the
thoroughfares. Moreover, grown-ups
as well as juveniles were taking part.
The beatsmen concerned were Constables
Sherwood and Cooke. I spoke to both
of them about these offences, especially
the kite flying, but neither, apparently,
had bothered to caution the offenders
or to put a stop to them in any way.
I overtook Constable Cooke at the
corner of Snugville Street and Upper
Charleville Street, and as I approached
the corner a youngster ran past into
Charleville Street within a yard of the
constable flying a kite. The constable
never even spoke to him. Constable
Cooke told me when I spoke to him
about it that he did not stop them
unless there was a danger of the kite
catching in a telegraph wire. Constable Sherwood's only excuse for not
doing something about these offences
was that it was hard for a
man in
uniform to get near them. I can only
say that I found it hard to drive round
the beats without running down those
engaged in these pastimes. I have
noticed this going on before, and I have
spoken to the beatsmen about it, but
something will have to be done to stop
it now. I have questioned the reports of
prosecutions brought by the plainclothes men in sub-districts on several
occasions within the past few months,
and you have endeavoured to explain
why they had so few cases. In future,
if I have any occasion to find fault in
regard to the detection of offences by
either the uniformed or plain-clothes
men I shall have to report to the Commissioner on the subject."
Nobody will deny in the face of that that
the police are being intimidated on the
Shankill Road into prosecuting people for
trivial offences that could be very well
dealt with in the majority of cases without any prosecution whatever.
All that was leading up to the transfer
of these six good Protestant men, some of
them men who had served in Belfast
faithfully and well through all the
troubles. I do not know whether it
strikes the Government or not, but I am
sure it strikes any sensible man that a
policeman who makes himself a nuisance
by prosecuting every child and everyone
who commits any trivial offence is, as a
matter of fact, a danger to the community. The best police are the police who
can stop these trivial offences by going
to the parents of the children and complaining, or by checking them in some
way. Of course there does come a time when
there would have to be a summons. But
here is a definite report by a gentleman
saying that he questioned the number of
prosecutions and, because the number of
prosecutions was not up to his standard,
there came a time when the police had
to go. You would imagine that a Government with a sword hanging over its
head, a sword that will fall one day or
other-I do not refer to the sword that
may fall through an election, but to
another sword-instead of persecuting
the police who do their duty well without becoming unpopular, would help
those police. There is quite enough
serious crime to occupy our police without endeavouring to make them antagonistic to the whole community by prosecuting for trivial offences.
Before this there was another sergeant
on the Shankill Road-Sergeant Stevens.
He had been on the Shankill Road for
thirty years, and thirty years is a long
time. Everyone on the Shankill Road
liked Sergeant Stevens. He brought up
his family to be a credit to him. His
oldest son, I understand, is practically
graduated in the Queen's University for
the honourable profession of the ministry in the Church of Ireland. But,
although Sergeant Stevens served for
thirty years faithfully and well on the
Shankill Road, he was not good enough
for the Lundy Government that sits over

good many factors to be taken into
account. Cities across the Channel might
have a more law abiding people than we
have, and their suburbs might not be so
widely scattered. Indeed, I think we are
too prone in this Parliament to follow the
financial lines of England, or the greater
Britain, forgetting that we are a poorer
area, that our individual wealth is twoand-a-half times less than that of our
neighbours in England. That is a fallacy
that has brought us to a straining point
in our finances.
While I do not believe in economising
at the expense of our police protection,
I say we should cut our cloth according
to the material we have. I know that our
excellent police force is available and
ready at all times to cope with any serious
trouble, and I think it might here be well
to pay a well deserved tribute to the
readiness which our police have at all
times shown to deal with trouble when it
arose. One cannot but regret the
dastardly crime that took place on Sunday
night, whereby a very excellent member

of repression could not be too drastic in

These people and those who are connected

should be taken against them. This deed
has caused a thrill of horror amongst all
law-abiding citizens, and no words are
too strong to condemn such an outrage.
I have an open mind on this question
of the charge for the police force, but I
am inclined to think the charge is not
excessive, and that in comparison with the
cost under the old regime it is a moderate
charge, and I shall support the Bill.
