That, in the opinion of this House,
the Government should take over the
full responsibility for the unemployed
of Northern Ireland, or provide work
or maintenance.
The Motion standing in my name is one
of great importance to many thousands
outside this House. The matter is so
important as to warrant those people
assembling together for the purpose of
demonstrating the serious position they
are placed in by certain Acts of Parliament that have been passed in the
British House of Commons from the year
1912. I take this opportunity to make
the strongest possible protest to the
Minister of Home Affairs against the
suppression of the demonstration which
was to be held in our city to-morrow
against poverty in abundance in
midst. If Christianity-as the Government claim it to be-is to assist one
another and help the lame dogs over the
stile, I feel disposed to say that the Government are laming the dogs more
seriously than previously. I cannot see
why an expression of thought as to the
hunger existing in Northern Ireland
should be suppressed.
our
My Motion is down for the purpose of
asking the State to share the responsibility of the unemployed of Northern
Ireland. I move it in all sincerity, with
the object of getting the Government to
realise fully that unemployment is not
due to the unemployed. For that reason.
I placed the Motion on the Order Paper
with the hope of having an audience, and
an attentive audience in this House, to
see could we not come together with the
object of devising a newer system of
maintaining those unfortunate people who
are unemployed at the present moment.
I will build up my case against the most
rotten system that ever I had the sorry
experience to deal with-I refer to the
present Unemployment Insurance Acts.
The first Act in 1912 was confined to
special sections of the community-shipbuilding and engineering. That Act
went on to 1916. In that year
extension of that Act took place, covering
many classes of workers who were at that
time drawn into industry. That was due
to the Great War having taken place in
1914. As there was little or no uneman
ployment during the war the scheme was
never tested.
After the Armistice in 1918 the Government of the day, realising that demobilisation would bring unemployment, faced its
responsibilities. This is a point I would
have wished the Minister of Finance, if he
had been present in his place, to clearly
understand. What I am asking now is
not a new departure within the State.
What I am asking now really took place
from 1918 to 1920 and as far as 1921. I
hope to give illustrations to this House in
the course of my remarks as to the change
over of this great fraud called insurance.
The Government of the time introduced
an out-of-work donation scheme for the
purpose of meeting the amount of unemployment amongst ex-Servicemen which
would take place on demobilisation. The
Government also included in that scheme
civilians, and the civilians and the ex-
Servicemen, who had never contributed
anything to the insurance scheme of the
State, received benefit without paying
any contributions. It is significant to
note here that after the out-of-work donation scheme came into operation it was
thought that fraud would likely happen
in a scheme of the kind. A committee
was set up with Lord Aberconway as
chairman to go into the working of that
scheme as regards fraudulent claims, and
Lord Aberconway's committee in 1919
reported that there was no ground for
supposing that there had been extensive
fraudulent abuses of the scheme. I think
that was most creditable to those persons
who were unemployed at that time and
who were claiming maintenance under
that scheme.
The out-of-work donation scheme came
to an end in 1919 so far as civilian
workers were concerned, and was replaced
by the 1920 Act, which embraced textile
and other workers, including females.
That scheme was introduced on a three
party contributory principle. At that
time an expression of opinion was sought
from the representatives of labour as a
whole, and that expression of thought
was conveyed in a definite protest against
a three party contributory scheme.

Speaking in the British House of
Commons,
March 28,
on
1930, Mr.
Snowden said:
"I was the only man in the Parliament when the first Unemployment
Insurance Bill was before the House
who opposed the employer's contribution, and I have never had any
occasion to change my view on the
matter. The incidence is very heavy,
and it comes very unfairly. It is
equally a charge on the employer
whether he is making a profit or a
loss."
The employer's contribution becomes incorporated in the cost of production,
raises prices, and restricts consumption.
This becomes particularly serious when
the products of his firm have to meet
the competition of commodities which do
not contain a similar item of cost.
I was reading in the paper that Sir
William Beveridge suggested a direct tax
on employers for dismissals. This seems
strange reasoning. It implies that employers dismiss workers whom they might
keep employed at a profit, as I cannot
conceive his suggestion to be that employers should keep workers employed at
a loss. In any event, the cost would be
added to production, and, on the other
hand, if the employer found it cheaper
to dismiss workers and pay the dismissal
tax, that also would be added to costs
and so handicap industries in which the
economists are always telling us that
costs are too high. I am at a loss to
understand how anybody can prefer increasing costs in that way, instead of
reducing the cost of unemployment to
industries by spreading the burden over
the State as a whole. The crude and
wasteful method of wage
reductions
seems to be the only idea many people
have for reducing costs. That crude
and wasteful method of reducing wages
as a means of reducing costs has become
part of the policy of the marketing of
goods to such an extent that I hope the
Government will now discard it and think
along different lines altogether with a
view to taking the cost of unemployment
insurance away from industry and spreading it over the general taxpayers as a
whole.
The evidence of the Accountant-General
to the Ministry of Labour in Great
Britain showed that with a live register
of 17 per cent. unemployed contributions
would need to be increased by 2s 6d per
week in order to make the fund solvent
and self-supporting. The imposition of
any further burden on industry would
be quite impracticable apart from the fact
that it would be most inequitable to
penalise so heavily a section of the people
to meet what is really a national charge.
The inclusion in insurance of persons
with incomes up to £500 per year, except persons in the service of public
authorities, national and local statutory
companies, civil servants, teachers, railway servants, agricultural workers, and
domestic servants, and the cancellation of

Events since 1920 have strengthened
the view which I have always held that
unemployment benefit should be a
national charge. That this view is growing in other
other quarters the following
quotation will show. During the debate
on the Unemployment Insurance Bill on
April 4, 1930, Mr. Winston Churchill
said:—
"It might well be that an increase of
indirect taxation borne by the whole
of the consumers would be preferable
to raising the millions for the maintenance of the Insurance Fund directly by
a tax upon the regularly employed workmen in the prosperous industries."
I do not agree with his method of
taxation, although he agrees with the
principle which I am outlining. But
indirect taxation is no cure for the
present position of the Unemployment
Insurance Fund. A direct tax is the
only thing that will save the situation,
and give to the many thousands of people
their just rights in unemployment insurance benefit.
I repeat again what I have said many
times, that a scheme such as I have in
mind, the full weight of which would be
borne by the State, would I believe prove
a powerful incentive to the State to take
all possible measures to prevent unemployment which is absent when it contributes
but a fraction of the cost of maintaining
the unemployed. I am convinced that the
abolition of the present form of workers'
and employers' contributions, and maintenance becoming a direct Exchequer
charge, will result in putting matters on a
proper footing by abolishing the present
pretence of insurance, relieving industry of
an unjust burden, and compelling the
nation as a whole to realise its responsibilities to the unemployed, and, therefore,
its responsibility for organising employment.
The debt of the present fund has been
incurred largely because the Exchequer
failed to meet its obligations to the unemployed. In addition to being unfair,
to expect a limited number of people to
shoulder the responsibility for the debt,
any new scheme that may be proposed
would be doomed from the start if it had
to begin with a huge debt. I, therefore,
strongly urge that the debt should be cancelled. I appreciate that my proposal for
the abolition of the present contributory
system involves a heavy charge on the
Exchequer, but it is a burden which must
be borne not only in common fairness to
the unemployed, but in the best interests
of the State itself.
There can be no question of reducing the
benefits-in fact, I think they are already
too small-but I will deal with that matter
later. My presence in this House is responsible for bringing one-eighth of an
inch of intelligence to the hon. Member
who is sitting forward (Mr. Gordon). I
am prepared to speak here until nine
oclock to-night if doing so could only increase that one-eighth. The present
abnormal unemployment, which, unfortunately may last some time, is not wholly
within the control of either workers or
employers, or even of the Government. It
is due to the loss of trade owing to industrial development and to political upheaval in some other countries. International monetary policy also plays a prominent part, and rationalisation is no
small factor in the situation. The nation
is fighting for its industrial life, and the
whole position should, therefore, be treated
as a national emergency calling for special
measures. I realise that the abolition of
the workers' and employers' contributions will probably necessitate fresh taxation, when the Exchequer has to meet the
full cost of the present abnormal unemployment.

Government Responsibility
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
Whilst agreeing with the principle of
Mr. Churchill's statement, I do not agree
that the money should be raised by an
increase of indirect taxation, which is
always unfair in its incidence to the
poorest people who have to buy in small
quantities. I am of opinion that the
present emergency should be met by a
special unemployment levy on all incomes
whether from earnings or from interest
and profit. The levy would be on a
percentage basis, and it could be varied
from time to time in accordance with the
amount required for the maintenance of
the unemployed. The percentage basis
would ensure payment according to income as against the present inequitable.
flat rate which operates irrespective of
earnings. The levy should not in any case
exceed one per cent. on incomes up to
£200 per annum, but it would be a matter
for the Exchequer to adjust other percentages on a graduated scale according to
requirements. Unearned income should
be charged at a higher rate than earned
income. In this way the community, as
a whole, would contribute its quota to the
maintenance of the unemployed, and unemployment benefit would be payable to
any member of the community who was
unemployed and could fulfil the statutory
conditions.
The proposed levy would be really a
national effort to meet the present
emergency. It would spread the burden
equitably on all incomes; it would remove
the present burden on the low-paid
workers; it would relieve industry by
removing the contribution which has to
be paid irrespective of the state of trade,
and would substitute for it a levy on
profits; it would ensure a proper share
of the cost of unemployment being borne.
by those who, though not directly engaged
in industry, derive income from it. In
short, it would be a special national
effort to provide for the maintenance of
the unemployed, which would focus more
attention on the problem of unemployment and expedite measures for the
solution of it. The levy could be reviewed as conditions improved with a
view to the cost of maintaining the unemployed becoming an Exchequer charge
to be met from ordinary taxation.
The benefit should be for the loss of employment only, and there should be no
means test of any kind as regards wholly
unemployed persons. This country has
always been in the forefront of progress,
and I am confident that the people are
quite prepared now, as always, to respond
to a strong lead on the lines of national
responsibility and national co-operation,
which I trust the Government will be
prepared to give.

to receive this Motion. I hope the Motion

I have put it forward. I beg to move.

Major HALL-THOMPSON: As the

I think it is well that I should clear the

To-day there are thirteen automatic signals in operation, and it is estimated that
those save the services of ten pointsmen,
and, therefore, save the State £3,000 a
year. It is ultimately hoped to introduce
39 of these automatic signals and presumably the saving to the State will be
approximately £9,000, while the cost cf
the upkeep of these automatic signals to
the local authority will be £838 10s. So
therefore I hope that the Minister will
take this into consideration when he is
estimating what is a fair and reasonable
charge to make on Belfast for the use of
the police. I say this in spite of the
fact that when he mentioned the number
of police in the city he excluded the Headquarters Staff and also the men on point
duty.
In conclusion, let me say that I hope

this side of the House in opposing what
I think is at the present moment an unreasonable request, and what, I fear, in
the future will become a very serious
burden upon the local authority of Belfast, and ultimately upon the City of
Derry and the urban councils.

Under the old Constabulary Act the
system was that to every county and
every county borough in Ireland there
was assigned what was called a free quota
of police. That is, for each county there
was assigned a number of police, who
were supposed to be sufficient for the
normal requirements of that county.
Similarly to every county borough there
was assigned a free quota sufficient for.
the normal requirements of that county
borough. Any additional police above
the free quota were paid for, half by the
Government and half by the district to
which they had been assigned. The
whole of the free quotas were paid for by
the Government. When there was
trouble or riots and additional police had
to be sent to a district over and above
the free quota, a bill of expenses was
sent to that particular district for payment. The basis of the whole matter
was that the ordinary normal police
requirements of the district were supposed to be supplied and paid for by the
Government alone. The free quota was
supposed to represent the normal requirements of the district.
is

That brings me to the other consideration put forward, and that is the
consideration based on the report of the
committee on the financial relations
between the State and the local authorities. I may say at the outset that I do
not want to, and would not, reflect on
this Committee, because in my judgment
it was
a most excellent Committee. It
examined the very complicated subject referred to them in a most careful way,
and of all the documents produced by the
Government I think this report one of
the most valuable and would well repay
a detailed study of every paragraph by
everyone who is taking a part in public
life. I might also say that if a detailed
study is made of it by some hon. Members
from country constituencies they will find
in this document what will give them
considerable food for thought if they
study the sections dealing with derating.
But that is digressing from the subject.
With regard to the report itself I would
say that, in order to understand the situation, you have to consider the difference
in the organisation and control of the
police in England from that in Northern
Ireland. In England the police are
organised and controlled by the various
counties and are paid by the county
authority, who get a certain grant from
the Government, amounting to about 50
per cent. of the total cost.
In Northern Ireland we have adopted
quite a different system. It is not a
county system of police. We have a centralised system. The force is a central
organisation and centrally controlled. It
is a question, to my mind, not of detail,
but of high policy, which is the better
system. To my mind the only possible
system we can have in Northern Ireland
is the present system, and it would be
a great mistake to make any inroad on
the present system of the mode of controlling the police. It would be a mistake
to establish anything in the way of a
local force here. The police ought to
remain centralised and controlled as at
present. If the police are to be organised and controlled centrally it follows
as a matter of course that they should
be paid for by those who organise and
control them. I know that in some Continental countries, I think Germany, the
police are organised by the National Government, but they are paid for to some
extent by the local authorities. Under
a Constitution such as ours it is well
recognised that the people who pay the
piper should, at any rate, have some say
in calling the tune, and if you are going
to put any portion of the cost of the
police on the local authority here you will
find that the local authorities will, as a
right, demand some share in the control
of the police, and I think that would
be a disaster in Northern Ireland.
It is a claim that will, undoubtedly, be
put forward so long as you seek to collect
any expenses from the local authorities,
and it will be a demand difficult to resist.
We have had a claim made by the hon.
Member (Mr. Nixon) on the ground that

is a claim impossible to say "No" to.
This is a question of very substantial
policy, and the whole organisation and
control of the police here should remain
in the hands of the Government.
Nothing should be done to give local
authorities any say in the control.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I have listened
with great interest and care to the

Member (Major Hall-Thompson) and the
hon. and learned Member (Mr. Black).
The strong point they were making was
an appeal to the rural Members to come
here and support their views. The hon. and
gallant Member (Major Hall-Thompson)
pointed out that this was only the thin
end of the wedge, and that, therefore, we
country Members should be on the alert
to come to his support and help him in
this case. I may point out to the hon.
and gallant Member for Clifton that the
thin end of the wedge was put in two
years ago when the Revaluation Bill was
introduced, and I remember at that
time when some Members on this side of
the House opposed that Bill very strongly
we did not receive any help or support from the hon. and gallant Member for Clifton or the hon. and learned
Member for Willowfield. If the bigger
question has to be fought we country
Members will fight it when we are faced
with it, but this, it strikes me, is only
the smaller question and only deals with
a short period.
The hon. and learned Member (Mr.
Black) who has just sat down asked why
Belfast should be treated differently from
other parts of the Six Counties. The
answer must have been obvious to him when
he put the question. There is more trouble
in Belfast, there is more danger in Belfast, there is more lawlessness in Belfast
than there is in other parts of the Six
Counties, and, therefore, it is necessary
for the Government to keep a strong
police force in the city. And may I say
that I agree thoroughly with the hon.
and learned Member that the force should
be a centralised force. If we are to follow
the step-by-step policy, which has been so
highly praised by some Members on this
side of the House, then of course we will
find ourselves in a very different position,
because, as the hon. Member for South
Derry (Mrs. Parker) has pointed out, in
England the local ratepayers have to pay
fifty per cent. of the cost of the police
force as they have to pay fifty per cent.
of the education rate. Probably that is
the direction in which Ministers are
moving.
But this small question cannot be taken
by itself, and if the City of Belfast is
getting an extra police force surely it is
as well able to pay for it as any other
part of the Six Counties. The hon. and
learned Member for Willowfield (Mr.
Black) in an optimistic mood, says, and
I hope it will be justified, that trade is
improving and that there will be more
revenue coming into my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance. I hope that
will be so, but if it is so the first place
that the reaction will be felt will be in
Belfast itself, and I think Belfast, on the
whole, is better able to pay than the
other parts of the Six Counties.
But we can narrow this issue down to a
very small point indeed, and that is that
there are a certain number of extra police
required in the City of Belfast and somebody has to pay for them. Who is going

that
(Mr. Murphy) has dealt with
matter. He has pointed out to the
House that this is not a new matter.
This is not a new principle that has been
invented for the first time by the hardhearted Government of Northern Ireland.
It is a matter which goes back a great
many years. It goes back to the foundation, to the beginning, of the Royal Irish
Constabulary. We had, as hon. Members are aware, prior to 1921, a quota
system, by which the country as a whole
was assessed as to how many police it
required upon the basis of population.
My hon. and learned Friend, the Member for Willowfield (Mr. Black) objects to
that principle, but I think hon. Members
of this House will agree that that
principle is sound, especially when I call
attention to one or two other matters connected with the City of Belfast, which
will show that this is the only basis upon
which the quota could be calculated.
Prior to 1921 the payments for the Royal
Irish Constabulary in Belfast varied
between £27,000 in 1914 and 1915, and
£40,000 per annum in 1919 and 1920,
and then they fluctuated and down
for the first few years of the life of this
Parliament, when the police were very
much under strength, not only in
Belfast but in the whole of the Six
Counties.
up
Eventually the Corporation were liable
in 1928 upon the quota system for a payment of somewhere about £40,000 or
£42,000 a year. They had paid, by
agreement with the Government, a sum
of £66,000 in respect of Special Constabulary employed during the years 1922
and 1925, when the Royal Ulster Constabulary were under strength, and it
was necessary to enrol Special Constabulary to ensure the peace of the city.
Therefore, in order to put this matter
upon a proper footing, my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
held an inquiry, and this sum of £25,000
was agreed upon, and it became law until
March, 1933. This Bill is merely to
extend that period for another 12 months
in order that the matter may be again
reconsidered.
In England, as my hon. and learned
Friend, the Member for Willowfield, has
said, payment for the police in all the big
cities is made upon the basis of half and
half-half by the Imperial Government
and half by the local authority-and if
there is any argument to be derived from
the question of control, the system in
England is against the argument of the
hon. and learned Member for Willowfield,
because although the Imperial Government pay half the cost of the police in
England the police are controlled by the
local authority. Here, although a payment is made by the Belfast Corporation
towards the cost of the police they are
controlled by the central authority and
by the Government, so that that is not a
matter of principle.
The matter to be determined as a
matter of principle is where the incidence
of payment is to fall. In England,
though it is not really material to this
argument, I think some Members of this
House may be interested to know that,
taking cities like Bristol, Leeds and
Sheffield, the rate for police worked out
between 11d and ls ld in the £. In
Belfast the amount in rates that this
£25,000 charge represents is only 3d in
the £, so that, as compared with other
cities, comparable in importance and
comparable in population and in size,
Belfast is very much better off than
similar cities across the water.
Let me take it another way. If Belfast
were to pay upon the basis upon which
the English cities pay for their police
force the amount to be paid by the
Corporation would be approximately
£140,000 a year, or 1s 7d in the £,
whereas in fact they pay only 34d in the
£. The total amount that the Corporation pay represents only 9 per cent. of
the total cost of the police in the City of
Belfast. On the question of principle as

to whether Belfast should carry any part

There has always been a payment made

capital city, a large proportion of the
business of the community is transacted in
the city. It has in close proximity or
within its borders these Parliament
Buildings; it has all the staff of the Government itself, the law courts, and all
the staff connected with the law, and it
reaps, by reason of its position as a capital
city, many advantages which are denied
to other areas whether they be urban er
rural. Consequently Belfast requires a
larger force of police than the ordinary
urban or rural area.
The normal number of police that
would be required for Belfast, as has been
stated in the House this afternoon, is, I
think, in or about 950 men. That is the
quota that Belfast would be entitled to
if it were on the same footing as the
rest of the country, whereas in fact the
strength that is necessary to maintain
order and discipline in the city is 1,200
men. If over and above its proportion
the City of Belfast would pay for all the
extra men that are required, namely,
250 men, the charge would be somewhere between £60,000 and £70,000 per
annum; and as there has been some misconception about this, it should be noted
that the charge which has been made in
respect of these extra men upon the City
of Belfast takes no account of extra men
that are required in an emergency.
When police are drafted into the city
under the present system to deal with disturbances which require in some cases a
great number of men and, consequently,
greatly added expense-the cost is borne
by this Government and not by the City
of Belfast. I should have thought that
under this arrangement the members of
the Corporation of Belfast-I quite agree
that they are trying to treat this as a

to liquidate all their liabilities for police,

all
those liabilities for £25,000 was
not at all a bad stroke of business upon

It really comes to this, that if Belfast
does not contribute to the cost of the
additional police force in Belfast, in fact
that extra cost must be thrown upon the
rest of the country. It is said that that
may be a sound principle. It may be
sound from the point of view of Belfast,
but I doubt if the Members for the other
areas would consider it sound. Therefore, it is a question of principle that
has to be determined, and what the Government has had to do is not to place a
burden upon any one area or another,
but to try to ascertain as nearly as possible what is an equitable arrangement
with reference to the police. That was
ascertained by this agreement which fixed
the charge at £25,000. This matter will
be considered again. I need not labour it
any further. But I could not, on behalf

that in future they will escape from all

Mr. McNEILL: It is incumbent upon us
to find revenue. We can only find
revenue in Northern Ireland in two ways
having regard to the particular limitations
imposed by the Act of 1920. The first
way is by economies. That method was
attempted some years ago.
I believe it
was a perfectly genuine attempt. I have
never been a wholehearted supporter of
this economy campaign, because no matter
how much we succeed in saving supposing
we were to save to the extent of £40,000
or £50,000 a year without impairing our
Civil Service, that sum, having regard
to our great social commitments at the
present time, would really be of very little.
effect. We cannot save to any considerable or effective extent, that is from an
economic point of view, and the only
alternative then which faces the Minister
is the imposition of taxation. I, for one,
would be very loath to be a member of
any Government in this House that would
suggest the imposition of taxation upon
the people of Northern Ireland. What
would be the effect of such taxation?
The effect of any taxation in respect of
our transferred services would be to
render the citizen of Northern Ireland
more highly taxed than his fellow citizen
in Great Britain.
At the present time, as hon. Members
are aware, the great bulk of taxation is
both imposed and collected by the Imperial Parliament, and the small amount
of taxation which we have inflicted upon
the community is only about one-eighth
of the total, and those two sources of
taxation in Northern Ireland bring upon
a citizen of Northern Ireland the same
incidence as there is upon a citizen of
Great Britain, so that I apprehend that
it is only in the last resort that this House
can fall back upon additional taxation.
Therefore, on the whole, I commend the
Minister of Finance for having introduced
this Bill. He has averted taxation for
another year.
He and the Members of
the Government are banking on the idea
that trade is going to improve and that
in a few years we shall be back into what
was regarded in the past as normal ways
of going. I hope that these anticipations
of the Minister and the Members of the
Government will be realised. I, myself,
have no such optimistic view with regard
to the future.
I believe the situation in which we find
ourselves to-day, and in which other
countries also find themselves, is one
really without parallel, and if we look
back through history we will find no precedent for the like, but as I say, I may
be wrong and the Minister may be right.
If he is right and if trade will improve
then his present expedient is a necessary
and useful one for avoiding taxation. If,
on the other hand, trade does not improve
then this present Measure will only
accelerate the economic downfall of this
Government, and similar Governments
throughout the world.

Mr. POLLOCK: With the leave of the

and questions that have been submitted

hon. Members did not appear to realise
the desperate financial conditions that
have obtained in every country in the
world, Britain included. The last two
Chancellors of the Exchequer, in order to
balance their Budgets, have had to resort
to expedients of a very extraordinary
character the utilisation of capital
moneys to meet current expenditure. That
is certainly very wrong finance if it can
be avoided.
What did Mr. Chamberlain do this year
in order to balance his Budget for the
year 1933-34 ? He had no hesitation
whatever in taking money from any fund
that he could lay his hands upon because
his revenue from income-tax alone was
down by 12 millions. Our revenue from
income-tax, customs and excise, and other
matters fell in one year by over one million
pounds. The question then arose, how
was the gap created by that one million
to be bridged this year? That was no
fault of the Ministry of Finance.
It was
no fault of the Government. It was
something that was inevitable. The
people of Ulster were not taking enough
whisky to provide us with the money.
They were not taking certain foodstuffs
and other commodities, and the result was
we were £250,000 to the bad. Then,
again, the question arose, how in the year
1933-34 was the gap created by that estimated loss to be bridged?

so far as any terminable resources of the

Order for Second Reading read.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This
Bill continues temporarily certain enactments, some of them enactments of the
Parliament of the United Kingdom and
some of this Parliament, which may be
regarded as liable to revision. There is
only one date fixed for their continuation,
and that is 31st December, 1934. The
Bill is framed so as to fit in with the
corresponding Bill of the Imperial Parliament which applies to Northern Ireland
in so far as it deals with any enactments
relating to subjects with respect to which
our Parliament has no power to legislate.
Hon. Members will see what these
Measures are. The first one is the Glebe
Loan Act of 1870. There have been two
loans under that Act in recent years. The
Courts (Emergency Powers) Act continues a War provision which has not yet
expired, and the Statutory Undertakings
(Temporary Increase of Charges) Act is a
necessity for canal and other companies,
and the same applies to the Harbours,
Docks, and Piers Act. The other two
Acts in Part 1 are the employment (Relief
Works) Act, and the Employment of
Women, Young Persons, and Children
Act. In Part II are the Local Government (Emergency Powers) Act, under
which the Minister has power to supersede local bodies if he thinks they have
not carried out their Statutory duties,
and the Canals (Continuance of Charging
Powers) Act, which is a matter of not
very much importance, but which has the
effect of continuing the right of these companies to make charges in respect of their
undertakings which derive validity under
the Road Transport Act. I do not think
hon. Members will find anything controversial in this Measure. I beg to move.

R.U.C. BOXING TOURNAMENT.
9. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he is aware that the
sanction of a body in Dublin, with Mr.
Frank Aiken, Free State War Minister,
as Patron; General W. R. E. Murphy,
Civic Guard Assistant Commissioner, as
President; Colonel M'Kenna, Free
State Army, as Vice-President; and a
committee composed largely of Civic
Guard and Free State Army Officers,
and without a representative from Northern Ireland is required to hold a boxing tournament for the R.U.C. in Belfast,
and if such an arrangement is in accord
with the dignity of the force maintained
by the Northern Government.
are
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): All boxing tournaments organised by the R.U.C.
carried on under the jurisdiction of the
Ulster Provincial Council of Amateur
Boxing a body which is composed of a
representative of each affiliated club in
Ulster, and which has authority to
approve of all such tournaments without
any reference to the Dublin organisation
referred to by the hon. Member. Permission for the R.U.C. tournament which
is to be held on the 13th instant was
granted by the Ulster Council at their
meeting on the 21st ultimo.
Mr. GRANT: Will the right hon.
Gentleman inform the House whether had
this body mentioned in the question refused permission for the boxing tournament there would have been no boxing
tournament?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid I am
unable to answer my hon. Friend, because,
I understand with regard to boxing, like
all other sports, it has to be held under
some recognised organisation.
For my
own part, I do not understand why
Ulster cannot have its own organisation
without reference to Dublin. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
LIABILITY OF GUARDIANS FOR
DESTITUTE PERSONS.
10. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state the liability of boards of
guardians as regards destitute persons
coming into Northern Ireland, and their
powers for transferring destitute persons
to their country of origin or domicile,
what are their powers of dealing with
persons whose domicile is the Irish Free
State, but who are at present in Northern Ireland, and who are a charge on the
Unemployment Fund and other means of
benefit from public funds; and whether
he will introduce legislation where necessary to deal with the manifestly unfair.
burden upon ratepayers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: For some
time past I have been causing careful
inquiries to be made throughout the
various unions in Northern Ireland regarding the problem which is apparently
exercising the mind of the hon. and
gallant Member who has put down this
question, and I am glad to be able to
report that from the reports received
from time to time from our inspector,
the situation is not one to cause any real
concern.
The hon. and gallant Member may
rest assured that if at any time it is
found that an unfair burden on the ratepayers of Northern Ireland was being
caused by reason of having to provide
poor relief for persons who are not residents of Northern Ireland, I will bring
the matter before the House with the
object of securing additional powers for
dealing with the situation.
Major MCCORMICK: Will the Minister of Home Affairs not say now that
there is an unfair burden on the taxpayers?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I am
not prepared to say that.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
SPECIAL POWERS OF MINISTER
OF HOME AFFAIRS.
11. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the murder of a police constable
by gunmen in Belfast, he will put into
force his powers under the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act, to
deport all known members of the Irish
Republican Army, and all such persons
known to the police authorities as being
sympathisers with that or other disloyal
bodies.
The following question also stood upon
the Order Paper:-
12. Major McCORMICK: To ask
the Minister of Home Affairs whether,
owing to the destruction of property and
grave loss of life caused by disaffected
persons consequent on the setting up of
this Government he will debar by regulation such persons, and all other persons suspected of having designs against
the laws of this area, from entering
Northern Ireland; and whether he will,
if necessary, apply to Parliament for
more drastic and immediate steps to cope
with this menace to authority.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the
permission of the hon. and gallant Member, I propose to answer questions Nos.
11 and 12 together.
The hon. and gallant Member may
rest assured that the Government are
using and will utilise the powers conferred by Parliament under the Civil
Authorities Act with the object of maintaining law and order.
I can also assure the hon. and gallant
Member that if it is found that the
powers which have already been vested
in the Government in this respect are
not sufficient I will have no hesitation in
coming to this House and asking for
further powers, and I feel sure that if
it is necessary to adopt such a course I
will receive the fullest possible support
from all the Members of the House who
realise the necessity for the preservation
of peace in our Province.
TOLL BRIDGE LABOURER'S
HOUSE.
13. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
a female farm worker resides at a place
called Toll Bridge, in Ballymoney Rural
District, in a house where the only light
admitted is by an open door, there being
no windows in the house, and where the
smoke goes out through the open door,
there being no chimney in the house;
that there is no empty cottage in the
district to which this labourer could be
transferred; and if he has arranged to
remove the suspension of the Improvement Scheme of Ballymoney Rural District Council, so that sanitary cottages
may be erected for the accommodation of
labourers who reside in such places.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon.
Member will furnish me with more precise particulars of the case referred to,
I shall have inquiries made.
With regard to the second part of the
question, this matter is covered by my
reply to question No. 7. I do not think
that has yet been answered.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Minister if I supply him with a full
list of unsanitary dwellings in Ballymoney Rural District, after having
viewed the dwellings will he be prepared
to remove the suspension on the building
of labourers' cottages.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not prepared to say I can alter the policy
already adopted by the Government, that
is, the suspension of the provision of further labourers' cottages in the country.
At the same time, if my hon. Friend
supplies me with cases of unsanitary
dwellings I will look into the matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: I ask whether he is
prepared to review Hansard of June this
year when I presented to this House a
full list of unsanitary dwellings in this
district.

3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he is aware that the
late Commissioners of National Education sent a circular to all their senior
inspectors asking them to do what they
could to discover if the statement made
by so many authors that many managers
sell school appointments to the highest
bidders was correct; and whether the
Ministry of Education has done the same,

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

the nature referred to by the hon. Member, although it is possible that such a

long time before the transfer of services
to this Ministry. The answer to the last
part of the question is in the negative.

REPAIRS TO BALLYMONEY
WORKHOUSE HOSPITAL.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
the total amount of money the present
Clerk of Ballymoney Union expended,
out of the rates, on repairs and improvements of the premises lately used as a
workhouse, and on the premises which
serves as a hospital, accommodation of
the Rural District Council and Board of
Guardians, without consulting the
Council or Board, or obtaining their
authority; whether any advertisement
was issued for tenders; and whether the
Ministry approves of this.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The minutes
of the meetings of the Ballymoney Board
of Guardians do not obtain any reference
to such an occurrence as is suggested in
the question, and the Ministry has no
information that it has taken place.
Speaking as a general rule, I can
assure the hon. Member that the Ministry would not regard with approval any
such action on the part of any officer of
a local authority unless, of course, there
were urgent reasons for carrying out repairs or improvements and that owing to
the urgency it would not be possible for
the officer concerned to obtain the prior
approval of his local authority.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister prepared to send his inspector to this place
to obtain first-hand information of the
charge contained in this question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am quite
prepared to send an inspector if the hon.
Member can give me particulars which
the inspector can go into and verify.
HOUSING OF RURAL LABOURERS.
7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
what rural district councils were engaged
in formulating improvement schemes when
the order for suspending the erection of
labourers' cottages was issued; whether
he is aware that the houses which these
councils proposed to supersede by sanitary
cottages are, as a rule, utterly unsanitary;
and what steps he proposed to take with
the object of having the unfortunate
occupiers of these unsanitary houses transferred to houses where health and comfort
are possible.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard
to the first part of the question, I would
refer the hon. Member to the answer
given to a similar question on the 12th
May 1932, of which I am sending him a
copy.
As the hon. Member is aware, it
became necessary, owing to the serious
financial situation some little time ago, to
suspend operations under the Labourers'
Acts and to concentrate on the Housing
Acts, which now apply to rural as well
as to urban districts in Northern Ireland.
It is a fact that in the various rural
centres in Northern Ireland there are a
considerable number of small cottages in
Occupation which do not conform to
modern sanitary standards, and I can
assure the hon. Member that if, and when
the financial situation permits, I will take
into consideration the resumption of
building operations by rural district
councils in Northern Ireland under the
Labourers' Acts, but, for the present at
any rate, I can only express the hope that
Oral Answers
Bills Presented
12 OCTOBER 1933
the rural district councils will make full
use of the powers which are being
accorded to them in the Housing Bill at
present before Parliament, and which, if
availed of, should, to a considerable
extent, meet the situation.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister prepared to say that finance is of more
importance than the health of the
residents who are compelled to live in
these unsanitary dwellings, and is he prepared to give an extended loan for the
provision of houses required in this
district?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think
that rises out of my answer to the
question. So far as the Government is
concerned it is willing to do everything
possible to improve housing in Northern
Ireland. I have already pointed out that
if the rural district council concerned had
availed themselves of the Housing Acts
which were passed some time ago the
situation would not be as bad as it is
to-day.

Section eight of the Act of 1929 shall
have effect subject to the following
amendments:-
(a) The following proviso shall be
added to sub-section (2):-
"Provided that, where additional
land is required for the purposes
of the scheme and it is not proposed to acquire such land compulsorily, the Ministry may,
instead of acquiring such land by
means of a supplemental scheme,
acquire it by agreement."
(b) after sub-section (3) the following
new sub-section shall be added:-
"(4) If it is found in the case of any
land proposed to be acquired by
the scheme that a portion only of
such land is required for the purposes of the scheme, the Ministry
may, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed, enter
into an agreement with the person
from whom it was proposed to
acquire such land, for the acquisition of such portion only as is
required for the purposes of the
scheme, and upon the execution
of such agreement the remainder
of such land shall cease to be
subject to the provisions of the
scheme."

Mr. POLLOCK: Hon. Members will
recall that, in moving the Ways and
Means Resolution, which was the necessary preliminary to the introduction of
this Bill, I gave the Committee a brief
explanation of each of the five matters
with which the Bill deals. It will, therefore, be difficult for me, if I am to refer
to these matters again, to avoid a certain
amount of repetition, especially as the
proposals in the Bill are comparatively
simple and free from complications, but
I will refresh the memories of those who,
perhaps, may have overlooked what I
explained on the Money Resolution.
Three of these deal with stamp duty. The
first effects a reduction from £1 to 10s
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
12 OCTOBER 1933
in the ad valorem duty payable, on registration, by companies and limited partnerships. This reduction is, I submit,
necessary in view of a corresponding reduction having been made in Great
Britain. If the British rates were to be
lower than ours many Northern Ireland
companies might register in Great Britain
instead of in Northern Ireland, thus entailing a considerable loss to our revenue.
The provision in the Bill is retrospective,
since during the course of the discussion
following upon my Budget statement
last May I gave an undertaking that
legislation on these lines would be introduced in the Autumn with retrospective
effect.
The second proposal relates to an agreement entered into by His Majesty's
Government at an International Conference held at Geneva in June, 1930. Under
this agreement the contracting parties
undertook to alter the laws in their respective countries so that the vàlidity of
obligations arising out of bills of exchange
or the exercise of the rights that flow
therefrom should not be subordinated to
the observance of the provisions in force
concerning stamp duty. In other words,
the effect of the proposed provision will
be that bills of exchange presented for
acceptance, accepted or payable outside
the United Kingdom will not be invalid.
by reason only of their not being properly
stamped in accordance with the law relating to stamp duty in Northern Ireland.
The object of the International Agreement is to remedy the feeling of insecurity
felt by holders of international bills of
exchange by reason of the fact that such
bills, owing to their non-compliance with
the stamp laws of the country in which
they ought to have been stamped, may,
without the holder being aware of the
fact, be invalid, and therefore unenforceable and valueless. It is hoped that the new
arrangement will be of considerable value
to the commercial community, since it
will render less risky the international
circulation of commercial instruments.
now come to Clause 3. Under the
existing law it is provided that certain
documents used in connection with local
government are exempt from stamp duty.
Since the exemption was first introduced,
nearly a century ago, many radical
changes have taken place in our system of
local government administration, with
the result that the original provisions relating to exemption are quite out of keeping with the conditions now in existence.
The present position is extremely chaotic
and it is sometimes very difficult to ascertain whether a particular document
does or does not come within the terms
of the exemption. The only methods of
remedying this state of affairs would be
either to extend the exemption to all local
government documents or else to abolish
the exemption altogether. I am satisfied
that the latter is the proper course to
adopt, especially as, even under the existing
law, local authorities in Northern Ireland
are in a much more privileged position
than those in Great Britain. Hon. Members
will agree that there is no sound reason
why local authorities should be exempt
from the payment of these duties, which
is, of course, obligatory on all other persons in the State.
Clause 4, like Clause 1, deals with a
remission of duty. It has become the
practice for the organisers of certain
agricultural shows to include in their
programme items not strictly germane to
an agricultural show, but rather designed to attract the general public, and
thus to interest them in the show as a
whole. Such efforts on the part of the
promoters are, I think, praiseworthy,
not only because, as I have said, they
increase the public interest in the shows,
but also because they augment the funds
of the societies responsible for their
organisation. At present the inclusion
of such items as I have mentioned
renders a show liable to Entertainments
Duty. The object of this Clause is to
remit duty in such cases subject to the
consent of the Ministry of Finance.
Clause 5 is rather a technical matter.
It exempts from death duties securities
issued by the Treasury so long as such
securities are in the beneficial ownership
of persons who are neither domiciled nor
ordinarily resident in the United Kingdom. Similar legislation was passed in
Great Britain in 1931 in regard both to
income-tax and British Death Duties, and
we have been asked by the Imperial
Authorities to grant similar exemption
from duties under the control of this
Parliament. The object of this Clause
is to provide for such exemption, so that
in issuing securities it may be possible
for the Treasury to state that they are
exempt from all United Kingdom taxation without having to make any special
exception in regard to Northern Ireland
taxation. I beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DISTRESS RELIEF WORK-
MR. R. TORBITT, BELFAST.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the claim for distress relief work by Mr. Robert Torbitt,
57 James Street, Belfast, has been rejected; whether this man has no means
to maintain his wife and family; and
whether the Minister will take steps to
see that these respectable destitute people
get some maintenance.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have no jurisdiction to question the discretion or to interfere with the action of the Belfast Board
of Guardians in connection with individual
claims for outdoor relief.
At the same time, I have caused inquiries to be made into the case referred
to in the question, and understand that
the claim was rejected after the most
detailed inquiries and investigations by
the Guardians' officers, who were
apparently of opinion that there was no
sign of distress or poverty in this particular case, and that the applicant could,
if he exerted himself at his trade of
tailoring, earn sufficient to keep himself
and family.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
relief is administered by an officer who
does, or at least did, belong to the Ministry of Home Affairs?
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is an
officer who is lent by the Ministry to the
Board of Guardians, and for the time
being that officer becomes a servant of the
Board of Guardians.
DUNDONALD SEWERAGE SCHEME.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
on what date work is to be commenced
on the Dundonald Sewerage Scheme.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that the plans for the extension of the
sewerage scheme referred to by the hon.
Member will come before the Castlereagh Rural District Council for approval
early in November, after which immediate
steps will be taken for the ratification of
the plans and for the issue of and the
acceptance of tenders.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would ask the
Minister whether he is prepared to impress upon these local authorities the
immediate needs of the people in this
locality in regard to work owing to the
distress that now exists.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly.
This is a matter of negotiation between
the Belfast Corporation and the Rural
District Council concerned. I have done
all I can to have the matter cleared up.
INTOXICATING LIQUOR ACT,
1923-SUNDAY OPENING.
3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
consider the advisability of amending the
1923 Intoxicating Liquor Act with a view
to stimulating the tourist traffic throughout Northern Ireland, especially with regard to prescribed hours of opening on
Sundays.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In reply to the
hon. and gallant Member's question, I
can only repeat the statements which
have already been made on several
occasions by my right hon. Friend, the
Prime Minister, to the effect that it is
not intended to introduce any further
legislation dealing with the Intoxicating
Liquor Acts.

CLAUSE 5 (Maintenance of watercourses and power of county council to
execute work).
(1) It shall be the duty of the
occupier of any agricultural lands on
or through which a watercourse runs
or of which a watercourse forms a
boundary to scour out and cleanse so
much of the watercourse as runs on or
through or bounds the lands occupied
by him and to maintain it in such a
condition that the proper flow of the
water is not obstructed:
Provided that, where a watercourse
forms a boundary between agricultural
lands in the occupation of different
persons, the liability of each person to
scour out, cleanse and maintain the
watercourse shall extend only to the
centre of the watercourse measured
from the boundary of the said land.
For the purposes of this section the
expression "scour out and cleanse"
shall be deemed to include the cutting,
topping or removal of any bush, shrub
or tree causing or likely to cause, or
contributing to the causing of, an
(6
obstruction to the proper flow of any
watercourse, the expression agricultural lands" shall include turf bog,
and the expression "watercourse" shall
not include so much of any rivers as
may be prescribed by the Ministry of
Home Affairs after consultation with
the Ministry.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Crawford]
This harmless looking Clause 3 proposes
to repeal that enactment and all contracts to be entered into by the various
public bodies throughout Northern Ireland will be subject to stamp duty in
future. So far as I can make out about
4,000 contracts will be entered intothis is a guess, but I think I am pretty
near it and even if a sixpence for Stamp
Duty were placed on each document it
would mean at least £100 a year being
placed upon the ratepayers, and, consequently the Exchequer would be freed
from the expense.
The County Treasurers Act, 1838, is to
be repealed. That Act exempted payment of Stamp Duty by county councils,
rural district councils, boards of
guardians, education authorities and such
people. That Act is going to be
repealed, and the bodies I have mentioned
have to put a stamp on each of the paying orders they issue. I calculate that
there will be at least 100,000 of these
orders issued in the Six Counties, and the
Stamp Duty on these will mean at least
£1,000 or £1,800 a year which is going
to be placed upon the already overburdened ratepayers. The Poor Relief
Act, 1838, exempted all poor rates from
Stamp Duty, and this Bill proposes to
repeal that and make the poor rate liable
to Stamp Duty. I have only to point
out to Members of this Committee who
have experience in this matter that this
will give a tremendous lot of trouble to
the various county councils and other
authorities. They will have to segregate
the items over £2 to discover how many
people are liable for the Stamp Duty.
The rate collectors will be bound to order
the stamps and the various bodies will
have to make a refund to the rate collectors. These bodies will have to provide
additional staff to do this work.
The privileges granted to us by Parliament a hundred years ago are being
gradually filched from us, and we are
bearing the name of freedom at the end
of a heavy chain. Everyone of these
Measures is for the purpose of saving the
Exchequer and putting the burden on
the ratepayers. The rate-collectors'
bonds were free from Stamp Duty in the
past, but in future the cost of the Stamp
Duty on these bonds will be a charge on
the rates. If collectors are unfortunate
enough not to be able to get a guarantee
insurance society to undertake the risk
they will have extra expense to meet.
There was freedom from Stamp Duty
under the Dispensary Houses Act, 1879,
but it is now proposed to repeal that and
make all these buildings liable to duty
in the time to come. I do not think that
will be so heavy a burden, as there are
not many dispensary houses being built,
but it will be part of a burden.
In
The Labourers Act, 1906, is going to
be repealed too, and this is a serious
thing. We will, in future have to find
stamps for all the various contracts and
arrangements in order to build labourers'
cottages. These are at present free from
duty. The nearest approach I can make
is that this change will cost the ratepayers £4,000 a year. The Exchequer
will be freed from that and it will be put
on the ratepayers. I protest against this
in the strongest possible manner.
addition, too, I want to say that the
Association of County Councils was
promised many months ago that before
any Measure would be brought into the
House affecting their interests they would
be consulted on the matter. That
promise was made definitely and decidedly
and so far as I can learn it has not been
carried out. There was no consultation
in regard to taking money from the Road
Fund or in regard to this Bill. If I am
wrong in that I will apologise.
I would like to say that the time has
come when this sort of thing must be
put a stop to. Again and again, without our knowing much about them, we
have passed Measures in this House which
have enabled the Chancellor to free himself from many liabilities, and the burden has been thrown on the ratepayers,
who cannot bear any more burdens.
They are loyal to the Government and
SO am I. They want no change of
Government, but in their interests and
in the interests of the Province, I beseech
the Government to put a stop to this
sort of thing. The Government are
gradually easing themselves of the burden they ought to bear. I do not want
to move the deletion of the Clause,
although I feel I ought to do it, but I

this Clause. In other words, it is in

I am put in a very delicate position
in my relations with the British Government over matters of this sort when I am
faced with the fact that we here claim
British citizenship, that we have agreed
that we should accept all the burdens of
British citizenship, having regard to all
the advantages that accrue from that, and
also having regard to the fact that at the
present time every penny of the revenue
that is received here-or of the burdens,
if you wish, that are imposed upon our
people is spent in Northern Ireland and
that we are not paying one penny for all
the protection we receive by reason of
the existence of the British Army in our
midst and of the Navy protecting our
shores. In view of the fact that we have
all that protection without contributing
one penny towards it the consideration of
matters such as I have mentioned becomes
all the more imperative. If you and I
have to impose a receipt stamp when we
receive money, why should local authorities necessarily be put in any invidious
position because they must do the same?
In other words, the law should be harmonious and should apply universally,
and that is the intention. It is not that
there is so much money involved in this.
It may be £4,000 or it may be less. I

it is a very small thing, and it tends to

arrangements in regard to all citizens and
all institutions in the community. Those,
shortly, are the reasons that necessitated
the introduction of this Clause. It is
mainly based, however, on the fact that
I cannot answer any claim or charge that

Housing Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill is
introduced to implement the promise
made in the House on the 8th June last.
Having regard to the fact that it is now
over ten years since the first Housing Act
was passed by this House, during which
period some 26,000 houses have been
built and a sum of over 21 millions has
been spent by the Government in subsidising building, it might be expected that
there was no need for further legislation.
But it is within the knowledge of everyone that the housing shortage is still a
long way from being met, and that
people belonging to the working class still
find the greatest difficulty in getting a
house at a rent which is within their
means. In this connection it must be
remembered that we have not only to.
meet the shortage which came about
during the war, and the increase of
population, but a number of new houses
are required annually to replace houses.
falling into disuse, and at present the
cost of building is still too high for
working-class houses to be erected at a
profit without assistance.
I have before me a return relating to
empty houses made to the Belfast Corporation on the 20th February last, from
which it appears that on that date the
total number of vacant houses in the city
was 937, but of these only 143 were
houses with a valuation of £8 or under.
Moreover, this number was less than the
number of similar houses vacant on the
date of the previous return, which showed
166 houses.
This is a very small margin in view of
the large working-class population of the
city. The question of unemploment is
an important factor. For every reason,
therefore, it is highly desirable that some
method should be found of giving a
stimulus to the building trade.
The Government hoped that the subsidy
of £25 per house, provided under the
Housing Act of 1932, might have been
found sufficient, and quite possibly it
would have been had the local authorities recognised their responsibility and
exercised their power of giving a similar
grant. Unfortunately, few of these
authorities, and included among them
the Belfast Corporation, saw fit to give
any assistance additional to the Government subsidy, and consequently operations under the Act of 1932 have been
disappointing.
Mr. HENDERSON: They ceased.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The extent of
the falling off may be seen from these
figures:-During the year ended 31st
March, 1931, when the subsidy was £100,
the number of houses approved for
erection was 4,083 and the number completed 5,160. During the year ended
31st March, 1932, when the subsidy was
£50, the number approved for erection
was 1,472, and the number completed
2,596. During the year ended 31st
March, 1933, when the subsidy was £25,
the number of houses approved for
erection was only 240, and the number
completed 50.
There has been a slight improvement
during the current year, the number of
houses approved for erection from the 1st
April to the end of September being 306,
and the number completed 138; but it is
necessary that building should be
accelerated to a much greater extent than
this if it is to meet the needs of the
people.
Suggestions for meeting the situation.
have been made to the Government from
various quarters, some requesting an
increase in the rate of the Government
subsidy, and others advocating the
advancing of money at a cheap rate or
the guaranteeing of loans to builders.
In view of the general financial situation, the Government is unable to
consider any increase in the amount of
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
the subsidy given by it. It considers,
also, that it has given more than its
share of assistance and that it devolves
upon the local authorities to shoulder
their responsibility in the matter and
supplement the aid given by the Government.
Accordingly in the Bill it is proposed
to continue the Government subsidy of
£25 per house for a further period of
two years, i.e., to 1936, but only on
condition that the local authority makes
a grant of a similar amount, or gives
an exemption from rates for a period of
10 years.
The Government has given careful
consideration to the other proposals submitted, and has included in the Bill
provisions enabling local authorities to
advance money, subject to certain safeguards, to persons or bodies of persons
building houses of the type which qualify
for Government subsidy. The money
may be advanced by the local authority
at the ordinary rate of interest, in which
case the builder will be eligible to receive subsidies paid by the Government
and the local authority, or it may be
advanced at a rate of interest of 2 per
cent. under the rate at which the local
authority is able to borrow, and in this
case the persons receiving the advance will
not be entitled to receive any Government subsidy or supplemental grant from
the local authority. The Government
will recoup to the local authority the
per cent. which they allow to the
borrower.
There is also included in the Bill a
provision enabling local authorities to
guarantee loans advanced by any company or other body of persons approved
by the Ministry to persons for the purpose of enabling them to build houses of
the prescribed type. The guarantee may
extend to not more than two-thirds of
the difference between 70 per cent. of the
value of the building, which is the
amount usually advanced by these bodies,
and 90 per cent. of the value, and the
Government will recoup to the local
authority half of any loss for which it
may become liable under the two-thirds
guarantee. In other words, the lending
society, the local authority, and the Government share equally the risk of any
in respect of 20 per cent. of the loan.

I beg to move.

Conduct of School Inspector.
Mr. McNEILL: I beg to move.
"That in the opinion of this House
the Ministry of Education should direct
an Inquiry forthwith into the complaints
preferred by Mr. Patrick Burns, assistant
teacher, Star of the Sea Boys' P.E.
School, against Mr. S. Kirkpatrick, one
of the Ministry's inspectors.'
""
In rising to propose the Motion that is
down in my name I may say for the benefit of the House that it is a most invidious task for me to have to perform,
but I strongly feel that in this particular
case
an injustice has been done by an
inspector of the Ministry to a member of
the teaching profession, and I am fortified by the thought that the teacher is
not alone and that he has behind him a
powerful organisation, the Irish National
Teachers' Organisation
The facts have already been set before
Members on both sides of the House. I
understand that hon. Members have been
furnished by the teachers' body with a
copy of the correspondence between Mr.
Burns and the Ministry and between the
Irish National Teachers' Organisation and
2351 School Inspector's Conduct HOUSE OF COMMONS
School Inspector's Conduct 2352
[Mr. McNeill]
the Ministry. Hon. Members, if they
have read the correspondence, as I am
sure they have, will agree that there
is a prima facie case against Mr. Kirkpatrick, the Ministry's inspector. They
will remember that this Star of the Sea
School, to which Mr. Burns belongs, was
inspected on the 17th and 18th November
of last year. It was inspected by Mr.
Kirkpatrick in the course of his annual
inspection. As a result of that annual
inspection, just two or three days afterwards, Mr. Burns, who felt himself
aggrieved by the manner in which Mr.
Kirkpatrick conducted that inspection,
wrote to the Ministry asking that he be
allowed an official inquiry. That official
inquiry has been refused.
In his letter to the Ministry Mr.
Burns gave the reasons why he asked for
the official inquiry. Those reasons may
appear to some hon. Members of this
House to be somewhat insignificant when
you regard them one by one, but when
you take their cumulative effect and when
you see that the principal reason is a
charge of discourtesy against Mr. Kirkpatrick, discourtesy not merely towards
Mr. Burns, but towards the children
attending the school of which Mr. Burns
is the teacher, then I think hon. Members will agree that the charges were substantially founded.
Now the charges are, firstly, that Mr.
Kirkpatrick, the Ministry's inspector, did
not know what was contained in the
Ministry's official programme, and that
when Mr. Burns informed him that some
of the questions which he was asking the
children were quite outside the scope of
the programme, Mr. Kirkpatrick said in
the hearing of the children, "Education
is above programmes. I do not care what
is in the programme." Assuming for
one minute that Mr. Kirkpatrick made
such a statement as that publicly and in
the presence of the children I suggest to
this House that it was a very improper
statement for an inspector to make, because it conveyed the impression, not only
to Mr. Burns but to the children attending the school, that Mr. Burns was being
publicly reprimanded by one of the Ministry's inspectors.
Mr. Burns, in the same letter to which
I have referred, the letter in which he
referred his complaint to the Ministry,
says that, in addition to the inspector
behaving in this somewhat discourteous.
way, the inspector, as though to put Mr.
Burns in a somewhat unpleasant situation, proceeded in his examination of the
children to ask each of them questions
which the children were not competent
to answer because the questions were inappropriate and unfitting questions. I
do not wish to go into that in detail,
but I shall take one example which was
characteristic of the conduct of Mr. Kirkpatrick on this particular occasion.
The classes which were being examined
were Grades 3 and 4, and in the matter
of composition, or shall I say?—in the
matter of the reading test, although the
children had only been receiving instruction for some ten weeks, Mr. Kirkpatrick deliberately chose the very last
reading of the Fourth Standard Reader,
the very last page, and asked them to
read, I think it was page 187. Mr.
Burns said it was not a fair test, but I am
not complaining about that. In the matter of geography, which has now become,
as all hon. Members are aware, a very
important subject-vastly different from
the geography which hon. Members were
taught when they were at school-Mr.
Burns endeavoured to assimilate his
teaching to the rules of the Ministry,
that is he tried not to teach geography in
the old-fashioned way but to teach it in
the more humanised fashion of to-day,
bringing in the natural situation of the
country, its resources and ethnological
possibilities. The children were taught
in that fashion by Mr. Burns, according
to the Ministry's annual report, and I
have seen the Ministry's annual report
in which this practice of teaching
geography is inculcated. But Mr. Kirkpatrick, for some reason or another, asked
them individually questions which had no
bearing whatever on what Mr. Burns had
taught, that is they had no bearing whatever upon what the Ministry had determined should be taught in the schools.
I do not wish to go into the details of
instruction, but it appears to me quite
clearly from the documents which have
been submitted to me, that Mr. Kirkpatrick, feeling aggrieved, perhaps,
because he did not know the Ministry's
official programme, when his attention
was courteously drawn to that by Mr.
Burns determined to humiliate Mr. Burns
before the children attending that class,
and did humiliate Mr. Burns. And
Mr. Burns accordingly wrote to the
Ministry asking for an inquiry, as he was
perfectly entitled to do and as it was perfectly competent for him to do.

Now,
as hon. Members are aware,
under the present, and, I should say,
most deplorable system, a teacher's promotion and a teacher's increments depend
upon what are known as merit marks,
which are awarded by the inspector
annually at the annual examination of
the school. I say, by way of digression,
that that system is one which can be no
longer maintained. It is condemned
wholeheartedly in the Report of the Vice-
Regal Commission of 1913, which I have
in my hand, and which was presided over
by no less an authority on education than
the late Sir Samuel Dill, our very distinguished townsman.
The materiality
of what I have said is that in Mr. Burns's
case everything, his grading, his emoluments, his promotion, his increments,
depended upon the result of this particular inspection, and his complaint to
the Ministry is that this particular
inspection was not carried out in a way
to give him a fair chance.
Shortly after the examination was held
in this school the inspector brought in his
report, as he was entitled to do, and as a
result of his report Mr. Burns was graded
as efficient instead of highly efficient, as
he anticipated he would be entitled to be
graded. That is an ambition which I
hope animates the mind of every teacher.
Mr. Burns appealed against his grading
to a committee known as the Rating
Appeals Committee. The Rating Appeals
Committee, acting within their powers,
determined that on the facts submitted to
them in the correspondence of course
Mr. Burns was not called as a witnesshe had been graded appropriately by the
inspector on this particular occasion.

Appeals Committee has nothing to do

after the inspection, Mr. Burns says "I
am not concerned really about my grading. I demand an inquiry, no matter
whether I am graded highly efficient or

Mr. Kirkpatrick.' As I said at the

and if there is any substance in the complaint we will give you an official
inquiry." It is a most remarkable factif I am wrong in stating this I am sure
I shall be correctly informed by the

If that is the case, how can it be said

concrete case. It is a prima facie case.
If the statements of Mr. Burns are true,

should have an opportunity of giving

Mr. Burns's position is this-I wish to
make it plain-he does not wish to prejudge the case of Mr. Kirkpatrick in any
way. I am perfectly sure that if this
inquiry be held Mr. Kirkpatrick will

I do suggest that it is a proper case for

the situation. I have no doubt that they
