TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I have no
complaint whatever to make of the
manner in which this Motion has been
moved or seconded. I will suggest, perhaps, as I go on, that it is a little bit misconceived. The demand in this case is
that a public inquiry should be instituted
by the Ministry of Education into certain
allegations made by Mr. Burns against
Mr. Kirkpatrick. Before I deal with the
allegations made, may I say something
about the parties to this dispute.
Mr. Burns is 54 years of age, and he
has 35 years' service as a teacher. He is
one of a group of teachers who are called
untrained teachers. That means that he
never served a period of training in a
training college. He might be a very
good teacher notwithstanding that fact,
but it is a fact that has a bearing upon
his chance of promotion in his profession.
Under the Regulations of the Ministry an
untrained assistant is not eligible for a
post as either a principal or vice-principal
of a school unless he is rated as "highlyefficient."
When speaking on the Education Estimates in the early part of this year I was
asked by my colleague from the University to say something about our system of
inspection in Northern Ireland, and I explained that under the system in vogue
here for years, teachers, as a result of the
impression their work makes upon the
inspectors at their periodical inspections,
are placed in four classes. The highest
class is " highly efficient." Below that
is the "efficient" class; below that again
is the "fairly efficient," and at the
bottom of all is the "not efficient" class.
Unless Mr. Burns, as an untrained assistant, is in the rating of "highly
efficient," he is ineligible for promotion
to a principalship of a school.
In the early part of his career the
reports of Mr. Burns's work were such
that he would have fallen into the
"highly efficient" class. In 1922, however, at an inspection which was not
held by Mr. Kirkpatrick, but was held
by the then inspector of the school in
which Mr. Burns was an assistant, he
was rated only as "efficient." That
rating has been continued at subsequent
inspections by different inspectors since.
that time down to November, 1932, when
these matters occurred. But in the year
1931 the principalship of the school in
2361 School Inspector's Conduct
School Inspector's Conduct 2362
17 OCTOBER 1933
which Mr. Burns is employed fell vacant,
and the manager of the school put forward Mr. Burns for the vacancy. The
Ministry pointed out that under the
Regulations Mr. Burns was ineligible.
At that time Mr. Burns, with a persistence that might seem to some people
justifiable, brought pressure both personal and political upon the Ministry to
waive the Regulations in this particular
case. The Ministry refused to do so, and
I have no doubt that Mr. Burns was
correspondingly disappointed.
Mr. Kirkpatrick is the sort of man
who one might say had been born and
bred in school. His father and his
mother were both public elementary school
teachers. He himself, from an early age,
was entered as a monitor, became a
teacher, and after a successful career as
principal was appointed by the Commissioners of National Education an inspector in the year 1914. The House
may be quite satisfied that he is a man
familiar with all aspects of school work,
both from the point of view of a teacher
and from that of an inspector.
In the
course of his ordinary duties on 17th and
18th November, 1932, Mr. Kirkpatrick
came to inspect the Star of the Sea School
in Halliday's Road, Belfast, where Mr.
Burns is employed, and it fell to him.
to examine the third and fourth standards
which were taught by Mr. Burns.
That inspection was held, and on 21st
November Mr. Burns wrote to
the
Ministry a long letter making a number
of allegations touching the inspection
that was held that day. I will deal with
them in detail afterwards. He followed
that up by formally appealing against
the rating which Mr. Kirkpatrick had
on that occasion assigned to him, which
was the rating of 'efficient" and not
"highly efficient" which, as my colleague
(Mr. McNeill) says, he anticipated. It
may be possible that the mover of this
Motion left the impression that Mr.
Kirkpatrick had altered the rating which
Mr. Burns had enjoyed, but, as I have
already said, and, I think, made quite
clear to the House Mr. Burns had not
been rated as "highly efficient" since the
year 1922. The rating assigned to him
by Mr. Kirkpatrick was the same rating
assigned to him on previous inspections
within the last ten years by different
inspectors.
I said Mr. Burns appealed against
that rating. When speaking on the
Education Estimates-I must repeat it
although I hate to weary the House with
it-I pointed out that some years ago
the Ministry of Education in Northern
Ireland set up what is called an Appeals
Committee. The duty devolves upon
that committee of hearing appeals by
teachers against the rating assigned to
them by inspectors at the periodical inspections. That committee was composed
of three persons (1) a chief inspector
of the Ministry; (2) the president for
the year of one of the four teachers'
organisations they take it in turn-and
(3) a retired teacher of wide experience.
A committee so constituted, everyone
must agree, is if anything weighted in
favour of the teacher. In the ordinary
course Mr. Burns's appeal against his
rating came before that committee.
In his letter he gave four general heads
of complaints against the inspection that
had been given. They are the same
heads as are now set forth by the Belfast
branch of the Irish National Teachers'
Organisation as the grounds upon which
the inquiry that is demanded should be
held. Those heads are as follows: The
first is want of knowledge by Mr. Kirkpatrick of the Ministry's official programme. The second is that no allowance was made at the examination for
the period of year at which the examination was held. The examination was
held in November. Of course, that is
early in the school year, but it is obviously
impossible for inspectors to do all their
inspections at the end of the year.
inspections must be spread all over the
year, but allowance is always made for
that fact. The third head was the adoption of methods of examination condemned in the Ministry's general report
and inferentially in the official programme
of instruction. The fourth head was
discourtesy towards him, and loud bullying tones adopted throughout.
-
The
Of those several heads Mr. Burns proceeds in his letter to give details. The
first three are obviously matters dealing
with the examination and the resulting
rating. If allowance was not made for the
period of the year and if wrong methods
of examination were adopted those
were matters eminently suitable for decision by the Teachers' Appeals Committee. The appeal and all the correspondence touching the appeal, were before
that Appeals Committee, who fully investigated the matter, and decided that
the rating be confirmed.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
So far as the Ministry is concerned
that disposes of the first three heads of
these charges. If we set up a committee
weighted, as I have said, in favour of
the teacher before whom such appeals as
this can be brought, then the finding
of that committee is and must be binding,
for no committee can be expected to
function if after their investigation as
a court of appeal they were to be subjected to Motions in this House for an
inquiry or a direction for a public inquiry
by the Ministry itself.
There remains then the charge of discourtesy brought by Mr. Burns against
Mr. Kirkpatrick. Now, I would just
like to make one remark. The mover
and seconder of this Motion were very
anxious to discuss generally the merits
or demerits of our system of inspection.
in Northern Ireland. It is not, I understand, alleged by any person that there
should not be some form of inspection of
schools, and I should like to point out
that under any form of inspection, merit
marks or other, there is a liability to
allegations of discourtesy, so that the
merits or demerits of any system of inspection are in any event irrelevant to this
Motion. There remains, as I have said,
the charge of discourtesy towards Mr.
Burns and his pupils.
Alleging discourtesy, Mr. Burns says
that when taking up the examination of
the fourth standard in reading, Mr. Kirkpatrick said to them: "Have you read
all this book?" and that when he came
to examine them in arithmetic he said:
"Have you done all this arithmetic
book?" Mr. Burns says that those were
ridiculous questions. Further, he saysand this is the ground of discourtesythat those questions should have been
addressed to him, he being the teacher
on the spot and ready to answer, and
that they should not have been addressed
to the pupils.
Mr. Kirkpatrick says: "Yes, I did
ask them those questions. That is the
most usual thing in the world. The inspector wants to try to break the ice with
a class, and when he is going to take
them in reading he takes up the book,
and asks: 'Have you read all this book?'
The class says 'No.' Then he says:
'Well, how far have you gone?' and they
tell him, and the examination proceeds.'
But Mr. Burns regards as an act of
discourtesy to himself that little intro-
""
ductory talk which I myself have heard
often from inspectors when I have been
present in schools at inspections. He
says he was there and should have been
asked how far the class had gone.
The second head is that when the inspector was preparing for the drawing
lesson for the third standard he needed
a blackboard and went to get it and put
it up on the easel for himself, that he
(Mr. Burns) went to put it up for him.
and that Mr. Kirkpatrick refused his
assistance. Mr. Kirkpatrick says, "I
did put up the blackboard. I wanted it,
and knew where I was going to put it.
Mr. Burns came forward to help me, but
I said, Thank you, I can put it up
myself; I can manage.'
Mr. Burns
construes that into an act of discourtesy
towards himself in that the inspector
refused his help.

The fourth head is the loud tone of
voice in which he says Mr. Kirkpatrick
addressed himself and the pupils Mr.
Kirkpatrick says that he is not a very
good judge of his own tone of voice, but
whatever tone he used, it was the same
on that occasion as he uses in other
schools.
Those are the incidents upon which
Mr. Burns asks the Ministry to set up a
sort of State trial in the form of a public
inquiry. It seems to me, and I hope it
will appear to the House, that to set up
a public inquiry in this case would be
the height of folly. The incidents alleged
are trivial in the extreme, and the substantiation of them upon one side or the
other, would involve the calling as witnesses of a class from the school. It
would mean the elevation into a State
trial, as I have said, of what were construed into acts of discourtesy. That is
not the sort of thing for which courts
of inquiry are held. Courts of inquiry
are serious things for serious matters,
and it seems to me, and has seemed to
the Ministry all through, that once the
question of the teacher's rating was
settled by the Appeals Committee,
a tribunal set up for the purpose and
weighted, as I have said, in favour of
the teacher-once that matter was settled
there remained only what could at the
best be described as a storm in a teacup.
It was not in any event a suitable subject
for a public inquiry.
Inspectors and teachers have difficult
jobs to perform. It may be, I do not
doubt it is a fact, that from time to

inquiry. It would not help at all.
can only express the hope that should

I do not know in view of the ruling

In our opinion, from the correspondence, the fact emerges clearly that a
prima facie case existed for an inquiry. In

point was made by the hon. and learned
Member (Mr. Robb) that when complaints
of this character are brought before the

and for the teacher to come along and put
his cards on the table and say what is
wrong. They have actually almost taunted
the teachers with failure to come forward
and give specific cases and evidence. May
I say that the results achieved by the
representations made in this particularly
glaring instance will not, we suggest, enhance the opinion held by the teaching body
of the honesty of the Ministry's previous
pronouncements on the subject. Rather

Burns as a teacher, and yet this is the
teacher that the Ministry accuses of lack
of intelligence in order to defend their
inspector, a gentleman failing in judgment
and perspective, and one whose method of
teaching is wrong. Why? What is the

because Mr. Burns has the courage to
stand up to the insults and strictures of
the inspector who, according to our information, has a reputation for rudeness.
This whole affair which, in our view, has
seriously aggravated the situation in the
school, as has been said by the hon.
Member for Pottinger and the hon. and
learned Member for the University (Mr.
McNeill), is full of the gravest possibilities, because the teacher has at his back
his entire organisation. It is quite
apparent from the changed tone of the
last of the Ministry's letters that there was
a certain amount of embarrassment and
anxiety felt in the Ministry at the public
ventilation of this whole matter, and that
was coupled with a desire at all costs to
exonerate their own official. May I say
that the affected desire expressed by the
Ministry for the maintenance of good relations in the interests of the system, even
if it could in the circumstances be accepted
as sincere, is entirely nullified by what we
regard as a highly improper attempt to
cloak the conduct of their own official in
this case.
On a careful and dispassionate survey
of all the circumstances it is perfectly clear
to us, and we believe to the House, that
a very unpleasant and disquieting situation is revealed, a situation capable of
inflicting untold injury on the whole
educational system. The matter appears
to us so grave that we have no doubt
whatever that it has been cloaked, and it
is aggravated by the fact that the
Ministry, instead of acceding to the very
fair and proper request, instead of, even
when the question of an appeal arose,
sending an inspector to the school to ascertain whether this other inspection was
right or not, and instead of holding this
inquiry, deliberately first assailed the
character of the teacher in question, and
then, having done that, endeavoured to
cloak over and conceal the whole question.
We think that the Ministry have handled
the subject from beginning to end in a
very unworthy manner, but, so far as the
group of which I am a Member here is
concerned, it is our opinion that nothing
whatever would be gained by putting this
question to a Division, and if it were put
to a Division we would not participate in
it, because it would merely enable the
Government to reveal that stereotyped
majority which will walk into the Lobby
irrespective of whether justice is done or
not. We say that grave injustice has pecn
done to a teacher of very high repute and
of great ability. Like the hon. Member
for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie), we have nothing but admiration for the courage of
the gentleman who can assail the Ministry,
beard the lion in his den, and do as he is
doing in the interests of the whole educational system, because if this sort of thing
is not stopped, and this petty tyranny of
the inspectors does not cease a very grave
and serious position will have arisen in
this area.

Mr. HENDERSON: I wish to take
this opportunity of criticising the
methods adopted by the Government in
dealing with the housing problem in
Northern Ireland. During the past
week or two this House was responsible
for setting up a Committee known as the
Pigs Marketing Board. Would it not
have been very advisable for the Minister
of Home Affairs and his Parliamentary
Secretary to set up a Central Housing
Board, because human beings who are
compelled to live in slums are of more
importance to the State than a glut of
pigs. Next to starvation bad housing is.
the worst thing any community could
have. The open confession which the
Minister of Home Affairs made yesterday
in this House proved conclusively that
the policy of his Department had failed
in regard to housing in Northern Ireland.
There was no necessity for the right hon.
Gentleman to make an open confession
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattie
at all. One has only to go throughout
the length and breadth of Northern Ireland to find what the conditions are.

see the condition of some of the houses in

This Bill contains nothing that will

Belfast that there will be any houses of

learned Gentleman go so far as to say
that any of the local authorities in the

mostly composed of farmers' representatives who are always opposed to putting
anything on the rates, no matter who is
going to benefit, will build houses under
this scheme? I know that there are a
few good authorities, such as that with
which the hon. Member for Mid-Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) is connected.
The fact of the matter is, that you are
leaving it to the local authorities throughout Northern Ireland to take advantage
of this £25, but none of these small local
authorities outside Belfast will take
advantage of this subsidy. Would the
hon. Member for Mid-Antrim be prepared to advocate that the Antrim
County Council should add £25 to the
Government's £25 for the erection of
houses in their area? You are leaving
this hopeless mess, in which you have
been for the past year, to the local
authorities. You only got ninety houses
built in the whole of last year.
Yet you
are the brilliant statesmen who, backed
by your housing experts, came into this
House last year and told sensible Members of Parliament that that Bill-this
Bill is an Amendment to it would be
responsible for clearing away the slums
throughout the length and breadth of
Northern Ireland. And after all those
promises by the Minister of Home Affairs
the total number of houses built under
the scheme has been ninety.
Much as I regret to say it, there is no
community in the world in which it is
more necessary to have a proper housing
policy than in Northern Ireland. I am
not surprised that hon. Members should
get up in this House and say that the
houses in Northern Ireland are all right.
I say they are all wrong. There has
been no comprehensive scheme of any
importance to house the people in the
agricultural areas. What is the plight
of some of these people? They are
living in dilapidated houses, which are,
in a good many cases, like old barns with
corrugated iron roofs. Some of the
houses with thatched roofs have been
badly thatched; if they were well
thatched they would be fairly comfortable. There are no drains, no nothing.

responsible member of the community
realises that it is the duty of the local

giving it that the members of these

properly housed themselves, and who do
ot care whether or not the rest of the

farmers on the county councils, for

properly.

so far as its aim was concerned, and I consider that the same will apply to this Bill,
though I stand here in support of it.
I feel very much the importance of
stressing those very pertinent points which
were discussed on the past Bills. I refer
especially to the question which has exercised this House during the past ten years
in regard to low or economic rents for
people who are not able to build houses.
That is the question that is facing us today, and I say that what was aimed at
in those previous Bills is still aimed at in
this Bill, namely, a low rent which the
average working man can pay. I give the
Minister credit for having the idea that
houses were largely wanted for workingclass people, and that those people who
would get the subsidy were able to build
houses themselves without any subsidy;
that what the working-class people really
wanted were houses at rents which they
could afford to pay and which were, in
some way, based on their earning capacities. I will state what has not been stated
here to-day, namely, my idea of an
economic rent. My idea of an economic
rent is one of 7/6 or 8/6 per week.
After all these years, during which we
have passed half-a-dozen Housing Bills,
we are still following after that will-o'-
the-wisp, a low or economic rent. I
sometimes think I will never see it in
my constituency, and I am afraid most
Members of this House will not see it.
But no matter, we are striving after it,
and I sincerely hope that this Bill will
bring about the desired object for which
we have so long been looking. When we
gave subsidies to builders and owners-as
I say people well able in many respects
to build houses without the Government
subsidy we surely expected that the
rents which they demanded would be
reflected in some measure of benefit to the
tenants by a reduction of rents. In many
cases these subsidies amounted to upwards
of £150, and in addition there was the
possible exemption from rates. I say it
was reasonable that people should expect
that they would get some benefit from all
that, and that rents would be much reduced. But no, it would seem that the
principle that was gone on was rather,
to quote a Biblical truth,
"To him that hath shall be given,
and from him that hath not shall be
taken away even that which he hath."
Certainly it is true in this instance.
The hon. Member for Shankill spoke
about slums. I would like to know what
he or the Members of this House would
define as slums. I go through the
countryside, and see many nice little
thatched houses. They are small, and
certainly not up to the superficial area
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major McCormick]
of 550 feet. I would dearly love to live
in one of those little houses. They are
picturesque and easily kept. If my hon.
Friend would describe that type of house
as a slum I differ from him, and I cannot
see in all my experience either in my own
constituency or in other constituencies in
the city that there are any slum areas.
Mr. HENDERSON: The Minister
himself says there are slums.
Major McCORMICK: There are no

Mr. HENDERSON: The Minister says
there are slums.
Major McCORMICK: I do not assent
to the assertion that there is slumdom in

for houses of 650 superficial feet, but
pressure was brought to bear on him,
and I am sorry he did not resist that
The result was that we had
pressure.
houses of 700 superficial feet, houses
away above what the working-class man
demanded. Yet the essence of that Bill
was to get houses for the working-class
people.
and
In previous Housing Bills I
other hon. Members on these benches
urged that a Clause should be included protecting tenants from high
rents, but without avail. I am human
enough to understand and to appreciate
the difficulties facing the Minister in this
matter, but I am only sorry that he did
not resist the pressure that was brought
to bear on him. I will even testify that
in discussing the 1929 Act, placing the
superficial area at 700 feet, he said it
was going to hurt the small or workingclass person.
But the interests of these
builders or owners prevailed, and the
result was that, with the help of this
House, the larger house was again provided for. But I say to his credit that
he realised the necessity for the economic
or smaller-rented house.
To deal with the Bill as it stands, it
is in the main to continue this subsidy
of £25, which I say at once is very small,
but I understand the financial needs of
the Government, and that they cannot
give more, and, therefore, we have to
deal with what we have got. It also
gives assistance to local authorities in
borrowing money, and aims generally at
encouraging the providing of housing in
their areas. I am quite in sympathy
with the Bill and hope for its success,
although I am not fully satisfied with it
as it stands.
The hon. Member for South Fermanagh
(Mr. Healy), who I regret is not in the
House, was very strong in a vocal way in
urging the claims of housing in rural
areas. The hon. Member has been very
quiet in this House of late. He is now
such a humanitarian that he only raises
his voice when murder appears. But in
this matter of housing he was very vocal.
Possibly he does not remain in the House
because those who follow him are such a
very small number to lead. As I say, the
hon. Member was the most vocal of his
party in his diatribes against the Government and accusing them of not providing
houses in the rural areas, whereas it was
up to those rural areas and the authorities
there to bring in their own housing
schemes. It is right that there should
be a call on rural authorities to do what
is plainly in their own power to do. 1
mention this in the sense that I know that
the local bodies have been slow as far as
providing houses in their own areas is concerned. But if the Government provide a
subsidy and the local bodies are slow to
take advantage of it, well they are the
people's representatives, and it is up to
the people to act when an election comes
round. The Government do not lay down
who shall build. It is for anyone to build,
but in this Bill they are giving extra facilities so far as the borrowing powers of
local authorities are concerned. In passing, I may say that if the hon. Member
for South Fermanagh pays the same attention to the needs of his local area as he
does to this House then he does not require
a Housing Bill, but rather an Attendance
Bill.
Mr. BYRNE: On a point of order. Is
it in order for the hon. and gallant
Gentleman to attack an hon. Member who
is absent from this House?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. and gallant
Gentleman is in order. It is purely a
matter of good taste.
Major McCORMICK: It is up to any
hon. Member who represents a constituency
to be in his place in this House, and to
be able to retort personally to what is said.
We have now over 26,000 houses built in
our area by means of this subsidy, and
Housing Bill—

over £2,500,000 has been paid in this way.
That is a huge amount, and yet the main
point has only been gained in a slight
degree so far as getting houses built at
smaller rents is concerned. I think I am
right in saying that in our first Housing
Bill ten years ago we set out to attain that
object, and we have only succeeded in a
slight way, although plenty of houses have
been built. The Corporation have built
--and much credit is due to them-houses
that cost about 7/6 or 8/6 weekly. More
houses of that class are required, but I am
sorry and I am sure the hon. Member
for Shankill (Mr. Henderson) will take

to give the subsidy themselves when the
Government were giving a subsidy in

I suggest that the main point in dealing with this problem is not so much the
building of more houses as the conditional
Clause that those houses must be let at
an economic rent. I do not think there
is anything to be said against the houses.
Personally, I do not object if a house is.
650 feet and it is added to and made 800
feet. The thing that has appealed to me
throughout these Housing Bills has been
the necessity for a house for which a
working-class person could pay. I think
the Government subsidy has only partly
helped to solve that problem. In my own
constituency of St. Anne's there is a great
need for that class of house. I have inquired very minutely into the rents which
are payable by people in that constituency
and I find that there are very few houses
let at less than 12/6 weekly, which is far
too high for the people to pay. I would
like the House to consider this matter
more closely, but possibly at this late
hour of the day it is too much to expect.
But I may say that the Rents Restriction
Act, which deals with private property
and houses in which the State has no
money invested at all, dictates limitations
as to the rents to be charged by the
owners of those houses. But here in this
Subsidy Bill wherein the Government have
undertaken to pay or guarantee certain
moneys, there is a complete absence of
dictation as to what a fair or economic
rent shall be. I say it is wrong-there
is no equity in it.
Again we are told that the law of supply
and demand will bring down rents but,
in ten years of house building and
subsidies, and although there are
thousands of vacant houses at present,
the extraordinary fact remains that whilst
everything else has been reduced rents
remain very high, and I am forced to the
conclusion that only by powers in this
Bill-as to these particular houses anyhow can we secure this very necessary
benefit to the people. I see by the Press
that the Corporation, who should be the
guardians of the people in the matter of
rent have discussed the question. One
report states:
The provisions of the Housing Bill,
which has been introduced
in the

of that contained in the Housing Act
passed by the Imperial Parliament in
the year 1923, which authorised conditions to be prescribed where a housing
subsidy is given.
a
Whilst I give the Ministry credit for

a considered protest is due to the Ministry
of Home Affairs from these Benches for
the continuous refusal of amendments and
clauses in previous Bills of this character
in regard to Housing and lower or

deputation appears before the Ministera deputation from the Corporation-insisting on this very clause, we find it is

nullified and we find the thing is possible,

consideration shown by the Government
to Back Benchers. I emphasize this because it has occurred more than once.
It amounts to this, that apparently our
views are not wanted, and have no
weight.

in insisting that economic rents should be

The number of houses built under this

of rents. The subsidy by the Government

Grants by local authorities might be given

But no

Major BLAKISTON - HOUSTON: I

for the simple reason that members of a

meantime, all the loose bricks were thrown

Oral Answers to Questions.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
RURAL DISTRICTS.
1. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state the number of labourers'
cottages that have been built in each
of the rural districts in Northern Ireland during the past twelve years.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As the reply consists of a tabular statement of figures,
I propose, with the hon. Member's permission, to circulate it with the Official
Report.
HACKNEY CAR OWNERS.
2. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that hackney car owners, especially
in seaside resorts, have suffered severely
in recent years; and whether he will give
sympathetic consideration to their claim
for the redress of their grievances.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that, owing to the rapid development of
motor transportation in the Province involving increased numbers of private
cars, motor omnibuses, and chars-a-bancs,
the demand for motor hackney vehicles
by the community has decreased, not only
in seaside places but generally throughout the country.
Oral Answers
Housing (Money)
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
If, however, the hon. Member can let
me have any suggestions which he may
have in mind under which motor hackney owners can be safeguarded without
prejudice to the interests of the public, I
will be happy to consider them.
SUGGESTED GUARANTEED PRICE
FOR OATS.
3. Mrs. PARKER asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state what
representations, if any, have been made
to the Imperial Government to grant a
guaranteed economic price for oats in
Northern Ireland as a counterpart to the
guaranteed price for wheat, which accrues
almost entirely to the advantage of the
English farmers.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): As
the hon. Member is doubtless aware,
successful representations have been
made by oat producers and millers
to the Import Duties Advisory Committee
for an increase in the duties on oats and
oatmeal. As a consequence the duties on
oats and oatmeal have recently been increased from 10 per cent. to 20 per cent.
ad valorem, but I regret to say that the
increased duties have not had the desired
effect of securing for farmers a better
price for their oats.
One of the principal factors causing a
disturbance in the oat trade is the indirect assistance given by the German
export bond system to the export of oats
from Germany. A merchant in Germany
who exports oats or oat products receives
a bond entitling the holder to import
into Germany a corresponding quantity
of feeding barley or other cereals at rates
of duty below the normal rates. These
bonds have a sale value which at present
amounts in effect to an export bounty of
approximately £5 per ton of oats exported. Representations have been made
by my Ministry to the Imperial authorities with a view to securing the withdrawal of this export bond system by
the German Government.
In regard to the introduction of an
oat subsidy similar to the wheat deficiency
pavments made under the Wheat Act,
1932. I would point out to the hon.
Member that there is no import duty
upon wheat entering this country and
that only a small part of our wheat supplies is home produced. It has therefore been possible to subsidise the home
produce by means of a small levy on
flour imported or milled in this country.
The position is totally different in regard
to oats which are largely home produced
and of which only a relatively small proportion is imported from overseas.

the Housing Bill now before the House,
to offer financial assistance from Government funds towards the provisions of
housing accommodation in Northern Ireland. I may perhaps at this stage point
out that the three methods are mutually
exclusive, and that not more than one
can be utilised in connection with the
building of any particular house.
The first Resolution is designed to make
provision for the payment by the Ministry of Home Affairs of grants of £25 for
each house provided in accordance with
the statutory requirements. The making
of a Government Grant under this
arrangement is conditional upon either a
subsidy of £25 being paid in respect of
the house by the appropriate local
authority, or exemption from rates being
granted by the rating authority for a
period of ten years.
The second method of financial assistance is, I think, a new one so far as
Northern Ireland housing legislation is
concerned. Under the Bill local authorities are empowered to guarantee the repayment of a proportion of the advances
made by building societies and such like,
to persons, or bodies of persons for the
purpose of enabling them to build houses.
Normally a building society will advance
up to 70 per cent. of the price of a house
on its own risk, the borrower having to
find 30 per cent. himself. Now, as an
incentive to the society to increase that
70 per cent.. the local authority can,
under the Bill, guarantee such excess
over 70 per cent, but the guarantee will
not extend to any portion of the loan in
excess of 90 per cent. of the value. If
having given such guarantee a local
authority sustains any loss as a result of
its guarantee, the Ministry of Home
Affairs may, with the consent of the
Ministry of Finance, reimburse to the
local authority a sum of not more than
one-half of the loss sustained by it. It
is in order to make financial provisions
for such reimbursement that I move this
second Resolution.
I now come to the third method by
which financial assistance may be given.
Where a local authority borrows money
for the purpose of building houses itself,
or for the purpose of lending it to other
persons in order to enable them to build
houses, it is proposed that the Ministry
of Home Affairs may, for a period not
exceeding 20 years, make to the local
authority annual contributions equal to
one-half per cent. per annum upon the
loan raised by it; it will be a condition
that if the local authority borrows money
for houses erected by the private builder,
the local authority must itself lend the
money to the builder at one-half per
cent. less than the rate at which it itself
borrowed, that is to say, it must pass on
the advantage of the Government contribution to the builder.
In conclusion, I may point out that all
houses in respect of which assistance may
be given under the terms of these, three
Resolutions must comply with the appropriate statutory conditions as to dimensions and so forth. I beg to move.

Sea Fishing Industry Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. BARBOUR: The Bill which I
now ask the House to read a Second time
is not, I think, likely to call forth any
marked differences of view. Hon. Members are
no doubt aware that a few
months ago the Imperial Government,
impressed by the difficulties confronting
the sea fishing industry of the United
Kingdom, introduced and secured passage
of, a measure-the Sea Fishing Industry
Act, 1933-designed to improve the
situation in the industry, in so far as
improvement could be effected by legislation.
The great difficulty under which
British fishermen have been labouring for
several years is "low prices"-prices insufficient to leave even a bare margin for
livelihood when capital and maintenance
charges have been met. In the Imperial Act this problem is attacked in
several ways.
In the first place protection has been afforded to United
Kingdom fishermen by subjecting the
landings in the United Kingdom of sea
fish caught by foreign fishermen to a
quota and licensing system, the details
of which were left to be embodied in
Orders made by the Board of Trade in
conjunction with the Ministers directly
concerned in the constituent parts of the
Kingdom.
With the same object in view the Act
empowered the Secretary of State for
England and Wales and the Secretary of
State for Scotland to prohibit the landing
of fish from Arctic waters during a
portion of each year. Fish from these
fishing grounds tend to be of rather lower
value than fish from, for example, the
North Sea, and their arrival in large
quantity usually had a depressing effect
upon market prices, which reacted to the
detriment of other fishermen.
The next line of attack was the elimination, so far as possible, of undersized
fish from the catches of deep sea trawlers.
This is to be secured by fixing a minimum
size of mesh to be used in the cod-ends
of net carried by British fishing vessels.
for use outside territorial waters.
I may
mention in passing that the exclusion of
territorial waters from the areas to be
covered by restrictions of this kind was
necessitated by the fact that within such
waters, both in Great Britain and in
Northern Ireland, local fishery authorities
-in the case of Northern Ireland the
Ministry of Commerce-already possessed,
and had exercised, power to make regulations prescribing the size of mesh to be
used. The elimination of immature fish
from the landings is desirable on two
counts. In the first place the preservation of young fish until they have
reached maturity and have reproduced
themselves is a fundamental principle in
fishery administration, and in the second
place, the enormous quantities of small
fish recently landed were of very small
unit value. As a corollary to the mesh
restriction power was taken to prohibit
by Order the sale in Great Britain of
sea fish of less than prescribed minimum
sizes.
In order to guard against the new conditions reacting unduly to the disadvantage of consumers, the British Act
provides for the setting up of a Sea Fish
Commission to investigate any matter
relating to the catching, landing, storage,
treatment, distribution, or sale of sea
fish, and to report to the appropriate
Ministers as to what steps should be taken
for reorganising any branch of the sea
fishing industry of the United Kingdom
or any branch of industry in the United
Kingdom which is engaged in dealing
with sea fish. It also provides for the
utilisation of the Market Supply Committee to furnish the appropriate Ministers
with information and advice upon any
specified matter relating to the supply
of sea fish in the United Kingdom.
Briefly, therefore, the Imperial Government has taken steps, on the one hand,
to regulate the landings, means of
capture, and saleable size of sea fish and,
on the other, to ensure that such regulation will not react to the detriment of
the public.
All the provisions of the Westminster
Act, with one exception, apply to the
whole of the United Kingdom, the
2451 Sea Fishing Industry Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Barbour]
exception being that relating to the sale.
of undersized fish, the operation of which
is confined to Great Britain. As hon.
Members are aware, the regulation of
sale within Northern Ireland is a matter
which lies within the jurisdiction of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, and it
was to avoid encroaching upon that jurisdiction that the "sale" section in the
Westminster Measure was made to apply
to Great Britain only.
Hon. Members will see, however, that
unless some control over sales is enforced
here the Northern Ireland market might
well be inundated with undersized fish
excluded from cross-Channel markets.
Moreover, the establishment of legal
minima in the size of fish to be sold affords
a very real protection to the stocks of
young fish upon which the future prosperity of our fishing industry depends.
The Government have, therefore, concluded that it is in the interests of
Northern Ireland that identical powers
should be taken to control the sale of
sea fish here, and the present Bill, which
follows closely upon the English Measure,
proposes to place such powers in the
hands of the Ministry of Commerce. It
does not purport, however, to fix for all
time the legal saleable sizes of fish.
Obviously the matter is one which calls
for flexibility in order to meet varying
conditions. The Bill, therefore, merely
provides for the making of Orders by the
Ministry of Commerce, as the central
fishery authority, prescribing the minimum sizes of fish to be sold in Northern
Ireland, and constitutes it an offence to
sell fish of a size smaller than that prescribed by the Ministry. I am sure no
Member of the House will deny the
wisdom of conferring such powers and it
is, therefore, with the utmost confidence
that I beg to move.

now read a Second time."

Electricity (Supply) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:

Mr. BARBOUR: The Bill to which I
desire the House to give a Second Reading this afternoon is of a miscellaneous
character. It is designed mainly to give
general application to certain provisions
which have in recent years been included
in numerous local Acts of Parliament,
both in Great Britain and in Northern
Ireland and at the same time the opportunity is taken to effect certain amendments in the existing law relating to the
supply of electricity, which experience
gathered since the passing of the 1931
Act, has shown to be desirable. In a
miscellaneous Measure of this kind there
is, of course, no broad principle underlying the whole Bill and, accordingly, it
is incumbent upon me, in submitting it
to the House, to review the various
Clauses.
2457 Electricity (Supply) Bill-

19 OCTOBER 1933
Second Reading
Clause 1 is self-explanatory and will
enable supply undertakers to use for
general purposes any transformer installed for the purpose of affording a
supply to a particular consumer, the interests of that consumer being, of course,
properly safeguarded.
Clause 2 is designed to meet cases
where the areas of supply of two different
undertakings abut on each other and the
centre
line of the roadway is
boundary. It enables the undertakers to
carry their lines on the side of the street
outside their area, where this may be
necessary owing to the presence of post
office lines or trees. The Clause of course
does not authorise them to supply in the
other party's area.
Clause 3 is a minor amendment for the
purpose of removing doubts as to the
necessity for serving on a rural district
council notice of works (on the county
roads for example) in cases where the
local authority concerned is in practice
the county council.
Clause 4 will enable undertakers to discontinue supplies where payments are
overdue in respect of hired apparatus.
Under existing legislation the undertaker
has power to discontinue the supply
where the consumer fails to pay for current used or for the use of fittings. This
provision is necessary in view of the
steadily growing practice of hiring out
the more expensive types of apparatus,
such as cookers.
The object of Clause 5 is to remove
doubts as to the interpretation of Clause
37 of the Act of 1931, which deals with
the granting by the Ministry of Commerce of consents to wayleaves for
electric lines. Under that section, where
a wayleave is sought by an undertaker
and refused by the owner or occupier of
the property, it is open to the former to
apply to my Ministry for a consent to a
wayleave, and provision is made for a
hearing before this is granted. At such
hearing an effort is made to secure an
agreed settlement.
A question has arisen, owing to a
recent court decision in England, as to
whether the Ministry in determining the
matter has power to award the amount of
compensation or rental to be paid in
respect of the wayleave. The Clause in
the 1931 Act states that the Ministry
may give its consent on such terms and
subject to such conditions and stipulations as it thinks just, and it is desirable
that it should be made clear that the
Ministry has power to award compensation. The principle enunciated is not a
new one and the Clause follows the wording of the Telegraph Act of 1878, which
deals with the erection of telephone and
telegraph lines. We now ask Parliament to confirm my Ministry in dealing
with wayleave matters in the future in
the same way as it has successfully dealt
with them for a number of years past.
In point of fact, the number of applications for the Ministry's consent to a wayleave in recent years has been compara-
In the
tively small.
case of the
Electricity Board, for instance, out of a
total of 3,900 wayleaves obtained up to
the 30th September last, only 1.28 per
cent. were obtained compulsorily. These
figures bear eloquent testimony to the
cordial co-operation which landowners
and occupiers in Northern Ireland are
giving to the efforts being made to provide cheap supplies of electricity in rural
areas.
Clause 6 provides for the attachment
to buildings of brackets or fixtures for
the support of electric service mains. A
considerable number of low tension distribution lines have been attached to
buildings by agreement with the owners,
a practice which leads to economy and
renders it a simple matter to connect up
consumers' premises. It also has the
advantage of avoiding the necessity for
placing polies in narrow and congested
streets. It may happen that in cases
where this form of construction is desirable, arrangements for a whole street
may be held up through one householder
refusing his consent. The second part of
the Clause gives the Ministry power to
deal with such a case under its ordinary
wayleave procedure. Having regard to
the increasing popularity of wiring of the
under-eaves type, references to the Ministry under this section will probably be
rare.
Clauses 7 and 8 are self-explanatory
and provide penalites for interference
with electricity supply lines. In the past
year there have been, I am sorry to say,
several cases of interference with overhead lines and, now that a large number
of towns and industrial concerns
drawing their supplies of electricity by
means of main transmission lines from
Belfast, it is highly important that there
should be no interruption of supplies
from such a cause.
are
2459 Electricity (Supply) Bill-.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment
[Mr. Barbour]
Clause 9 makes the provisions of the
Bill applicable to the Electricity Board.
This is all it is necessary for me to say
in respect of the Clauses of the Bill.
The House will have observed that the
object of its Clauses taken together is to
promote development and to provide such
additional protection to the supply
authorities as is required by the altered
conditions under which the supply of
electricity is now being so rapidly extended to rural districts and to the
smaller householders with such enormous
benefit to the community as a whole. I

Oral Answer to Question.
THE PIGS MARKETING SCHEME.
Mr. STEWART asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is prepared to compensate farmers for the heavy losses they
have sustained by reason of the operation
of the Pigs Marketing Scheme.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply. I am not aware of the heavy
losses experienced by farmers through the
operation of the Pigs Marketing Scheme
to which the hon. Member refers. On
the contrary, the action of the British
Government in limiting the imports of
bacon into the United Kingdom during
the nine months ended 30th September
to seven million cwts., as compared with
eight and a half million cwts. during the
corresponding period of last year, has
resulted in farmers in Northern Ireland
obtaining a standard price of 58s 6d per
dead cwt. for their pigs as contrasted
with about 40s per dead cwt. a year ago.
I would remind the hon. Member that
last week more than eight thousand
Northern Ireland pigs were bought by
curers at the standard prices, while between sixteen and seventeen hundred
Northern Ireland pigs were shipped to
Great Britain. Altogether some 9,930
Northern Ireland pigs were marketed
last week. I regret that in some areas
farmers have experienced difficulty in
selling their pigs to curers, but the Pigs
Marketing Board will buy all live pigs
offered to it, and if the hon. Member
knows of any group of farmers who have
difficulty in disposing of their pigs I am
confident that if he communicates with
the Pigs Marketing Board arrangements
can be made to market the pigs, provided they are alive.
Mr. STEWART: I would like to
know if the Minister is aware that several
farmers in Tyrone and Armagh have had
to put their pork in cold storage, and is
he prepared to pay for the cost of that
storage pending the release, or, at least,
make representations to the Pigs Marketing Board to release the pork in cold.
storage?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I regret
that such is the fact. We are trying to
see what can be done.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The object of the paragraph, as my hon. Friend has said, is a
slight concession on the part of private
owners. It would not be difficult to
imagine a row of terrace houses, possibly
under different ownerships, the bulk of
whose tenants desired to take in electricity. The simplest form of doing the

attached to the front of the houses underneath the eaves. In the case of
single individual in a row of terrace
houses objecting to the wires being
attached to his house it would necessitate
starting off from the next house and then
putting a pole in the thoroughfare to
carry the wire over the house of the

being attached to his house. In narrow
thoroughfares the poles would block the
thoroughfare in addition to being an
a

CLAUSE 8 (Interference with works
with intent to cut off supply of
electricity).
(1) If any person unlawfully and
maliciously cuts, injures or tampers
with any electric line or work with the
intent to cut off or injuriously affect
any supply of electricity, such person
shall be guilty of a felony and be liable
to be kept in penal servitude for any
term not exceeding five years, or to
imprisonment for any term not exceeding two years; but nothing in this
section shall exempt a person from any
proceeding for any offence which is
punishable under any other provision
of the Electricity (Supply) Acts
(Northern Ireland), 1882 to 1931, or
this Act, or under any other Act or at
common law, so, however, that no
person shall be punished twice for the
same offence.

So far then as the main principle of
this Clause is concerned it seems to me

no doubt that by-laws governing the
supply of electricity are very desirable.
It is a new convenience, and local
2475 Electricity (Supply) Bill— HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee

authorities have not yet controlled it in
the same way as they control the use of
some other conveniences. For example,
every local authority has power to adopt

their respective areas. They can require
builders to have rooms of a specified size,
adequate lighting, and so on, and streets
of the proper width. Such by-laws are
absolutely necessary in many directions.
Here we have a new convenience being
introduced into our civilised life, and
there is nothing more certain than that
such by-laws are desirable, because
electricity, as has been suggested already,
is a somewhat dangerous commodity. I
presume that any of us who have had
experience of it have had the discomfort
of having wires fused even in our own
homes. Not very long ago I had rather
an unpleasant experience of this sort
myself. I bought a little radiator from a
local firm. It seemed to me to be of quite
a satisfactory type, but I discovered that
when it was brought into contact with
anything in connection with the ground
the wire immediately fused with a loud.
report. It was an exceedingly dangerous
article, and anyone in the house handling
that radiator in a room, say, in which
there was oilcloth, or on a tiled floor,
would almost certainly have received a
very severe shock. The instrument was not
made in a satisfactory way but was
seriously defective. It may interest hon.
Members to know that within recent
years the most dangerous room in the
modern house is the bathroom. Bathrooms are now usually wired; the wiring
is occasionally defective, and defective
wiring in the presence of water or with
a floor that is likely to be wet is exceedingly dangerous.
I do not want to seem to urge this with

Ireland are in favour of it, or certainly
not opposed to it.
Then the hon. and gallant Member

supply by making unnecessary by-laws.
On that ground itself and on the ground
of the very desire of these undertakers

there is very little danger of the power
which it is proposed to give here being

May I say in conclusion that the work
of the Electricity Board in Northern Ireland is giving wide satisfaction? People
all over the country are gratified when

home towns and when they realise that
a short time they will have an

venture, therefore, to support the appeal

emanating from the Belfast Corporation
should receive the sympathetic consideration of the Minister.

the Unemployment Fund it is estimated

I wish to add that the Government cannot accept the Motion because in the first
place it would cut right across the re-insurance agreement, and that I will not
be a party to. In the second place, as
hon. Members know, his Majesty's Imperial Government at the present time is
considering the question of unemployment
insurance and also public relief, and proposes to bring in a Bill dealing with those
two important matters at no distant date.

I have been careful to-day to say little
or nothing of a party nature or of a
political description, because I I have
always tried to raise the problems associated with the administration of these
great social services above the level of
mere party politics. I do not know that

with the view that hon. Members want

I have simply told a plain unvarnished

brought forward year after year.
The
Socialist party in Great Britain have had

before the House, and have it placed

We are told very often by members of

of which unlimited supplies of money
might be obtained; but the fact of the
case is that at the present time we are
over-taxed to such an extent that the
Federation of British Industries and the
National Chambers of Trade have stated
that a reduction in taxation would benefit
trade and lead to more spending power in
the community. The Financial Relations
Committee which was set up in 1931,
referring to taxation, said:
The limit of our resources has been
reached, and the only effective remedy
is for both Government and local
authorities to concentrate on the
utmost measure of economy.
If more money is taken for these services then education, and, shall we say,
old-age pensions, and other necessary
services are bound to suffer, whilst we
are running the risk of returning to the
position we were in in 1931, when money
was leaving the country, exports were
decreasing, imports of manufactured
goods were increasing, and unemployment was going up by leaps and bounds.
But what do we find to-day? We find
to-day that the position is such that the
world as a whole has confidence in the
future, and it is confidence in the future
that is needed for the restoration of
trade. That confidence has already
affected trade to such an extent that we
find exports going up, and imports of
manufactured goods coming down; the
revenue of the country is going up, and
for the first nine months of this year
the deficit is only £48,000 against
£118,000 last year, with the result that
it is not unreasonable or too optimistic
to say that for the last six months of
this year there will be a surplus, and
that surplus will have a very far-reaching
effect upon the trade of the community.
Already we see the effect in what may
be described as a small boom in the industrial market on the Stock Exchange,
where shares in good industrial concerns
are going up from day to day. All the
more recent balance-sheets of wellmanaged firms show a gradual improvement in trade, while the unemployment
figures, as a result of improved trade,
are going down, and for this year show
a
reduction of approximately half
million. In Northern Ireland they have
decreased during the last six months by
almost 15,000. The Member for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon), I think it was, referred to the unemployment among men
in Belfast at the present moment. He
said the figure was 30,000. I do not
dispute his figures. The exact figures are
28,366. But he will be pleased to know
Government Responsibility 2518
The Unemployed-
24 OCTOBER 1933
that that shows a decrease of approximately 1,000 on the previous return, and
I have not the least doubt that those
figures are improving daily.
In fact, only the week before last,
I am glad to say, some bricklayers and
plasterers were sent to fill jobs on the
other side of the Channel. I only hope
that more will be required, and that
there will be an increased demand for
at least that type of employment in
Northern Ireland itself. Even the linen
industry, which has been spoken of this
afternoon, shows a distinct improvement,
due almost entirely to the action which
has been taken by the Imperial Government, with the support and at the request
of the Government of Northern Ireland,
in introducing tariffs, quotas and agreements, resulting in imports being down
£296,000 during the last nine months,
while exports are up £244,000. Another
sign of trade revival is to be found in
the figures for the railways, which show
an increase of £1,251,000 in the last six
months.
In my opinion there is no country in
the world better fitted at the present
moment to take advantage of the general
improvement in trade, and I believe that
with the co-operation of employers and
employees, labour and capital, we will
do so. But I appeal to the Member for
Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) to look to the
future, and to take such steps through
his organisations as will prevent Japan
in a very few years under-selling this
country, owing to the fact that in that
country longer hours are worked and
lower wages are paid.
In conclusion, let me say that if any
Member of the Opposition is dissatisfied
with the Government of Northern Ireland, or the prospects or state of the
country, let him go to De Valera's

claimed and, accordingly, he called upon

challenged his decision, successively, to

challenged his decision, having stood up.
Resolved: "That in the opinion of
this House the Government is doing
everything possible within its resources to
assist financially the unemployed and to

Electricity (Supply) Bill.
As amended considered.
NEW CLAUSE (By-laws as to wires,
apparatus, and fittings).
(1) Any authorised undertakers may,
for the purpose of preventing fire in
or injury to any building or premises
supplied or proposed to be supplied
with electricity by them, or injury to
any person, make by-laws with respect
to the nature, material, workmanship
and mode of arrangement of the wires,
apparatus and fittings in any such
building or premises or required or
used for the purpose of such supply,
and may refuse to supply electricity or
cut off and discontinue the supply of
electricity to any building or premises
in or in respect of which such by-laws
are not complied with.
(2) Any dispute as to whether any
wires, apparatus and fittings comply
with the provisions of any by-laws
made in pursuance of this section shall
be referred for decision to an electric
inspector appointed under the special
Acts or Orders of the undertakers, and
that inspector shall also order by
which of the parties the costs of and
incidental to the proceedings before
him shall be paid and the decision of
the inspector shall be final and binding
on all parties.
(3) The undertakers may by any bylaws made under this section impose
on offenders against the same such
reasonable penalties as they think fit
not exceeding the sum of five pounds
for each offence and in the case of a
continuing offence a further penalty
not exceeding forty shillings for each
day after written notice of the offence
from the undertakers and such penalties be recovered in a summary
may
manner.
(4) By-laws made under this section.
shall not have any force or effect unless
and until they have been confirmed by
the Ministry of Commerce and published in such manner as the Ministry
of Commerce may direct.
(5) No by-law made under this
section shall apply to or in respect of
any premises (not being a dwellinghouse) belonging to a railway company,
harbour authority, navigation authority or gas or water undertakers and
used for the purposes of their undertaking, or to or in respect of any
premises occupied as a factory or workshop to which the Factory and Workshop Act, 1901, applies.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I beg to move, in
page 4, line 8, leave out the words "two
hundred" and insert the word "sixty."
The Clause to which this is an Amendment deals with the power of local
authorities to make loans for the purpose of enabling persons to build
houses. In the Clause, as it was originally
drafted, it was provided that in the case
of leaseholds no loan should be made by
a local authority where the term of the
lease was for less than 200 years, unexpired. On consideration, however, I
am of opinion that it is unnecessary to
insist on so long a term, and that it will
be sufficient to revert to the practice in
connection with the Small Dwellings
Acquisition Act, where a term of not less
than sixty years is sufficient.

will never make for those conditions, and

under this Clause from 10s to 20s.

NEW CLAUSE (Payment of Grants
where Conditions are imposed by Local
Authority).
(1) A local authority or rural district
council may resolve that the grant or
exemption from rates to be given by
the authority or council under section
one of this Act in respect of an
approved house may be made subject
to such conditions as the authority or
council may, with the approval of the
Ministry, impose, including a condition
that for a period of three years the
house shall not be let at a rent in
excess of that fixed by the authority or
council with the approval of the
Ministry.
(2) Where a resolution has been
adopted under sub-section (1) of this
section, then, notwithstanding anything in section one of this Act, the
following provisions shall have effect:-
(a) Grants made by the Ministry
under section one of this Act (not
being grants to local authorities
carrying out schemes for the provision of houses for the working
classes under the Housing of the
Working Classes (Ireland) Acts,
1890 to 1921) shall be paid to the
local authority or rural district
council in whose area or district the
houses are situate;
(b) Before paying any such grant
the Ministry shall be satisfied that
the house has been completed in a
proper and workmanlike manner.
(c) A grant paid to a local
authority or rural district council
under paragraph (a) of this subsection shall be subject to the same
conditions as are imposed by the resolution on grants or exemptions
from rates given by such authority
or council, and shall be paid by the

(1) of section one of the Act of 1932

Sir DAWSON BATES: First of all,
might I explain that, as hon. Members

Paper have been considerably altered from

Paper; but, while the alterations are extensive, they are alterations of form
rather than of substance, and portion of

avoid legislation by reference.
These new Clauses are designed to carry
out the alterations which I indicated in
my speech on the Second Reading of the
Bill. They provide that a local authority
may resolve to give a subsidy or the
equivalent exemption from rates, subject
to such conditions as they may decide with
the approval of the Ministry, and included
in this power is the power of making a
condition restricting the rent at which the
houses may be let for a period not exceeding three years from the date on which
the subsidy is paid.
as
Where the local authority does not pass
a resolution deciding to impose such conditions, the subsidy will be regulated by
the provisions of the Bill as it now stands,
and the procedure will be the same
heretofore, but where the local authority
passes a resolution imposing restrictions
the procedure will remain as heretofore up
to the point at which the Ministry is satisfied that the house or houses have been
completed in a workmanlike manner, but
from that point the administration will
be taken over by the local authority. The
Government subsidy will be paid not to
the builder of the house but to the local
authority, and that authority will be responsible for paying over not only its own
subsidy, but also that contributed by the
Government to the builder, and it will
further be responsible for seeing that the
conditions imposed under its resolutions
are observed.
Members of the Committee will
remember that there are already certain
restrictions as to enlargement and so
forth, which are enforceable by the
Ministry. It would not be practicable,
however, that the Ministry should be
responsible for enforcing some restrictions
and the local authority responsible for
others, and, accordingly, the amendments
provide that, where there are what I may
call local authority restrictions in force,
the local authority shall be responsible for
the enforcement of the restrictions imposed
by themselves under the powers now given
and also for the statutory restrictions for
which the Ministry are now responsible.

Mr. HANNA: That is a point of very
considerable importance, but the view
that has been put forward by the representatives of the local authorities to the
Government, and one that I have a great
deal of sympathy with, is this. Let me
instance a case. A builder approaches
a local authority to make arrangements
to build six houses, and he wants a subsidy in respect of those six houses. If
the local authority tell him he must not
charge more than, let me say, 5s a week
for those houses for three
years the
builder might be induced to go on and
build the houses on those terms. But if
the local authority says that the builder
must not increase the rent of those houses
for, say, ten years, we think the number
of houses that would be built would be
fewer.
The period of three years which we
arrived at was something in the nature of
a compromise. I do not think it would
be wise for the Committee in the meantime to increase the number of years to
which this rent would be limited, because
we think it would militate against the
building of houses. I am sure the hon.
Member for South Derry (Mrs. Parker)
will appreciate that that is a factor in
the situation. The point has already
received a good deal of consideration, and
I would be very loath to increase the
period of three years at the present
stage. It is an experiment we are
adopting at the request of the local
authorities, and I would not like to place
it in any greater jeopardy than it is at
the present moment.

LAND PURCHASE ACT, 1925.
3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the approximate number of farms taken
over under the Land Purchase Act, 1925;
the number which have not been completed and registered by certificate as
transferred; and whether he can state
the cause of the delay.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
to reply.
According to the last report furnished
to me, which shows the position on the
1st September last, the total number of
holdings, particulars of which have been
lodged by the owners pursuant to the
provisions of Part II of the Northern
Ireland Land Act, 1925, is 39,057.
In the case of 37,906 of these the
purchase money has been advanced and
annuities have been set up.
In 12,113 the holdings have been revested in the tenants.
I may add that the progress which is
being made in the process of re-vesting
is quite satisfactory, and I can assure my
hon. Friend that it is, in fact, being
considerably expedited.
Major McCORMICK: Would the
Minister state approximately when the
whole matter of land purchase will be
completed at the present rate of progress?
Mr. BARBOUR: Every effort is being
made to expedite the completion of this
transaction. I may say that the number
of cases now dealt with each year is nearly
14,000, and if that can be maintained
all the vestings should be completed
within eighteen months or two years.
Major McCORMICK: Thank you.

Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked to
reply.
My Colleagues and I regret the low
prices which prevail in respect of many
agricultural products at the present time.
The Government is, however, endeavouring to ameliorate the position of
producers by the introduction of schemes
for the better marketing of their produce.
It is not the case that pork markets have
been closed through the Government's
policy. Certain difficulties have occurred
which, however, are disappearing.
The position was fully explained to the
hon. Member by my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Agriculture, on Tuesday.
In regard to the proposal contained
in the latter part of the hon. Member's
question, I would point out that my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
dealt fully with the Land Purchase
Annuity Sinking Fund when explaining
the Resolutions relating to the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Bill, which was
before this House only a few weeks ago.
The fund will be just sufficient to meet
its statutory requirements, and my right
hon. Friend regrets, therefore, that it is
impossible to accede to the hon. Member's request.

or

under their Ministry and their total cost.

reply.
Since the 1st January, 1933, the following nine inspectors have been appointed
by the Ministry:-
Two temporary veterinary inspectors at
£383 per annum inclusive.
Three ship inspectors at £117 per
annum inclusive.
One ship inspector at £94 10s per
annum inclusive.
Three junior inspectors on the scale.
£200 £15-£400 with bonus.

staff at salaries of £3 13s 6d per week for

Fourteen potato inspectors for a period

Ten egg instructors for the period from

be justified in keeping them any longer.
I know that they were anxious to get
away about half-past three. I protest
against the adjournment of the House.
I feel that as a professional politician I
am justified in doing that. Every one of
you on the opposite side of this House is
a professional politician. There are no
amateurs
over there. It is not like
sport. I wish you were sportsmen. We
have only met for a few weeks, and I
protest in the strongest possible manner
against the proposed adjournment, as our
services could be usefully employed here
in doing something for the people. I am
speaking on behalf of the electors that I
represent, on behalf of the hundred
thousand unemployed workers in Northern
Ireland-I know that the Minister of
Labour disputes those figures-on behalf
of the single men and the single women
who are in destitution and a burden to
their parents. You have no reason to be
proud of yourselves. You have met for
a few weeks. You have done nothing,
and now you are going to do nothing
until the 9th November. Representing,
as I do, the intelligent electors of
Shankill, I protest.
Major McCORMICK: Before this
Motion is put to the House I should like
to remind the Members that this proposed
adjournment precludes the discussion of
the Betting Bill, which is down for Second
Reading on Tuesday next. I feel that I
should make a protest on that ground. I
understand that Government business has
precedence over a Private Member's Bill,
but I claim that this Bill deals with a
matter of public interest. Whilst I shall
agree with the decision of the House in
the matter, I wish to say that the Bill
deals with vital matters, the healthy
ventilation of which would do no harm.
A Bill will be brought forward in the
Imperial House of Commons on this subject sooner or later, and it is a vital issue
that must be faced. Therefore, I wish
to ask if the adjournment of the House
will prevent my moving the Second Reading of this Bill. Certain opposition has
been shown to the Bill, but I think in
avoiding the issue at the present time
those Members have shown great weakness.
On the other hand, I would say
that hon. Members on my left and some
in front were anxious to hear the discussion on the Bill. I say that to their
credit. I beg to make this mild protest.
Mr. BYRNE: I should like to say a
few words with regard to a very important
matter. Some time ago the Poor Law
Guardians, the Corporation, and the
Government came to an arrangement
whereby a scheme was introduced to provide a very great deal of employment
and relief from distress. I understand
that the Government have now refused to
contribute to that scheme, and that they
are awaiting the introduction of a Bill
on the other side of the water. The
people who have been getting this employment and relief feel very much dissatisfied. I have them coming to me
every day to find out what is going to
happen. As soon as the Bill is introduced across the water, I hope no time
will be allowed to lapse before this Government takes up the proposals and continues the relief works. We all know
very well that these people are in great
distress when they apply for this relief.
I know from my own experience that
they would far rather be working than
getting money for nothing. They feel
that the schemes instituted by the Corporation are coming to an end, and that
they will be paid off. I sincerely hope
there will be no reduction in the allowances they get. I hope that this matter
will receive serious consideration, and
that as soon
as this Bill is introduced
across the water no time will be lost in
giving it effect here. There is another
matter to which I should like to draw
attention. I meet single people who can
get no relief of any kind either from
the Labour Exchange or the Poor-law
Board.
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not see how
the hon. Member's remarks relate to the
Motion before the House.
Mr. BYRNE: I only wanted to express the hope that the Government
would lose no time in connection with
this matter. I want to speak with regard
to single people. A lady called with me
the other day. She has two brothers,
single men, walking about. She has 16s
a week on which to maintain herself and
her daughter and two brothers. I hope
the Government will at an early date
consider this important matter.

Mr. HENDERSON: On looking over

and back passages. I contend that anyone who receives the subsidy for constructing these houses should be compelled
to complete the streets and back passages.
I am not quite satisfied with the condition of affairs that exists in the
different localities where the houses were
erected under the £140 subsidy. Many

streets, and that was with the knowledge

Then take Clause 2, where it says
rents can be restricted. This restriction
is only for three years.
That means that
these people who have received the subsidy for the erection of these houses can,
at the end of three years, charge whatever rent they like. That is a most
outrageous proposal. If unrestricted
rent is bad for three years it should be
bad as long as these houses exist. Why
should the right hon. Gentleman introduce this term of three years? Some
person gets into one of these new houses
for which the Government give a grant
of £25. The local authorities will not be
tripping over themselves to give this
additional grant.
few of the
Very few
councils will increase this grant from £25

Sir DAWSON BATES: I never said

Mr. HENDERSON: You said it in the

side Belfast this Bill will just be as great

I am supporting this Bill as the lesser

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am sure it
will interest the House to know that this

the agricultural Members even a few

I was
rather intrigued yesterday or the day before when this Bill was discussed, to hear
the Member for Pottinger assuring the

Affairs.
I sympathise with the Minister of
Home Affairs in dealing with the housing
problem. I think it is one of the most
terrible legacies that could have been
left. He and I are old enough to remember when there was no housing
problem in the city of Belfast, when, as
a matter of fact, the population of this
city was not only the best housed but the
most cheaply housed in the United
Kingdom. Indeed, I believe the rents
then were only 47 per cent. of what they
were in corresponding cities in other parts
of the United Kingdom. But owing to
a variety of circumstances the housing
question has become an exceedingly difficult one, and a man with less courage
than the Minister of Home Affairs might
very well have been daunted by its difficulties. I do not for a moment pretend
to believe that this Bill is going to finally
settle the housing problem, but at any
rate it is an attempt on the part of the
Minister of Home Affairs and the Government to continue their efforts to solve a
problem which was not of their own
creation.
I rise especially to draw the attention
of the Minister of Home Affairs to the
plight of the Labouring classes. I think
there is no class in Northern Ireland
that deserves more at the hands of the Government than the agricultural labourers
of this Province. They are a loyal, industrious, and honourable class, and they
cannot be put on a comparison with the
industrial classes in the City. I do not
know if in the matter of legislation the
Minister would not be wiser to keep their
case apart from the industrial question.
There is no doubt about it that in the
rural districts there is an urgent need
for a big, generous policy in connection
with housing. To-day we are spending
a large sum of money in building new
schools, and I for one am very glad to see

these new schools being erected all over

spent five hours a day in these palaces
they have to spend the rest of the day
in what are little better than hovels.
I would also say this; that it is poor
economy to spend money in trying to cure
people of disease and not try to prevent
it. Bad housing is certainly one of the most
general causes of disease, and I do appeal
to the Minister of Home Affairs to take
this question up in a very large spirit.
We who know the Minister of Home
Affairs realise that he is a man of great
courage, and I would ask him in this
respect to take his courage in both hands
and see to it that not a single hovel is
left in Northern Ireland. The Minister
has rendered very notable service to this
Province, and he could not crown those
services better than by being able to say,
when he lays down the reins of his office

left in the rural districts, or indeed in
the urban districts of Northern Ireland.
I am well aware that this is largely a
question of money. Unfortunately the
Minister of Home Affairs has not got unlimited cash to deal with this problem,
but I was very glad to note that in the
course of the discussion on the Second
Reading of this Bill the right hon.
Gentleman promised to give sympathetic

that help should be given towards the

expense in building new cottages. Hon.
Members know that the Scotch are not
