out very well.
The local councils-and I speak particularly for my own constituency-are
anxious to co-operate in every possible.
way with the right hon. Gentleman in
solving this housing problem. I am sorry
the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie)
is not here to-day because he has spent

glad that the Member for Pottinger takes
even
a second-hand interest in North
Antrim, because even when he gets so
closely in touch with the constituency as
second-hand knowledge it will be an advantage to him. The Ballymoney Rural
District Council is most anxious to help
forward a real big housing scheme for
agricultural labourers. Two years ago,
the Council had 400 applications for new
cottages, and I am assured by members of
that Council that most of those applications would have been granted, but owing
to the money restrictions it was found
impossible to go on with the scheme.
Might I point out to the Minister that
if there is not enough money to help
everyone and I presume that is the
position he finds himself in-then our

first, and in this Province there is no
class who are poorer than the agricultural
labourers. The majority of the farmers,
anxious as they are to help forward any
scheme for the building and repair of
cottages, are not able to do it. Housing
in the country districts is becoming
a really serious problem, and I can assure
the Minister of Home Affairs that the
two rural district councils in my own
division will help him in every way they
can to solve this housing problem.
In spite of the criticism of the Member
for Pottinger I say that these councils
are composed of generous hearted and
kindly men who realise the suffering
caused by bad housing, and they are
anxious to help in every way they can.
They are really hampered because of the
lack of money, and I would appeal with
all the strength I can to the right. hon.
Gentleman to give particular attention
to this agricultural housing problem and
to help us in the agricultural districts to
wipe out the hovels that are a danger to
health and a menace to the well-being

Oral Answers to Questions.
NORTHERN IRELAND APPLES.
1. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is satisfied as to
the effect of the spray fluid recommended
by his officials for the spraying of apples
last spring; whether the apple crop has
been ruined by this spray fluid, and, if
so, whether he is prepared to compensate
the apple growers.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I assume the
hon. Member is referring to certain
mineral oil sprays recommended in a
leaflet issued by my Ministry last spring
for the better control of the pest known
as the capsid bug. If this assumption be
correct, I am not only quite satisfied but
I am convinced that the sprays referred
to gave excellent results when applied in
accordance with the directions given in
the leaflet. No crops have been ruined
by this spray, but I am advised that in
a few cases where growers omitted to
follow the Ministry's directions, and consequently sprayed their trees at a later
stage than that recommended by the
Ministry, growth was temporarily checked,
although, fortunately, no serious or permanent damage was done. The hon.
Member will, I feel sure, be interested
to know that in the apple orchard competition for 1933 the two premier awards
went to crops on which one of the mineral
oil sprays recommended by the Ministry,
and to which he refers, was used.
In view of those facts the hon. Member
will realise that the question of compensation obviously does not arise.
2. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if only
ten per cent. of the apples grown in
Northern Ireland are free from all
blemish; whether a large tonnage of the
very largest and best Bramleys grown have
more than three-quarter inch blemish,
and under the Ministry's regulations are
thereby not available for exportation except in bags to a factory at the price of
£1 per ton to the grower, and, if so,
whether he is prepared to compensate the
growers and alter the regulations.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I do
not accept the view that only ten per
cent. of the apples grown in Northern Ireland in the past season are free from
blemish, nor can I agree with the suggestion that a large tonnage of the largest
and best Bramleys have more than the
maximum percentage of blemish permitted
by the Ministry's regulations in regard to
apples for export under approved grades.
Further, I am satisfied that where orchards
have been properly cared for there is no
difficulty in exporting a large proportion
of the fruit under one or other of the
authorised grades. Consequently, the
question of compensating the growers or
altering the regulations does not arise.

SALE OF GERMAN OATMEAL.

aware that German flake oatmeal is being

quarter-stone bags without any indication
as to the country of origin, and that
patriotic housewives in Northern Ireland
are buying this meal under the impression.
that it is made from home-grown oats, and
what steps he proposes to take to put an
end to this, and so protect the interests of
Northern Ireland farmers.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply to this question.
The hon. Member will be aware that the
marking of foreign produce exposed for
sale in the United Kingdom is a matter
falling within the ambit of the Merchandise Marks Acts, the administration of
which is reserved to the Parliament of the
United Kingdom.
to
My attention has, however, been drawn
an alleged infringement of the
Merchandise Marks (Imported Goods)
No. 5 Order, 1928, in respect of the sale
of certain foreign oat products in Northern Ireland.
I am having careful inquiries made
into the matter, and I can assure the hon.
Member that, if a prima facie case is
established, the attention of the appropriate authority will be drawn to it.

RENTS OF DECONTROLLED AND
SUBSIDY HOUSES.
5. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received
copies of protests sent by tenants of decontrolled and subsidy-built houses to the
owners against the heavy rents they are
compelled to pay; whether the Government will bring those dwelling-houses,
de-controlled at the passing of the 1932
Act, back to the controlled rent as recommended by the Select Committee set up
by the Prime Minister, or set up a fair
rents court so that these tenants of noncontrolled dwelling-houses and business
premises may have an opportunity to
appeal for relief; whether it is a fact that
the owners of subsidy-built houses have a
return of about 25 per cent. on their
outlay as compared with 8 per cent. to
owners of controlled property.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to reply.
Individual complaints have been received
from time to time regarding rents charged
by landlords, but, at the same time, it
is only fair to say that representations
have also been received from owners of
controlled property pointing out that after
payment of the outgoings on their property they are getting little or no return.
All these factors were carefully considered and debated at the time when the
Rent and Mortgage Interest (Restriction)
Act of 1932 was passed by Parliament,
which Act provides that houses which
were subject to control at that time would
continue to be subject to control until the
1st May, 1936. Under those circumstances it would be inequitable and
improper to introduce any further legislation at present.

They are not going to see their income,
their ill-gotten gains, cease flowing into
their lockers. If you do not prevent

who will stop the exploitation of the
tenants. I hope that I will be one of the
blockades. I am a man in a block-house,
if you know what that means.
the war I visited a block-house, which
existed for the purpose of checking

approaching. I have seen for a long

the people of Northern Ireland, and I
have seen through the glasses of the right

shortly for some Members of the Government. The question will be asked them,
Why did they make promises. Why did
they put laws on the Statute Book and
fail to see them executed in the same way
as other laws on the Statute Book? One
law was placed on the Statute Book that
they did see carried out, and that was
they saw the landlord got the 30 per
cent. over and above the pre-war rent,
and if any tenant failed to pay that the
landlord has the law to evict him out of
his home. You see that side of the
picture all right, but you cannot see the
right and justice of the tenants' claim,
when that claim is against the powerful
class called landlords.
That is the protest I make on behalf
of that section of the community, who
are fortunate enough to have the little
protection they have got. If they are
not careful in the very early future that
protection will be taken away from them,
because I know the minds of the Government have been concentrating on how
best to take away the law as it stands
and open an avenue for the propertyowning classes to exploit and get easy
gains from those who cannot afford it.
That is all I have to say on that point
of the question.
I come now to another question, of

Mr. Byrne asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number
of claims for the Widows' and Orphans'
Pension which have been refused owing

Unemployment Act being exhausted
prior to their death; whether most of
these men were insured persons for
many years before becoming unemployed; whether the Government can
take any action to remedy this hardship.
I need not go over the other part. The
Minister of Labour's answer was as

:
The Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) No claims for widows' or
orphans' pensions have been disallowed
on the grounds that the husbands'

to death.

accordance with the facts, and a statement
likely to create misapprehension in the

claims have passed through my hands. I
have dealt with large numbers of claims

BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall, in His Majesty's name, summon,
prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF SAINT
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the fifth day of
December, one thousand nine hundred
and thirty-three, to be then holden.
Given this eighth day of November,
one thousand nine hundred and thirtythree.
(Signed by his own hand) ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.

who spoke although they may have very

That is as it should be, because
if we had not an independent Speaker,

May I say that it is a very great

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
elections for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or

misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that

offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I feel confident that the deliberations
of this, the Fourth Parliament of
Northern Ireland, now being inaugurated, will be conducted with the care,
wisdom and moderation which have in
in past years characterized the work of
both Houses.
I am gratified to learn that a substantial increase in the volume of
employment has taken place during the
current year and that the number of
persons registering for work has fallen
by about one-fifth, the improvement
being particularly marked in our staple
industries of shipbuilding and linen
manufacture. There are indications of
still further improvement, so I am
not without hope that the progress
already made towards general industrial
recovery will not only be maintained,
but accelerated. In the course of
twelve months about 24,000 persons
have been assisted in securing employment through the medium of our
Employment Exchanges.
The identity of our economic and industrial interests with those of the rest
of the United Kingdom has been demonstrated very clearly during the past
few months by the figures for trade and
employment both in Great Britain and
in Northern Ireland, which coincide to
a remarkable degree. It is evident that
Northern Ireland is sharing fully the
advantage of all those far-reaching
changes which the British Government
have initiated in the sphere of Imperial
and International relationships. My
Government will continue to give sym-
King's Speech
Debate on the Address
18 DECEMBER 1933
pathetic and unremitting attention to
all practicable measures for the development of the resources of the country
and will use every available means of
stimulating the demand for the agricultural and industrial products of our
area.
You will be invited to give consideration to a comprehensive measure designed to place Unemployment Insurance
on a sound and permanent footing and
to establish a new system for the ablebodied unemployed who are outside
insurance. By these proposals the social
standards of our unemployed workpeople will be maintained equal in every
way to those enjoyed by their fellowcountrymen elsewhere in the United
Kingdom.
Under the Agricultural Marketing
Act schemes are being prepared by the
Ministry of Agriculture dealing with
the Marketing of Milk and Potatoes.
It was found impracticable last Session
to consider proposals for the reform of
certain aspects of Local Government
Administration; a Bill dealing with
this matter will be laid before you.
The number of accidents on our
roads, resulting in loss of life and injury
to persons and property is causing my
Government much concern; you will be
invited to give consideration to a Bill
designed with the object of remedying
this state of affairs.
A measure will also be laid before
you dealing with the qualifying period
of residence governing the registration
of voters in Northern Ireland.
Other Bills will be introduced regarding the following matters:—
Agricultural Marketing.
Destructive Insects and Pests.
Charitable Donations and
Bequests.
Fisheries.
Railways.
Donaghadee Harbour.
Printers.
Coroners.
Members of the House of Commons.
The estimates for the public services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am gratified to learn that law and
order continue to be effectually maintained, and I am sure that the steps
taken by the authorities to this end
have the whole-hearted support of all
law-abiding citizens.
The policy of my Government in
aiming at a prolonged period freed, as
far as possible, from contentious legislation and during which the business
community and our unrivalled agriculturists and artisans may pursue their
respective vocations meets with my
highest commendation.
Outstanding progress has been made
with the work of electrification, and
much encouragement can be derived
from the fact that not only rural communities, but also outlying industrial
establishments, are readily taking
advantage of the cheap power rendered
available to them by this method.
The educational system continues to
develop satisfactorily, and notwithstanding the difficulties occasioned by
the present strain on public finance,
substantial progress has been made in
the replacement of unsuitable buildings
by modern structures, with resulting
improvement in the well-being of both
scholars and teachers.
It is gratifying to learn of the marked
success which continues to attend the
skilfully organised voluntary efforts to
stimulate the demand within Northern
Ireland for goods produced by manuhome
facturers at
and within the
Empire, and also the measures
instituted to attract tourists to our
shores, and thus to turn to account
in the interest of our people generally
those natural assets with which our
country has been so generously endowed.
And I pray that the blessing of
Almighty God may rest upon your
deliberations.

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HousE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
In
All hon. Members will agree that
throughout the last Parliament the most
serious, most difficult, and most insistent
problem with which this House was concerned was that of unemployment.
Northern Ireland the problem of unemployment is a peculiarly urgent problem.
Those of us who live in the city of Belfast
and who have the honour to represent
Belfast constituencies have been brought
daily into close touch with the acute
hardship and suffering which a prolonged
period of unemployment, such as we have
recently been going through, must of
necessity bring in its train.
It is accordingly with very great pleasure
that we welcome the clear note of optimism
at the outset of the Gracious Speech. It
is gratifying to learn that a substantial
increase in the volume of employment has
taken place during the current year. It
is still more gratifying to learn that there
are indications of still further improvement, and I am sure every Member of this
House will fervently and sincerely re-echo
the expression of hope contained in the
Gracious Speech that the progress already
made towards a general industrial recovery
will not only be maintained but will be
accelerated. (Hon. Members :
Hear,
hear.)
In dealing with the problem of unemployment the duty of a Government such
as our Government of Northern Ireland
is, as I conceive it, two-fold. In the first
place, it is the duty of the Government to
endeavour by all means to mitigate the
evil of unemployment by fostering work
within its area. This our Government has
steadily endeavoured to do during the
whole period for which it has held office.
I need only refer to the long series of
Statutes passed with that object, to the
loans made under the Loans Guarantee
Acts, which have had the effect of providing the shipyards of Belfast with a very
considerable volume of work which would
not otherwise have come to the city.
But it is not only by legislation and by
loans under the Loans Guarantee Acts
that service has been rendered by the
Government to the Province in this
respect. The Prime Minister and every
single Member of his Cabinet have by their
own unceasing personal efforts done much
to attract work to Northern Ireland which
otherwise would not have come here, and
I hope that some day the people of Northern Ireland will adequately appreciate how
much has been done in that regard by the
Members of the Government by their own
personal, unremitting efforts in exercising
influence in every quarter in which they
could possibly exercise their personal influence, and that the people will also learn
how great success in many instances has
resulted from their efforts.
When we have been passing through
a period of world-wide depression for a
number of years, it is impossible for a
Government in an area like ours to abolish
unemployment by securing that every man
should have work. Unemployment is not
a local thing. It is a world-wide thing,
and you cannot abolish it simply by passing an Act of Parliament. There will be
in such circumstances a number, be it
small or be it great, of persons in the community who are unable to obtain work,
and are accordingly unable to obtain by
the fruits of their labour the ordinary
means of subsistence. The Government,
in such circumstances, has a duty to discharge a duty to see that provision is
made for those who become the victims of
unemployment through no fault of their
own. That duty has been faced by the
Government, and in addressing itself to
the task our Government here has one
great piece of good fortune, and that
piece of good fortune is the close link
existing between Northern Ireland and
Great Britain.
It has been the good fortune of us in
Northern Ireland that in the times of
stringency and hardship through which
the country has been passing during a
number of years, we have been able
in this little area of ours to make the same
provision for the victims of unemployment as has been made in the great
and wealthy country of Great Britain. It
is a source of great satisfaction that that
link has been maintained, and that in
the Unemployment Bill, which has been
introduced into the British Parliament,
the British Government propose to take
power to make reciprocal agreements with
the Government of Northern Ireland for
the purpose of dealing with unemployment. That is a provision which we
welcome with great satisfaction. In the
British Bill it is proposed that a statutory
unemployment insurance committee
should be set up, a committee of great
prestige, to deal with the whole problem
which at times arises out of the very complex and difficult subject of unemployment insurance. That committee is to
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
18 DECEMBER 1993
consist of five members. It is with great
satisfaction that we in Northern Ireland
have learned that one of the five members
shall be appointed after consultation with
the Minister of Labour for Northern Ireland, showing, I think conclusively, that
the close relationship which exists between the British scheme of unemployment insurance and the Northern Ireland
scheme of unemployment insurance is to
continue in the future as it has done in
the past.
In the Gracious Speech, the intention
of the Government is announced to introduce a comprehensive Measure designed
to place unemployment insurance on a
sound and permanent footing, and to
establish a new system for the able-bodied
unemployed who are outside insurance.
One gathers from these words that the intention of the Government is to introduce
a Measure somewhat on the lines of the
Measure to which I have already referred,
and which is now passing through the
British House. If the Bill to be introduced here is at all on the lines of the
English Bill, it will indeed be a very comprehensive and far-reaching Measure.
The British Bill well merits the description of the Imperial Minister of Labour,
Sir Henry Betterton, when, in moving the
Second Reading in the British Imperial
House, he described it as
The greatest Measure of social
progress which has been presented to
the country by any Government for
many generations.
It
The aim of the British Bill and of the
Bill which will be presented to our House
is twofold. In the first place it aims at
maintaining the unemployment insurance
scheme as a true insurance scheme.
aims at placing the scheme on a true insurance basis, and to keep it and maintain
it as a solvent and self-supporting scheme.
In the second place it recognises that the
poor-law does not provide the proper
machinery for relieving persons who,
through no fault of their own, in a time
of unemployment, have found themselves
unable to support themselves. Accordingly the Measure provides that the unemployed industrial worker who is outside
the benefits of the insurance field is not
to be brought into contact with the poorlaw administration. The proposal is that
the State should accept general responsibility for the industrial able-bodied unemployed worker who is not entitled to
benefit in the insurance scheme, or,
having been so entitled, has ceased to be
entitled by reason of his insurance benefits having run out.
This is the first attempt, I think, by
any Government to deal comprehensively
outside the poor-law with the position of
able-bodied unemployed workers who are
not embraced within the insurance
scheme. It will be seen that the changes
proposed are radical. They are changes
which cannot be carried through by
a simple one-or-two-Clause Bill. They
are changes which deal with the subject
of unemployment insurance which has
become exceedingly complex, and accordingly the Measure which proposes to carry
through such changes must of necessity
be a complicated Measure. When the
Measure indicated in the Gracious Speech
is introduced here, it will be the duty of
the House in the first place to consider
the broad outlines of the Measure, and
whether they commend themselves to the
wisdom of the House as likely to bring
benefit to Northern Ireland. If they do
commend themselves to the wisdom of the
House, it will be the duty of the House
in Committee to examine in detail those
provisions, and I venture to say that it
will be the duty of every Member of this
House, whatever his political faith, whatever interest he represents, whatever side
of the House he sits on, to contribute
to the consideration and to the discussion
of this Measure all the experience and all
the wisdom which he personally can bring
to bear upon it, for not only as a House
is it our duty, but it is the duty of every
individual, to do everything we can to
improve the measures which are suggested
for the alleviation of unemployment and
the improvement of unemployment insurance.
One other matter which is referred to in
the Gracious Speech which I think is of
paramount importance is the intimation.
that under the Agricultural Marketing
Act schemes are being prepared by the
Ministry of Agriculture dealing with the
marketing of milk and potatoes. In formulating these schemes under the Agricultural Marketing Act, it is sometimes
lightly assumed that there are only two
parties to be considered: first, the producer, and, secondly, the distributor.
That I conceive to be a great mistake.
There are three interests to be considered.
First, the producer; secondly, the distributor; and, thirdly, the consumer; and I
venture to say that the most important
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
of these three interests to be considered
is the interest of the consumer, especially
in regard to such a commodity as milk,
which is practically an essential of life to
everyone, and which is an essential food
of the most helpless members of our community.
Accordingly, the consumer must be safeguarded first in regard to the quality of
the product, and, secondly, in regard to
price. In regard to the quality of milk,
I suggest that any scheme which is formulated under the Agricultural Marketing
Act for the marketing of milk must have
as one of its cardinal provisions something
that will endeavour to raise and maintain
the average of the quality which is supplied in Northern Ireland. Its aims should
be that within a very short space of time,
within a very few years, the milk placed
on the market of Northern Ireland should
be of the same quality as Grade "A" T.T.
milk. That is one of the things which I
think ought to be aimed at by such a
scheme.
The
The other matter which must be dealt
Iwith in the interests of the consumers is
price. A milk marketing scheme differs
in one essential from many other marketing schemes for agricultural products. It
differs from the Pigs Marketing Scheme
or a Potato Marketing Scheme. And the
difference is this, in the case of pigs or
potatoes only a relatively small percentage of the produce of Northern Ireland
is marketed in Northern Ireland.
principal market for pigs and potatoes is
to be found outside Northern Ireland, and
the price to be obtained for pigs or potatoes in Northern Ireland must of necessity
be controlled by the prices obtainable in
the principal market for those commodities. So in regard to the marketing of
pigs and potatoes, the prices of necessity
must be largely controlled by the prices
obtainable in Great Britain.
With milk the position is totally
different. Substantially speaking, all
milk produced in Northern Ireland will be
consumed in Northern Ireland. Substantially speaking, all milk consumed in
Northern Ireland must be produced in
Northern Ireland, and so we have not in
the case of milk the factor of cross-
Channel milk affecting the price.
consumer in Northern Ireland will be
largely affected by the price fixing operations of such a board as a Milk Marketing
Board, and the consumer will be entitled
The
to look to the Board to see that a fair
price, and nothing more than a fair price,
is fixed.
1S
The justification of any marketing
board for agricultural produce is surely
this, that it will bring about a more
economical marketing and distribution of
the produce. If the Milk Marketing
Board succeeds in effecting a more
economical distribution of the produce,
if it succeeds in effecting savings in the
production and marketing of milk, the
consumers, the ordinary people, will be
entitled to ask that those savings, or at
any rate a proportion of those savings, be
passed on to the consumers. Accordingly
when the Milk Marketing Board
established, I think it will be vital to see
that as well as the producers being represented on that Board, and the distributors
being represented on that Board, there
will be ample representation of the consumers on that Board. From events
which took place in the milk trade some
time ago, the ordinary consumer got the
impression, rightly or wrongly—I think,
rightly that both producers and distributors are well able to look after their
own interests. There is no one to protect
the consumer except the Board, and it is
essential, when the Board is established,
that a very large representation of the
interests of the consumers shall be on that
Board.
I have ventured to deal at some length
with these two topics, the topic of the
proposed Unemployment Insurance Bill
and the proposed marketing scheme in
regard to milk, because I think they are
the two most important topics dealt with
in the Gracious Speech so far as it affects
the ordinary individual residing in an
urban area in Northern Ireland. There
are other provisions outlined in the
Speech, not I think of such cardinal
importance but yet of considerable
importance in themselves. The result of
all appears to be that this Parliament will
have work before it worthy of our best
thoughts and our best acts which will
engage, and will require to engage, our
earnest attention and the best efforts of
every individual Member. I venture to
promise on behalf of every Member of this
House that the best thought and the best
efforts of every individual Member will be
given unremittently to the great and
difficult questions we will have to consider
in the legislation adumbrated in the
Gracious Speech. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

Debate on the Address
18 DECEMBER 1933
Dr WILSON (in morning dressy: I
rise to second the Address, and in doing
so crave the indulgence of the House in
the performance of a duty which is both
pleasant and arduous, arduous because of
my lack of Parliamentary experience.
This occasion confers a signal honour
upon the constituents of the Iveagh
Division, and upon myself a great compliment. Of both I am indeed duly
appreciative. The strongest impression
made upon me by the Gracious Speech is
that it demonstrates a full and sympathetic knowledge of the present day
needs of Northern Ireland and a sincere
desire to improve the positions of both
farmers and artisans. Keference is made
to the prime essential of maintaining law
and order, and I take advantage of this
opportunity to assure the Minister of
Home Affairs of the hearty support and
co-operation of the Iveagh Division of
Down in all his efforts in that direction.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It
Something has already been accomplished to improve the condition of the
farmers, and it is a delight to me as representing an extensive farming community
to note that legislation is in view to provide schemes for the marketing of two
staple products, milk and potatoes.
seems absurd that milk for which the producer is paid at the rate of 10d per gallon
should cost the consumer exactly double
that amount. The production of milk is
at present most unprofitable and the farmer will welcome any scheme to set the
industry at work on sound financial lines.
My earnest hope is that these marketing
schemes will be brought into force at the
earliest possible date and that they may
be faithful pointers to the fact that our
idea is to continue to advance step by
step with Great Britain and thus enjoy
the advantages accruing from the closest
relationship with the other units of the
British Empire, and especially with Great
Britain.
a
Mention is made of a Measure designed
to place unemployment insurance on
sound footing, and surely it is a source of
gratification that the basis of these proposals is the maintenance of the social
standards of our unfortunate unemployed
upon an equality with those of their
fellows in Great Britain.
The reference in the Gracious Speech
to the number of accidents on our roads is
timely, and any legislation destined to
improve traffic conditions will be most
welcome and should receive the commendation of all parties. May I express
the hope that no further restrictions will
be laid upon careful motorists, but
rather that slow moving traffic, including pedestrians, may be brought
to realise the necessity for care
of self and consideration of others
in their use of the highways.
To my
mind a very important point tending
towards safety first is the care and upkeep
of roads of all classes, and I suggest that
here is an opportunity to lower the number of those registering at the unemployment exchanges. The country by-roads
are in many cases far from safe and at
little expense could be rendered not only
much safer for traffic, but also a useful
source of employment.
The introduction of a Measure dealing
with the qualifying period of residents in
Northern Ireland governing the regis
tration of voters is an urgent necessity to
counteract the influence of those who
being unable to exist in their own
country invade Northern Ireland, not
always with peaceful intentions, and who
after a short sojourn here reap advantages to which they are not in justice
entitled.
It is most encouraging to note that
progress is being made in the electrification of many districts, and I should like
to think that in the near future all industrial concerns may receive equal
benefits from the scheme. Districts
where the new electricity supply is not
yet available are at a serious disadvantage
so far as running costs are concerned compared with those who are already fortunate enough to obtain their supply from
the Electricity Board.
The policy of the Government as outlined in the Gracious Speech is singularly
free from what may be termed contentious
legislation, and it is our duty as Members
of this House to set an example to
our constitutents by working together
harmoniously to pass into law these ideas
which are so obviously intended for the
benefit of all law-abiding citizens. I beg
to second. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I extend my

dog for the hard road, and to the seconder
as a new Member of this House not yet
tested on that hard road which one has
to travel in this House? I want to say

HOUSE OF COMMONS

my
that the Address has brought
mind back once again to what I
have advocated in this House in regard

Ireland. In the King's Speech there is
one measure of importance mentioned in
a way that will never touch the fringes
of unemployment as far as the situation
in Northern Ireland is concerned. I feel
that the Government are following the
lead given by the National Government,
who have proved their inability to deal
with any question affecting the welfare
of the country. That being so, I fail to
see why the Government of Northern
Ireland should conduct their legislation
on similar lines. If we want to get free
from the disease we have to get at the
root of the disease and remove it, and
perhaps the foundations will come to a
more purified state when the root of this
evil, unemployment, is removed.
I have looked over the King's Speech
at the few moments at my disposal, and
in it I fail to recognise any solution of the
unemployment situation. In the last
Parliament I placed before the House a
solution, but that solution was ignored
and voted out. Whether you may like
that solution or not you will have to
recognise that with your financial responsibilities there must be real effort to get
for those who are unemployed a decent
standard of life. There must be a decent
standard of life whilst in work, and for
those who are thrown out of work through
no fault of their own you will have to
provide a decent standard of maintenance
for themselves, their wives, and their
families. You cannot but realise the
great changes that are taking place
throughout the world. Every country
seems to change. Northern Ireland will
also change. It may not be to-day or
to-morrow, but the change is bound to
come sooner or later, and the sooner the
better. The more patched-up work you
perform the sooner will the change come.
I am not prepared to eulogise the new
Unemployment Insurance Bill for the
simple reason that the British Government
has agreed to put a representative from
Northern Ireland on the Statutory Board
to be set up.
I want to know how far
they are in agreement as to giving the
financial assistance necessary for the
maintenance of the unemployed on
decent standard. I have heard no
a
mention of that, either in the King's
Speech or from the mover or seconder of
the Address in reply. That being so, the
financial part is of more importance to

Board which will be established in
London.
I would like to ask the mover-I know
he is a far-seeing Member and an able
Member-what explanation have we been
given. We have juveniles brought in-or
it is suggested that they should be brought
in-and they are to be made pay 2d. per
week until they are sixteen years of age.
If they become unemployed their parents
are to get 2/- a week on which to keep
them. I have in my hand the report of
a medical expert, and his opinion is that
it would take 5s 11d a week to nourish
and maintain a child and bring it up in
a proper state of health. The lowest
figure is 5s 11d, and still we are being
told the great boon our new Unemployment Insurance Act is going to be to the
children from fourteen to sixteen years
of age.
The other point is that the unemployment problem can never be solved whilst
the present system remains. Professor
Clay in his article on finance says that
the wealth of the country to-day is
centred in 2 per cent. of the population.
Just imagine trying to solve the problem
and make the wheels of industry go when
they are clogged by such conditions. We
are labourers worthy of our hire, and we
expect to get a reasonable return for our
labour. We desire security, we desire
decency and the comforts of life for our
wives and children, and we desire to enjoy
the beauties which the Lord put on this
earth for our eyes to enjoy. Are we
getting those to-day? We are not because of the mist of poverty covering our
eyes.
We cannot see the beauty. We can
see nothing but the degradation of ourselves and our families owing to our want
of purchasing power. That is due to the
system under which we are compelled to
live, and whilst that system remains I
can see no hope for the salvation or relief
of those unfortunate victims who are
walking the streets and cannot find work
to do.
It is all right getting a ship or two, or
even getting half a dozen ships. We are
highly delighted to know that there are
half a dozen or so to come, but that does
not give you a solution of the unemployment difficulty. Your unemployment

difficulty will arise again when the ships

I feel that the new Unemployment Insurance Bill is only another clog in the
wheels of progress, to prop up the old
system and to keep it from falling

Mr. HENDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would challenge you,
without any figures at my disposal at the
moment, when you say that 24,000 people

twelve months. I know the tricks of the
game of making up figures of this kind.
I have had them too often challenged. How

classified six times through having had

general public and your friends, but it
does not deceive anyone on this side of

in Northern Ireland. We know that
there are many thousands of people
to-day who are roaming about receiving neither unemployment insurance, exceptional distress, nor Poor
Law relief because of the harsh administration of the Minister of Labour in
Northern Ireland. That harsh administration is due to the fact that within the
past two years, under the parity arrangement, we ourselves have failed to live up
to our responsibilities in so far as taking
full advantage of the financial arrangements is concerned.
A day or so ago I was reading the
financial account for 1932-33 and was
surprised to find that for unemployment
insurance we claimed no financial assistance last year or the year before under that
financial arrangement. Why have we not
claimed that financial assistance when we
required it? Solely because we have disallowed from 20,000 to 25,000 people their
rights under the unemployment insurance
code. That proved to England that we
were endeavouring to make our fund selfsupporting, and from that point of view.
we would be more likely to get an arrangement under the new Unemployment Insurance Bill which is before the British
House. I am not prepared to make that
sacrifice on behalf of the unemployed for
the sake of this new arrangement, which
I believe will not be an arrangement suitable to you.
How can you expect local
authorities in England to bear part of
your financial responsibility in Northern
Ireland? I can foresee an outcry among
British local authorities which will mean
that you will be turned down and will
receive no financial assistance from the
fund which is to be established under the

now have to buying those commodities which are on the market from

That we do not desire to do, and

Again, we know that some of the people

If those labourers only get that for

if he were not here neither the Prime

of their livelihood is concerned.
The other thing I want to mention, and

away. I would

enjoy in Great

We are not living in a fool's paradise.
We know the wealth of this Province,

We know it has wealth to the extent that

beauties and we could be provided with

that stands between the consumer and the
producer, and we intend to remove that

The PRIME MINISTER:
occasions of this sort it is always one great
pleasure, in the first instance, to congratulate the Mover and Seconder of the
Address, and to my old bachelor Friend
from Willowfield I extend most cordial
congratulations on the way he presented
those particularly interesting points with
which he has associated himself on more
than one occasion in the past. And then,
if I may say so, much as we regret the
loss of the lady Member for the Iveagh
Division, who was a distinguished ornament to this House, we congratulate the
married Member who has come here today and made his maiden speech. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
As a rule when one meets after a
General Election or a prolonged adjournment of any kind, one naturally expects
to find a considerable amount of attack
for the sins and omissions of the Government, and my Colleagues individually
have to answer many a charge. But if
the Leader of the Opposition to-dayand, if I may say so, he has put his case
very moderately and very modestly—is to
be taken as a guide of what grumbles
there are in the Ulster area, I do
not think that any of us will do
anything else except enjoy a very
happy Christmas and a merry New
Year, because, after all, he concentrated
most of his remarks on the subject of unemployment. While we listened to all
that has been said-and we are not deaf
at any time to suggestions made on any
side of the House-I think that thoughtful persons here in Ulster will agree that
the benefits that accrue to us from working
harmoniously with Great Britain in connection with the social services of unemployment are, perhaps, the greatest that
can possibly be conferred on a small community like our own.
It fills me with horror to suggest that we
should depart in any material way from
the system which is in existence in Great
Britain. And perhaps the most valuable
part of this intertwining of the two great
systems is that we have full reciprocity
secured for our workmen who might possibly go over to the Clyde, Tyneside, or
any other shipbuilding centre.
If you
once vary in even a small degree the contributions made by the workers and the
State and the employers-if you vary in
the slightest degree from what is the
custom on the other side, or if you vary
with regard to the benefits received by the
unemployed, then you break the connection between the two, the ill-effects of
which would fall upon the working classes
whom my colleagues and I are desirous to
protect. Therefore, I hope this House

Then I should like to make a short
reference to the marketing of milk, which
has been referred to by all three speakers
who have preceded me.
I can assure
them all, and especially my hon. and
learned Friend behind me (Mr. Black),
that the public will be safeguarded as
far as it possibly can be done in connection with the scheme to be brought
forward. I suppose I have consumed as
much milk as anyone else in my time,
and I have at least a limited knowledge
of the trade gained from my talks with
those who came to me in connection with
the strike that took place a year ago. To
all concerned with this question I say, we
have a young, virile and extraordinarily
clever Gentleman on this Bench who is
going to take charge of this milk question.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is he a farmer?
The PRIME MINISTER: He has been
a farmer from a time when the hon.
Gentleman opposite was probably not
acquainted with any of these farm
problems at all. He is a farmer, like his
father and his grandfather before him.
Mr. HENDERSON: Does he know
anything about pigs?
The PRIME MINISTER: He knows
all about pigs too. The point is, we have
now a new Minister of Agriculture, who
will be charged with the duty of producing
a scheme, which, with patience, will do
away with what everybody recognises
to be, unfortunately, an unsatisfactory
position. Undoubtedly, whatever else
may be said, the farming community
deserve a fair return for the work
that they carry on in connection with the
production of milk. I think they deserve
a little bit more than that, for this reason,
that they run risks that no one else has
to face, because of the nature of their
calling, and because they sometimes meet
with the most unforeseen difficulties
in connection with the weather, the
climate, or a disaster over which they
have no control. Therefore I think that
something satisfactory will have to be
evolved in order to get this milk marketing placed on an equally sound footing
with the marketing of pork. I am
delighted that the right hon. Gentleman
behind me, the Member for Lisnaskea,
will be able to take up this work, fresh
and vigorous as he is, and I am perfectly
certain that he will be as successful in that
direction as he has been in all the rest of
his public work.
The next point I should like to make
is this, that when you look at the Address,
I think you will realise that the Government have done all they possibly can to
keep clear of acrimony or anything likely

with a widowed mother dependent upon
him to be in. Your policy for providing
work for the single young man has
failed deplorably. It is the youth that
is required to build up the wealth of a
country, and you are doing absolutely
nothing for the youth of this country.
You talk about your love of Ulster, and
at the same time you allow these tender
flowers to fade away and die, and then
forget about them.
It is absolutely incorrect to say that
the number registering for work has
fallen by one-fifth. What has really
happened is this. These young men who
have been signing on for ten or twelve
years are getting tired of signing, and
because of that the Minister of Labour
takes it for granted that they have
secured employment. Unfortunately, the
people believe such a statement when
they see it in the Unionist Press, and I
want to ask the Government if it would
not be advisable to have a census taken
of the number of persons who are really
unemployed. You will not agree to that
suggestion, because it would bring out
the truth. There is another charge I
want to make against the Minister of
Labour. I can scarcely find Parliamentary words to express sufficiently what
I feel, but I will express my real feelings
outside this House. The Minister of
Labour has thousands of young men
starving to-day because they are in the
category of seasonal workers, two days a
week men. You are compelling men
who have been driving buses throughout
the country to register, and you are
doing the same with quarrymen and
others. What does the Minister of
Labour care whether any young men in
Northern Ireland starve so long as he
has plenty. How would you like your
post as a Cabinet Minister to be classed
as seasonal work, and be paid accordingly.
You are paid for doing fifty-two weeks
work in the year, and you draw £2,000
a year for two or three weeks' work.

The proper time to discuss that matter is

will include parasites. There are a lot

Then we are going to have more fishery

Milk Board. I hope the new Minister of
Agriculture will have a very successful

although if I had been selecting a gentleman for that job my choice would not
have fallen on the hon. and gallant Member (Sir Basil Brooke). There are other
Members on the same side of the House
who have greater qualifications for that

When he sets up this Milk Board I hope

Gentleman will appoint a practical farmer

Board is set up I hope it will enable the
farmer to get a reasonable profit for his
milk, and that he will sell it at a reasonable price. At the same time, I am
afraid these marketing boards will be very
detrimental to the industrial workers I
have the honour to represent.
I am delighted with the reference in

Harbour. I am glad that any little thing

harbour at Donaghadee has at last borne

Government's neglect of Donaghadee and

There is another matter that requires

that the recommendations brought forward

What you ought to do is this: if it is

you should boost your own, and thus help

much to attract tourists to our country.
Of course there is the natural beauty and
the scenery.
We all realise that the
scenery in Northern Ireland cannot be
equalled in any part of the world; but
there are some other things you require to
do to encourage tourists.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: What are they?
Mr. HENDERSON: I will tell you.
The tourists in Northern Ireland should
have the same rights and privileges as they
enjoy in every other country. They
should be allowed to obtain whatever food
they like, and whatever sort of drink they
like; they should get more freedom. There
is no freedom for tourists in Northern
Ireland at all. What is the position? It
is well known-no one understands it
better than the Prime Minister-that a
tourist who comes to Northern Ireland
has to go to the Free State on Sunday if
he wants to enjoy himself. Would it not
be far better to keep him in Northern
Ireland, to provide for his wants, instead
of letting him stay in Northern Ireland
on Saturday and compelling him to go to
the Free State on Sunday? If you are
anxious to help Northern Ireland, do
something to facilitate the tourists. Here
is an opportune time to see that tourists
are not exploited. The Ministry of Commerce should take drastic action against
anyone who supplies tourists with linen
that is not Irish linen. I know that
tourists coming to our country purchase
what they are told is Irish linen, but when
they go home they find out in all probability that it was made in Czechoslovakia.
That is the curse of the linen industry in
Northern Ireland, and the Minister of
Commerce is taking no action to end it.
In conclusion-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear)-I appeal to the noble Lord to use
his powerful influence with his friends
inside and outside the House against the

how to make linen. That is one of the

appeal to the right hon. Gentleman to

I hope the Minister of Labour will not

huge army of unemployed, and if every
linen factory in Northern Ireland was
working to its full capacity there would
still be large numbers of linen workers

The only hope the noble Lord or the
Minister of Labour has at the present
time is to get new industries created in
an endeavour to absorb the people who
worked previously at those particular industries. You will not get it by sitting
in Glengall Street and denouncing the

Nationalists. The only way you can
bring about peace and contentment in
this country is by taking drastic action

It is not the responsibility of individual

Lord that he should pay a visit to Germany. There a determined effort is
being made to provide work for the people
who are unemployed.
The Prime Minister a minute or so ago

We have always helped anything like

get our wholehearted support. I suggest

Instead of wasting their time gallivanting

He gets about £1,000 more for looking
after one and a quarter million
people-

them and take extracts from them, he

fact correct, and is borne out by these

people employed in the linen trade. Will
hon. Members opposite say that no
improvement is to be found?

Again, the imposition of the import
duties, combined with the effect of the
departure from the gold standard, resulted in a decided falling off in foreign
linens imported into the United Kingdom. During the eleven months ended
30th November, 1933, the value of all
linen goods imported, amounted
£243,000, as compared with £361,000 in
1932, and going further back to 1931 we
find the amount was £664,000. Therefore, hon Members will see there has been
a great drop since 1931 of very nearly
two-thirds of the imports of foreign linen
into the United Kingdom. This again
supports my contention that the trade is
improving.
It is not possible to give with any precision the value of the United Kingdom
market to Northern Ireland manufacturers either immediately prior to the
imposition of the import duties or at the
present time, but it may be accepted that
one of the results of the changed fiscal
policy has been to increase the value of
the home market for the home producer
by at least the value of the decline in
imports of foreign linens, and that in
round figures is an increase in our home
market of half a million pounds per
annum.
There again the figures cannot
be either contradicted or disputed.
The value of linen goods exported from
the United Kingdom during the eleven
months ended 30th November, 1933, was
£5,285,000, or about 11 per cent. more
than the value of those exported during
the corresponding period last year. Further, although the figure I have just
given falls short of the 1930 exports the
fall in the wholesale price level more
than accounts for the decrease.
The increased activity in the export
market is best illustrated by an examination of the quantities of piece goods exported, which in 1933 was higher than
at any time during the past seven years.
Take the figure for 1930 of 61,450,000
square yards, while in 1933 it was
77,601,000 square yards. These figures
are a reflection of our increased trade and,
consequently, increased employment and
so refute the statement made yesterday
from the opposite benches.

of unemployment did not necessarily

Take this question of unemployment.
There is no question so loosely handled,
either in Parliament or elsewhere, as the
question of unemployment. In this connection, may I say at the outset that I
challenge the validity or the method of

one-fifth. In another section of the

interested persons is that those 24,000
are separate and distinct entities, but

I presume the Minister of Labour will

one-fifth, even if it were true that onefifth of the unemployed population has

lay the flattering unction to their souls

humanity, even if one-fifth of the unemployed population has been absorbed into
industry. I have taken considerable
pains with, and given considerable study
to, the whole problem of unemployment,
and I have made myself as familiar with

I have gone to the libraries, and I have

What do we find? We find that the
basic condition which creates unemployment to-day is not a feature of our postwar civilisation, but that this feature
manifested itself in our pre-war conditions. I have here a report issued by
the Engineering and Allied Industries
Association, in which they deal very
comprehensively with this problem of
unemployment. They point out that in
pre-war days we had a standing army of
500,000 persons unemployed, and that in
the post-war period we are going to be
left with a standing army of 12 million.
That is a condition of affairs that is
simply appalling, and ought to command
the respect and serious consideration of
every student of sociology, and I presume
there are some in this House.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
public feeling in many other constituencies where hon. Members were allowed to
be returned unopposed. We could then
have submitted this question of unemployment to the acid test.
The position in regard to unemployment is this. Unemployment is caused
to-day, just as it was in pre-war days, by
something inherent in our social system.
Members may theorise as much as they
like about this, but boiled down it
amounts to this, that unemployment is
caused, generally speaking, by those who
produce goods not getting sufficient back
in the shape of wages or salaries to buy
the goods they have produced; and as
industry is carried on for profit, as soon
as the profit-making motive goes out of
industry, factories, and mills, and workshops have to stop until the glut in the
market has eased itself and some of the
unemployed can again be absorbed into
industry.
This is a basic statement in regard to
unemployment, and I would challenge in
the subsequent debate any Member on
the other side of the House to controvert
that on economic grounds. Now, that
being so, whatever you have got to do
in regard to this problem of unemployment you have got to face up to the implications of it. It is not good enough to
come forward and say that your only
policy is to keep step with the actions of
another Government or another Parliament. That may sound nice from a sentimental point of view, and by the way,
in passing, may I say that if prosperity
in Northern Ireland could be restored by
sentiment, which is poured out by the
bucketful by members of the Unionist
Party, who are true to type-Winston
Churchill said it years ago-if prosperity
could be brought to Northern Ireland by
sentiment or by political slogans Northern
Ireland would be the most prosperous
place on the face of the earth, but at the
present time it is not, because slogans
and sentiment will not do.
You must have some regard to facts.
We have to face up to this, that merely
to come forward to the public time and
again and live in past history-and that
is the curse of Ireland in my opinion,
this desire to live in the realms of the past
-to come forward to the public and say
that you have a policy for all social questions and that is to keep step by step, or
fall into line, or develop on parallel lines
with the Imperial Parliament, is not good
enough in modern-day thought with regard to social problems. To start with,
no Member of the Government can claim
there is any originality of thinking in
dealing with a problem like that.
Almost without exception every question that has been dealt with in Northern
Ireland since its inception is a question
which the Northern Government have not
had to do any thinking about. All they
have contented themselves with doing was
to say, "We will wait and see what they
will do on the other side, and when they
do it we will follow their example as far
as we possibly can." But all the time
while they talk about reciprocity of
arrangements and community of interests
they never face up to the economic implications of the whole situation.
I am privileged to be a member of the
Belfast Corporation, and a few weeks ago
I was summoned to a Committee which
has to have regard to the financial

civic chancellor tell us on that occasion?
He told us that the finances of Belfast had
reached such a parlous condition that there

with a huge increase in its poundage rate
in the near future. And he went on to
add this is the significant thing, and I
am only quoting it to show you the
opinion of this man, a man who certainly
does not share my political faith-that
the time has arrived when some publicspirited person must stand forth in Belfast
and say that we are so poverty stricken
that we cannot possibly follow this traditional policy of maintaining equal standards in our social services with Great
Britain. That is what he said.
I do not want any member of the
Government to twit me afterwards, as
they sometimes do, by saying, “Oh, do
you wish to depart from the social standards?" Certainly not. The highest
social standards are not too high for me,
and I am not going to agree to a bringing
down of the social standards. What I

I was asked in the recent campaign-I

I believe in bringing the rates down to
the level of the poor or the poor up to the

in bringing anybody down, but that I
believed in bringing the submerged tenth

designed to place unemployment insurance on a sound and permanent footing.
I have read through the Clauses of this
Unemployment Insurance Bill which you
are going to try to copy in Northern Ireland, but I venture to predict that it is
going to be more difficult to copy this Bill
in Northern Ireland in its entirety than
some of the other Acts which you have
copied in the past.
For instance, there is the problem
of the local authorities. The amount
of the Bill they would have to foot
it is deemed at the moment would be
about 60 per cent. A burden of 60 per
cent. in Belfast presents one problemit presents an entirely different problem
in some of the great municipalities across
the water-when you remember that
Belfast is the chief industrial centre of
the area of Northern Ireland. That is
only one aspect of the question. I believe I am justified in saying that the
Minister of Labour will have to do some
hard thinking along with his colleagues
before he can harmonise in every way the
principles of this Bill when it comes to be
introduced into the industrial life of
Northern Ireland.
I want to deal for a few moments with
the question of shipbuilding and linen.
Unlike the last speaker I do not profess
to be an expert in any particular
industry. I am perhaps a fairly decent
authority on every industry, but I do not
specialise in any one. I have gone to
great trouble in looking into the shipbuilding industry. When I got home
last night after hearing the eloquent
testimony of the Members of this House
to the improved social conditions, I took
up the "Telegraph" and, in addition to
Alderman Duff's statement, which I have
already quoted, I saw a suggestion with
regard to shipbuilding in Belfast.
Then I went to the Ulster Year Book.
I would like those Members of the House
who have not consulted the Ulster Year
Book to know that there are some little
bits of propaganda issued by this Government which can be used by almost every
section of the community. I do not know
whether that is done unconsciously or not
on their part, but it happens that way.
The hon. and gallant Member for East
Down quoted the shipbuilding-

There is nobody who would gainsay the fact
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
that every additional order that comes to
Belfast should make the heart of every
individual rejoice no matter to what
political party he belongs. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In this connection
might I reply to the Prime Minister?
The Prime Minister was good enough
yesterday to address a request to the hon.
Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) and
myself. He stated that he hoped that
one of the two of us would be good enough
to have a word in the ear of the Labour
Members across the water, particularly
Mr. Kirkwood, with regard to their attitude towards orders coming to Belfast.
So that there may be no misunderstanding
about this question, I want to put the
facts before the House. The fact is that
in a time of languishing industry, particularly in shipbuilding, representatives
of the working-class people in constituencies across the water, particularly
shipbuilding constituencies, are perturbed
when they see orders passing their own
doors, so to speak. They begin to make
inquiries and they find that a certain
policy is being pursued-I am not now
expressing any opinion on the policy;
understand that by the Ministry of
Finance in Northern Ireland in relation
to the shipbuilding industry under the
Loans Guarantee Acts.
When they find out those facts, and
when they arrive at the conclusion that
the assistance given by the Northern
Ministry of Finance, along with the
business acumen of the heads of the firms,
may be responsible for orders coming to
Belfast, they raise the question in the
House of Commons from the point of
view of trying to get the Imperial
Chancellor to embark upon the same
policy in Great Britain as is pursued in
Northern Ireland. It is not a question
of trying to inflict economic injury or
hardship upon the working classes of Northern Ireland. Why should it be? You
are always boasting about being Ulster
Scots, and, therefore, why should the
Scots, from whom you spring, try to do
you an economic injury? But what are
the facts in the Imperial House, if I
may be permitted to use them? The
facts are that when this question of shipbuilding was raised in the Imperial
House the Imperial Chancellor intimated
to the House that he was not prepared to
adopt the same policy for Great Britain.
He did not deem it expedient to adopt
the same policy, and yet he is a member
of the same Unionist Party as the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Labour in
Northern Ireland. He said he did not
deem it expedient, in the interests of the
working-class people of Great Britain,
that such a policy should be embarked
upon.
as
In making his request the Prime
Minister suggested that we should use our
endeavours with Mr. Kirkwood and
others across the water. May I now ask
the Prime Minister to use his endeavours
in regard to another industry, namely,
the textile industry? Some months ago
a representative deputation of employers.
and employees of the Scottish textile industry went to the Imperial Parliament
and made a complaint to the Imperial
authorities that, owing to the absence of
trade-regulating machinery, known
trades boards, in the spinning and weaving ends of the linen industry in Northern
Ireland, employers were paying their employees lower wages and were able to
undercut the employers of Great Britain
and so secure orders which should have
gone to them in the normal course of
events. It was charged against us that
our people were being paid on lower
scales, and in relation to the spinning and
weaving ends that charge was largely substantiated. As the Prime Minister was
good enough to address a request to us,
I now wish to address one to him and
ask him to use his influence with the
Minister of Labour so as to ensure that
the same safeguards will be given to the
wage earners in the textile industry in
Northern Ireland as are at present given
to textile workers across the water.
So much for shipbuilding. Now let
us come to linen. If we were to interpret or to accept the statements made by
the right hon. and hon. Gentlemen in
this House at their face value we would
believe that industry had made such a
startling recovery that everything in the
garden was lovely, and we might if I
may paraphrase the words of the Prime
Minister go home and have a very
happy and peaceful Christmas. But
such are not the facts. The position is
that, despite the improvement, there is
no basic change in either the textile or
the shipbuilding industry in Northern
Ireland. In shipbuilding it is definitely.
for the worse, and I will tell you whv.
A statement was made by the hon. Member for Shankill (Mr. Henderson) here

Debate on the Address
19 DECEMBER 1933
yesterday, and I saw some people on the
other side of the House smile because they
thought he had overstated himself. I
was content to take his meaning rather
than his words, and I think those who
desired to get his right meaning saw what
he was at. The hon. Member for
Shankill mentioned that if every slip in
our shipyards were utilised there would
still be a certain number of employees for
whom no work could be found. That is
absolutely true. He also stated that if
the mills and factories in our textile industry in Northern Ireland were working
to full capacity-that is what he intended.
and what any intelligent person would
have taken out of his statement-there
would still be a surplus army of unemployed.
Why? Here is the explanation, apart
from anything else. A few months ago
a naval architect came to Belfast and delivered an address to the Rotary Club.
He made certain statements with regard
to shipbuilding which we know to be true.
He said:
"I should like to make a prediction
which some of you will say is merely the
dream of youth. If welding advances
as rapidly in the next ten years as it
has in the past two, then the revolution in the methods of joining metal
parts will be complete, and the
riveting hammer, with its staccato
clatter, may be just as hard to find in
the shipyards as it is to find a horse and
trap in Donegall Place."
Then he added these significant words:
"The new process is going to eliminate a multiplicity of operationspunching, reaming, counter-sinking,
riveting, and caulking and obviously
some trades will be wholly or partially
displaced as the process develops."
Now, apart altogether from the development of electrical arc welding-and, by
the way, in passing, it may interest hon.
Members of this House to know
that shipbuilding employers are not
allowing the skilled artisans to work
that electrical arc welding process:
already they are laying down the principle that a semi-skilled man can do that
job with a few weeks' training, and are
going to throw the skilled artisan
on the scrap heap-I should like
to ask the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Labour what policy they
have in view of that inevitable
development of industry along mechanical
lines. The same thing is true of the textile industry. The same mechanical processes are being introduced into every
phase of our life. It is reported by
scientific authorities-and you can take
this as a basis upon which to make some
calculation as to the mechanical development of the age in which we live-that in
thirty years if the development of
mechanical devices and scientific principles
in industry goes on for the next thirty
years at the same rate as it has proceeded.
for the last twenty years-it will be possible to carry on the work of Great
Britain and Ireland on a basis of 500,000
super craftsmen. In face of that development-whether it is an exaggeration or
not, the trend of development is in that
direction-I should like to ask right hon.
Gentlemen on the front bench what proposals they are prepared to put before
this House and the country in order to
relieve or to deal comprehensively and
scientifically with this permanent problem
of unemployment. Because, remember
that under our present conditions of
society this is becoming a permanent
problem, and the Government so far,
apart altogether from the policy of following step by step and giving a little assistance here and there to dig holes and fill
them up again, have not put forward one
statesmanlike expression or proposal.
I
Just come to the textile industry for a
moment. In connection with that industry the hon. and gallant Member for
East Down made some quotations.
have taken the Census figures from the
Ulster Year Book, and what do I find?
You may quote output for one year and
output for another year, but I want you
to take the Census figures of those
employed in the industry and face up to
the inevitable consequences of those
figures. In the Census of 1924 in Northern Ireland the figures for the textile
industry in all branches in Northern Ireland were 86,762 persons employed. In
the Census of 1930 those figures had
dropped to 67,000. There is the discrepancy recorded in the Ulster Year Book,
and I should like to ask the Minister of
Labour and his colleagues on the Front
Bench what they propose to do in face of
that development which is taking place
right throughout our industry.
Now, I want to make an appeal to this
House. I realise that it is a little bit out
of place, perhaps, to make an appeal to
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
the House in the ordinary sense of the
term, but I am going to ask the Minister
responsible to face up to this test in
dealing with the question of unemployment. The best the Government can
hope to do under the step-by-step policy
is not going to solve the problem of unemployment. Even take the great experiment that is being undertaken in the
United States of America at the present
time, and upon which the eyes of the
world are focussed. That is doomed to
inevitable defeat, because the same forces
that are at work in our state of society
must inevitably assert themselves there
and so defeat the object which the policy
has in view.
But, notwithstanding this stop-gap, we
see statesmen being driven to the
expedient of trying to increase the purchasing power of all members of the community. I commend to the Minister of
Labour and all concerned the thought
that one of the things that must be considered by the statesmen in Northern
Ireland is the question of some method of
increasing purchasing power. I knowand I am not now indulging in sob stuff,
and I hope that after I have sat down no
Member, either on the front or back bench,
will suggest that I have been indulging in
sob stuff or sentiment-I am a product of
poverty-stricken conditions and have rebelled against poverty all my life. I have
fought all my life against people being
kept in poverty. It is not God's will or
the work of nature.
In the Division I represent in this
House there is most appalling destitution. I took a census of 450 people
in my Division last year and intend
taking another this year at Christmas.
I found that for a population of
450, taken indiscriminately from my
Division, the average allowance for
the maintenance of each person, adult
and juvenile, for every phase of life, rent,
food, clothing, comfort of every kind that
goes to make up civilisation, was 2/31d
per head over those 450 people. I only
take that section as representing many
more throughout the Division. And the
same conditions are existing to-day.
There is very distressing poverty throughout my Division. In face of that I put
this challenge and this test to the Government: You may claim that you are doing
all you can. I say that no Government
and no statesman are doing all they can,
or all he can, while one man, woman, or
child is deprived of food or of the
standard of life God intended that person
to enjoy. Ulster, or the portion of it
under your control, is rich enough to
guarantee to every man, woman, and
child a decent standard of subsistence, but
they are not getting it at the present time,
and it is not through their own fault. It
is not because of their individual thriftlessness or their lack of control in household affairs. I know some of the most
magnificent parents and guardians in
Northern Ireland who are facing very
very degrading and appalling poverty at
the present time.
Because of that I am emphasising the
question of unemployment. It is because
of that, and also as a result of generations
of propaganda on the part of people like
myself, that you are compelled to bring
in your social legislation. I have been
pioneering social measures in Belfast
since Ι was fourteen years of age.
I had the privilege of fighing an
election for the Imperial House against
a Member of this House, who sits on the
opposite Benches, and some of the things.
that were said by him to be absolutely
wild and visionary are to-day on the
Statute Book as a result of the pioneer
efforts of people like myself. It is
because of that I want to ask this House
to face up to the fact that although they
are compelled to do their best according
to their standpoint of social legislation,
that best is not good enough, and that
the time has arrived in the history of
our Province and country when we ought
to ask ourselves are there any other
avenues which may be explored, are there
any other methods or propositions which
may be tested, in the hope that we may
do the greatest work that men may do,
that is, stamp out this problem of inequality, social injustice, and poverty,
which is a stigma on every Christian
community wherever it exists? That is
the question of unemployment.
There is one other question mentioned
in the King's Speech with which I wish
to deal, that is the question of education.
I have served an apprenticeship for nine
years on the local education authority.
Therefore, I take it that the House will
agree that I know something about the
subject.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, with your
permission, I should just like to say that
in quoting census figures in reply to the
hon. and gallant Member for East Down
