Debate on the Address
19 DECEMBER 1939
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) I do not want
him to think I was shirking the responsibility. I have looked up the statistics
of exports, and if he can find any great
comfort for his soul on the basis of the
export figures he is a greater optimist
than I take him to be. There is no
revelation of a permanent and fundamental improvement in the linen industry
on the basis of exports. Piece goods
have gone down in money value and have
increased in yardage, but come to the
handkerchief end, which is the end I was
always told by the protagonists of safeguarding would show the most beneficial
results when safeguarding was embarked
upon.
We find that the exports in handkerchiefs went down from 3,480,000 dozens
in 1930 to 1,922,000 dozens in 1932, and
the cash value dropped from £649,000
to £338,000. Those are the figures, and
I wish to state on the basis of those
statistics and census returns, as to those
employed in the textile and kindred
industries, that the claim cannot be
justified in this House that there is a
fundamental change in the state of society
so far as shipbuilding and linen are
concerned.
Now I come back to education. The
statement is made in the King's Speech:
The educational system continues to
develop satisfactorily and notwithstanding the difficulties occasioned by
the present strain on public finance,
substantial progress has been made in
the replacement of unsuitable buildings.
by modern structures, with resulting
improvement in the well-being of both
scholars and teachers.
The latter part of that statement is
correct, substantially correct; the first
section is incorrect in my opinion. "The
educational system continues to develop
satisfactorily."
It all depends upon
what you mean by those words. If we
can accept the political outlook of
Northern Ireland in regard to education
we might say that that is true, because
it is a matter of common knowledge that
politicians in Northern Ireland never did
believe in education. In years gone by,
working-class children were sent halftime to the mill and half-time to school.
That system was changed; we abolished
the half-time system, and we allowed the
school age to be raised to 14. Before
that children of 12 years of age were sent
out to work to augment the family income.
Because we have raised the school
leaving age to 14 it may be contended
that we are doing all that is required of
us in the way of education.
There used to be a kind of social
superiority outlook in Northern Ireland
which some of us experienced-why should
workers have any education at all;
education is reserved for the sons and
daughters of the so-called better class?
That was the attitude to education.
Education in Northern Ireland is in a
lamentable condition. I want to tell this
House that elementary education in
Belfast is better now from the point of
view of facilities and training centres for
the children than it was in the past, when
Lord Carson-he was then Sir Edward
Carson-poured such bitter scorn upon
the educational system in Belfast and
Northern Ireland. But I want to point
to some aspects of education which are
lost sight of. We have been told by the
Front Bench Members here, and will be
told again, that we follow step by step
with Great Britain in the matter of education generally. We do not. In England
and Wales for 50 years all the children
have been provided with free books. It
Belfast and Northern Ireland they are
not.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is a matter for
the Corporation.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The Minister of
Labour says that that is the fault of the
Corporation. Under the Act as it stands
at present that is undoubtedly true, and
I have tried in vain, by appeal, by the
force of example, by great persuasive
powers (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
and all the rest of it, to get the Corporation to recede from that position. I will
make another attempt next week, but I
have not succeeded yet. There is a very
easy way out. When the Minister of
Labour, the Minister of Education, and
the other Cabinet Ministers see me
ploughing my lonely furrow-it is not so
lonely now as it used to be, thanks to the

we will come forward in the Northern
Parliament and amend the Education Act
again, so as to make it obligatory on the

lccal authorities to do what the education

is the easy way out. And the reason for

Last week the Corporation of Glasgow
decided to give free books to every child
in the City of Glasgow attending the
public elementary schools at a cost of
£40,000. Incidentally, I may mention
that on the same afternoon they decided
to restore the cuts to the unemployed,
amounting to £100,000, and I commend
to the Minister of Labour the consideration of restoring here the cut of 10 per
cent. imposed on the unemployed, which
inflicted the most grevious injury amongst
the section of the community least capable
of bearing any additional burden. Upon
the question of education, I wish to say
that we have not the facilities, as I claimed
before, that they have across the water.
Not only does that apply to books; it
applies also to the right or the possibility
of the elementary school children going in
for higher education.
I want to tell my experience to this
House to show how erroneous things are
palmed off on the public of Northern Ireland. A certain newspaper in Belfast on
one occasion came out with a placard,
"Education in Northern Ireland," and
because the placard contained that
announcement I thought: "That is something unusual in that paper, because they
do not deal with educational topics in
their placards," as the right. hon. Gentleman opposite (Mr. Moles) can tell you.
I was so astounded that I got that newspaper, and I found in it a full-page
article, which claimed that education in
Northern Ireland was placed on such a
high pinnacle that every child from the
humblest cottage in Northern Ireland had
the right to the highest education obtainable in Northern Ireland. That was
palmed off on the public of Belfast as
being true; it led them to lick their lips
with satisfaction and to say:
"We are
going on beautifully."
I rang up the editor of that newspaper
and told him that the article was teeming
with inaccuracies. He told me that it
had been written by a celebrated authority
on education. I said: "I do not care
who it was written by; I am a member
of the education authority in Belfast, and
I will give you some facts to controvert
those statements." He sent over an
interviewer. My article appeared the
next morning-I did not get paid for it,
I am sorry to say-controverting about
90 cent. of the claims of the authority,
per
and from that day to this not another
word has appeared in that newspaper
on this subject from an expert or anybody
else. The inference to be drawn is that
my position was unassailable, and, on the
question of education, it is unassailable
this afternoon.
With regard to higher education, let us
consider the position in Northern Ireland
at the present time. There are little over
12,000 children in the whole of Northern
Ireland getting secondary education. It
works out about 7 per cent. of the school
population of Northern Ireland. What
does that mean? I will prove what it
means by giving you another figure. The
next figure is the amount of assistance
given for higher education in the way of
free places in the secondary schools of
Northern Ireland. There is less than one
per cent. of the school population in
receipt of free places in our secondary
schools. I am very glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education (Mr. Robb) here, because I want
him to face up to some of these figures
which I have been hammering at for
years, in vain, in the Belfast Corporation.
Less, slightly less, than 7 per cent. of
the total school population is getting
higher education at all. I hate to have
to say a thing like that. I do not want to
create the feeling in the minds of right
hon. and hon. Gentlemen opposite that I
am filled with class envy and hatred and
all the rest of it. I am not. I am not
filled with hatred of anybody, but I am
filled with hatred of a bad social system.
I hate a bad social system which makes
certain things inevitable, but sincerely I
do not hate anyone. I am out against
policies and social evils. I say this is a
consequence of our bad social system.
These statistics demonstrate beyond the
shadow of a doubt that higher education
in Northern Ireland is still the prerogative of the rich. You may not like that
phrase, but it is absolutely true, and
education ought not to be the prerogative
of any section of the community.
I am a bit of a revolutionist in education. I understand that a few years ago
there was brought into operation in Germany a system called the democratisation
of education, whereby every boy and girl
in the community was compelled to attend
an elementary school. I should like to
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
19 DECEMBER 1933
see that system introduced into Northern
Ireland. I should like to see every boy
and girl, no matter about origin or social
status, compelled to attend a public elementary school. As it is, they are not,
and the poor are precluded from attending
the higher schools because of the incidence
of their poverty. The Belfast Corporation
gives 50 scholarships every year, 30 for
boys and 20 for girls. I want to tell the
Members of this House that it is absolutely pathetic to see the unrealised aspirations of the working-class mothers and
fathers of Belfast in regard to the education of their children.
Belfast gives four scholarships to the
University. A city with a population of
450,000 provides four scholarships in the
University. I collected statistics for
Queen's University and the Universities
of Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester, and
Liverpool. What did I find? I found
that in Queen's University the free
places are represented by 8 per cent., and
that in the other Universities I have mentioned the figure is 50 per cent. Think
of that. Fity per cent. free places in
the Universities in the principal municipal
centres of Great Britain, and 8 per cent.
in Belfast and Northern Ireland. I want
to
urge here that the working-class
children of Northern Ireland are not
getting the educational chances that they
ought to be getting. When the results
of the examinations come through every
year I find there are hundreds of
children intellectually well equipped to
profit by a higher education who are
knocking at the doors of educational
opportunity, but are precluded from
having that opportunity because of the
limited support given to a higher
education and the limited number of tree
places. So long as this condition of affairs
exists in Northern Ireland it cannot be
claimed that our educational system is
developing satisfactorily.
A few days ago I looked at the "Belfast
Telegraph" and saw in it a statement by
a former teacher trained at Stranmillis
who has now gone to live in London and
to play as a professional footballer because
he could not find employment in Northern
Ireland. If that teacher had been able to
find employment in Northern Ireland he
would have stayed here, but he went to
London. He was under a contract with
the Ministry of Education to stay for five
years, but he could not get a job, in
Belfast at any rate.
Mr. CHRISTIE: Coleraine.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I did hear that somebody guaranteed him a job in Coleraine,
but how anyone could guarantee a job
passes my comprehension because these
appointments are supposed to be based on
merit. I know he tried in every way
possible to get a job in Belfast.
What does he say? He wrote in the
"Star, I think it was, and it was quoted
by the "Telegraph." He said that the
educational standard was far greater there
than it was in Northern Ireland. It may
be a case of one leaving his own city and
finding nothing good to say of it. I say
that the educational opportunites for the
children of the poorer class here are not
what they ought to be. Before I conclude
on education let me say this, I repeat with
all the emphasis at my command that in
Northern Ireland seven per cent. of the
school population get a higher education
and less than one per cent. free places.
In England to-day from 25 per cent. to
40 per cent. of the working class have
access to higher education and from 25
per cent. to 50 per cent. are in receipt of
free places. That is the acid test.
I do not need to say that no section
of the community would be prouder of
a real industrial recovery in Northern
Ireland than the Members who sit on
these benches. We are just as jealous of
the good name of our part of the country
as any other section of the community.
We want to see the people well housed,
well fed, and well clothed. The necessity which exists we attribute to the
pernicious principles which govern our
present social order. In regard to the
future, when I read the King's Speech
yesterday I felt like quoting Shakespeare,
but I refrained because if I am in doubt
about the exact words of a quotation I
do not attempt to repeat the quotation.
The phrase I thought of was "sound
and fury signifying nothing."
When I read the Speech I realised
it was "sound and fury signifying
nothing." There is nothing fundamental or constructive in it. If hon.
Members have "listened in" to talks on
the subject or have read text books by
eminent authorities and students all over
the world they will find that increasingly
they are turning to new methods of
solving the social problem. The perpetuation of a bad social system will not
solve the problem. The best that has
been promised here is this new Unemployment Insurance Bill, which we are told
is going to place unemployment insurance
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
on a permanent and firm foundation.
God help us.
If you read all the Clauses of that
Bill you will find that it is not a
comprehensive Insurance Bill at all. So
far as Great Britain and Northern Ireland
are concerned it leaves out between
4,000,000 and 5,000,000 people who
could have been brought in by an
extension of the scope of the Bill. It
is also assumed that the Bill is going to
bear the burden of this liability, instead
of making unemployment what it ought
to be, a national liability to which every
section of the community would contribute. That is the best we can expect.
That is not reconstruction, that is not
statesmanship; and in the name of the
people who sent me here, who want slums,
and bad health, and all the paraphernalia of an evil civilisation based upon
injustice swept away-in the name of
those people I appeal to the Government
to take their courage in their hands and
come out with a bold, constructive programme, aiming at the rebuilding of
our country and the rehousing of our
people with proper sanitary decent homes,
with the best medical service, the best
schools, best equipped from the point of
view of teachers and pupils, and the best
educational opportunities. If they do
something like that in their day and
generation, although they may not build.
the New Jerusalem in Ulster, they will
at least be able to lay down the reins
with the consciousness that they have
done their duty, and done something for
the permanent recovery of the people.

It is quite an attractive thing to say
that the purchasing power of the people
should be increased. We would all like
to see the purchasing power of the people
increased just as much as hon. Members
opposite. The difficulty is that they seem
to look upon Northern Ireland as one little
unit. They forget that three out of every
four articles we produce have to find a
market in other lands, and if the purchasing power of the people here
increased, and the cost of production put
up as a consequence, the effect would be
that we could not sell those things that
we must sell in other countries (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and unemployment would be created to a greater extent
than even exists at the present time.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is
the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and
the end of the problem as I see it. If
we were a little unit, if we could consume
all we produce, then the whole position
would be quite different. But hon. Members opposite know that we are internationalists to a great extent. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Hon. Members
go further than I would go in that
direction-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-but at any rate, we are internationalists to the extent that we cannot live
without other lands.

Then, again, you must remember the
Reinsurance Agreement. The position is
that we cannot have an agreement based
on parity and then not have parity.
Further, I would like to point out that,
if we had kept in step with Great
Britain and had not had the Reinsurance
Agreement, the debt on our Unemployment Insurance Fund would now have been
over £12,500,000, which, of course, would
have been impossible. It is through the
Reinsurance Agreement that we have
been able to maintain our social standards
in parity with those of Great Britain.
The hon. Member for Pottinger went
on to refer to the Unemployment Insurance Bill as another clog in the wheels of
progress. Those are his words. I wonder
does he recollect that this Bill, which no
doubt he has read, proposes to increase
the twenty-six weeks which was the maximum period for benefit under the old
arrangement to a possible maximum of
fifty-two weeks according to the insurance
record of the claimant during the previous five years. That will have the effect
of removing from the means test, for that
period at any rate, those persons who
qualify for unemployment benefit for a
longer period than twenty-six weeks.
Another advantage will be that benefit
will be paid to juveniles from sixteen

of those juveniles between the ages of
fourteen and sixteen.

whether they remain at school or whether

Then again an Unemployment Assistance

Mr. HEALY: I read carefully the
Gracious Speech from the Throne in the
hope of discovering that there was some
mention of material benefit for the most
important class in the Six Counties,
namely, the farmers, and although I
found mention of one or two rather
unimportant Measures. I cannot see that
they are likely to alter the existing position very much. Farming, as is sometimes forgotten in this House, is by far
the most important industry, and it employs the largest number of people, and
yet the plight of that important industry
to-day is such that the majority of the
farmers are quite unable to pay their
debts. 1 am not going to exaggerate the
parlous plight in which they find themselves, because if I quoted from speeches
delivered at meetings up and down the
country it might be held that they were
exaggerated.
I am going to quote statistics sent out
by the Ministry of Finance as to the
number of civil bills issued in nine months
of this year against farmers for the nonpayment of land annuities, with the
object of showing that this important class
is passing through one of the most difficult
periods they have experienced for a long
while. I find that no fewer than 6,263
civil bills for rent were served in that
period, and of those no fewer than 1,127
were issued in the County of Fermanagh,
the constituency of the present Minister
of Agriculture and of the late Minister
of Agriculture. Whilst every Dominion
has been doing what it possibly can by
means of subsidies and tariffs to assist the
farming class, the Northern Government
have been folding their arms and regarding the plight of the farmers with the
utmost complacency.
As a matter of fact, the Northern
Government have no agricultural policy.
The hon. Member who spoke from these
Benches last stated that they were following piecemeal the legislation of Great
Britain. I hold that that more particularly applies to the legislation concerning
the farming class than it does to the
industrial community and to unemployment. The farmers have asked the
Government to legislate not on matters of
pests, not on the marketing of milk,
however desirable that may be; they have
put to the Government a concrete case for
the reduction of the land annuities, and
the Prime Minister, who should sympathise with the farmers, almost told a
recent deputation that went to him that
no honest men from Ulster would have
made the demand that they made. That
put to the proof, to the acid test, the right
hon. Gentleman's sympathy, expressed on
many occasions, but particularly on the
occasion of his return from New Zealand,
when he was going to make the land
blossom like the rose, and when he told
us that he was going to set up some
wonderful system for the reclamation of
bogs. I think that in that respect the
right hon. Gentleman is in the bog still.
At a time when the farming community
had to sell milk at 34d a gallon, butter at
10d a pound and eggs at 8d per dozen,
a deputation from this most deserving
class was almost told by the Prime
Minister to clear out, and that the case
they had presented was one that no
honest man could support. There was
surely nothing socialistic in the farmers
of Northern Ireland asking for a remission of the land annuities for a period
of five years. I do not think that, if the
Government had conceded the demand
made, they would have suffered either
economical or political shipwreck. By
going through the Departments, and particularly through the Department of
Agriculture, they could have so reduced
their overhead expenses that practically
the whole of the demand of the farmers
could have been met without any loss of
efficiency. The late Minister of Agriculture and the present Minister of

in the County of Fermanagh-their
county and mine. I have no objection,
when appointments are going, to their

say that we Catholics are getting fair
play. Let me refer him to the hon.
Member for South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy). I have considered several

passed I think is a most unjust Bill as
far as we Catholics are concerned. We
have always endeavoured, as it is well
known and has been admitted by Members of this House, to raise money for
our schools. We raised the money before
an Education Act was passed in Northern
Ireland. We raised it from the poorest
section of our community, and it was
admitted that before the Education Act
of 1923 was passed our schools were
superior to any others in the city.
Under the recent Act the only grant
we could extract from the Government
was one of 50 per cent. Could anyone
say that that is justice? We are people
who respect our religion; in fact, we
would die for our religion. We are most
anxious that the members of our community will be brought up in the faith
to which we belong. I say that we will
never surrender our schools to any community outside the Catholic community.
You may penalise us as much as you
wish, and you may impose as many restrictions as you wish, but we will retain
control of our schools.
It is most unfair that we who contribute our share to the rates of the city
should have also to raise 50 per cent. of
the cost of running our schools. Yet the
hon. Member for North Antrim says we
are better treated here than in any other
country. I do not agree with that statement. We never will be content as long
as that state of affairs exists, under which
the poorest section of the community have
to pay 50 per cent. of the costs of their
education.
There are many other things I would
like to refer to. I think the Government
could do more than it is doing with
regard to unemployment. Recently the
Corporation had a scheme in connection
with distress relief amounting to some
thousands of pounds, but when that
scheme was submitted to the Government
they refused to sanction it or to give us
any assistance, the reason given being
that a Bill was being introduced across
the water. That means that 4,000 of
our people are on distress relief and the
ratepayers have to contribute that amount.
I know a great many of those people. I
know they would rather work than get
money from charity, and I maintain
that at the very earliest moment the
Government should meet the Corporation
and introduce at least a partial scheme,
so that those people would get employment. That would be a very great
benefit to the city.
The Corporation have another scheme
which is very urgent and necessary, that

number of people could be employed and

earliest possible moment the Government

With regard to the last Housing Act,
there are in it some deficiencies, and I
would like to see an Amending Bill introduced. Large numbers of houses are decontrolled, and there are people paying
5s or 10s a week more than their
neighbours for the same class of houses.
Then again, there are subsidy houses
which are not controlled and for which
very high rents are being charged. No
less than £140 of the ratepayers' money
was invested in each of those houses, and
I know from experience that exorbitant
rents are exacted.
There is another matter that has not
been brought before the Government for
a long time, the Landlord and Leaseholders Bill. That has been promised by
the Government, but for some reason or
other nothing has been done. Numbers
of shopkeepers in different streets in the
city when their leases expire are treated
most unjustly by the landlords, who
charge exorbitant rents. At an early
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Byrne]
date the Government should bring in a
Bill to deal with this matter.
Then there is another section of the
people for whom I have a great sympathy,
namely, the widows without pensions.
There are a number of widows in the city
of Belfast who have been deprived of the
widows' pension because their husbands
had been unemployed. Some of these
people are in starvation, and that is a
matter to which I would like the Government to give attention at the earliest
possible moment.
Great stress has been laid upon
industrial development. I could give the
Government a hint as to how they could
raise money for this purpose. In 1923 a
Licensing Act was passed in a great hurry.
The hon. and gallant Member for East
Down (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) stated very
truly earlier to-day that when people
come to visit this part of the country they
are amazed and surprised that they cannot
get refreshments later than half-past nine
at night. That is a great grievance, and
the Government should take this matter
into consideration at an early date and
do something to encourage people to come
here. I hope that soon a reasonable
Licensing Bill will be produced by which.
the people of Northern Ireland can be
treated in the same way as are people in
other parts of the country. Although I
am in the licensed trade I am not advocating drinking at random. I am only
advocating liberty for the people, and I
may say that there is no one more opposed
to the abuse of drink than is the licensed
trade.
I think that is all I need refer to at
present, but those are matters of great
urgency, and I would appeal to the
Government to bring in legislation at the
earliest possible moment to do away with
some of these grievances in regard to
widows' pensions, housing, licensing, and,
last but not least, education. I hope the
Government will bring in an amending
Education Bill in order that we may not
be penalised to the extent we are at the
present time.
Mr. MURPHY: I desire at the outset
to associate myself with the congratulations which have been tendered to the
mover and seconder of the Address. There
are one or two aspects of the Gracious
Speech to which I wish to refer very
shortly. Reference is made in the Speech,
and I say properly made, to the fact that
law and order continue to be effectually
maintained. It seems to me that that
should be put in the forefront in considering the various matters that have
been discussed during this debate, because
without the effectual maintenance of law
and order in our Province the prosperity
for which we are all hoping cannot be
attained. I desire to congratulate our
Government upon the effectual manner
in which law and order have been maintained. I wish to go further in this
respect and congratulate the Government,
the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates)
who is Minister of Home Affairs, on the
fact that nothing which the Government
have recently done has given more satisfaction in the constituency which I have
the honour to represent than the latest
Order made by the Ministry of Home
Affairs prohibiting the use of what has
been properly described as a Republican
emblem. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I was at first surprised and afterwards.
somewhat grieved to hear in the speeches
made, firstly, by the hon. Member for
South Fermanagh (Mr. Healy) and,
secondly, by the hon. Member for Falls
(Mr. Byrne) complaints against the
Government in connection with education
in this Province. We heard, not for the
first time, the suggestion that in some
way Roman Catholics in this Province
were being penalised in connection with
education. That fallacy has been frequently exploded, and I am surprised to
hear it suggested once again that in some
unexplained fashion our Roman Catholic
fellow-countrymen are being penalised.
As every Member of the House must
know, every advantage that is open to
other denominations is open to the members of the Roman Catholic denomination.
Roman Catholics, so far from being
penalised, have, it seems to me, determined
not to avail themselves of the privileges
offered. So far from being in any less
favoured position than their co-religionists
in England the Roman Catholics in this
Northern Province have deliberately refused to do what their co-religionists in
England have done. They have refused,
and continue to refuse, not merely to
transfer their schools but to appoint the
four-and-two committees which have been
appointed by their co-religionists throughout England. I am surprised to hear
that that should be laid to the charge of
this Government in view of the explana-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
19 DECEMBER 1933
tions that have been so frequently given
in the debates on the education question
in this House.
I notice that legislation is to be introduced in connection with the very grievous
additions to the accidents on our roads.
In the Gracious Speech it is stated that
a Bill will be introduced to afford a
remedy for that state of affairs. I would
only wish to make two suggestions.
Perhaps in respect of one of those suggestions I am like a voice crying in the
wilderness. My first suggestion is that
improvements in our roads may to some
extent operate to reduce the actually
dangerous character of certain places in
the roads, but I submit that by itself the
process of improving the roads will not
necessarily reduce the number of road
accidents. When this matter comes to be
considered, if that be the remedy suggested, it would be well to remember that
road accidents on the great arterial roads
out of London, so far from being reduced,
are rapidly increasing.
It has occurred to me that at some time
-I do not think the country is at the
moment ripe for such a development—and
eventually something will have to be done
to reduce the speed of motor vehicles on
the roads (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-and to reduce that speed not by police.
regulations, which cannot effect an actual
reduction in the speed, but by some system of mechanical control.
As I say,
probably we are not ripe for legislation
on those lines at the moment; nevertheless, it seems to me that when we consider
the future of the roads and the safety of
the population something on those lines
will have to be done.
I wish also to make one contribution to
what has been said in connection with the
improvement in the unemployment position. Reference has been made, both in
the Gracious Speech and in the speeches
delivered by Members on both sides of
the House to the improved position in the
two staple industries of Northern Ireland,
namely, the shipbuilding and the linen
industries. I am very glad to be able
to say that that improvement is not confined only to those two industries, but that
there has been a substantial improvement
at least in employment in the staple
industry of Londonderry, namely, the
shirt and collar industry. It is
contending with very grave difficulties.
but it has a feature of hope in
that during the last year that industry
has managed to give employment to a
substantially greater number, especially
of female workers, than it did in the previous year.
Might I also, in conclusion, refer to the
legislation that is
promised in the
Gracious Speech dealing with the qualifying period of residence for the franchise.
I trust that, when it is introduced, that
legislation will be found to be retrospective in operation, and I think I am entitled also to say this, that in connection
with that legislation consideration ought
to be given to the subject already referred
to by the hon. and gallant Member for
East Down (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) that
in our electoral system it should be made
impossible for any person to be nominated
as a candidate for Parliament unless that
person was prepared before nomination to
take the Oath of Allegiance. I trust that
that matter will receive the due consideration of the Government, and that in the
future we shall not see what I can only
describe as the scandal of persons being
nominated as candidates for seats who not
merely avow their contempt for our Constitution, but also avow their intention,
if elected, not to serve in this House.

Oral Answers to Questions.
OFFICIALS OF PIGS MARKETING
BOARD.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
number of officials the Pigs Marketing
Board has already appointed, their names,
positions, total remunerations, and terms
of appointment; and whether it is the
intention of this Board to make any further appointments before the elected
representatives of the pig producers get
an opportunity of voicing their opinions.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): As will have been
observed from the public advertisements
of the Pigs Marketing Board and their
Press statements, the board has appointed, with the Ministry's approval, a
secretary at a salary of £1,000 per annum,
an accountant at a salary of £500 per
annum, and a marketing officer at a
salary of £500 per annum. My Ministry
has also approved of the employment of
three junior officials at salaries ranging
from £104 to £250 per annum.
The secretary of the board is Mr. A. N.
Duckham; the accountant Mr. J. Monteith; and the marketing officer Mr. C. P.
MacAuley.
I have no information as to the future
intention of the board with regard to the
appointment of additional staff.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, may I ask
whether it is a fact that in addition to the
officials enumerated in his reply, the
members of the Pigs Marketing Board receive three guineas per day, plus expenses, for their services?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I should require
notice of that question.

MENTS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to the serious loss both to
farmers and traders caused by the upsetting of long-standing marketing
arrangements for the marketing of pork;
and whether he will make representations

to having the pork markets restored.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I an
am not
aware of the serious loss to which the
hon. Member refers. It is unanimously
agreed that the operation of the pigs.
marketing scheme has secured for
farmers a price for pigs very substantially higher than would have been the case
if no such scheme had been framed.
The purchase of pigs by curers in the
markets in Northern Ireland is a matter
for the Bacon Marketing Board and not
for the Pigs Marketing Board. I would
remind the hon. Member that in offering
to compensate curers in respect of any
losses experienced during the period 1st
November, 1933, to 28th February, 1934,
the Government attached two conditions,
one of which was that curers should
continue to purchase their pigs in the
manner which was customary in the past.
My Ministry has drawn the attention of
the Bacon Marketing Board to numerous
instances in which it was claimed by
farmers and market authorities that in
purchasing pigs bacon curers were departing from the methods which were hitherto followed. I am not aware that there
are now any markets which have not been
re-opened for the sale of pigs but, if the
hon. Member can
with
supply me
particulars of any markets which are still
closed, I shall be happy to have inquiries
made and to make representations to the
Bacon Marketing Board with a view to
arranging for curers who have attended
these markets in the past to resume their
attendance.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: In accordance

persons who were named in the pigs
marketing scheme, and these persons will

In accordance with the provisions of

are being made by my Ministry to hold

unable at the moment to indicate who

Act, 1932, for the first cereal year, and

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am desired by
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) to
reply to this question.
The Wheat Commission has published
no particulars of the amount of payments
made by millers or of the deficiency payments received by farmers in any particular area of the United Kingdom. I

deficiency payments received by farmers

£6,500, while the amount of quota payments made by millers in Northern

BILL PRESENTED.
Destructive Insects and Pests Bill,
"to amend the Destructive Insects and
Pests Acts, 1877 and 1907," presented by
the Minister of Agriculture, supported by
the Minister of Finance; to be read a
Second time to-morrow and to be printed.
(Bill 6.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Railways Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The brief Measure to
which I now invite the attention of the
House is of a non-contentious character
and does not involve considerations of
major policy. Hon. Members will be
aware that in the early days of railways
the new form of locomotion was regarded
with a certain degree of suspicion. The
recent Royal Commission on Transport
speaks of how early railway promotions
"were initiated and carried out in an
atmosphere of ignorance and prejudice,
which has left a lasting mark on the
economics of our railways."
It is not surprising, therefore, that the
legislature thought fit to impose many
restrictions and regulations on the new
form of transport. During the past
hundred years something like 200 Public
Acts dealing with the regulation of railways have been placed on the Statute
Book. These Acts were based on the fact
that railways had a virtual monopoly of
transport, and on the assumption that
such a monopoly would continue.
The enormous strides made in the
development of the internal combustion
engine have, however, revolutionised
transport, and the railways, as we all
know, no longer possess a monopoly either
of passenger or of goods transport. The
result has been that railway legislation
in recent years has been mainly designed
to free the railways from the shackles
which bound them, and to place them in
a position to compete on a fairer basis
with other forms of transport which had
the advantage of commencing operations
in a more advanced age.
If hon. Members will turn to.Clause 1
they will observe that it is proposed to
confer powers upon railway companies to
enable them to dispose of land not
required for the purposes of their undertakings. The greater part of the land
owned by railway companies was acquired
under statutory powers, in many cases on
a compulsory basis, though in recent
years, where railway companies have
developed road transport services, they
have acquired any necessary additional
land and buildings by agreement.
With the transfer to the road of a substantial proportion of the traffic previously
borne on rail, it occasionally happens that
land held by a railway company is no
longer necessary for the transport undertaking, but under existing law difficulties
arise in the way of disposing of superfluous lands. The railway companies
have power to buy land but virtually no
power to dispose of land. The whole
tendency in Great Britain, I may say, has
been to confer such powers on the companies to free them from this disability.
Clause 2 of the Bill is designed to
enable a railway company, with the consent of my Ministry, to keep the gates at
a level-crossing closed against the railway,
instead of against the road.
In many
cases the railway company is under legal
obligation to keep the gates closed against
the road. With the enormous growth of
road traffic, however, conditions have
changed, so that in a number of cases the
balance of advantage to all concerned will
lie in having the gates closed across the
railway.
Sub-Clause 3 of Clause 2 will repeal the
first part of Section 48 of the Railway
Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845, which
requires all trains crossing a turnpike road
or a level-crossing adjoining a railway
station to slacken speed and to cross the
road at a speed of not more than four
miles an hour. This provision is out of
keeping with modern transport conditions.
Railways Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
Under Clause 3 of the Bill it is proposed
to relieve railway companies from the
obligation to make reports, or immediate
reports, upon accidents of a minor
character. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should have liked
the Minister to have indicated to this
House just exactly what this Bill proposes
to do with regard to bringing the transport problems of Northern Ireland up
to date. I have received some communciations with regard to the point of
view expressed by the different transport
authorities in Northern Ireland. I
understood that at least it was contemplated that some of those questions would
be dealt with in any proposed railway
legislation introduced in Northern
Ireland.
The question of what speed a train is
going to approach a level-crossing and
whether the gates are going to be closed
on the railway side or the road side may
be matters of importance in the opinion
of some people, but from the public point
of view they are so ridiculously small
that it seems an absurdity to have to
come to the Northern Commons to listen
to such proposals. I should have thought
that it would have been the duty of the
Minister to bring forward legislation
designed for the purpose of bringing our
transport facilities up to date and for the
purpose of co-ordinating them, that is,
with regard to railways and roads.
No proposals seem to be included in
this Bill to do anything like that. We
have expressions here from competent
transport authorities that the time has
arrived for the State to bring in some coordinating scheme for rail and road.
transport, and also for seeing that in any
reorganisation of transport in Northern
Ireland the principle of uniformity of
conditions in regard to
to the people
employed should be embodied in the Bill.
There is nothing revolutionary about that
proposal. It has already been done by
other Parliaments for the benefit of the
community.
I am such a newcomer to this House
that although I am usually full of
audacity I have not acquired sufficient.
audacity yet to suggest that this is a
waste of time, but when I am here
another week I will probably say that
about other Bills. I am suggesting, at
the moment, that the Bill is not comprehensive enough, and even yet I should
welcome some declaration from the
Minister of Commerce as to whether this
Government has considered the question
of transport in the light of some well
co-ordinated scheme embodying within
it uniformity of working conditions in
regard to all the people employed both
by rail and road.
It is something like a decade since, by
invitation, I appeared before the Transport Commission set up by the Government of Northern Ireland. I was one of
the persons who gave evidence. The
main point of view emphasised at that
time was the necessity of bringing about
co-ordination in regard to the new modes
of transport. Ten years have passed
away and nothing has been proposed outside, of course, what has been done by
the Minister of Commerce in regard to
the internal problems of transport, which
commenced with the problem in Belfast.
I am speaking now of the problem in its
general sense.
Ten years have passed away and
nothing comprehensive has been done
here in that regard, and now, if the
Minister is not going to be credited with
having spoken to a Bill which purports
to do a lot and actually does nothing, if
he is not going to be accused of perpetuating that practice, surely he will
take the opportunity this afternoon of
presenting this Bill to make a statement,
not only to this House, but through this
House to the public, indicating to all
people interested in transport problems
what the policy of the Government is
and what they ultimately hope to do.
Those are the thoughts in my mind this
afternoon. I was not sure, on account
of my newness to the House, whether this
problem was going to be debated or not,
but had I known the business was going
to be gone through with such facility I
should have taken steps to see that hon.
Members were detained a little longer
than they are likely to be detained on
this particular question to-day.
Mr. MURPHY: In rising to support
this Bill, I do not intend to follow the
hon. Member who has just sat down in
discussing the general question of the co-

to
Many Members of the House are
probably aware that that has led to considerable trouble even in the City of
Belfast of late, where railway companies
have been anxious to dispose of certain
portions of land superfluous so far as they
are concerned, but cannot sell. Clause 1
is clearly designed to remove that
anomaly. All that I would wish to say
about the Bill is this, that while the
purpose of Clause 1 is obvious and while
it would appear that the Clause, as
drafted, secures to the railway companies
the power to dispose of lands surplus to
their undertakings, I am aware that very
recently, in England, where the Southern
Railway were anxious to dispose of a
portion of Gosport station on their line,
to enable the local authority concerned

portion of the station into the roadway, a
difficulty arose in connection with
Clause in the Southern Railway Bill,
which was drafted on very much the same
lines as the Clause in the Bill at present
before the House. I am aware that in
the 1933 Act of the Southern Railway
additional powers were taken by a somewhat more general Clause, and I would
suggest to the Minister in charge of this
Bill that possibly, before the Committee
Stage is reached, the matter should be
looked into, when an alteration in the
drafting of Clause 1 might be found
desirable. I cannot say who raised the
difficulty in connection with Gosport

Agricultural Marketing Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The purpose of
this Bill is to implement certain undertakings which were made by my predecessor in office with the approval of the
Prime Minister and the Minister of
Finance to the Pigs and Bacon Marketing
Boards at the end of October, 1933.
Those undertakings were made in order
to overcome certain difficulties which were
experienced in regard to the initial working of the Pigs and Bacon Marketing
Schemes, and were complementary to a
similar arrangement, which was made in
Great Britain.
It will be recalled that the Lane-Fox
Re-organisation Commission, on whose
recommendations the Pigs and Bacon
Marketing Schemes were introduced in
Great Britain and in Northern Ireland,
advocated the restriction of the quantity
of bacon and hams marketed in the
United Kingdom to a figure of 10,670,000
cwt. On the basis of the information
available from the census of production
of 1930-31 it was assumed that at the
commencement of the Pigs Marketing
Scheme the home production of bacon
and hams would be at the rate of about
1,750,000 to 2,000,000 cwt. per annum.
This figure allowed for an expansion of
between 25 and 50 per cent. on the rate
of bacon production in this country in
recent years. On the assumption that
home production would not
exceed
2 million cwt. per annum, the Imperial
Government had brought about a restriction of imports from foreign countries
down to a level of about 83 million cwt.
per annum.
Towards the end of October, however,
when particulars became available regarding the numbers of contracts signed by
farmers in Great Britain for the delivery
of hacon pigs, it was discovered that the
rate of production of bacon and hams in
the United Kingdom during the first
quota period, viz., from 1st November,
1933, to 28th February, 1934, would be
at the rate of about 3 million cwt. per
annum.
The Government of the United Kingdom was faced with the necessity for an
immediate further severe restriction of
imports from abroad. Some delay
necessarily occurred before these further
restrictions could be effected, and it was
also uncertain whether the restrictions
which had already been imposed were
sufficiently severe to enable bacon curers
to pay the standard prices which had
been fixed for pigs and sell the bacon made
from these pigs at a reasonable profit.
Consequently, an assurance was given to
the Bacon Marketing Board that curers
would be indemnified in respect of any
losses which they were shown to have
sustained during the first quota period
through their adherence to the standard
prices which had already been fixed by
the Pigs Marketing Board in Northern
Ireland.
It is proposed to set up a small committee, representative of the Government,
of the Pigs Marketing Board and of the
Bacon Marketing Board, in order to
assess the losses which have been experienced by curers during the period
from the 1st November to the 28th
February. When the claims of individual curers have been assessed the
procedure to be followed will be as
follows:
A loan will be raised by the Bacon
Marketing Board, with a guarantee by
the Ministry of Finance, and out of the
proceeds of this loan the Bacon Marketing Board will be enabled to compensate
curers in respect of losses shown to have
been sustained by them. The service of
the loan will be met by the Pigs Marketing Board, and that Board will, if
necessary, be required to impose a special
levy upon pig producers in order to cover
the service of the loan.
Clause 5 of the present Bill contains
such amendments of the Northern Ireland
Act of 1933 as are required to enable the
Ministry, by Order, to provide for the
carrying out of this arrangement.
It is anticipated that, arising out of
the experience of the present quota
period, an arrangement will probably be
arrived at between the Pigs and Bacon
Marketing Boards in order to secure a
co-partnership arrangement to be operated
225 Agricultural Marketing Bill--

between the two Boards. An arrangement to this effect has already been
arrived at in Great Britain. Accordingly, in addition to the special ad hoc
power granted to the Ministry under
Clause 5 of the Bill, provision is also
made in Clauses 1, 2 and 3 to enable
arrangements similar to those which have
been adopted on this occasion to be incorporated in future schemes drafted under
the principal Act of 1933.
Clause 4 extends the provisions of a
scheme in one direction, which has been
found desirable on the basis of recent
experience. It empowers a board, in
respect of some past period, to allow a
discount below the standard price. In
order to avoid any possibility of the misuse of this power, the special approval of
the Ministry is required.
a
Clause 6. Under Section 6 of the
Agricultural Marketing (No. 2) Act,
1933, marketing boards in Great Britain
are empowered to purchase the regulated
product from board in Northern
Ireland. Owing to the rapid increase in
the pig population in Northern Ireland,
a considerable surplus of pigs now exists,
which has at present to be exported to
Great Britain. It is hoped that an
expansion in the bacon curing industry
will soon take place, which will avoid the
necessity for large quantities of pigs
being exported to Great Britain, as is
being done at present. In the meantime,
however, provision has been made to
enable surplus pigs, which cannot be
cured in Northern Ireland, being taken
over by the Pigs Marketing Board in
Great Britain and disposed of to British
curers. Clause 6 of the present Bill
enables the necessary arrangements in
Northern Ireland to be made.
Clause 7. The main object of this
Clause is to continue in force certain
modications of the Northern Ireland Act
of 1933, which were made by Order in
Council subsequent to the passing of that
Act, as a result of amendments which
had been made in the United Kingdom
Act of 1933. It will be recalled that the
modifications were required because the
Northern Ireland Act received the Royal
Assent before the United Kingdom Act
had been passed, and that in order to
provide that the Northern Ireland Act
should be in conformity with the United
Kingdom Act power was given by Section
20 of the Northern Ireland Act to modify
that Act by Order in Council, so as to be
consistent with the United Kingdom Act.
Modifications made by Order in Council
under Section 20 of the Northern Ireland
Act, would, under the terms of that
section, cease to have effect after 12
months unless kept in force by resolutions passed by both Houses. The enactment of the modifications by the present
Clause will make them part of the
permanent law. The Clause adds also
three further verbal modifications of the
Northern Ireland Act of 1933.

the curers had to pay the pig dealers such

When a similar Bill to this was brought

information than we have been given

It was said that the loss in England to

--was 7s 6d or 7s 9d per pig, and that

when the Bill was introduced into the

dealing with. They knew that the loss

pay
amount. This Bill has to be passed to

any, this House is going to have over

the
open market which now exists for this

of bacon. Again, anybody wishing to

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Chairman
of the Board receives a good salary. He
is undertaking a scheme which is worth
some £3,000,000 to the farmers of Northern Ireland. If you choose to have a
chairman at a wage of £50 a year you
would have a £50 a year scheme. The
point which everybody must have noticed
is that so far as Northern Ireland is concerned there have been no difficulties
whatever in the working of the scheme
through the Pigs Board, whereas on the
other side there have been considerable
difficulties. However, that is a point I
understand I cannot go into here; otherwise I should be only too glad to argue
with the hon. Gentleman on that point.
May I go a little bit further than I have
gone for the moment? I am most anxious
that the Pigs Marketing Board and the
Bacon Marketing Board, and all those
interested in this scheme should realise
that the Ministry are anxious and willing
to do everything they can to make the
scheme a success, and to bring prosperity
to agriculture on this particular line on
which we are working. Criticism has
been aimed at the Board which is, after
all, a board of directors, a business board,
although, of course, for the time being it
was appointed by the Ministry. I should
like to say in reference to that that some
50 per cent. of the gentlemen appointed
by the Ministry have been re-elected on
the Board. That, I think, goes to prove
that, at any rate, 50 per cent. of the
farmers approved of the selection the
Ministry made.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: There are no
consumers' representatives because the
price of the article is really controlled on
the other side. That is our main market.
The price in England will rise or fall
according to
to the amount consumed.
Where hon. Members wish to criticise,
although I have not reached such a stage
of Cabinet proficiency that I can say I
welcome criticism, I would prefer that

at the present moment most delicate
negotiations. If continual criticism is

the moment it will make things more
difficult for them, and if they are made
difficult for them it will mean that the
negotiations which they are carrying out
will not be carried through in the most
satisfactory manner.
Hon. Members have appealed to me
that the scheme should be of a very simple
nature. The pigs scheme in England is
certainly more complicated than our
scheme over here. It is a new scheme.
It is a scheme for which there is no precedent, and, therefore, one must anticipate that improvements will take place.
There are bound to be additions, and I
would ask farmers and others interested
before they criticise any new point which
has been introduced to realise that that
new point is an advancement, and is not

purpose. I feel I will not appeal in vain

who have acted on these Boards for the

they bought was by handing them over to

equal citizenship and also with the best
trade union practice. Therefore, as I
said, it is obviously the best that can be
done.
Mr. HENDERSON: I wish to associate
myself with the suggestions and remarks
made by the hon. Members for Dock,
Pottinger, Woodvale, Duncairn, and by
the Minister himself. What strikes me
forcibly about this debate is that all the
pig Members have gone.
Mr. GRANT: They are all away.
I
Mr. HENDERSON: This would have
been a great opportunity to show how
something could be done for the widows
in Northern Ireland. There are many
anomalies that could be fixed by the
Minister. Hundreds of widows have
been denied pensions owing to a day in
many cases. I know one case in my own
division where a day was the cause of a
widow being disallowed a pension.
would like to ask the Minister of Labour
why, when an ex-Service man has given
his life for his country, the pension
granted to his widow should be taken into
consideration when she makes a claim for
a widow's pension. The Government
never intended that, if a widow is
receiving an Army pension, that pension
should be taken into consideration. It is
a mean action, and you ought to be
ashamed of yourselves, as should any
government under whom a widow, who is
receiving an Army pension of 8s, only
receives 2s of a widow's pension. That is
one case in which the Minister of Labour
requires to get out of step with Great
Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: It would be the
slippery slope.
Mr. HENDERSON: You are always
on the slippery slope when it comes to
widows' pensions. I do not agree with
the hon. Member for Duncairn (Mr.
Grant) when he says that we have no
right to complain and that the officials
are carrying out the law as it is on the
Statute Book. We have a right to complain. Many of us are opposed to any
statute which denies a pension to a widow
who we think is justly entitled to it.
Why should a widow be denied her
pension for the sake of one stamp? The
whole thing is outrageous, and I suggest
to the right hon. Gentleman that he and
his Parliamentary Secretary should take
this matter up and see that these
anomalies, which have been responsible
for 8,000 widows being denied their
pensions, are remedied. Whether they
get the pension in England or not does
not concern me. I want to see the widows
in Northern Ireland getting even fairer
play than their sisters across the water.
I hope that before this debate finishes the
only lady Member in the House will tell
us something with regard to the many
widows in her constituency who are being
penalised in the same way as are the
widows in our constituencies. I am quite
satisfied that dozens of cases have been
brought to her notice where the Government have denied pensions to widows who
were entitled to them.
I support whole-heartedly the hon.
Members who have spoken on this matter.
I hope, during this Session, you will forget about pigs and amend your Widows'
Pensions Act in such a way that these
7,000 widows from whom you have taken
pensions will get them in the near future.
You have no right to deduct 8s from any
widow whose husband was killed during
the Great War. You talk about loyalty.
There is no loyalty there. If you were
loyal you would give that widow her
pension. Her husband paid for it under
the National Health Insurance Act. Why
do you give her 2s? It is because she is
entitled to the widow's pension.
You
Adjournmeal-
Pensions for Widows
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
only give her 2s, but you would give her
10s if she gave up the 8s she is receiving
from the British Government.
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Gentleman
is wrong.
Mr. HENDERSON: The hon. Gentleman is not wrong. Will the Parliamentary Secretary be prepared to give
this widow the pension of 10s if she gives
up her Army pension? The Minister of
Labour wants her to give up the 8s that
she received from the British Government for the sacrifice by her husband of
his life. A more outrageous thing could
not be done in any part of the world.
The whole thing is wrong.
The country
gave that woman 8s a week because her
husband sacrificed his life. What greater
sacrifice could a man make than giving
his life for his country? But that
amount is taken into consideration when
she applies for a widow's pension, and her
other pension is reduced to 2s a week. I
do not care what the British Minister of
Labour does. We have a Parliament of
our own. We should be able to make
laws to better the conditions here. The
Minister of Labour ought to take this up
immediately. He should get into touch
with the British Minister of Labour.
Mr. ANDREWS: I thought you said
you would not take anything to do with
the British Minister of Labour.
Mr. HENDERSON: We have a Parliament of our own here, and we ought to
deal with these anomalies. This wrong
should be remedied. I support the hon.
Members who have spoken. I hope that
the Government will amend the Act
during the present Session.
I wish to take this opportunity of drawing the attention of the Ministry of
Labour to a very important thing that
has happened during the past week or so.
This Government has sanctioned expenditure by the Belfast Corporation of a sum
in the region of £500,000 for the carrying
out of schemes. I am given to understand that only £250,000 of that money
has been spent, and that the Corporation.
can carry on and spend the other
£250,000. But something serious has
happened. A conference took place
between the Minister of Labour and representatives of the Belfast Corporation in
regard to unemployment relief schemes.
Will the Minister of Labour tell me if he
was a party to the arrangement that
schemes for the relief of unemployment
should be stopped?
I ask this question because it is of
paramount importance to the unemployed
worker. It is of interest to the Minister
of Labour, because many of the men who
have been displaced will receive no benefit.
Some of them will draw benefit. I want
to know whether this was part of the
agreement entered into between the representatives of the Corporation and the
representatives of the Government. At
the present time almost 600 men have
been thrown on to the streets. Can the
right hon. Gentleman say what sort of
policy is that? Immediately he saw that
in the Press he should have got into touch
with the Belfast Corporation and
demanded why these schemes-schemes in
connection with which the Government
were contributing 60 per cent. of the
wages were stopped. There is no reason
why these schemes should be stopped. In
view of the fact that orders for some ships
have been obtained, I appeal to the
Minister of Labour on this matter. I
know that the Government take credit
for the orders for these ships. It is said,
"The Northern Government get three
more ships." Let us forget about that.
Mr. GRANT: We will never forget
about that.
Mr. HENDERSON: The Northern
Government never got an order for a ship
in their lives.
Mr. POLLOCK: Do not talk nonsense.
Mr. GRANT: Of course, they did.
Mr. HENDERSON : Harland &
Wolff's and Workman & Clark's got the
contracts because they were the cheapest.
It was not you who got the ships at all.
Mr. GRANT: Who was it? You?
Mr. HENDERSON: You want to take
up my time, but I am not going to be
drawn. What is the use of finding
employment for men in the shipyards
when you are depriving them of work in
other directions. Who was responsible
for these 600 men being put on the
streets?
Adjournment-
Pensions for Widows
6 MARCH 1934
Mr. GORDON: Alderman Duff.
Mr. HENDERSON: If you say it was
Alderman Duff you know more than I
do. In view of the fact that the Corporation has received sanction to spend
£250,000 on relief schemes I demand to
know now from the Minister of Labour
what steps he is taking to see that employment is provided for these 600 men who
have been thrown on to the streets.
Mr. ANDREWS: With
the permission of the House I would like to say
this. The hon. Member has just made a
great many very wild statements, and he
has asked a great many questions. It
would really be impossible for me, in the
two minutes the hon. Member has left
me, to reply to his speech and, therefore,
I do not propose to attempt to do so.
Mr. HENDERSON: And the 300 to
400 men will be starving.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Two
Minutes before Seven o'clock.
